lessons.title: Support vector machines and kernels
yt: support vector machine kernel trick explained

blocks.x: A **support vector machine (SVM)** finds the separating hyperplane w.x + b = 0 with the **largest margin**. The margin width is **2 / ||w||**; for w = (3, 4), ||w|| = 5 and the margin is **0.4**. Only the points closest to the boundary, the **support vectors**, decide it.

x: **Hard margin:** no point may violate the margin (needs separable data). **Soft margin:** slack variables allow some errors; the parameter **C** trades margin width against errors (large C = few errors but narrow margin, risk of overfitting).

**Kernel trick:** replace dot products by a kernel K(x, z) so a linear SVM works in a high-dimensional space without computing it. **RBF kernel** K(x, z) = exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2). For gamma = 0.5, x = (1, 2) and z = (2, 0): ||x - z||^2 = 5, so K = e^-2.5 = **0.0821**. Other kernels: linear, polynomial.
Scale features before an SVM. It works well on small and medium datasets and in high dimensions; training is slow for very large data.

blocks.x:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X, y = make_moons(300, noise=0.2, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
for kern in ("linear", "rbf"):
    print(kern, round(SVC(kernel=kern, C=1).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte), 2))
The RBF kernel scores higher than the linear one on this curved (moons) data.
Hindi saransh
SVM sabse bade margin wala hyperplane dhoondhta hai; margin = 2/||w||. Kernel trick data ko bade dimension mein le jaata hai. C bada ho to margin chhota aur overfitting ka khatra.
Always scale features before using an SVM with an RBF kernel.

qa.q: What is the margin of an SVM and how is it computed?
qa.a: The distance between the two classes' boundaries; it equals 2 / ||w||.

qa.q: What are support vectors?
qa.a: The training points closest to the decision boundary; only they determine the hyperplane.

qa.q: What does the kernel trick do?
qa.a: It computes dot products in a high-dimensional feature space through a kernel function, so non-linear boundaries are learned without explicitly mapping the data.

qa.q: Effect of a very large C?
qa.a: Fewer training errors but a narrower margin and a higher risk of overfitting.

lessons.title: Ensembles: bagging, boosting and random forests
yt: random forest gradient boosting adaboost explained

blocks.x: An **ensemble** combines many models to beat a single one.

x: **Bagging:** train models on bootstrap samples (random draws with replacement) and average or vote. Reduces **variance**. A bootstrap sample leaves out about **36.8%** of rows (1/e), which become the free **out-of-bag (OOB)** test set; each row is in the sample with probability about 63.2%.
**Random forest:** bagged decision trees that also pick a random subset of features at each split, which decorrelates the trees.

**Boosting:** build models one after another, each correcting the previous errors. Reduces **bias**. **AdaBoost** weights misclassified points up; a weak learner with error e gets weight alpha = (1/2) ln((1 - e)/e). For e = 0.2: alpha = 0.5 ln 4 = **0.693**. **Gradient boosting** (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) fits each new tree to the residual errors (the negative gradient of the loss).
**Stacking:** a meta-model learns to combine the outputs of different models.

blocks.x:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
for m in (RandomForestClassifier(200, random_state=0), GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)):
    print(type(m).__name__, round(cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5).mean(), 3))
Both reach about 0.96 accuracy on this dataset.
Hindi saransh
Bagging variance kam karta hai (random forest), boosting bias kam karta hai (AdaBoost, gradient boosting). Bootstrap sample mein lagbhag 36.8% rows chhoot jaati hain (OOB).
Bagging = parallel and reduces variance. Boosting = sequential and reduces bias.

qa.q: Difference between bagging and boosting?
qa.a: Bagging trains independent models in parallel on bootstrap samples to cut variance; boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on earlier mistakes, to cut bias.

qa.q: What is the out-of-bag error?
qa.a: The error measured on the rows left out of each tree's bootstrap sample, a free validation estimate.

qa.q: AdaBoost weight for a learner with error 0.2?
Why does a random forest pick random features at each split?
qa.a: To make trees less correlated, so averaging reduces variance more.

lessons.title: PCA, clustering and anomaly detection

blocks.x: PCA (Principal Component Analysis)

PCA projects data onto directions of maximum variance. Steps: centre the data, compute the covariance matrix, find its eigenvectors (components) and eigenvalues (variance along each). Example: covariance [[2, 1], [1, 2]] has eigenvalues **3 and 1**, so the first component explains 3/(3 + 1) = **75%** of the variance (direction (1, 1)). Keep enough components to reach about 90 to 95% variance. PCA is linear and needs scaled features.
Clustering

x: **k-means:** assigns points to the nearest of k centres and recomputes centres; needs k; finds round clusters. Use the **elbow method** or the **silhouette score** (between -1 and 1; higher is better) to choose k.
**DBSCAN:** groups dense regions using eps and min_samples; finds odd shapes and labels outliers as noise; needs no k.
**Hierarchical:** builds a dendrogram by merging nearest clusters.

blocks.x: Anomaly detection

**Z-score** (flag |z| > 3), **IQR rule** (outside Q1 - 1.5 IQR and Q3 + 1.5 IQR), **Isolation Forest** (anomalies are isolated in fewer random splits), **autoencoders** (large reconstruction error). Example: for [1, 2, 3, 4, 100]: Q1 = 2, Q3 = 4, IQR = 2, upper fence 7, so 100 is an outlier.

import numpy as np
C = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)
print(vals, vals / vals.sum())     # [1. 3.] [0.25 0.75]
Hindi saransh
PCA maximum variance ki direction chunta hai: eigenvalues 3 aur 1 se pehla component 75% variance samjhata hai. DBSCAN density se cluster banata hai aur outliers pakadta hai.
Scale the features before PCA; otherwise large-valued features dominate.

qa.q: What do eigenvalues represent in PCA?
qa.a: The variance captured along each principal component.

qa.q: Why scale features before PCA?
qa.a: Otherwise features with large units dominate the variance and the components.

qa.q: When is DBSCAN better than k-means?
qa.a: For clusters of arbitrary shape and when outliers must be detected, with no need to fix k.

qa.q: IQR rule upper fence for [1, 2, 3, 4, 100]?
qa.a: Q3 + 1.5 IQR = 4 + 3 = 7, so 100 is an outlier.

lessons.title: RNN, LSTM and attention
yt: lstm explained attention is all you need

blocks.x: **RNNs** process sequences by keeping a hidden state h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_(t-1) + b). Training uses backpropagation through time; gradients vanish or explode over long sequences. **LSTM** adds a **cell state** and three gates (forget, input, output) that decide what to erase, write and reveal, so it remembers long-range information. Parameter count for hidden size h and input size x: 4 (h (h + x) + h). For h = 64 and x = 32: 4 (64 x 96 + 64) = **24,832**. **GRU** uses two gates and is lighter.
Attention and transformers

**Scaled dot-product attention:** Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V. Example with Q = [1, 0], K = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], V = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], d = 2: scores [0.707, 0] -> softmax [0.670, 0.330] -> output [1.660, 2.660]. **Self-attention** lets every token look at all others in parallel; **multi-head attention** repeats it with different projections; positional encodings add order information. The **transformer** (encoder, decoder) replaced RNNs for most NLP tasks and underlies BERT and GPT-style models.

import numpy as np
Q = np.array([1, 0.]); K = np.eye(2); V = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4.]])
s = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(2); p = np.exp(s) / np.exp(s).sum()
print(p.round(3), (p @ V).round(3))   # [0.67 0.33] [1.66 2.66]
Hindi saransh
RNN purani jaankari hidden state mein rakhta hai; LSTM gates se lambi yaaddasht sambhalta hai. Attention = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V; transformer mein sab tokens parallel mein ek doosre ko dekhte hain.
Transformers process tokens in parallel; RNNs process them one at a time.

qa.q: Why do plain RNNs struggle with long sequences?
qa.a: Gradients shrink (or blow up) as they pass through many time steps, so early information is lost.

qa.q: What are the three LSTM gates?
Why divide by sqrt(d) in attention?
qa.a: To stop dot products growing with dimension, which would make softmax saturate and gradients tiny.

qa.q: Why are transformers faster to train than RNNs?
qa.a: All positions are processed in parallel instead of sequentially.

lessons.title: Model evaluation, regularisation and MLOps

blocks.x: Evaluation

Use a train / validation / test split or k-fold cross-validation; for time series, split by time (never shuffle). Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, **log loss** (-ln p for the true class: p = 0.9 gives **0.105**, p = 0.1 gives **2.303**, so confident wrong answers are punished hard), RMSE and MAE for regression. Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match real frequencies.
Regularisation

**L2 (ridge)** shrinks weights; **L1 (lasso)** drives some weights to exactly zero (feature selection); **dropout**, **early stopping**, **data augmentation**, and **batch normalisation** help generalise.
Hyper-parameter tuning
Grid search, random search, Bayesian optimisation; always tune on validation data, never on the test set.
Pitfalls

**Data leakage** (information from the test set or future leaking into training, such as scaling before splitting), class imbalance (use stratified splits, class weights, SMOTE), and concept drift (data changes after deployment).
MLOps

Version data and code (Git, DVC), track experiments (MLflow), package models (Docker), serve through APIs, monitor accuracy and drift, and retrain on schedule. **Responsible AI:** check bias across groups, explain predictions (SHAP, LIME) and protect privacy.
Hindi saransh
Cross-validation aur sahi metric chuno. L1 weights ko zero kar deta hai, L2 chhota karta hai. Data leakage se bacho; deploy ke baad drift monitor karo.
Fit the scaler on the training data only, then apply it to the validation and test data.

qa.q: What is data leakage?
qa.a: Information from outside the training data (test or future data) influencing the model, giving over-optimistic results.

qa.q: Difference between L1 and L2 regularisation?
qa.a: L1 can set weights to exactly zero and select features; L2 shrinks weights smoothly without zeroing them.

qa.q: Log loss for a correct class predicted with probability 0.9?
Why not shuffle time-series data when splitting?
qa.a: It would let the model train on the future and test on the past, which is unrealistic.

lessons.title: Reinforcement learning and generative models

blocks.x: Reinforcement learning (RL)

An **agent** takes **actions** in an **environment**, receives **rewards** and learns a **policy** that maximises the cumulative discounted return G = r1 + gamma r2 + gamma^2 r3 + ... **Markov decision process:** states, actions, transitions, rewards. **Q-learning** updates Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha [ r + gamma max Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) ]. Example: Q = 0, alpha = 0.5, r = 1, gamma = 0.9, next max Q = 2: new Q = 0 + 0.5 (1 + 1.8 - 0) = **1.4**. **Exploration vs exploitation** is handled with epsilon-greedy. Deep RL (DQN, policy gradients, PPO) powers game-playing and robotics; RLHF tunes language models with human feedback.
Generative models

x: **Autoencoder / VAE:** compress to a latent code and reconstruct; VAEs sample new data.
**GAN:** a generator and a discriminator compete.
**Diffusion models:** learn to remove noise step by step; behind many image generators.
**Large language models:** transformers trained to predict the next token, then fine-tuned.

blocks.x:
Q, alpha, r, gamma, nxt = 0, 0.5, 1, 0.9, 2
Q = Q + alpha * (r + gamma * nxt - Q); print(Q)   # 1.4
Hindi saransh
RL mein agent reward se seekhta hai; Q-learning update: Q += alpha(r + gamma maxQ' - Q). Example mein Q = 1.4. Generative models naya data banate hain (GAN, diffusion, LLM).
Epsilon-greedy: with probability epsilon explore randomly, otherwise take the best known action.

qa.q: What is the Q-learning update?
qa.a: Q(s,a) <- Q(s,a) + alpha [ r + gamma max Q(s',a') - Q(s,a) ].

qa.q: What is the exploration-exploitation trade-off?
qa.a: Trying new actions to learn more versus using the best known action to earn reward.

qa.q: How do GANs train?

lessons.title: Image formation and pixels
yt: how digital images work pixels and color channels

blocks.x: **Computer vision** is the field that lets computers understand images and video: detect objects, read text, track motion, measure the world.
What is a digital image?

A grayscale image is a 2D grid of numbers called **pixels**. For 8-bit images each pixel is 0 (black) to 255 (white). A colour image has three channels, **R, G, B**, so a 1920x1080 colour image holds 1920 x 1080 x 3 = 6,220,800 numbers (about 6.2 MB uncompressed).
Resolution and bit depth
Resolution = width x height. Bit depth = bits per value (8 bits give 256 levels). More bits give smoother gradations; more pixels give more detail.
Colour to grayscale

Gray = 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B. Green gets the largest weight because the eye is most sensitive to it. Other colour spaces: **HSV** (hue, saturation, value; easy for colour thresholding) and **YCbCr**.
Image formation: the pinhole camera

Light from a scene passes through a small hole and forms an inverted image. With focal length f, a point at (X, Y, Z) projects to **x = f X / Z, y = f Y / Z**. Farther objects (bigger Z) look smaller. Real cameras use lenses to collect more light.
Sampling and quantisation
Digitising an image samples it into pixels (spatial sampling) and rounds brightness to levels (quantisation). Too few samples cause **aliasing** (jagged edges, moire).
Histogram
A histogram counts pixels per intensity. A narrow histogram means low contrast. **Histogram equalisation** spreads it out to increase contrast.

import numpy as np
img = np.array([[0, 50], [200, 255]], dtype=np.uint8)
print(img.shape, img.mean(), 1920 * 1080 * 3)   # (2, 2) 126.25 6220800
Hindi saransh

Image pixels ka grid hai; 8-bit mein 0 se 255 values hoti hain. Colour image mein R, G, B teen channels hote hain. Gray = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Pinhole camera mein x = fX/Z, isliye door ki cheez chhoti dikhti hai.
Z is in the denominator: double the distance and the object appears half the size.

qa.a: x = f X / Z and y = f Y / Z, where f is the focal length and Z is the depth of the point.

qa.q: What is aliasing?
qa.a: Distortion caused by sampling too coarsely, so fine detail appears as false patterns or jagged edges.

qa.q: What does histogram equalisation do?
qa.a: It redistributes pixel intensities to use the full range, improving contrast.

lessons.title: Convolution and image filtering

blocks.x: **Filtering** replaces each pixel by a combination of its neighbours. A small matrix called a **kernel** is slid over the image; at each position we multiply overlapping values and add them up (convolution/correlation).
Smoothing (noise removal)

x: **Box (mean) filter:** the 3x3 kernel with all values 1/9. Output = average of the neighbourhood.
**Gaussian filter:** weights fall off with distance. Blurs edges less harshly than a box filter.
**Median filter:** replaces the pixel by the median of the neighbourhood. Excellent against **salt-and-pepper noise** and keeps edges sharp. It is not a linear filter.

blocks.x: Example (box filter)

Neighbourhood [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]: mean = 45/9 = **5**. Median is also 5. A salt noise pixel: [[10, 10, 10], [10, 255, 10], [10, 10, 10]]: the mean gives (8 x 10 + 255)/9 = 37.2 (smeared), the median gives **10** (removed).
Sharpening
Add edges back to the image: sharp = original + k (original - blurred). The kernel [[0,-1,0],[-1,5,-1],[0,-1,0]] sharpens.
Output size
For an N x N image and an F x F kernel with no padding, output size is N - F + 1. With padding P the size is N - F + 2P + 1. "Same" padding uses P = (F - 1)/2 for odd F.
Properties
Convolution is linear, shift-invariant and separable for Gaussian kernels (one 2D pass = two 1D passes, cost drops from F^2 to 2F per pixel).

import numpy as np
a = np.array([[10, 10, 10], [10, 255, 10], [10, 10, 10]])
print(round(a.mean(), 1), np.median(a))   # 37.2 10.0
Hindi saransh

Kernel ko image par slide karke pixel ko padosiyon ke combination se badalte hain. Box filter average leta hai, median filter salt-and-pepper noise hatata hai aur edges bachata hai. Output size N - F + 1 hota hai.
Use a median filter for salt-and-pepper noise and a Gaussian filter for general smooth noise.

qa.q: What is a kernel in image filtering?
qa.a: A small matrix of weights that is slid over the image to compute each output pixel from its neighbourhood.

qa.q: Why is the median filter better than the mean filter for salt-and-pepper noise?
qa.a: The mean spreads an extreme value into neighbours, while the median ignores outliers and removes them while preserving edges.

qa.q: What is the output size for a 7x7 image and a 3x3 kernel with no padding?
What is a separable filter?
qa.a: A 2D kernel that can be written as a product of two 1D kernels, such as the Gaussian. It is faster to apply as two 1D passes.

qa.q: How does sharpening work?
qa.a: It boosts differences between a pixel and its neighbours, for example by adding a scaled version of the original minus a blurred copy.

lessons.title: Edge detection: Sobel and Canny

blocks.x: **Edges** are places where brightness changes sharply, usually object boundaries. We detect them with the **gradient** of the image: the change in intensity in x and y.
Sobel operator
Gx = [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]] detects vertical edges; Gy = [[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]] detects horizontal edges. Magnitude = sqrt(Gx^2 + Gy^2); direction = atan2(Gy, Gx).
Worked example
A big magnitude means a strong edge.

import numpy as np, math
p = np.array([[10,10,10],[10,10,200],[10,10,200]])
kx = np.array([[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]])
gx = (p*kx).sum(); gy = (p*kx.T).sum()
print(gx, gy, round(math.hypot(gx, gy), 1), round(math.degrees(math.atan2(gy, gx)), 1))   # 570 190 600.8 18.4
Canny edge detector (4 stages)

x: **Gaussian smoothing** to reduce noise.
**Gradient** magnitude and direction (Sobel).
**Non-maximum suppression:** keep only local maxima across the edge to thin it to 1 pixel.
**Hysteresis thresholding:** two thresholds (high and low). Pixels above high are edges; pixels between are kept only if connected to a strong edge.

blocks.x: Laplacian
A second-derivative operator. Edges are at its zero-crossings; very noise-sensitive, so use it after smoothing (Laplacian of Gaussian).
Hindi saransh

Edge matlab jahan brightness tezi se badle. Sobel x aur y gradient nikalta hai (is example mein 570 aur 190, magnitude 600.8). Canny mein smoothing, gradient, non-max suppression aur hysteresis threshold hote hain.
Smooth first, then differentiate. Derivatives amplify noise.

qa.q: What does the Sobel operator compute?
qa.a: Approximate horizontal and vertical derivatives of the image, which give gradient magnitude and direction.

qa.q: List the stages of the Canny edge detector.
qa.a: Gaussian smoothing, gradient computation, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis thresholding.

qa.q: Why does Canny use two thresholds?
qa.a: Strong pixels above the high threshold are surely edges; weaker ones above the low threshold survive only if connected to strong edges, which keeps real edges continuous and rejects noise.

qa.q: How do you compute edge strength from Gx and Gy?
Why smooth before edge detection?
qa.a: Differentiation amplifies noise, so smoothing avoids false edges.

lessons.title: Feature detection: corners, SIFT and ORB

blocks.x: A **feature** is a distinctive, repeatable image location (a corner, a blob) with a **descriptor** (a vector describing the neighbourhood) so that the same point can be found in another image. Uses: panoramas, 3D reconstruction, tracking, AR.
Why corners?

x: A flat region looks the same when you shift the window in any direction.
An edge looks the same when shifted **along** the edge.
A **corner** changes in every direction, so it is easy to localise.

blocks.x: Harris corner detector
Compute the matrix M from gradients Ix, Iy summed over a window: M = [[sum Ix^2, sum IxIy], [sum IxIy, sum Iy^2]]. Corner response R = det(M) - k (trace M)^2, with k about 0.04 to 0.06.

x: R large and positive: corner.
R negative with large magnitude: edge.
|R| small: flat region.

blocks.x: Harris is rotation-invariant but not scale-invariant.
SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform)

Finds keypoints in scale space (difference of Gaussians), assigns an orientation, and builds a 128-dimensional descriptor from gradient histograms (4x4 cells x 8 orientations = 128). It is robust to scale, rotation and moderate lighting change but slower.
ORB
Oriented FAST keypoints plus a rotated **BRIEF** binary descriptor. Fast and free to use, matched using **Hamming distance** (count differing bits).
Matching

For each descriptor in image A find the nearest in image B. **Lowe's ratio test**: keep a match only if the best distance < 0.75 x the second-best distance. **RANSAC** then estimates a homography/fundamental matrix while ignoring wrong matches (outliers).
Hindi saransh

Corner har disha mein change hota hai isliye feature ke liye achha hai. Harris mein R = det(M) - k(trace M)^2. SIFT scale aur rotation invariant hai (128-dim descriptor). ORB binary descriptor hai jo Hamming distance se match hota hai. RANSAC outliers hatata hai.
Flat: no change. Edge: change in one direction. Corner: change in all directions.

qa.q: Why are corners better features than edges?
qa.a: A corner can be located precisely in both directions, while a point on an edge can slide along the edge.

qa.q: What does the Harris response R = det(M) - k (trace M)^2 tell us?
qa.a: A large positive value means a corner, a large negative value means an edge, and a small value means a flat region.

qa.q: How long is a SIFT descriptor?
qa.a: 128 numbers: a 4x4 grid of cells, each with an 8-bin orientation histogram.

qa.q: What distance is used to match ORB descriptors?
qa.a: Hamming distance, the number of differing bits, which is fast to compute.

qa.q: What does RANSAC do?
qa.a: It repeatedly fits a model to random minimal samples and keeps the model with the most inliers, so wrong matches are ignored.

Harris response is strongly negative at
quiz.why: One large and one small eigenvalue give negative R.

o: cosine of angles in colour space

o: clearly smaller than the second best (for example below 0.75 times)

quiz.q: RANSAC is used to
o: reject outlier matches while fitting a model
quiz.why: It keeps the model with the most inliers.

  • A feature is a distinctive, repeatable image location (a corner, a blob) with a descriptor (a vector describing the neighbourhood) so that the same…
  • Uses: panoramas, 3D reconstruction, tracking, AR
📌

Why corners?

  • A flat region looks the same when you shift the window in any direction.
  • An edge looks the same when shifted along the edge.
  • A corner changes in every direction, so it is easy to localise.
🧠

Harris corner detector

  • R large and positive: corner.
  • R negative with large magnitude: edge.
  • |R| small: flat region.
🌟

SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform)

  • Finds keypoints in scale space (difference of Gaussians), assigns an orientation, and builds a 128-dimensional descriptor from gradient histograms…
  • It is robust to scale, rotation and moderate lighting change but slower
🔬

ORB

  • Oriented FAST keypoints plus a rotated BRIEF binary descriptor
  • Fast and free to use, matched using Hamming distance (count differing bits)
📊

Matching

  • For each descriptor in image A find the nearest in image B
  • Lowe's ratio test: keep a match only if the best distance < 0.75 x the second-best distance
  • RANSAC then estimates a homography/fundamental matrix while ignoring wrong matches (outliers)
🎯 Remember Flat: no change. Edge: change in one direction. Corner: change in all directions.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Corner har disha mein change hota hai isliye feature ke liye achha hai. Harris mein R = det(M) - k(trace M)^2. SIFT scale aur rotation invariant hai (128-dim descriptor). ORB binary descriptor hai jo Hamming distance se match hota hai. RANSAC outliers hatata hai.

lessons.title: CNNs for recognition and object detection
yt: IoU intersection over union and mAP

blocks.x: **Image classification** gives one label per image. **Object detection** gives a **bounding box** and class for every object. **Segmentation** labels every pixel (semantic: class; instance: each object).
Evolution
Classical methods used hand-made features (HOG + SVM). Since AlexNet (2012), **CNNs** learn features automatically. ResNet added skip connections.
Detectors

x: **Two-stage (R-CNN family, Faster R-CNN):** first propose regions, then classify and refine them. Accurate.
**One-stage (YOLO, SSD):** predict boxes and classes directly in one pass over the image. Fast, suitable for real-time and mobile use.

blocks.x: IoU (Intersection over Union)

IoU = area of overlap / area of union. A prediction is usually counted correct if IoU >= 0.5. Example: box A = (0,0) to (4,4) (area 16), box B = (2,2) to (6,6) (area 16). Overlap = 2 x 2 = 4. Union = 16 + 16 - 4 = 28. **IoU = 4/28 = 0.143**.
Non-maximum suppression (NMS)
Many boxes cover the same object. Keep the one with the highest confidence and delete other boxes whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold (for example 0.5).
Metrics
**Precision** and **recall** at various confidence thresholds give a precision-recall curve; the area under it is the **average precision (AP)**; **mAP** averages AP over classes.
Segmentation models
U-Net (medical images), Mask R-CNN (instance masks), and modern **vision transformers** (ViT) that split the image into patches.
Hindi saransh

Classification mein ek label, detection mein box + class, segmentation mein har pixel ka label. YOLO tez one-stage detector hai. IoU = overlap/union (example 0.143). NMS duplicate boxes hatata hai. mAP detector ka score hai.
A box with IoU 0.5 or more with the ground truth is normally called a correct detection.

qa.q: What is the difference between classification, detection and segmentation?
qa.a: Classification assigns one label to the image, detection finds objects with boxes and classes, and segmentation labels every pixel.

qa.q: What is IoU?
qa.a: Intersection over Union: the overlap area of predicted and true boxes divided by the area of their union.

qa.q: Why is YOLO faster than Faster R-CNN?
qa.a: YOLO predicts boxes and classes in a single pass without a separate region-proposal stage.

qa.q: What does non-maximum suppression do?
qa.a: It removes duplicate overlapping boxes, keeping the highest-confidence box for each object.

qa.q: What does mAP mean?
qa.a: Mean average precision: the area under the precision-recall curve averaged over all classes.

def iou(a, b):
    x1, y1 = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1]); x2, y2 = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3])
    inter = max(0, x2 - x1) * max(0, y2 - y1)
    area = lambda r: (r[2] - r[0]) * (r[3] - r[1])
    return inter / (area(a) + area(b) - inter)

lessons.title: Camera geometry and stereo depth

blocks.x: To measure the 3D world from images we need a model of the camera.
Camera matrix
A 3D world point P = (X, Y, Z) maps to pixel (u, v) by u = f_x X / Z + c_x, v = f_y Y / Z + c_y

x: **Intrinsic** parameters: focal lengths f_x, f_y (in pixels), principal point (c_x, c_y), skew.
**Extrinsic** parameters: rotation R and translation t from world to camera coordinates.

blocks.x: In matrix form s [u v 1]^T = K [R | t] [X Y Z 1]^T.
**Calibration** (checkerboard images, Zhang's method) estimates K and lens distortion (radial: barrel, pincushion).
Example
Stereo vision

Two cameras separated by a **baseline B**, with focal length f (pixels). A point appears at x_L in the left image and x_R in the right image. **Disparity d = x_L - x_R**. Depth: **Z = f B / d**. Example: f = 700 pixels, B = 0.12 m, d = 14 pixels: Z = 700 x 0.12 / 14 = **6 m**. Nearer objects have larger disparity.
Finding correspondences

Using **epipolar geometry**, the match for a pixel lies on a line in the other image, so we search only along that line (a row in rectified images). Block matching and semi-global matching produce a disparity map.
Other depth sensors
LiDAR (time of flight lasers), structured light, ToF cameras; and monocular deep networks that estimate depth from one image.
Hindi saransh
Camera model u = fX/Z + cx. Intrinsic parameters camera ke andar ke hote hain (f, principal point), extrinsic bahar ke (R, t). Stereo mein depth Z = fB/d; disparity jitna zyada, object utna paas.
Disparity and depth are inversely related: half the depth means double the disparity.

qa.q: What are intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters?
qa.a: Intrinsic: focal length, principal point and distortion of the camera itself. Extrinsic: the camera's rotation and translation in the world.

qa.q: Write the stereo depth formula.
qa.a: Z = f B / d, with focal length f in pixels, baseline B and disparity d in pixels.

qa.q: Why does a larger disparity mean a closer object?
qa.a: Depth is inversely proportional to disparity: Z = f B / d.

qa.q: What is camera calibration?
qa.a: Estimating the camera's intrinsic parameters and lens distortion, usually from images of a checkerboard.

qa.q: What does epipolar geometry give for matching?
qa.a: The matching point must lie on a known line (the epipolar line) in the other image, reducing the search from 2D to 1D.

lessons.title: CIA triad, threats and malware

blocks.x: Cyber security protects systems, networks and data. The **CIA triad**: **Confidentiality** (only authorised people read data; encryption, access control), **Integrity** (data is not altered; hashes, signatures), **Availability** (systems work when needed; backups, redundancy). Add **authentication** (who are you?), **authorisation** (what may you do?) and **non-repudiation**.

x: **Threat** (something that can cause harm), **vulnerability** (a weakness), **risk** (likelihood x impact), **attack** (an attempt to exploit).
**Malware:** virus (attaches to files), worm (self-spreads), trojan (pretends to be useful), ransomware (encrypts files for payment), spyware, botnet.
**Social engineering:** phishing (fake emails), vishing (calls), smishing (SMS). Humans are the most common weak link.
**Defence in depth:** many layers (firewall, antivirus, patching, backups, training) so that one failure is not fatal. **Least privilege:** give only the access needed.

lessons.title: Passwords, hashing and authentication

blocks.x: **Password entropy** = length x log2(alphabet size). Eight random characters from 62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9): 8 x log2(62) = **47.6 bits**. Four random words from a 2048-word list: 4 x 11 = **44 bits** and far easier to remember. Twelve random lowercase letters: **56.4 bits**. Length and randomness matter most; reused or common passwords are weak. **Storing passwords:** never store plain text. Store a **salted, slow hash** using bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 (not plain MD5 or SHA-1). A **salt** is a random value per user so equal passwords have different hashes and precomputed (rainbow) tables fail. A slow function makes guessing expensive. **Multi-factor authentication (MFA):** something you know + have + are. **TOTP** codes (authenticator apps) are made from a shared secret and the current 30-second time step using HMAC; the RFC 6238 test value for the standard secret at T = 59 s is **94287082** (8 digits). Prefer passkeys / FIDO2 and use a password manager.

import hashlib, os
salt = os.urandom(16)
h = hashlib.scrypt(b"my-password", salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
print(len(h), h != hashlib.scrypt(b"my-password", salt=os.urandom(16), n=2**14, r=8, p=1))   # 64 True
Hindi saransh
Password entropy = lambai x log2(akshar-samuh). Password ko salt ke saath dheemi hash (bcrypt/Argon2) se store karo. MFA mein do alag cheezein chahiye; authenticator app ya passkey behtar hai.
Use a long unique passphrase for each account plus MFA, managed by a password manager.

qa.q: Why add a salt to a password hash?
qa.a: So identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables become useless.

qa.q: Why use bcrypt or Argon2 rather than SHA-256 for passwords?
qa.a: They are deliberately slow and memory-hard, making brute-force guessing costly.

qa.q: What are the three authentication factors?
qa.a: Something you know, something you have, and something you are.

qa.q: How is entropy computed?
qa.a: Length x log2(number of possible symbols), assuming random choices.

lessons.title: Network security and safe browsing
yt: network security firewall vpn https explained

x: **Firewall:** filters traffic by rules (IP, port, protocol); next-generation firewalls inspect applications. **IDS/IPS:** detect (and block) suspicious traffic. **Segmentation / VLANs** limit spread.
**HTTPS = HTTP over TLS:** encrypts traffic, authenticates the server through a **certificate**, and protects integrity. Check the padlock *and* the domain name.
**VPN:** an encrypted tunnel; hides traffic from the local network but you must trust the VPN provider.
**Wi-Fi:** use WPA2/WPA3 with a strong passphrase; avoid open public Wi-Fi for logins.
**Common attacks to defend against:** DoS/DDoS (flooding a service), man-in-the-middle, DNS spoofing, ARP spoofing, and rogue access points.
**Safe habits:** update the OS and apps (patches close known holes), use a standard (non-admin) account, check the sender, avoid cracked software and unknown USB drives.
**Basic hygiene checklist:** automatic updates, MFA, backups (3-2-1: three copies, two media, one off-site), screen lock.

qa.a: Many machines flood a service with traffic so legitimate users cannot reach it.

  • Firewall: filters traffic by rules (IP, port, protocol); next-generation firewalls inspect applications. IDS/IPS: detect (and block) suspicious traffic. Segmentation / VLANs limit spread.
  • HTTPS = HTTP over TLS: encrypts traffic, authenticates the server through a certificate, and protects integrity. Check the padlock *and* the domain name.
  • VPN: an encrypted tunnel; hides traffic from the local network but you must trust the VPN provider.

lessons.title: Web application security and safe coding
yt: owasp top 10 explained sql injection prevention

blocks.x: The **OWASP Top 10** lists common web risks: broken access control, cryptographic failures, **injection**, insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable components, authentication failures, integrity failures, logging failures, and server-side request forgery. Developers defend by never trusting input.

x: **SQL injection:** user input is mixed into a query so it changes its meaning. **Defence: parameterised queries** (prepared statements), which keep data separate from code.
**XSS (cross-site scripting):** untrusted text is shown as HTML. Defence: escape output, use a Content-Security-Policy.
**CSRF:** a browser is tricked into sending an authenticated request. Defence: anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
**Broken access control:** always check on the server that the user may see the record.
**Secrets** (API keys) go in environment variables, never in Git.

blocks.x: The demo below shows why parameterised queries are safe:

import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("create table users(name text, pw text)")
db.execute("insert into users values('asha','x')")
evil = "nobody' OR '1'='1"
unsafe = db.execute("select * from users where name='" + evil + "'").fetchall()
safe = db.execute("select * from users where name=?", (evil,)).fetchall()
print(len(unsafe), len(safe))   # 1 0
The string-built query returns a row it should not; the parameterised one correctly returns none.
Hindi saransh
Kabhi bhi user input par bharosa mat karo. SQL injection se bachne ke liye parameterised query, XSS se bachne ke liye output escape, CSRF ke liye token. API keys ko code mein mat likho.
Use parameterised queries for every database call that includes user input.

qa.q: Why must access checks happen on the server?

lessons.title: Risk management and incident response

blocks.x: **Risk management:** identify assets, threats and vulnerabilities, then estimate and treat risk (**mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid, accept**). Quantitative example: an asset is worth Rs 1,00,000 and one incident would damage **30%**, so **single loss expectancy SLE = Rs 30,000**; it happens **0.5 times a year** (ARO), so **annual loss expectancy ALE = SLE x ARO = Rs 15,000**. A control costing less than the ALE it removes is worth considering. **Incident response (NIST-style):** **1) Preparation, 2) Detection and analysis, 3) Containment, eradication and recovery, 4) Post-incident review.** Keep logs, preserve evidence, communicate clearly and fix the root cause. **Digital forensics** records evidence carefully and keeps a **chain of custody**. **Security frameworks:** ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF, CIS Controls. **Zero trust:** never trust, always verify.
Hindi saransh
Jokhim = sambhavna x asar. ALE = SLE x ARO; example mein 30,000 x 0.5 = Rs 15,000. Ghatna prabandhan: taiyari, pehchan, roktham aur sudhar, samiksha.
Preserve evidence and logs first; do not wipe a compromised machine before you have copied what you need.

lessons.title: Cyber law, privacy and careers (India)
yt: cyber crime reporting india it act 2000

blocks.x: **India's legal framework** (verify the latest text before relying on it): the **Information Technology Act, 2000** covers hacking, identity theft, cheating by impersonation and cyber offences; the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** governs handling of personal data. The **Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)** handles incident reporting and advisories. **Reporting a cyber crime:** use the national portal **cybercrime.gov.in** or the helpline **1930** for financial fraud, report quickly so money can be frozen, and keep screenshots and transaction details. Never share OTPs, PINs or card details, and be wary of fake "KYC" or "customer care" calls. **Ethics:** only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Unauthorised access is a crime. **Careers and certifications:** SOC analyst, penetration tester, security engineer, forensics analyst, GRC; certifications such as CompTIA Security+, CEH, CISSP; practice legally on platforms such as TryHackMe and Hack The Box, and learn Linux, networking and Python.
Hindi saransh

IT Act 2000 aur DPDP Act 2023 mukhya kanoon hain. Cyber fraud ho to 1930 par turant call karein ya cybercrime.gov.in par shikayat karein. OTP kisi ko na dein. Sirf anumati wale system par hi testing karein.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"age": [22, None, 30, 22], "city": ["Delhi", "delhi ", "Pune", "Delhi"]})

lessons.title: Descriptive statistics and probability
yt: statistics for data science mean variance standard deviation

blocks.x: **Central tendency:** mean, median, mode. **Spread:** range, variance, standard deviation (sd), IQR. For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mean 5, population variance 4, population sd **2**, sample sd (divide by n - 1) = sqrt(32/7) = **2.138**. Use sample sd when the data is a sample. **Probability basics:** P(A) between 0 and 1; P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); independent events multiply. **Conditional probability** P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). **Bayes' theorem:** P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A)/P(B). Example: a disease affects 1% of people; a test is 99% sensitive with a 5% false-positive rate. P(positive) = 0.99 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99 = 0.0594, so P(disease | positive) = 0.0099/0.0594 = **16.7%**: a positive test is far from certain when the disease is rare. The **normal distribution** has about 68% of values within 1 sd, 95% within 2 sd and 99.7% within 3 sd of the mean.

import statistics as s
d = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
print(s.pstdev(d), round(s.stdev(d), 3))   # 2.0 2.138
print(round(0.0099 / 0.0594, 3))           # 0.167
Hindi saransh
Mean, median, mode kendra batate hain; sd failav. Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Rare bimari mein positive test ke baad bhi sambhavna sirf 16.7%. Normal mein 68-95-99.7 niyam.
Rare event + imperfect test = many false positives. Always use Bayes, not intuition.

qa.q: Difference between population and sample standard deviation?
qa.a: Population divides by n; sample divides by n - 1 to correct for bias.

qa.q: State Bayes' theorem.
What does the 68-95-99.7 rule say?
qa.a: In a normal distribution, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.

qa.q: Why is a positive result of a good test still often a false alarm for a rare disease?
qa.a: Because the healthy population is so large that even a small false-positive rate produces more false positives than true positives.

formulas

Big idea

  • Central tendency: mean, median, mode
  • Spread: range, variance, standard deviation (sd), IQR
  • For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mean 5, population variance 4, population sd 2, sample sd (divide by n - 1) = sqrt(32/7) = 2.138
  • Use sample sd when the data is a sample
import statistics as s
d = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
print(s.pstdev(d), round(s.stdev(d), 3))   # 2.0 2.138
print(round(0.0099 / 0.0594, 3))           # 0.167
Read the full explanation

Central tendency: mean, median, mode. Spread: range, variance, standard deviation (sd), IQR. For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mean 5, population variance 4, population sd 2, sample sd (divide by n - 1) = sqrt(32/7) = 2.138. Use sample sd when the data is a sample. Probability basics: P(A) between 0 and 1; P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); independent events multiply. Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A)/P(B). Example: a disease affects 1% of people; a test is 99% sensitive with a 5% false-positive rate. P(positive) = 0.99 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99 = 0.0594, so P(disease | positive) = 0.0099/0.0594 = 16.7%: a positive test is far from certain when the disease is rare. The normal distribution has about 68% of values within 1 sd, 95% within 2 sd and 99.7% within 3 sd of the mean.

🎯 Remember Rare event + imperfect test = many false positives. Always use Bayes, not intuition.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Mean, median, mode kendra batate hain; sd failav. Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Rare bimari mein positive test ke baad bhi sambhavna sirf 16.7%. Normal mein 68-95-99.7 niyam.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

blocks.x: A **hypothesis test** asks whether data is consistent with a **null hypothesis H0** (no effect). The **p-value** is the probability of results at least this extreme if H0 were true. If p < alpha (usually 0.05) we reject H0. A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true. **z-test example:** n = 100, sample mean 52, mu0 = 50, sigma = 10. Standard error = 10/sqrt(100) = 1, so z = (52 - 50)/1 = **2**, two-sided p = **0.0455** (reject at 5%). A **95% confidence interval** is mean +/- 1.96 x SE = 52 +/- 1.96 = **(50.04, 53.96)**.

x: **Type I error:** rejecting a true H0 (probability alpha). **Type II error:** missing a real effect (beta); power = 1 - beta.

Use a **t-test** when sigma is unknown or n is small, **chi-square** for categorical counts, **ANOVA** for more than two means. In **A/B testing**, decide sample size before starting and avoid peeking.

H0 "koi asar nahi" hai. p-value chhota (<0.05) ho to H0 reject. Example mein z = 2, p = 0.0455. 95% confidence interval = (50.04, 53.96). p-value H0 ke sach hone ki sambhavna nahi hai.
A small p-value shows the data is unlikely under H0; it does not measure the size or importance of an effect.

qa.q: What is a p-value?
qa.a: The probability of seeing data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis were true.

qa.q: What is a Type I error?
qa.a: Rejecting a true null hypothesis; its probability is alpha.

qa.q: What does a 95% confidence interval mean?
qa.a: If the procedure is repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals contain the true parameter.

qa.q: When do you use a t-test instead of a z-test?
qa.a: When the population standard deviation is unknown, especially for small samples.

lessons.title: Correlation and regression

blocks.x: **Correlation** r measures linear association from -1 to +1. **Correlation is not causation.** **Simple linear regression** fits y = a + b x by least squares: b = sum((x - mx)(y - my)) / sum((x - mx)^2) and a = my - b mx. Worked example: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. mx = 3, my = 4, so slope **b = 6/10 = 0.6**, intercept **a = 4 - 1.8 = 2.2**, correlation **r = 0.7746** and **R^2 = 0.6** (60% of the variance in y is explained by x). Prediction at x = 6: 2.2 + 3.6 = **5.8**. Other ideas: **multiple regression** (several features), **residuals** should look like random noise, **multicollinearity** (correlated features) makes coefficients unstable, **logistic regression** for yes/no outcomes. Always plot the data; very different data can give the same r.

import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]); y = np.array([2, 4, 5, 4, 5])
b, a = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(b, 2), round(a, 2), round(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1], 4))   # 0.6 2.2 0.7746
Hindi saransh
Linear regression y = a + bx; example mein b = 0.6, a = 2.2, r = 0.7746, R-squared = 0.6. Correlation ka matlab karan (causation) nahi hota.
Plot your data: the same correlation can hide very different patterns.

qa.q: What does R-squared tell us?
qa.a: The fraction of variance in y explained by the model.

qa.q: Does a high correlation prove causation?
qa.a: No; a third factor or coincidence may explain it.

qa.q: What is multicollinearity?
qa.a: Strong correlation among input features, making individual coefficients unstable.

qa.q: What method fits the regression line?
qa.a: Least squares: minimise the sum of squared residuals.

lessons.title: Feature engineering and time series
yt: time series forecasting moving average exponential smoothing

blocks.x: Feature engineering

Better features beat fancier models: **one-hot encode** categories, **bin** numbers, take **logs** of skewed values, build **date features** (day of week, month), **interaction** terms, and text features (TF-IDF). Avoid target leakage.
Time series
Components: **trend, seasonality, noise**. Never shuffle; split by time. Simple forecasts:

x: **Moving average (window 3)** of 10, 12, 14, 13, 15 gives **12, 13, 14**.
**Exponential smoothing** s_t = alpha x_t + (1 - alpha) s_(t-1). With alpha = 0.5 and s1 = 10: **11, 12.5, 12.75, 13.875**.
Advanced: **ARIMA**, Prophet, gradient boosting with lag features, LSTMs. Measure error with MAE, RMSE or MAPE.

Achhe features model se zyada kaam aate hain. Time series mein trend, seasonality, noise hota hai; data time ke hisaab se baanto. Moving average aur exponential smoothing sabse saral forecasts hain.

internet-of-things.title: Internet of Things
internet-of-things.tagline: Sensors, ESP32, MQTT, cloud, edge and IoT security.

lessons.title: What is the Internet of Things? Definition and architecture
yt: internet of things introduction architecture layers
IoT applications smart home smart agriculture industry 4.0

blocks.x: The **Internet of Things (IoT)** is a network of physical objects ("things") with sensors, processing ability and connectivity that collect and exchange data over the internet, often acting on it with little human input.
Why now?
Cheap sensors and microcontrollers (an ESP32 costs a few hundred rupees), ubiquitous Wi-Fi/4G/5G, cloud computing, and better analytics and AI.
Basic building blocks

x: **Things / devices:** sensors (measure), actuators (act), a microcontroller or small computer.
**Connectivity:** Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, cellular.
**Data processing:** at the device (edge), a gateway (fog) or the cloud.
**User interface / application:** mobile app, dashboard, alerts.

blocks.x: Layered architectures

**Three-layer:** Perception (sensors, actuators) → Network (transport) → Application (services). **Five-layer:** Perception → Transport → Processing (middleware, storage, analytics) → Application → Business (policies, revenue, privacy). **Cloud-edge view:** Device → Gateway → Cloud, with decisions made at the most suitable level.
Characteristics
Connectivity, sensing, intelligence, scalability (billions of devices), low power, heterogeneity (many vendors and protocols), and security/privacy needs.
Examples

x: **Smart home:** lights, thermostat, door locks.
**Smart agriculture:** soil-moisture sensors control irrigation pumps.
**Healthcare:** wearables monitor heart rate and SpO2.
**Industry 4.0 / IIoT:** predictive maintenance of machines.
**Smart city:** street lights, waste bins, traffic and air-quality monitoring.
**Logistics:** GPS and temperature tracking of cold-chain goods.

blocks.x: India: Smart Cities Mission, smart electricity meters, FASTag, agriculture sensors.
IoT versus M2M
M2M is direct machine-to-machine communication, often over closed cellular networks. IoT adds internet-scale connectivity, cloud services and analytics.
IoT data flow example
Temperature sensor → ESP32 reads and averages → sends JSON over MQTT → broker → cloud database → dashboard graph → rule triggers a fan relay.
Challenges
Security, privacy, interoperability, power consumption, scalability, reliability in harsh environments, and data volume.
Sense → connect → process → act.

qa.q: Define the Internet of Things.
qa.a: A network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software and connectivity that collect and exchange data over the internet and can act on it.

qa.q: Describe the three-layer IoT architecture.
qa.a: The perception layer senses and acts on the physical world, the network layer carries the data, and the application layer delivers services to users.

qa.q: Difference between a sensor and an actuator?
qa.a: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal; an actuator converts an electrical signal into physical action such as motion or light.

qa.q: Give three IoT application areas.
qa.a: Smart agriculture, healthcare wearables, smart cities, smart homes and industrial predictive maintenance.

qa.q: Name key challenges in IoT.
qa.a: Security and privacy, interoperability, limited power, scalability and handling large volumes of data.

quiz.why: The perception layer senses the environment.

o: converts a signal into physical action
quiz.why: Examples are motors, relays and LEDs.

quiz.why: It is not a network technology.

visuals.title: A four-layer IoT architecture
visuals.data: Application layer: apps, dashboards and alerts; Network layer: Wi-Fi, LoRa, cellular and the protocols on them; Processing layer: edge, cloud, databases and analytics; Perception layer: sensors and actuators in the physical world

problems.q: Define the Internet of Things and name the four layers of a typical IoT architecture from bottom to top.
problems.a: The Internet of Things is a network of physical objects fitted with sensors, software and connectivity so they can collect and exchange data and act on it. Layers from bottom to top: perception (sensors and actuators), network (connectivity), processing (edge, cloud, storage, analytics) and application (apps and dashboards).

problems.q: Explain the data flow of a smart home temperature system from the sensor to the user's phone and back to a fan.
problems.a: A temperature sensor in the room (perception) reads the value, a microcontroller sends it over Wi-Fi using MQTT (network) to the cloud (processing) where it is stored and checked against a rule. The mobile app (application) shows the value. If the temperature is above the limit, a command goes back through the cloud to the device and the actuator (relay) switches the fan on.

problems.q: Differentiate IoT and M2M. Give three challenges of IoT with one example each.
problems.a:
M2M is direct device-to-device communication over a point-to-point link, often with cellular or wired networks and proprietary solutions. IoT connects devices to the internet and cloud platforms with open protocols, analytics and applications, so it scales to many services.
Challenges: security (default passwords on cameras), interoperability (devices from different vendors with different protocols), power and battery life (a sensor must run for months), scalability and privacy of collected data.

lessons.title: Sensors, actuators, ADC and signal conditioning
yt: iot sensors types DHT11 LDR PIR ultrasonic soil moisture
ADC analog to digital conversion voltage divider

blocks.x: Sensors
A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
Specifications: range, **resolution**, accuracy, precision, sensitivity, response time, power use.
Analog and digital signals

A microcontroller pin reads either a digital level (0 or 1) or, through an **ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter)**, a number proportional to the voltage. **ADC resolution:** an n-bit ADC has 2^n levels. ESP32 has 12-bit ADCs (0–4095) for 0–3.3 V, so one step is 3.3/4095 ≈ **0.806 mV**. Arduino Uno: 10-bit, 0–1023 over 5 V ≈ 4.88 mV per step. Voltage from reading: V = reading × Vref / (2^n − 1). LM35 gives 10 mV per °C, so 0.25 V means **25 °C**.
Voltage divider

Vout = Vin × R2/(R1 + R2). With Vin = 5 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 20 kΩ: Vout = 5 × 20/30 = **3.33 V**. It is used to read an LDR or to **level-shift 5 V signals to 3.3 V** for the ESP32 (whose pins are not 5 V tolerant).
Sensor reading in code (simulated)
Output:
Noise and filtering

Real readings jump. Common fixes: take the **average** of N samples, **moving average**, **median filter** (removes spikes), and add a capacitor across the sensor supply. Calibrate against a reference.
Actuators

x: **LED/buzzer:** digital output with a current-limiting resistor. For a 5 V supply, 2 V LED and 20 mA: R = (5 − 2)/0.02 = **150 Ω**.
**Relay module:** lets a low-voltage pin switch mains loads safely (fans, pumps). Mains voltage is dangerous; use isolation and proper enclosures.
**DC motor:** driven through a transistor or motor driver (L298N, L293D).
**Servo:** angle control by a PWM signal.
**Stepper:** precise steps.
**Display:** OLED (I2C), LCD.

blocks.x: **PWM (Pulse Width Modulation)** simulates analog output by switching quickly; duty cycle 25% on an 8-bit scale is 64/255.
Pull-ups and debouncing
Buttons use pull-up/pull-down resistors so the pin never floats; mechanical contacts bounce and need a small delay or capacitor.
A microcontroller only understands voltages; the ADC and a little maths turn them into meaning.

qa.q: What is the resolution of a 12-bit ADC with 3.3 V reference?
Why use a voltage divider with an ESP32?
qa.a: To scale 5 V signals down to 3.3 V, since ESP32 GPIO pins are not 5 V tolerant, or to convert a resistive sensor such as an LDR into a voltage.

qa.q: How do you compute the series resistor for an LED?
qa.a: R = (supply voltage − LED forward voltage)/desired current, for example (5 − 2)/0.02 = 150 Ω.

qa.q: What is PWM used for?
qa.a: Controlling average power by varying duty cycle, such as LED brightness, motor speed and servo angle.

qa.q: How can sensor noise be reduced?
qa.a: By averaging multiple samples, using moving-average or median filters, adding decoupling capacitors and calibrating.

problems.q: Differentiate between a sensor and an actuator with two examples of each.
problems.a: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal (temperature sensor LM35, soil moisture sensor, PIR motion sensor). An actuator converts an electrical signal into physical action (relay, servo motor, buzzer, water pump).

problems.q: A 10-bit ADC has a 5 V reference. Find the voltage step (resolution) and the voltage for a reading of 512. An LM35 gives 10 mV per degree Celsius: what temperature is a voltage of 0.25 V?
problems.a: A 10-bit ADC has 2^10 = 1024 levels. Step = 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV. A reading of 512 corresponds to 512 x 5 / 1024 = 2.5 V. LM35: 0.25 V / 0.01 V per degree = 25 degrees Celsius.

problems.q: A voltage divider uses R1 = 10 kilo-ohm and R2 = 10 kilo-ohm on 5 V. Find the output. Find the series resistor for a red LED (2 V, 20 mA) on a 5 V supply. Why is signal conditioning (filtering) needed?
problems.a:
Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2) = 5 x 10 / 20 = 2.5 V. Resistor = (5 - 2) / 0.02 = 150 ohm.
Sensor signals are small and noisy; amplification brings them to the ADC range and filtering removes noise, so readings are stable and accurate.

Analog and digital signals

  • A microcontroller pin reads either a digital level (0 or 1) or, through an ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter), a number proportional to the voltage
  • ADC resolution: an n-bit ADC has 2^n levels
  • ESP32 has 12-bit ADCs (0–4095) for 0–3.3 V, so one step is 3.3/4095 ≈ 0.806 mV
  • Arduino Uno: 10-bit, 0–1023 over 5 V ≈ 4.88 mV per step
Read the full explanation

A microcontroller pin reads either a digital level (0 or 1) or, through an ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter), a number proportional to the voltage. ADC resolution: an n-bit ADC has 2^n levels. ESP32 has 12-bit ADCs (0–4095) for 0–3.3 V, so one step is 3.3/4095 ≈ 0.806 mV. Arduino Uno: 10-bit, 0–1023 over 5 V ≈ 4.88 mV per step. Voltage from reading: V = reading × Vref / (2^n − 1). LM35 gives 10 mV per °C, so 0.25 V means 25 °C.

🧠

Voltage divider

  • Vout = Vin × R2/(R1 + R2)
  • With Vin = 5 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 20 kΩ: Vout = 5 × 20/30 = 3.33 V
  • It is used to read an LDR or to level-shift 5 V signals to 3.3 V for the ESP32 (whose pins are not 5 V tolerant)
🌟

def lm35_celsius(volts):

0.25 25.0
🔬

Noise and filtering

  • Real readings jump
  • Common fixes: take the average of N samples, moving average, median filter (removes spikes), and add a capacitor across the sensor supply
  • Calibrate against a reference
📊

Actuators

  • LED/buzzer: digital output with a current-limiting resistor. For a 5 V supply, 2 V LED and 20 mA: R = (5 − 2)/0.02 = 150 Ω.
  • Relay module: lets a low-voltage pin switch mains loads safely (fans, pumps). Mains voltage is dangerous; use isolation and proper enclosures.
  • DC motor: driven through a transistor or motor driver (L298N, L293D).
  • Servo: angle control by a PWM signal.

Pull-ups and debouncing

  • Buttons use pull-up/pull-down resistors so the pin never floats
  • Mechanical contacts bounce and need a small delay or capacitor

blocks.x: Microcontroller vs microprocessor

A **microcontroller (MCU)** puts CPU, RAM, flash memory and peripherals (GPIO, ADC, timers, UART, I2C, SPI) on one chip: cheap, low power, runs one program with no OS. A **microprocessor** (as in a PC or Raspberry Pi) needs external memory and runs an OS.
Popular boards
ESP32 features

GPIO pins (3.3 V logic), 12-bit ADC, 2 DAC, touch sensors, PWM, UART/I2C/SPI, Wi-Fi 802.11 b/g/n, Bluetooth, **deep-sleep** mode (microamp current), RTC memory, and OTA (over-the-air) updates. Some GPIOs are input-only (34–39) and ADC2 pins cannot be used while Wi-Fi is on.
Communication buses

x: **UART:** two wires TX/RX, asynchronous (GPS, serial monitor).
**I2C:** two wires SDA/SCL, many devices by address (OLED, BMP280).
**SPI:** four wires (MOSI, MISO, SCK, CS), fast (SD cards, displays).
**1-Wire:** one data line (DS18B20).

blocks.x: Programming

x: **Arduino IDE / PlatformIO** (C/C++): `setup()` runs once, `loop()` runs forever.
**MicroPython** on ESP32: Python on the board.
**ESP-IDF** (professional C framework with FreeRTOS).

blocks.x: Blink and sensor sketch (ESP32 Arduino, shown for reference)
Avoid long `delay()` in real products; use timers or non-blocking code with `millis()`.
Power management

Battery life = capacity / average current. A 2000 mAh battery with a constant 20 mA lasts **100 hours**. Wake for 5 s at 80 mA once a minute and deep sleep at 10 µA the rest of the time: average ≈ 6.7 mA, so about **300 hours (12.5 days)**. Sleeping is the key to battery IoT.
Choosing a board
Need Wi-Fi/BLE and low cost → ESP32. Heavy processing, camera AI, Linux → Raspberry Pi. Ultra-low power for years → special low-power MCUs with LoRa.
MCU = tiny computer for one job; Raspberry Pi = small Linux computer.

qa.q: Difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?
qa.a: A microcontroller integrates CPU, memory and peripherals on one chip for dedicated control tasks; a microprocessor is a CPU needing external memory and peripherals, typically running a full OS.

qa.q: Why is ESP32 popular for IoT?
qa.a: It combines a fast dual-core CPU, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, many peripherals, deep sleep and low cost.

qa.q: Compare I2C and SPI.
qa.a: I2C uses two wires and addresses many devices on one bus but is slower; SPI uses four wires (plus chip selects), is faster and full duplex but needs more pins.

qa.q: What do setup() and loop() do in Arduino code?
qa.a: setup() runs once at start for initialisation; loop() runs repeatedly forever.

qa.q: How does deep sleep extend battery life?
qa.a: The device turns off most circuitry and draws microamps, waking only briefly to measure and transmit, which cuts the average current.

lessons.title: IoT connectivity: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT and cellular
yt: iot communication technologies lora zigbee ble wifi comparison

blocks.x: Choosing a link means trading **range, data rate, power, cost and infrastructure**.
Short range

x: **Wi-Fi (802.11):** high data rate (tens–hundreds of Mbps), ~50 m indoors, high power. Good for mains-powered devices and cameras.
**Bluetooth / BLE:** ~10–100 m, low power, phones and wearables, beacons. BLE uses the GATT profile (services and characteristics).
**Zigbee (802.15.4):** ~10–100 m, 250 kbps, **mesh** network, low power, used in smart homes; a hub/coordinator is needed.
**Thread/Matter:** IP-based smart home standards.
**RFID / NFC:** very short range identification (NFC ≈ 4 cm): payments, access cards, inventory.

blocks.x: Low-Power Wide-Area Networks (LPWAN)

x: **LoRa / LoRaWAN:** long range (2–5 km urban, 10+ km rural), very low power, low data rate (0.3–50 kbps), unlicensed ISM band (865–867 MHz in India). Star-of-stars architecture: **end devices → gateways → network server → application server**. Great for agriculture, metering, tracking. Small payloads, limited messages per day.
**NB-IoT / LTE-M:** cellular LPWAN using licensed spectrum; good indoor penetration; needs a SIM and operator support.
**Sigfox:** ultra-narrowband (very small messages).

blocks.x: Cellular
2G/3G/4G/5G for mobile assets (vehicle tracking) and high bandwidth (video). 5G adds low latency (URLLC) and massive IoT (mMTC).
Comparison
Data volume example
One reading of 20 bytes every 10 seconds is 8,640 readings a day = 172,800 bytes ≈ **169 KB per day** — tiny, so LoRa or NB-IoT is enough. A video camera needs Wi-Fi or 4G/5G.
Network topologies
Star (BLE, Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN), mesh (Zigbee, Thread: devices relay for each other, extending range and resilience), tree, and point-to-point.
Addressing: IPv6
IPv4 (4.3 billion addresses) cannot name billions of devices; **IPv6** (128-bit) can. **6LoWPAN** compresses IPv6 headers for tiny 802.15.4 devices. NAT is used behind routers.
Choosing
Mains power + high rate → Wi-Fi; battery + phone → BLE; mesh in a building → Zigbee/Thread; battery + kilometres → LoRaWAN/NB-IoT.
Range, rate and power form a triangle: you can optimise only two.

qa.q: Why is LoRaWAN suited to agriculture?
qa.a: It has long range (kilometres), very low power use so sensors run on batteries for years, and uses unlicensed spectrum, though only for small, infrequent messages.

qa.q: What is a mesh network?
qa.a: A network in which nodes relay data for one another, extending range and providing alternative paths if a node fails; Zigbee and Thread use it.

qa.q: Compare BLE and Wi-Fi.
qa.a: BLE has low data rate, very low power and works with phones; Wi-Fi has high data rate but much higher power consumption.

qa.q: What is the role of a LoRaWAN gateway?
qa.a: It receives LoRa radio messages from end devices and forwards them over IP to the network server.

qa.q: Why is IPv6 important for IoT?
qa.a: Its 128-bit addresses provide enough unique addresses for billions of devices, which IPv4 cannot.

problems.q: Name four wireless technologies used in IoT and say what each is best suited for.
problems.a: Bluetooth Low Energy: short range, low power wearables and beacons. Zigbee: low-power mesh networks for home automation. Wi-Fi: high data rate for cameras and hubs. LoRaWAN: long range, low data rate sensors in fields or cities. NB-IoT (cellular): metering and tracking using the mobile network.

problems.q: Compare LoRaWAN and Wi-Fi for a soil sensor in a farm 3 km from the house. Which is better and why?
problems.a: LoRaWAN is better: it reaches kilometres, needs very little power so a battery lasts for years, and the small soil data packets fit its low data rate. Wi-Fi reaches only tens of metres, uses more power and needs a router coverage over the whole farm.

problems.q: A sensor sends 100 bytes every 10 seconds. How many bytes per day? A node uses 20 mA for 2 s every minute and 0.01 mA while sleeping for the other 58 s. Find the average current and the life of a 2000 mAh battery.
problems.a: Messages per day = 86400 / 10 = 8640, so 8640 x 100 = 864,000 bytes (864 KB). Average current = (20 x 2 + 0.01 x 58) / 60 = (40 + 0.58) / 60 = 0.676 mA. Battery life = 2000 / 0.676 = about 2957 hours, about 123 days.

lessons.title: IoT application protocols: MQTT, HTTP/REST, CoAP

coap vs mqtt vs http iot protocols

blocks.x: HTTP / REST
Request–response over TCP. Simple and universal (`GET /sensors/12`, `POST /readings` with JSON), but heavy headers and no server push, so poor for tiny battery devices. Use HTTPS.
MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport)
The most popular IoT protocol: lightweight **publish/subscribe** over TCP (port 1883, 8883 with TLS).

x: **Broker:** central server (Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ) that routes messages.
**Clients** publish messages to **topics** and subscribe to topics. Publishers and subscribers never talk directly (decoupled).
**Topic:** a hierarchy like `home/kitchen/temperature`.
**Wildcards:** `+` matches one level (`home/+/temperature`), `#` matches all remaining levels (`home/#`) (subscribe only).

blocks.x: Quality of Service
Other features

x: **Retained message:** broker stores the last message for new subscribers.
**Last Will and Testament (LWT):** message the broker publishes if a client disconnects unexpectedly (device offline alert).
**Keep-alive** ping, **persistent sessions**, small 2-byte minimum header.

Publishing from Python (needs a broker and the paho-mqtt library)

import json, paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
c = mqtt.Client()
c.connect("broker.example.com", 1883)
c.publish("farm/field1/soil", json.dumps({"moisture": 41, "unit": "%"}), qos=1)
CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol)

REST-like (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) but over **UDP** with tiny binary headers, designed for constrained devices; supports **observe** (subscribe to changes), multicast and optional reliability (confirmable messages). Secured with DTLS.
Comparison
Others
AMQP (enterprise queues), XMPP, WebSocket, DDS (robotics/industrial), OPC UA (industrial), LwM2M (device management).
Data format
Payloads are usually **JSON** (human readable) or CBOR/Protobuf (compact). Example: `{"id":"node1","t":28.4,"h":61}`.
MQTT: devices talk to a broker, not to each other.

qa.q: What is MQTT and why is it popular in IoT?
qa.a: A lightweight publish/subscribe protocol over TCP with a central broker. Its small overhead, simple API and QoS levels suit constrained devices and unreliable networks.

qa.q: Explain the three MQTT QoS levels.
qa.a: QoS 0 delivers at most once with no acknowledgement; QoS 1 delivers at least once, possibly duplicated; QoS 2 delivers exactly once using a four-step handshake.

qa.q: What are the wildcards in MQTT?
qa.a: + matches exactly one topic level and # matches any number of remaining levels.

qa.q: What is the Last Will and Testament?
qa.a: A message registered by a client at connect time which the broker publishes if the client disconnects unexpectedly, often used for offline status.

qa.q: Why is CoAP preferred over HTTP for very small devices?
qa.a: It runs over UDP with a compact binary header, so it needs less memory, energy and bandwidth, while still giving REST-style operations.

quiz.q: MQTT uses which model?
quiz.why: Clients publish to topics and subscribe through a broker.

quiz.q: MQTT QoS 2 means
quiz.why: The slowest but most reliable level.

problems.q: Explain the publish-subscribe model of MQTT with the roles of publisher, subscriber, broker and topic.
problems.a: Publishers send messages to a topic on a broker; subscribers register interest in topics with the broker; the broker delivers each message to every matching subscriber. Publishers and subscribers do not know each other, which decouples them. A topic is a hierarchical name such as home/room1/temp.

rubric.t: Roles of publisher, subscriber and broker

problems.q: Explain MQTT QoS 0, 1 and 2, and the wildcards + and # with an example.
problems.a: QoS 0: at most once (no acknowledgement, may be lost). QoS 1: at least once (acknowledged, may be duplicated). QoS 2: exactly once (four-step handshake, slowest). Wildcards: + matches one level (home/+/temp matches home/room1/temp), # matches all remaining levels (home/room1/# matches every topic below room1).

problems.q: Compare MQTT, HTTP and CoAP on transport, pattern and best use. What are retained messages and the last will message?
problems.a:
MQTT: TCP, publish-subscribe, small overhead, good for many devices pushing telemetry. HTTP: TCP, request-response, heavy headers, good for web APIs. CoAP: UDP, request-response similar to HTTP but lightweight, good for constrained devices.
A retained message is stored by the broker so a new subscriber gets the last value immediately. A last will message is sent by the broker if a client disconnects unexpectedly, so others know it is offline.

Topic matching (simulated and verified)

def match(flt, topic):
    f, t = flt.split('/'), topic.split('/')
    for i, part in enumerate(f):
        if part == '#': return True
        if i >= len(t): return False
        if part != '+' and part != t[i]: return False
    return len(f) == len(t)
print(match('home/+/temp', 'home/kitchen/temp'))
print(match('home/#', 'home/a/b/c'))

c.connect("broker.example.com", 1883)
c.publish("farm/field1/soil", json.dumps({"moisture": 41, "unit": "%"}), qos=1)
💡

CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol)

  • REST-like (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) but over UDP with tiny binary headers, designed for constrained devices
  • Supports observe (subscribe to changes), multicast and optional reliability (confirmable messages)
  • Secured with DTLS
📌

Comparison

FeatureHTTPMQTTCoAP
Modelrequest/responsepublish/subscriberequest/response (+observe)
TransportTCPTCPUDP
Overheadhighlowvery low
Best forweb APIstelemetry, many devicesvery constrained nodes
🧠

Others

  • AMQP (enterprise queues), XMPP, WebSocket, DDS (robotics/industrial), OPC UA (industrial), LwM2M (device management)
🌟

Data format

  • Payloads are usually JSON (human readable) or CBOR/Protobuf (compact)
  • Example: {"id":"node1","t":28.4,"h":61}
🎯 Remember MQTT: devices talk to a broker, not to each other.

blocks.x: Why a cloud?

qa.q: List the stages of an IoT data pipeline.
qa.a: Device sensing, ingestion through a broker or endpoint, processing and rules, storage in a database, analytics, visualisation and alerts, and control commands back to devices.

qa.q: What is a device shadow?
qa.a: A cloud-held representation of a device's reported and desired state, allowing applications to interact even when the device is offline.

qa.q: Why use a time-series database for sensor data?
qa.a: It is optimised for timestamped data, fast writes, range queries and downsampling over time.

qa.q: What is an OTA update?
qa.a: Remotely sending new firmware to a deployed device over the network, ideally signed and with rollback capability.

qa.q: How can message cost be reduced?
qa.a: By batching readings, compressing payloads, reporting only significant changes and lowering the sampling frequency.

Time-series databases store
A device shadow stores
Rules engines can
o: trigger alerts or actions based on conditions
quiz.why: For example, temperature above a threshold sends SMS.

visuals.title: An IoT data pipeline
visuals.data: Devices send readings > Gateway collects and forwards them > Cloud ingests with MQTT or HTTP > Database stores time-series data > Dashboard and alerts show results

problems.q: List the stages of an IoT data pipeline and name one tool or service for each.
problems.a: Ingestion (MQTT broker, AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub), storage (time-series database such as InfluxDB, or a cloud database), processing (rules engine, stream processing, Python), visualisation (Grafana, ThingsBoard) and alerting (email, SMS, push notifications).

problems.q: What is a time-series database and why is it better than a plain table for sensor data? Design the fields for temperature readings.
problems.a: A time-series database stores values with timestamps and is optimised for fast writes, time-range queries, downsampling and automatic retention of old data. Fields: timestamp, device_id, location, temperature, battery (optionally humidity). A plain table can store this but becomes slow and large without these optimisations.

problems.q: A cloud rule says: if temperature is above 40 for 3 consecutive readings send an alert. Explain why 3 readings are required and describe the storage cost of 1000 sensors sending 100 bytes every 10 seconds for one day.
problems.a: Requiring 3 readings filters out a single noisy spike or glitch and reduces false alarms. Storage per day = 1000 sensors x 8640 messages x 100 bytes = 864,000,000 bytes = about 864 MB (before indexing and compression).

rubric.t: Mentions indexing or compression or retention

lessons.title: Edge and fog computing, gateways and TinyML
yt: edge computing vs cloud computing vs fog computing iot

blocks.x: Why not send everything to the cloud?

x: **Latency:** a brake or safety system cannot wait 200 ms for a cloud reply.
**Bandwidth and cost:** raw video from a thousand cameras is huge.
**Reliability:** the network may fail.
**Privacy:** keep sensitive data local.

blocks.x: Edge, fog and cloud

x: **Edge computing:** processing on the device or right next to it (microcontroller, gateway).
**Fog computing:** an intermediate layer of gateways/local servers between devices and cloud.
**Cloud computing:** large-scale storage and heavy analytics.

blocks.x: Typical split: filter and react at the edge (milliseconds), aggregate in fog (seconds), long-term learning in cloud (hours or days).
Gateways
A gateway connects devices using local protocols (BLE, Zigbee, LoRa) to IP networks and the cloud. It can translate protocols, buffer data during outages, run rules and apply security.
Edge analytics example

A vibration sensor samples at 1 kHz. Sending 1,000 readings/second is wasteful. The edge device computes a feature (RMS value) each second and sends only that, or an alert when it exceeds a threshold. Data volume drops by about 1000 times.
TinyML
Running machine-learning models on microcontrollers with kilobytes of memory.

x: Train on a PC (TensorFlow/Keras, Edge Impulse), **quantise** weights to 8 bits, convert to **TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers**, and deploy as a C array.
Use cases: wake-word detection, gesture recognition (accelerometer), anomaly detection in motors, people counting.
Benefits: low latency, low power, works offline, privacy.
Limits: tiny models and memory, reduced accuracy.

blocks.x: Simple edge filter (simulated)

import statistics
samples = [0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.25, 4.0, 0.3, 0.2]   # one spike
clean = [s for s in samples if abs(s - statistics.median(samples)) < 1]
print(clean, round(sum(clean) / len(clean), 3))

Real-time operating systems
FreeRTOS and Zephyr schedule tasks with deadlines on MCUs (see Operating Systems: scheduling).
Fog use cases
Smart factory (local control loops), connected vehicles, smart grid, video analytics at the camera.
Do the urgent work near the data; send the summary to the cloud.

qa.q: Why is edge computing used in IoT?
qa.a: It reduces latency, bandwidth use and cost, keeps working during network failure, and improves privacy by processing data locally.

qa.q: Difference between edge and fog computing?
qa.a: Edge computing processes data on or very near the device; fog computing uses an intermediate layer of gateways or local servers between the edge and cloud.

qa.q: What is TinyML?
qa.a: Machine learning models optimised to run on very small, low-power microcontrollers.

qa.q: What is quantisation?
qa.a: Reducing the precision of model weights (for example from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers) to shrink size and speed up inference with small accuracy loss.

qa.q: What functions can an IoT gateway perform?
qa.a: Protocol translation, local processing and rules, buffering when offline, security enforcement and forwarding to the cloud.

quiz.q: FreeRTOS is a

visuals.title: Where the processing happens
visuals.data: Edge=On the device or next to it~Lowest delay, works offline~Limited power; Fog=A nearby gateway or local server~Combines data from many devices~Medium delay; Cloud=Far-away data centres~Huge storage and compute~Higher delay and cost

problems.q: Differentiate edge, fog and cloud computing in IoT.
problems.a: Edge computing processes data on the device or very close to it. Fog computing uses nearby gateways or local servers between the devices and the cloud. Cloud computing uses remote data centres with large storage and computing power. Moving from edge to cloud increases power and delay.

problems.q: 1000 sensors each send 1 KB per second to the cloud. If an edge gateway sends only a 1 KB summary per sensor every minute, find the data sent per second in both cases and the reduction.
problems.a: Raw: 1000 x 1 KB = 1000 KB per second. With edge summaries: 1000 KB every 60 s = 16.7 KB per second. Reduction = 1 - 16.7 / 1000 = about 98.3%. Edge processing also reduces latency and cost.

problems.q: What is TinyML? A model is 250 KB in 32-bit floating point. What is its size after 8-bit quantisation? Give one use case and one limitation.
problems.a: TinyML runs machine learning models on very small, low-power microcontrollers. 8-bit quantisation stores each weight in 1 byte instead of 4, so the model becomes 250 / 4 = 62.5 KB. Use case: keyword spotting or detecting vibration anomalies in a motor without sending data to the cloud. Limitation: small memory and compute, so models are small and may lose some accuracy.
