lessons.title: JEE Main: mole concept, solutions and titration
yt: jee main mole concept solutions titration

blocks.x: One mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles; n = mass/M; molarity M = moles/litre; molality m = moles/kg solvent; mole fraction x = n_i/n_total. Colligative properties: DTb = Kb m, DTf = Kf m, pi = C R T, relative lowering of vapour pressure = x_solute (Raoult). Van t Hoff factor i modifies each. Titration: N1 V1 = N2 V2 and M1 V1 n2 = M2 V2 n1.
Deep dive: mole concept

One mole is the amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 entities (Avogadro number N_A). Moles n = mass/molar mass = number of particles/N_A = volume at STP/22.4 L. Percentage composition and empirical formula: divide percentages by atomic masses, then by the smallest to get the simplest ratio; molecular formula = empirical formula x n where n = molar mass/empirical mass. Stoichiometry: balance the equation, convert masses to moles, use mole ratios; the limiting reagent is the reactant that gives the least product. Percentage yield = (actual/theoretical) x 100. Equivalent mass = molar mass/n-factor.
Deep dive: concentration terms and colligative properties

Molarity M = moles of solute/volume (L); molality m = moles of solute/mass of solvent (kg) (independent of temperature); normality N = gram equivalents/volume (L) = M x n-factor; mole fraction x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B); ppm = mass of solute/mass of solution x 10^6. Dilution: M1 V1 = M2 V2. Raoult law: P_A = x_A P_A^0; total P = sum x_i P_i^0. Relative lowering of vapour pressure (P^0 - P)/P^0 = x_solute. Elevation of boiling point DTb = i Kb m, depression of freezing point DTf = i Kf m, osmotic pressure pi = i C R T. Van t Hoff factor i = observed colligative property/calculated: i > 1 for dissociation (NaCl about 2), i < 1 for association (acetic acid in benzene). Molar mass from colligative data M = Kf w2 x 1000/(DTf w1).
Deep dive: titrations

At the equivalence point gram equivalents of acid = gram equivalents of base: N1 V1 = N2 V2; with molarity M1 V1 n2 = M2 V2 n1 for a reaction a A + b B. Redox titrations: KMnO4 in acid medium has n-factor 5 (Mn7+ to Mn2+), K2Cr2O7 has n-factor 6, oxalic acid 2, Fe2+ 1. Indicators: phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) for strong base titrations, methyl orange (3.1 to 4.4) for strong acid. Back titration is used for insoluble or volatile substances. Hardness of water is expressed in ppm of CaCO3.
Hindi saransh
n = w/M. M = n/V. DTf = i Kf m. pi = i C R T.
Normality = molarity x n-factor.

qa.q: What is Avogadro's number?
What is a mole?
qa.a: The amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 elementary entities.

qa.q: What is molarity?
qa.a: Moles of solute per litre of solution.

qa.q: What is molality?
qa.a: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.

qa.q: Which is independent of temperature, molarity or molality?
What is the mole fraction?
qa.a: The ratio of the moles of one component to the total moles.

qa.q: What is normality?
qa.a: Gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution.

qa.q: What is the limiting reagent?
qa.a: The reactant that is completely consumed first.

qa.q: State Raoult's law.
qa.a: The partial vapour pressure of a component is its mole fraction times its vapour pressure in the pure state.

qa.q: What are colligative properties?
qa.a: Properties that depend only on the number of solute particles.

qa.q: Name the four colligative properties.
qa.a: Relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure.

qa.q: What is the van't Hoff factor?
qa.a: The ratio of observed to calculated colligative property.

qa.q: What is osmosis?
qa.a: The flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane towards the higher solute concentration.

qa.q: What is reverse osmosis?
qa.a: Solvent flow from the solution to the pure solvent under pressure larger than osmotic pressure.

qa.q: What is an isotonic solution?
qa.a: Solutions with the same osmotic pressure.

qa.q: What is an azeotrope?
qa.a: A constant-boiling mixture that cannot be separated by distillation.

qa.q: What is the n-factor of KMnO4 in acidic medium?
What is the n-factor of K2Cr2O7?
What is the equivalence point?
qa.a: The point at which the reactants have reacted in chemically equivalent amounts.

qa.q: Which indicator is used for a strong acid and weak base titration?
What is a primary standard?
qa.a: A stable, pure substance of known composition used to prepare standard solutions.

qa.q: What does a positive deviation from Raoult's law mean?
qa.a: Weaker solute-solvent interactions than in the pure components.

  • Moles n = mass/molar mass = number of particles/N_A = volume at STP/22.4 L

Read the full explanation

One mole is the amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 entities (Avogadro number N_A). Moles n = mass/molar mass = number of particles/N_A = volume at STP/22.4 L. Percentage composition and empirical formula: divide percentages by atomic masses, then by the smallest to get the simplest ratio; molecular formula = empirical formula x n where n = molar mass/empirical mass. Stoichiometry: balance the equation, convert masses to moles, use mole ratios; the limiting reagent is the reactant that gives the least product. Percentage yield = (actual/theoretical) x 100. Equivalent mass = molar mass/n-factor.

🧠

Concentration terms and colligative properties

  • Molarity M = moles of solute/volume (L)
  • Molality m = moles of solute/mass of solvent (kg) (independent of temperature)
  • Normality N = gram equivalents/volume (L) = M x n-factor
  • Mole fraction x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B)
Read the full explanation

Molarity M = moles of solute/volume (L); molality m = moles of solute/mass of solvent (kg) (independent of temperature); normality N = gram equivalents/volume (L) = M x n-factor; mole fraction x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B); ppm = mass of solute/mass of solution x 10^6. Dilution: M1 V1 = M2 V2. Raoult law: P_A = x_A P_A^0; total P = sum x_i P_i^0. Relative lowering of vapour pressure (P^0 - P)/P^0 = x_solute. Elevation of boiling point DTb = i Kb m, depression of freezing point DTf = i Kf m, osmotic pressure pi = i C R T. Van t Hoff factor i = observed colligative property/calculated: i > 1 for dissociation (NaCl about 2), i < 1 for association (acetic acid in benzene). Molar mass from colligative data M = Kf w2 x 1000/(DTf w1).

🌟

Titrations

  • At the equivalence point gram equivalents of acid = gram equivalents of base: N1 V1 = N2 V2
  • With molarity M1 V1 n2 = M2 V2 n1 for a reaction a A + b B
  • Redox titrations: KMnO4 in acid medium has n-factor 5 (Mn7+ to Mn2+), K2Cr2O7 has n-factor 6, oxalic acid 2, Fe2+ 1
  • Indicators: phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) for strong base titrations, methyl orange (3.1 to 4.4) for strong acid
Read the full explanation

At the equivalence point gram equivalents of acid = gram equivalents of base: N1 V1 = N2 V2; with molarity M1 V1 n2 = M2 V2 n1 for a reaction a A + b B. Redox titrations: KMnO4 in acid medium has n-factor 5 (Mn7+ to Mn2+), K2Cr2O7 has n-factor 6, oxalic acid 2, Fe2+ 1. Indicators: phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) for strong base titrations, methyl orange (3.1 to 4.4) for strong acid. Back titration is used for insoluble or volatile substances. Hardness of water is expressed in ppm of CaCO3.

lessons.title: JEE Main: equilibrium, pH and electrochemistry

blocks.x: Kc = [products]/[reactants] with stoichiometric powers; Kp = Kc (RT)^Dn. pH = -log [H+], pH + pOH = 14, Ka Kb = Kw = 10^-14. Henderson: pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]. Ksp of AxBy = x^x y^y s^(x + y). Electrochemistry: E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode, Nernst E = E0 - (0.0591/n) log Q, DG = -nFE, Faraday m = Z I t.
Deep dive: chemical equilibrium

For aA + bB <=> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d/([A]^a [B]^b); Kp = Kc (RT)^Dn with Dn = (c + d) - (a + b). The reaction quotient Q is compared with K: Q < K forward shift, Q > K backward shift, Q = K equilibrium. Reversing the reaction inverts K; multiplying coefficients by n raises K to the nth power; adding reactions multiplies K values. Le Chatelier: adding reactant shifts forward; raising pressure favours fewer gas moles; heat favours the endothermic direction (K changes only with temperature, van t Hoff: log (K2/K1) = DH (T2 - T1)/(2.303 R T1 T2)). Degree of dissociation alpha: for A <=> 2B at total pressure P, Kp = 4 alpha^2 P/(1 - alpha^2).
Deep dive: ionic equilibrium

Water: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 at 25 C; pH = -log [H+]; pH + pOH = 14. Strong acid: [H+] = C. Weak acid: [H+] = sqrt (Ka C) = C alpha. Ka Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair. Buffer: pH = pKa + log ([salt]/[acid]) (Henderson-Hasselbalch); buffer capacity is maximal when [salt] = [acid]. Salt hydrolysis: for a weak acid-strong base salt pH = 7 + (1/2) (pKa + log C). Solubility product Ksp: for AB, s = sqrt (Ksp); for AB2 or A2B, s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3). Precipitation occurs when the ionic product exceeds Ksp; the common ion effect lowers solubility. Indicator pH range = pKin +- 1.
Deep dive: electrochemistry

A galvanic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy; anode (oxidation, negative), cathode (reduction, positive). E0_cell = E0_cathode - E0_anode; DG0 = -n F E0 and DG0 = -2.303 R T log K, giving log K = n E0/0.0591 at 25 C. Nernst equation: E = E0 - (0.0591/n) log Q. Concentration cell: E = (0.0591/n) log (C2/C1). Faraday laws: mass deposited m = (M/(n F)) I t; one faraday = 96500 C. Conductance: conductivity kappa = G (l/A), molar conductivity Lambda_m = kappa x 1000/C; Kohlrausch: Lambda_m0 = lambda+ + lambda-. Batteries: lead storage, Leclanche, Ni-Cd, fuel cell (H2-O2 with 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O). Corrosion is electrochemical rusting of iron.

🔑

Big idea

  • Kc = [products]/[reactants] with stoichiometric powers
  • Kp = Kc (RT)^Dn
  • PH = -log [H+], pH + pOH = 14, Ka Kb = Kw = 10-14
  • Henderson: pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]
Read the full explanation

Kc = [products]/[reactants] with stoichiometric powers; Kp = Kc (RT)^Dn. pH = -log [H+], pH + pOH = 14, Ka Kb = Kw = 10^-14. Henderson: pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]. Ksp of AxBy = x^x y^y s^(x + y). Electrochemistry: E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode, Nernst E = E0 - (0.0591/n) log Q, DG = -nFE, Faraday m = Z I t.

⚗️

Chemical equilibrium

  • For aA + bB <=> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d/([A]^a [B]^b)
  • Kp = Kc (RT)^Dn with Dn = (c + d) - (a + b)
  • The reaction quotient Q is compared with K: Q < K forward shift, Q > K backward shift, Q = K equilibrium
  • Reversing the reaction inverts K
Read the full explanation

For aA + bB <=> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d/([A]^a [B]^b); Kp = Kc (RT)^Dn with Dn = (c + d) - (a + b). The reaction quotient Q is compared with K: Q < K forward shift, Q > K backward shift, Q = K equilibrium. Reversing the reaction inverts K; multiplying coefficients by n raises K to the nth power; adding reactions multiplies K values. Le Chatelier: adding reactant shifts forward; raising pressure favours fewer gas moles; heat favours the endothermic direction (K changes only with temperature, van t Hoff: log (K2/K1) = DH (T2 - T1)/(2.303 R T1 T2)). Degree of dissociation alpha: for A <=> 2B at total pressure P, Kp = 4 alpha^2 P/(1 - alpha^2).

🧠

Ionic equilibrium

  • Water: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10-14 at 25 C
  • PH = -log [H+]
  • PH + pOH = 14
  • Strong acid: [H+] = C
Read the full explanation

Water: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 at 25 C; pH = -log [H+]; pH + pOH = 14. Strong acid: [H+] = C. Weak acid: [H+] = sqrt (Ka C) = C alpha. Ka Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair. Buffer: pH = pKa + log ([salt]/[acid]) (Henderson-Hasselbalch); buffer capacity is maximal when [salt] = [acid]. Salt hydrolysis: for a weak acid-strong base salt pH = 7 + (1/2) (pKa + log C). Solubility product Ksp: for AB, s = sqrt (Ksp); for AB2 or A2B, s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3). Precipitation occurs when the ionic product exceeds Ksp; the common ion effect lowers solubility. Indicator pH range = pKin +- 1.

🌟

Electrochemistry

  • A galvanic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy
  • Anode (oxidation, negative), cathode (reduction, positive)
  • E0_cell = E0_cathode - E0_anode
  • DG0 = -n F E0 and DG0 = -2.303 R T log K, giving log K = n E0/0.0591 at 25 C
Read the full explanation

A galvanic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy; anode (oxidation, negative), cathode (reduction, positive). E0_cell = E0_cathode - E0_anode; DG0 = -n F E0 and DG0 = -2.303 R T log K, giving log K = n E0/0.0591 at 25 C. Nernst equation: E = E0 - (0.0591/n) log Q. Concentration cell: E = (0.0591/n) log (C2/C1). Faraday laws: mass deposited m = (M/(n F)) I t; one faraday = 96500 C. Conductance: conductivity kappa = G (l/A), molar conductivity Lambda_m = kappa x 1000/C; Kohlrausch: Lambda_m0 = lambda+ + lambda-. Batteries: lead storage, Leclanche, Ni-Cd, fuel cell (H2-O2 with 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O). Corrosion is electrochemical rusting of iron.

lessons.title: Permutations and combinations (JEE Main)

blocks.x: Fundamental principle: m ways then n ways gives m x n ways (and), m + n (or). nPr = n!/(n - r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!). Circular arrangements of n objects: (n - 1)!. Arrangements with repeats: n!/(p! q! r!). Distribution and derangements use inclusion-exclusion; the number of ways to distribute n identical objects among r people is C(n + r - 1, r - 1).
Deep dive: counting principles

The multiplication principle: if one task can be done in m ways and a second in n ways, both in sequence can be done in m n ways. The addition principle: if either of two exclusive tasks can be done, the count is m + n. Factorial: n! = n (n - 1) ... 1 with 0! = 1. Permutations are ordered arrangements: nPr = n!/(n - r)! and with repetition allowed n^r. Combinations are unordered selections: nCr = n!/(r! (n - r)!) with nCr = nC(n - r), nCr + nC(r - 1) = (n + 1)Cr and r nCr = n (n - 1)C(r - 1). The maximum value of nCr occurs at r = n/2.
Deep dive: arrangements with conditions

Objects with repetition: n!/(p! q! r!). Circular arrangements: (n - 1)! (clockwise and anticlockwise distinct); if direction does not matter (necklace): (n - 1)!/2. Together condition: tie objects as one block and multiply by the internal arrangements: n people with 2 specific people together: 2 (n - 1)!. Never together = total - together. Ranking of letters of a word: count words below each letter. The number of words formed by the letters of MISSISSIPPI is 11!/(4! 4! 2!).
Deep dive: selection and distribution

Selecting at least one from n distinct items: 2^n - 1. Selections from identical objects: choose any number from p alike, q alike, r alike: (p + 1)(q + 1)(r + 1) - 1. Number of ways to divide 2n objects into two equal groups: (2n)!/(2 (n!)^2) when unlabelled. The number of non-negative integer solutions of x1 + ... + xr = n is C(n + r - 1, r - 1); the number of positive solutions is C(n - 1, r - 1). Derangements of n objects: D_n = n! (1 - 1/1! + 1/2! - ... + (-1)^n/n!). The number of diagonals of an n-gon is n (n - 3)/2; of triangles formed from n points with p collinear is nC3 - pC3.
Hindi saransh
nPr = n!/(n-r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!). Circular: (n-1)!. Repeats: n!/(p!q!).
nCr = nC(n-r), and nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr.

lessons.title: Binomial theorem (JEE Main)

blocks.x: (a + b)^n = sum nCr a^(n-r) b^r. General term T(r+1) = nCr a^(n-r) b^r. The middle term is the (n/2 + 1)th term for even n, and there are two middle terms for odd n. The sum of coefficients is found by x = 1, and the sum of the binomial coefficients is 2^n. The greatest coefficient is nC(n/2).
Deep dive: expansion and general term

(a + b)^n = nC0 a^n + nC1 a^(n-1) b + ... + nCn b^n, with n + 1 terms for a positive integer n. The general term T(r+1) = nCr a^(n - r) b^r. The r-th term from the end of (a + b)^n is the (n - r + 2)-th term from the beginning. Special cases: (1 + x)^n = sum nCr x^r, (1 - x)^n = sum (-1)^r nCr x^r. Pascal triangle gives the coefficients: the row for n = 5 is 1 5 10 10 5 1.
Deep dive: middle term, greatest term and sums

If n is even there is one middle term, T(n/2 + 1); if n is odd there are two, T((n + 1)/2) and T((n + 3)/2). The greatest binomial coefficient is nC(n/2) for even n and nC((n - 1)/2) = nC((n + 1)/2) for odd n. Putting x = 1 gives the sum of coefficients 2^n; x = -1 gives C0 - C1 + C2 - ... = 0; so the sum of even-indexed coefficients equals the sum of odd-indexed ones = 2^(n - 1). Identities: C0^2 + C1^2 + ... + Cn^2 = 2nCn; C1 + 2 C2 + ... + n Cn = n 2^(n - 1). Greatest term in (1 + x)^n: find the largest r with (n - r + 1)/r x > 1.
Deep dive: independent term, remainders and approximations

The term independent of x in (x^a + 1/x^b)^n: set the power a (n - r) - b r = 0 and solve for r. The coefficient of x^k: solve a(n - r) - b r = k. Remainder problems: express the number as (1 + multiple)^n and use binomial expansion: e.g. 7^100 mod 5 using (5 + 2)... To approximate: (1 + x)^n is approximately 1 + n x when x is small. For negative or fractional index (JEE Main uses |x| < 1): (1 + x)^n = 1 + n x + n(n - 1)/2! x^2 + ...

lessons.title: Sequences and series (JEE Main)

blocks.x: AP: a_n = a + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n - 1) d). GP: a_n = a r^(n - 1), S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1), S_infinity = a/(1 - r) for |r| < 1. HP: reciprocals form an AP. AM >= GM >= HM, with AM = (a + b)/2, GM = sqrt(ab), HM = 2ab/(a + b).
Deep dive: arithmetic progression

An AP has a constant common difference d: a, a + d, a + 2d, ... The n-th term a_n = a + (n - 1) d and the sum of n terms S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n - 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l) where l is the last term. If three numbers are in AP, take them as a - d, a, a + d; four as a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d. The n-th term in terms of the sum: a_n = S_n - S_(n - 1). Arithmetic mean of a and b: (a + b)/2; n arithmetic means between a and b have common difference (b - a)/(n + 1). Useful sums: sum of the first n natural numbers n(n + 1)/2, squares n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, cubes [n(n + 1)/2]^2.
Deep dive: geometric and harmonic progressions

GP: a, ar, ar^2, ...; a_n = a r^(n - 1); S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1) (r != 1); S_infinity = a/(1 - r) when |r| < 1. Three numbers in GP: a/r, a, ar. n geometric means between a and b have common ratio (b/a)^(1/(n + 1)); their product is (ab)^(n/2). HP: a sequence whose reciprocals are in AP; its n-th term is 1/(a + (n - 1) d). 🔑

Big idea

  • AP: a_n = a + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n - 1) d)
  • GP: a_n = a r^(n - 1), S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1), S_infinity = a/(1 - r) for |r| < 1
  • HP: reciprocals form an AP
  • AM >= GM >= HM, with AM = (a + b)/2, GM = sqrt(ab), HM = 2ab/(a + b)
📌

Arithmetic progression

  • An AP has a constant common difference d: a, a + d, a + 2d,
  • The n-th term a_n = a + (n - 1) d and the sum of n terms S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n - 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l) where l is the last term
  • If three numbers are in AP, take them as a - d, a, a + d
  • Four as a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d
Read the full explanation

An AP has a constant common difference d: a, a + d, a + 2d, ... The n-th term a_n = a + (n - 1) d and the sum of n terms S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n - 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l) where l is the last term. If three numbers are in AP, take them as a - d, a, a + d; four as a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d. The n-th term in terms of the sum: a_n = S_n - S_(n - 1). Arithmetic mean of a and b: (a + b)/2; n arithmetic means between a and b have common difference (b - a)/(n + 1). Useful sums: sum of the first n natural numbers n(n + 1)/2, squares n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, cubes [n(n + 1)/2]^2.

  • A_n = a r^(n - 1)
  • S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1) (r != 1)
  • S_infinity = a/(1 - r) when |r| < 1

blocks.x: Standard limits: sin x/x -> 1, (e^x - 1)/x -> 1, (1 + 1/n)^n -> e, (a^x - 1)/x -> ln a. L Hopital: if f/g is 0/0 or infinity/infinity then lim f/g = lim f'/g'. Integration: integral x^n = x^(n+1)/(n+1), by parts, substitution, partial fractions. Definite integrals use the fundamental theorem and properties such as integral_0^a f(x) dx = integral_0^a f(a - x) dx.
Deep dive: limits and continuity

A limit exists at a if the left and right limits are equal. Standard limits: lim sin x/x = 1; lim tan x/x = 1; lim (1 - cos x)/x^2 = 1/2; lim (e^x - 1)/x = 1; lim (a^x - 1)/x = ln a; lim ln (1 + x)/x = 1; lim (1 + x)^(1/x) = e; lim ((1 + x)^n - 1)/x = n; lim (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n - 1). For indeterminate forms 0/0 or infinity/infinity use L Hopital rule, factorisation, rationalisation or series. For infinity - infinity combine the terms; for 1^infinity use lim (1 + f)^(g) = e^(lim f g). Squeeze theorem: if f <= g <= h and the outer limits are equal, g has the same limit. A function is continuous at a if the limit equals f(a); differentiable implies continuous.
Deep dive: differentiation and applications

Derivatives: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1), (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = -sin x, (tan x)' = sec^2 x, (e^x)' = e^x, (a^x)' = a^x ln a, (ln x)' = 1/x, (sin^-1 x)' = 1/sqrt (1 - x^2), (tan^-1 x)' = 1/(1 + x^2). Rules: product, quotient, chain; logarithmic differentiation for x^x type; parametric dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Tangent slope = f'(a); normal slope = -1/f'(a). Maxima and minima: f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0 gives a local maximum. Mean value theorem: f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). Rolle theorem needs f(a) = f(b).
Deep dive: integration techniques

Standard: integral x^n = x^(n+1)/(n + 1), integral 1/x = ln |x|, integral e^x = e^x, integral sin x = -cos x, integral cos x = sin x, integral sec^2 x = tan x, integral 1/(1 + x^2) = tan^-1 x, integral 1/sqrt (1 - x^2) = sin^-1 x. Substitution u = g(x); by parts integral u v = u integral v - integral (u' integral v) with ILATE order; partial fractions for rational functions; integral e^x (f + f') = e^x f. Definite integral properties: integral_a^b f = integral_a^b f(a + b - x); integral_0^a f(x) = integral_0^a f(a - x); integral_(-a)^a f = 2 integral_0^a f if even and 0 if odd; for periodic f with period T, integral_0^(nT) f = n integral_0^T f. Area between curves = integral (upper - lower) dx; area under y = f(x) from a to b = integral_a^b f.

🔑

Big idea

  • Standard limits: sin x/x -> 1, (e^x - 1)/x -> 1, (1 + 1/n)^n -> e, (a^x - 1)/x -> ln a
  • L Hopital: if f/g is 0/0 or infinity/infinity then lim f/g = lim f'/g'

Standard limits: sin x/x -> 1, (e^x - 1)/x -> 1, (1 + 1/n)^n -> e, (a^x - 1)/x -> ln a. L Hopital: if f/g is 0/0 or infinity/infinity then lim f/g = lim f'/g'. Integration: integral x^n = x^(n+1)/(n+1), by parts, substitution, partial fractions. Definite integrals use the fundamental theorem and properties such as integral_0^a f(x) dx = integral_0^a f(a - x) dx.

📌

Limits and continuity

  • A limit exists at a if the left and right limits are equal
  • Standard limits: lim sin x/x = 1
  • Lim tan x/x = 1
  • Lim (1 - cos x)/x2 = 1/2
Read the full explanation

A limit exists at a if the left and right limits are equal. Standard limits: lim sin x/x = 1; lim tan x/x = 1; lim (1 - cos x)/x^2 = 1/2; lim (e^x - 1)/x = 1; lim (a^x - 1)/x = ln a; lim ln (1 + x)/x = 1; lim (1 + x)^(1/x) = e; lim ((1 + x)^n - 1)/x = n; lim (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n - 1). For indeterminate forms 0/0 or infinity/infinity use L Hopital rule, factorisation, rationalisation or series. For infinity - infinity combine the terms; for 1^infinity use lim (1 + f)^(g) = e^(lim f g). Squeeze theorem: if f <= g <= h and the outer limits are equal, g has the same limit. A function is continuous at a if the limit equals f(a); differentiable implies continuous.

💡

Differentiation and applications

  • Derivatives: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1), (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = -sin x, (tan x)' = sec2 x, (e^x)' = e^x, (a^x)' = a^x ln a, (ln x)' = 1/x, (sin-1 x)'…
  • Rules: product, quotient, chain
  • Logarithmic differentiation for x^x type
  • Parametric dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
Read the full explanation

Derivatives: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1), (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = -sin x, (tan x)' = sec^2 x, (e^x)' = e^x, (a^x)' = a^x ln a, (ln x)' = 1/x, (sin^-1 x)' = 1/sqrt (1 - x^2), (tan^-1 x)' = 1/(1 + x^2). Rules: product, quotient, chain; logarithmic differentiation for x^x type; parametric dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Tangent slope = f'(a); normal slope = -1/f'(a). Maxima and minima: f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0 gives a local maximum. Mean value theorem: f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). Rolle theorem needs f(a) = f(b).

🌟

Integration techniques

  • Standard: integral x^n = x^(n+1)/(n + 1), integral 1/x = ln |x|, integral e^x = e^x, integral sin x = -cos x, integral cos x = sin x, integral sec2…
  • Substitution u = g(x)
  • By parts integral u v = u integral v - integral (u' integral v) with ILATE order
  • Partial fractions for rational functions
Read the full explanation

Standard: integral x^n = x^(n+1)/(n + 1), integral 1/x = ln |x|, integral e^x = e^x, integral sin x = -cos x, integral cos x = sin x, integral sec^2 x = tan x, integral 1/(1 + x^2) = tan^-1 x, integral 1/sqrt (1 - x^2) = sin^-1 x. Substitution u = g(x); by parts integral u v = u integral v - integral (u' integral v) with ILATE order; partial fractions for rational functions; integral e^x (f + f') = e^x f. Definite integral properties: integral_a^b f = integral_a^b f(a + b - x); integral_0^a f(x) = integral_0^a f(a - x); integral_(-a)^a f = 2 integral_0^a f if even and 0 if odd; for periodic f with period T, integral_0^(nT) f = n integral_0^T f. Area between curves = integral (upper - lower) dx; area under y = f(x) from a to b = integral_a^b f.

lessons.title: JEE Main: kinematics and laws of motion
yt: jee main kinematics laws of motion

blocks.x: Equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2) a t^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as; projectile range R = u^2 sin 2 theta/g, maximum height H = u^2 sin^2 theta/(2g), time of flight T = 2 u sin theta/g. Newton second law F = ma, friction f = mu N, circular motion a = v^2/r, banking tan theta = v^2/(r g), and conservation of momentum in collisions.
Deep dive: motion in a straight line and projectiles

For constant acceleration use v = u + a t, s = u t + (1/2) a t^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s, and the distance in the nth second s_n = u + a (2n - 1)/2. For free fall use a = g downward. Area under a v-t graph is displacement; slope of an x-t graph is velocity. Relative motion: v_AB = v_A - v_B; river-boat problems resolve velocities along and across the stream (minimum time when the boat heads straight across; shortest path when it heads upstream at sin theta = v_r/v_b). Projectile motion from the ground: horizontal speed u cos theta constant, vertical speed u sin theta - g t; time of flight T = 2 u sin theta/g; maximum height H = u^2 sin^2 theta/(2 g); range R = u^2 sin 2 theta/g, maximum at 45 degrees; ranges at theta and (90 - theta) are equal; H = R tan theta/4 at... in general R/H = 4/tan theta. The trajectory y = x tan theta - g x^2/(2 u^2 cos^2 theta) is a parabola.
Deep dive: Newton's laws, friction and circular motion

Newton second law F_net = m a; weight apparent in a lift: N = m (g + a) accelerating up and m (g - a) accelerating down. For connected bodies (Atwood machine) a = (m1 - m2) g/(m1 + m2) and tension T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2). Friction: static f <= mu_s N, kinetic f = mu_k N; on an incline the body slides when tan theta > mu_s, and a = g (sin theta - mu cos theta). Angle of repose = tan^-1 mu. Circular motion: centripetal acceleration a = v^2/r = omega^2 r; a car on a level road is safe when v <= sqrt (mu r g); on a banked road with no friction tan theta = v^2/(r g); at the top of a vertical circle the minimum speed is sqrt (g r) and at the bottom sqrt (5 g r) to complete the circle on a string.
Deep dive: momentum and collisions

Linear momentum p = m v; impulse J = F Dt = Dp. In an isolated system momentum is conserved. In a perfectly elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved; for masses m1 and m2 with m2 at rest, v1 = (m1 - m2) u/(m1 + m2) and v2 = 2 m1 u/(m1 + m2). Coefficient of restitution e = (v2 - v1)/(u1 - u2): e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic (bodies stick). Rocket propulsion: thrust = u (dm/dt). For a variable mass system use F = d(mv)/dt. Centre of mass x_cm = sum m_i x_i / sum m_i; it moves as if all external forces act on the total mass.

Visual lesson

JEE Main: kinematics and laws of motion

Equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2) a t^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Motion in a straight line…›3Newton's laws, friction and…›4Momentum and collisions
🔑

Big idea

  • Equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2) a t2, v2 = u2 + 2as
  • Projectile range R = u2 sin 2 theta/g, maximum height H = u2 sin2 theta/(2g), time of flight T = 2 u sin theta/g
  • Newton second law F = ma, friction f = mu N, circular motion a = v2/r, banking tan theta = v2/(r g), and conservation of momentum in collisions
🚀

Motion in a straight line and projectiles

  • For constant acceleration use v = u + a t, s = u t + (1/2) a t2, v2 = u2 + 2 a s, and the distance in the nth second s_n = u + a (2n - 1)/2
  • For free fall use a = g downward
  • Area under a v-t graph is displacement
  • Slope of an x-t graph is velocity
Read the full explanation

For constant acceleration use v = u + a t, s = u t + (1/2) a t^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s, and the distance in the nth second s_n = u + a (2n - 1)/2. For free fall use a = g downward. Area under a v-t graph is displacement; slope of an x-t graph is velocity. Relative motion: v_AB = v_A - v_B; river-boat problems resolve velocities along and across the stream (minimum time when the boat heads straight across; shortest path when it heads upstream at sin theta = v_r/v_b). Projectile motion from the ground: horizontal speed u cos theta constant, vertical speed u sin theta - g t; time of flight T = 2 u sin theta/g; maximum height H = u^2 sin^2 theta/(2 g); range R = u^2 sin 2 theta/g, maximum at 45 degrees; ranges at theta and (90 - theta) are equal; H = R tan theta/4 at... in general R/H = 4/tan theta. The trajectory y = x tan theta - g x^2/(2 u^2 cos^2 theta) is a parabola.

⚖️

Newton's laws, friction and circular motion

  • Newton second law F_net = m a
  • Weight apparent in a lift: N = m (g + a) accelerating up and m (g - a) accelerating down
  • For connected bodies (Atwood machine) a = (m1 - m2) g/(m1 + m2) and tension T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2)
  • Friction: static f <= mu_s N, kinetic f = mu_k N
Read the full explanation

Newton second law F_net = m a; weight apparent in a lift: N = m (g + a) accelerating up and m (g - a) accelerating down. For connected bodies (Atwood machine) a = (m1 - m2) g/(m1 + m2) and tension T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2). Friction: static f <= mu_s N, kinetic f = mu_k N; on an incline the body slides when tan theta > mu_s, and a = g (sin theta - mu cos theta). Angle of repose = tan^-1 mu. Circular motion: centripetal acceleration a = v^2/r = omega^2 r; a car on a level road is safe when v <= sqrt (mu r g); on a banked road with no friction tan theta = v^2/(r g); at the top of a vertical circle the minimum speed is sqrt (g r) and at the bottom sqrt (5 g r) to complete the circle on a string.

🌟

Momentum and collisions

  • Linear momentum p = m v
  • Impulse J = F Dt = Dp
  • In an isolated system momentum is conserved
  • In a perfectly elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved
Read the full explanation

Linear momentum p = m v; impulse J = F Dt = Dp. In an isolated system momentum is conserved. In a perfectly elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved; for masses m1 and m2 with m2 at rest, v1 = (m1 - m2) u/(m1 + m2) and v2 = 2 m1 u/(m1 + m2). Coefficient of restitution e = (v2 - v1)/(u1 - u2): e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic (bodies stick). Rocket propulsion: thrust = u (dm/dt). For a variable mass system use F = d(mv)/dt. Centre of mass x_cm = sum m_i x_i / sum m_i; it moves as if all external forces act on the total mass.

blocks.x: Coulomb force F = k q1 q2/r^2; field E = k q/r^2; potential V = k q/r; potential energy U = k q1 q2/r. Gauss law: flux = q_enc/e0 giving E = sigma/e0 near a conductor. Capacitance C = e0 A/d, energy U = (1/2) C V^2; series 1/C = sum 1/Ci, parallel C = sum Ci; a dielectric multiplies C by K.
Deep dive: charges, fields and potential

Coulomb law F = k q1 q2/r^2 with k = 1/(4 pi e0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2; the force is along the line joining the charges (repulsive for like charges). Electric field E = F/q = k Q/r^2 for a point charge. Dipole of moment p = q (2a): axial field 2 k p/r^3, equatorial field k p/r^3, torque p E sin theta, potential energy -p E cos theta. Potential V = k Q/r; potential difference V_AB = -integral E . dl; E = -dV/dr. Potential energy of two charges U = k q1 q2/r; of a system of charges it is the sum over pairs. Work done in moving a charge q through potential difference V is q V.
Deep dive: Gauss law and conductors

Gauss law: closed-surface flux = q_enc/e0. Field of an infinite line charge E = lambda/(2 pi e0 r); of an infinite sheet sigma/(2 e0); just outside a conductor sigma/e0; inside a conductor zero. For a uniformly charged spherical shell: E = 0 inside, k Q/r^2 outside; for a solid insulating sphere E = k Q r/R^3 inside. All the charge of a conductor resides on its outer surface, and the surface is an equipotential. The potential of a shell is k Q/R on and inside the surface. Electrostatic energy density u = (1/2) e0 E^2.
Deep dive: capacitors

Capacitance C = Q/V; parallel plate C = e0 A/d; with a dielectric of constant K filling the gap C = K e0 A/d; a conducting slab of thickness t increases C to e0 A/(d - t); a dielectric slab gives C = e0 A/(d - t + t/K). Energy stored U = (1/2) C V^2 = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2) Q V. Series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 (same charge); parallel: C = C1 + C2 (same voltage). Two capacitors C1 (charged to V1) and C2 (uncharged) joined together share charge: common potential V = C1 V1/(C1 + C2) and energy loss (1/2) C1 C2 V1^2/(C1 + C2). If a battery stays connected V is constant; if disconnected Q is constant when the plate separation or dielectric changes.

blocks.x: Photoelectric effect: K_max = h f - phi, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s. de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/(m v). Bohr model for hydrogen: E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV, r_n = 0.529 n^2 angstrom, v_n = 2.19 x 10^6/n m/s; spectral lines 1/lambda = R (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2). Radioactivity N = N0 e^(-lambda t), half-life T = 0.693/lambda; mass defect gives binding energy E = Dm c^2 = 931.5 Dm (MeV).
Deep dive: photoelectric effect and matter waves

Einstein equation: h f = phi + K_max, where phi = h f_0 is the work function and f_0 the threshold frequency. K_max = e V_s (stopping potential). The photocurrent is proportional to intensity (for f > f_0); K_max depends only on f, not on intensity. Photon energy E = h f = h c/lambda = 1240/lambda(nm) eV; momentum p = h/lambda. de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v) = h/sqrt (2 m K); for an electron accelerated through V volts, lambda = 12.27/sqrt (V) angstrom; for a particle in thermal equilibrium lambda = h/sqrt (3 m k T). Davisson-Germer experiment confirmed electron diffraction.
Deep dive: atoms and spectra

Rutherford alpha scattering shows a small dense nucleus of radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 fm. Bohr postulates: angular momentum m v r = n h/(2 pi); energy E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV; radius r_n = 0.529 n^2/Z angstrom; speed v_n = 2.19 x 10^6 Z/n m/s; time period T_n proportional to n^3/Z^2. Emitted photon energy for a transition n2 -> n1: E = 13.6 Z^2 (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) eV, with 1/lambda = R Z^2 (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2), R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1. Series: Lyman (n1 = 1, UV), Balmer (n1 = 2, visible), Paschen (n1 = 3, IR), Brackett (n1 = 4), Pfund (n1 = 5). Number of lines for transitions from the nth level to the ground state is n(n - 1)/2. Ionisation energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV.
Deep dive: nuclei and radioactivity

Mass number A, atomic number Z; neutrons N = A - Z. Mass defect Dm = Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n - M; binding energy B = Dm x 931.5 MeV; binding energy per nucleon peaks near A = 56 (about 8.8 MeV) which explains fission of heavy and fusion of light nuclei. Radioactive decay law: N = N0 e^(-lambda t); half-life T = ln 2/lambda = 0.693/lambda; mean life tau = 1/lambda = 1.44 T; activity A = lambda N, SI unit becquerel (1 curie = 3.7 x 10^10 Bq). After n half-lives N = N0/2^n. Alpha decay reduces A by 4 and Z by 2; beta-minus raises Z by 1; gamma changes neither. Q value of a reaction = (mass of reactants - mass of products) x 931.5 MeV. Fission of U-235 releases about 200 MeV; fusion powers stars.

lessons.title: NEET Biology: human physiology, genetics and cell fact bank

blocks.x: High-yield NCERT facts for NEET Biology: vitamins and deficiency diseases, endocrine glands and hormones, cell organelles and their functions, and Mendelian genetics with worked crosses (monohybrid 3:1 and 1:2:1, dihybrid 9:3:3:1, test cross 1:1, incomplete dominance, ABO blood groups).
Deep dive: vitamins and deficiency diseases

Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts. Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K (stored in the body); water-soluble ones are B-complex and C (not stored, need regular intake). Vitamin A (retinol) deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia; B1 (thiamine) beri-beri; B2 (riboflavin) cheilosis and glossitis; B3 (niacin) pellagra; B6 (pyridoxine) anaemia and convulsions; B9 (folic acid) megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects; B12 (cyanocobalamin) pernicious anaemia (needs intrinsic factor from the stomach); C (ascorbic acid) scurvy; D rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; E infertility and fragile RBCs; K delayed blood clotting. Provitamin forms: beta-carotene gives vitamin A; 7-dehydrocholesterol gives vitamin D in skin with sunlight.
Deep dive: endocrine system

Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands into the blood. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary: anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) secretes growth hormone, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH; the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) stores and releases oxytocin and ADH made in the hypothalamus. Thyroid: thyroxine (T4, T3) controls basal metabolic rate (deficiency causes goitre, cretinism in children, myxoedema in adults; excess causes Graves disease); calcitonin lowers blood calcium. Parathyroid: PTH raises blood calcium. Pancreas islets: insulin (beta cells) lowers glucose, glucagon (alpha cells) raises it; insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus. Adrenal medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline (emergency hormones); adrenal cortex: cortisol and aldosterone. Gonads: testosterone (Leydig cells), oestrogen and progesterone. Gastrointestinal hormones: gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP.
Deep dive: Mendelian genetics

Mendel studied pea plants (Pisum sativum) and gave three laws: dominance, segregation (law of purity of gametes) and independent assortment. Monohybrid cross Tt x Tt gives phenotypic ratio 3:1 and genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (TT : Tt : tt). A test cross (unknown x homozygous recessive) gives 1:1 if the unknown is heterozygous and all dominant if homozygous. A dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy gives 9:3:3:1 with 16 combinations. Incomplete dominance (snapdragon, Mirabilis) gives 1:2:1 for both genotype and phenotype in F2; co-dominance (ABO blood group IA IB) shows both alleles. ABO: alleles IA, IB (dominant over i), genotypes: A = IAIA or IAi, B = IBIB or IBi, AB = IAIB, O = ii. A heterozygote makes two types of gametes; an individual heterozygous for n genes makes 2^n gametes. Sex determination in humans: XX female and XY male (XO in grasshoppers, ZW in birds with female heterogametic).

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };
struct Node *push(struct Node *head, int x) {
    struct Node *n = malloc(sizeof *n); n->data = x; n->next = head; return n;
}
struct Node *reverse(struct Node *h) {
    struct Node *prev = NULL;
    while (h) { struct Node *nx = h->next; h->next = prev; prev = h; h = nx; }
    return prev;
}
int main(void) {
    struct Node *h = NULL;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) h = push(h, i);      /* 4 3 2 1 */
    h = reverse(h);                                    /* 1 2 3 4 */
    for (struct Node *p = h; p; p = p->next) printf("%d ", p->data);
    printf("\n"); return 0;
}
Read the full explanation

An array stores elements of the same type in contiguous memory. Access by index is O(1); insertion or deletion in the middle is O(n) because elements must shift. A linked list stores each element in a node holding data and a pointer to the next node. Insertion at the head is O(1); access by position is O(n).

Output: 1 2 3 4. Always check that malloc did not return NULL and free() every node when done to avoid memory leaks.

Traversals

  • Inorder (left, root, right): visits a BST in sorted order.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
typedef struct N { int k; struct N *l, *r; } N;
N *ins(N *t, int k) {
    if (!t) { t = calloc(1, sizeof *t); t->k = k; return t; }
    if (k < t->k) t->l = ins(t->l, k); else t->r = ins(t->r, k);
    return t;
}
void in(N *t)  { if (t) { in(t->l);  printf("%d ", t->k); in(t->r); } }
void pre(N *t) { if (t) { printf("%d ", t->k); pre(t->l); pre(t->r); } }
void post(N *t){ if (t) { post(t->l); post(t->r); printf("%d ", t->k); } }
int main(void) {
    int a[] = {50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80}; N *r = NULL;
    for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) r = ins(r, a[i]);
    in(r); printf("\n"); pre(r); printf("\n"); post(r); printf("\n"); return 0;
}
🎯 Remember Inserting sorted data into a plain BST makes a linked list (O(n) operations).

#include <stdio.h>
int bsearch_(int a[], int n, int x) {
    int lo = 0, hi = n - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) { int m = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (a[m] == x) return m; if (a[m] < x) lo = m + 1; else hi = m - 1; }
    return -1;
}
int main(void) {
    int a[] = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11};
    printf("%d %d\n", bsearch_(a, 6, 7), bsearch_(a, 6, 4));   /* 3 -1 */
    return 0;
}
🎯 Remember Choose merge sort when stability and guaranteed O(n log n) matter.

lessons.title: Number systems and Boolean algebra

blocks.x: **Binary, octal, hexadecimal:** 1011 (binary) = 8 + 2 + 1 = **11**; 255 = 0xFF = 11111111. **Two's complement** represents negative numbers: invert the bits and add 1. -5 in 8 bits: 5 = 00000101, invert 11111010, add 1 = **11111011**. 8-bit range is -128 to +127. Addition ignores the carry out; overflow occurs if two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign. **Boolean algebra laws:** identity, null, idempotent (A + A = A), complement (A + A' = 1), De Morgan: (A + B)' = A' B' and (AB)' = A' + B'; absorption A + AB = A. NAND and NOR are universal gates. XOR: 1010 XOR 0110 = **1100** (12). Half adder: sum = A XOR B, carry = A AND B. Full adder adds a carry-in. **K-map** simplifies expressions: group adjacent 1s in powers of two.

lessons.title: Cache memory and pipelining

blocks.x: **Memory hierarchy:** registers, cache, main memory, disk: faster but smaller towards the top. **Locality of reference** (temporal and spatial) makes caches effective. **Average memory access time (AMAT)** = h x t_cache + (1 - h) x t_memory, where h is the hit ratio (simple model). For h = 0.9, t_cache = 10 ns and t_memory = 100 ns: AMAT = 9 + 10 = **19 ns**. **Mapping:** direct (one possible line), fully associative (any line), set-associative (a set of lines). Replacement: LRU, FIFO, random. Write policies: write-through, write-back. **Pipelining** overlaps instruction stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back). For k stages and n instructions: time = (k + n - 1) cycles; speed-up over non-pipelined = n k / (k + n - 1). For k = 5, n = 100: 500/104 = **4.81**, approaching k for large n. **Hazards:** structural, data (forwarding, stalls), control (branch prediction).
Hindi saransh
AMAT = h x tc + (1 - h) x tm. Pipeline speedup = nk/(k + n - 1).
Speed-up can never exceed the number of stages.

blocks.x: **Laplace transform:** F(s) = integral from 0 to infinity of f(t) e^(-st) dt. Standard pairs: L{1} = 1/s; L{t} = **1/s^2**; L{e^(at)} = **1/(s - a)**; L{sin at} = a/(s^2 + a^2); L{cos at} = s/(s^2 + a^2). Derivative: L{f'} = s F(s) - f(0). minutes

Big idea

  • Four pillars: encapsulation (data hidden behind methods), abstraction (hide complexity), inheritance (reuse a base class), polymorphism (one…
  • Compile-time polymorphism: function and operator overloading
  • Run-time polymorphism: virtual functions with a base-class pointer
  • Output: 12 and 12.5664
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
class Shape {
public:
    virtual double area() const = 0;          // abstract
    virtual ~Shape() {}
};
class Rect : public Shape {
    double w, h;
public:
    Rect(double w, double h) : w(w), h(h) {}
    double area() const override { return w * h; }
};
class Circle : public Shape {
    double r;
public:
    Circle(double r) : r(r) {}
    double area() const override { return 3.14159 * r * r; }
};
int main() {
    Shape *s[] = { new Rect(3, 4), new Circle(2) };
    for (Shape *p : s) cout << p->area() << endl;   // 12 and 12.5664
    for (Shape *p : s) delete p;
}
Read the full explanation

Four pillars of OOP

x: **Encapsulation:** private fields with public getters/setters.
**Inheritance:** `class Dog extends Animal` reuses code. Java allows single inheritance of classes, but many interfaces.
**Polymorphism:** one call, many forms. *Overloading* (same name, different parameters, compile time) and *overriding* (subclass redefines a method, run time).
**Abstraction:** `abstract` classes and `interface`s hide details and define contracts.

An **exception** is an event that disrupts normal flow. Hierarchy: `Throwable` → `Error` (not meant to be caught, e.g. `OutOfMemoryError`) and `Exception`.

x: **Checked** exceptions (`IOException`, `SQLException`) must be handled or declared with `throws`.

qa.q: Difference between overloading and overriding?
qa.a: Overloading uses the same method name with different parameters in one class and is resolved at compile time. Overriding redefines a superclass method in a subclass with the same signature and is resolved at run time.

qa.q: Checked versus unchecked exceptions?
qa.a: Checked exceptions are verified by the compiler and must be caught or declared; unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException) need not be.

qa.q: What does finally do?
qa.a: It contains code that runs whether or not an exception occurs, usually releasing resources.

qa.q: Why is String immutable?
qa.a: Immutability makes strings safe to share, cache (string pool), use as hash keys and in security-sensitive code.

qa.q: Difference between == and equals() on Strings?
qa.a: == compares object references; equals() compares the character contents.

problems.a: Encapsulation: private fields with public getters and setters. Inheritance: class Dog extends Animal. Polymorphism: a method overridden in a subclass and called through an Animal reference. Abstraction: an abstract class or interface that hides the details, such as interface Shape with area().

problems.q: What is printed by this code, and in what order? try { int x = 10 / 0; } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("A"); } finally { System.out.println("F"); } System.out.println("E");
problems.a: Output: A, then F, then E (each on its own line). The division throws an ArithmeticException, the catch block prints A, the finally block always runs and prints F, and since the exception was handled the program continues and prints E.

problems.q: For String s1 = "hi", s2 = "hi", s3 = new String("hi"); give the values of s1 == s2, s1 == s3, s1.equals(s3) and s1 == s3.intern(). Why are strings immutable and when should StringBuilder be used?
problems.a:
s1 == s2 is true (same pooled literal). s1 == s3 is false (new creates a separate object on the heap). s1.equals(s3) is true (same characters). s1 == s3.intern() is true (intern returns the pooled string).
Strings are immutable for security, thread safety, caching of hash codes and the string pool. Use StringBuilder when building strings in loops, because each concatenation of a String creates a new object.

public class Shapes {
    static abstract class Shape {
        abstract double area();
        public String toString() { return getClass().getSimpleName() + " area=" + String.format("%.2f", area()); }
    }
    static class Circle extends Shape {
        double r; Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
        double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
    }
    static class Rect extends Shape {
        double w, h; Rect(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
        double area() { return w * h; }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Rect(3, 4) };
        for (Shape s : shapes) System.out.println(s);
    }
}

public class ExDemo {
    static class LowBalance extends Exception {
        LowBalance(String m) { super(m); }
    }
    static void withdraw(int bal, int amt) throws LowBalance {
        if (amt > bal) throw new LowBalance("need " + (amt - bal) + " more");
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            withdraw(100, 150);
        } catch (LowBalance e) {
            System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally always runs");
        }
        try { int x = 5 / 0; } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
    }
}

Iterating
Enhanced for, `Iterator` (supports `remove()`), `forEach` with lambda. Modifying a list while looping with enhanced for throws `ConcurrentModificationException` — use the iterator's `remove`.
equals() and hashCode()
`HashMap`/`HashSet` use `hashCode()` to choose a bucket and `equals()` to compare. If two objects are equal they **must** have the same hash code. Override both together.
Comparable and Comparator

blocks.x: Generics
Generics give **compile-time type safety** and remove casts.
Output:

true
false

Wildcards: `List<?>` (unknown), `List<? extends Number>` (read-only producer), `List<? super Integer>` (consumer). Generics use **type erasure**: type information is removed at run time. Primitives are not allowed (`List<int>` is illegal; use `Integer` with autoboxing).
Hindi saransh
List में क्रम और duplicates चलते हैं, Set में duplicates नहीं, Map में key-value जोड़े होते हैं। Generics से type-safety मिलती है।
HashMap for speed, TreeMap for sorted keys, LinkedHashMap for insertion order.

qa.q: Difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
qa.a: ArrayList is backed by an array with fast random access but slow insertion in the middle. LinkedList is a doubly linked list with fast insertion and deletion at known positions but slow indexed access.

qa.q: How does HashMap work?
qa.a: It computes the key's hashCode to find a bucket, then uses equals() to find the exact key within the bucket. Collisions are chained in a list or tree.

qa.q: Why override hashCode when overriding equals?
qa.a: Equal objects must produce the same hash code, otherwise hash-based collections cannot find them.

qa.q: Difference between Comparable and Comparator?
qa.a: Comparable defines one natural ordering inside the class via compareTo; a Comparator defines a separate ordering and lets you have many.

qa.q: What is type erasure?
qa.a: The compiler removes generic type information after checking, so at run time List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class.

problems.q: Differentiate between List, Set and Map with one implementation of each.
problems.a: List: ordered, allows duplicates, access by index (ArrayList). Set: no duplicates (HashSet, no order; TreeSet, sorted). Map: stores key-value pairs with unique keys (HashMap).

problems.q: Write code to count the words of "to be or not to be" with a Map and show the result when a TreeMap is used.
problems.a:
Map<String,Integer> m = new TreeMap<>(); for (String w : "to be or not to be".split(" ")) m.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(m);
Output: {be=2, not=1, or=1, to=2}. TreeMap keeps keys sorted; a HashMap gives the same counts in no guaranteed order.

problems.q: Write a generic method that returns the larger of two values and explain the bound. Why is List<Integer> not a List<Number>, and what does List<? extends Number> allow?

public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } The bound T extends Comparable<T> guarantees compareTo exists.

Functional interface and lambda

A **functional interface** has exactly one abstract method (`Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Function<T,R>`, `Predicate<T>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`). A **lambda** `(params) -> expression` implements it concisely. A **method reference** `String::length` is shorthand.
Stream API

qa.q: What is a functional interface?
qa.a: An interface with exactly one abstract method, which can be implemented by a lambda expression.

qa.q: Difference between intermediate and terminal operations?
qa.a: Intermediate operations such as filter and map return a new stream and are lazy. Terminal operations such as collect or count trigger execution and end the stream.

problems.q: Use streams to find the sum of the squares of the even numbers from 1 to 10. What is the result?

problems.q: Group the words apple, fig, kiwi, plum, pear by length using streams and give the result. What is the difference between intermediate and terminal operations, and why is a stream lazy?

Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) return a new stream and do nothing yet; terminal operations (collect, forEach, sum) start the processing. Streams are lazy: elements flow through the whole pipeline only when a terminal operation runs, which allows short-circuiting like limit or findFirst.

blocks.x: A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process. Java lets one program run several tasks at the same time (for example downloading a file while the screen stays responsive). This lesson covers only creating threads and their life cycle.
Creating a thread

x: **Extend `Thread`** and override `run()`.
**Implement `Runnable`** and pass it to a `Thread` (preferred: the class can extend something else).
A lambda: `new Thread(() -> ...)`.

blocks.x: Call **`start()`** (not `run()`) to create a new thread of execution. Calling `run()` directly just runs the method in the current thread.
Output:

Hello from worker-1
Hello from lambda thread
main finished after joins
`join()` makes the caller wait until that thread dies; here it also keeps the output order fixed.
Life cycle states (`Thread.State`)

x: **NEW:** created, `start()` not yet called.
**RUNNABLE:** ready or running (the scheduler decides).
**BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING:** temporarily not running (for example `sleep(ms)` gives TIMED_WAITING).
**TERMINATED:** `run()` finished.

blocks.x: A terminated thread cannot be restarted.
Useful methods
`sleep(ms)`, `join()`, `isAlive()`, `getName()`, `setPriority(1–10)`, `Thread.currentThread()`, `interrupt()`. Daemon threads (`setDaemon(true)`) do not keep the JVM alive.
Thread priority
Hints to the scheduler (`MIN_PRIORITY` 1, `NORM_PRIORITY` 5, `MAX_PRIORITY` 10). The actual order is not guaranteed.
Hindi saransh
Thread एक हल्की execution unit है। `start()` नया thread बनाता है, `run()` सिर्फ़ method call है। Life cycle: New → Runnable → (Waiting) → Terminated।
start() creates a new thread; run() alone does not.

qa.q: Why use Runnable instead of extending Thread?
qa.a: A class can extend only one class, so implementing Runnable keeps inheritance free, and it separates the task from the thread that runs it.

qa.q: What happens if you call run() instead of start()?
qa.a: The code runs in the calling thread like an ordinary method, so no new thread is created.

qa.q: Name the states in the life cycle of a thread.
qa.a: New, Runnable, Blocked, Waiting, Timed Waiting and Terminated.

qa.q: What does join() do?
qa.a: It makes the calling thread wait until the target thread has finished.

qa.q: Can a terminated thread be started again?
qa.a: No. Calling start() again throws IllegalThreadStateException.

quiz.why: start() schedules the thread to run its run() method.

problems.q: Show two ways to create a thread in Java. What is the difference between start() and run()?
problems.a:
1) class Worker extends Thread { public void run() { ... } } then new Worker().start(); 2) class Task implements Runnable { public void run() { ... } } then new Thread(new Task()).start(). Implementing Runnable is preferred because the class can still extend another class.
start() creates a new thread of execution and calls run() in it; calling run() directly just executes the method in the current thread like an ordinary method.

problems.q: A thread t prints "T". The main thread starts t, calls t.join() and then prints "M". What is the output and why? What changes without join()?
problems.a: Output: T then M. join() makes the main thread wait until t finishes, so M is always printed after T. Without join() the order is not guaranteed because both threads run independently, so M may appear before T.

problems.q: Give the state of a thread t after: new Thread(r); t.start(); during Thread.sleep(1000) inside run; after run ends. What happens if you call t.start() twice?
problems.a: After new Thread(r): NEW. After start(): RUNNABLE. While sleeping inside run: TIMED_WAITING. After run ends: TERMINATED. Calling start() a second time throws IllegalThreadStateException, because a thread can be started only once.

blocks.x: Java's `java.net` package supports network programming.
Network basics

x: **IP address** identifies a host (IPv4 such as 192.168.1.5, IPv6). **Port** (0–65535) identifies an application on that host; 80 is HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH. Ports below 1024 are well-known.
**TCP:** connection-oriented, reliable, ordered (web, email). **UDP:** connectionless, faster, may lose packets (video calls, DNS, games).
**Socket** = IP address + port: an endpoint of two-way communication.

blocks.x: Classes

x: `InetAddress`: `getByName("localhost")`, `getLocalHost()`.
`URL`/`URLConnection`/`HttpURLConnection`: fetch resources over HTTP. Newer: `java.net.http.HttpClient`.
`ServerSocket` (server), `Socket` (client), `DatagramSocket`/`DatagramPacket` (UDP).

blocks.x: TCP client-server steps
Server: create `ServerSocket(port)` → `accept()` (blocks until a client connects) → get streams → read/write → close. Client: `new Socket(host, port)` → get streams → read/write → close.
Working example (server and client in one program)
Output:
ECHO: HELLO FUTURESELF
A real server handles each client in its own thread so one slow client does not block others.
UDP in brief
The sender builds a `DatagramPacket(data, length, address, port)` and calls `send`; the receiver calls `receive` on a `DatagramSocket(port)`. There is no connection and no delivery guarantee.
URL parsing

Big idea

  • Java's java.net package supports network programming
📘

Network basics

  • IP address identifies a host (IPv4 such as 192.168.1.5, IPv6). Port (0–65535) identifies an application on that host; 80 is HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH.…
  • TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered (web, email). UDP: connectionless, faster, may lose packets (video calls, DNS, games).
  • Socket = IP address + port: an endpoint of two-way communication.
🧠

Classes

  • InetAddress: getByName("localhost"), getLocalHost().
  • URL/URLConnection/HttpURLConnection: fetch resources over HTTP. Newer: java.net.http.HttpClient.
  • ServerSocket (server), Socket (client), DatagramSocket/DatagramPacket (UDP).
🔄

TCP client-server steps

  • Server: create ServerSocket(port) → accept() (blocks until a client connects) → get streams → read/write → close
  • Client: new Socket(host, port) → get streams → read/write → close
💡

Working example (server and client in one program)

  • Output: A real server handles each client in its own thread so one slow client does not block others
import java.io.*;
import java.net.*;
public class EchoDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(0);          // 0 = any free port
        int port = server.getLocalPort();
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            try (Socket s = server.accept();
                 BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(s.getInputStream()));
                 PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(s.getOutputStream(), true)) {
                String msg = in.readLine();
                out.println("ECHO: " + msg.toUpperCase());
            } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); }
        });
        t.start();
        try (Socket c = new Socket("localhost", port);
             PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(c.getOutputStream(), true);
             BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(c.getInputStream()))) {
            out.println("hello futureself");
            System.out.println(in.readLine());
        }
        t.join(); server.close();
    }
}
ECHO: HELLO FUTURESELF
📊

UDP in brief

  • The sender builds a DatagramPacket(data, length, address, port) and calls send
  • The receiver calls receive on a DatagramSocket(port)
  • There is no connection and no delivery guarantee
🔑

URL parsing

  • New URL("https://example.com:8080/path?q=1") gives protocol https, host example.com, port 8080, path /path, query q=1
🎯 Remember TCP for reliability, UDP for speed. A socket is IP plus port.

blocks.x: **JDBC (Java Database Connectivity)** is the standard API (`java.sql`) for Java programs to talk to relational databases.
Architecture
Application → **JDBC API** → **DriverManager** → **JDBC driver** (vendor-specific JAR) → Database. The database can be changed by switching the driver and URL, with little code change.
Driver types

x: Type 1: JDBC-ODBC bridge (removed).
Type 2: native API driver.
Type 3: network protocol (middleware).
**Type 4: pure Java thin driver** (used today: MySQL Connector/J, PostgreSQL, SQLite).

blocks.x: Steps to connect

x: Add the driver JAR to the class path (modern drivers auto-register).
Open `Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);`

blocks.x: URL examples: `jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/college`, `jdbc:postgresql://localhost/college`, `jdbc:sqlite:college.db`.

x: Create `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`.
Execute: `executeQuery` (SELECT, returns `ResultSet`), `executeUpdate` (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, returns row count), `execute`.
Process the `ResultSet`: `while (rs.next()) rs.getString("name")`.
Close resources (try-with-resources).

blocks.x: Statement types

x: `Statement`: plain SQL, vulnerable to **SQL injection**.
`PreparedStatement`: precompiled with `?` placeholders; safe and faster for repeated use.
`CallableStatement`: calls stored procedures.

blocks.x: CRUD example (needs a database driver, so shown without main)
Never hard-code real passwords; read them from configuration or environment.
SQL injection
With string concatenation `"... WHERE name='" + input + "'"` the input `' OR '1'='1` returns every row. With `PreparedStatement`, the input is treated only as data.
Transactions
`con.setAutoCommit(false); ... con.commit();` and `con.rollback()` on error, giving the ACID behaviour of the DBMS course. **Batch updates** (`addBatch`, `executeBatch`) speed up many inserts.
ResultSet types
Default is forward-only and read-only; scrollable and updatable result sets can be requested. `ResultSetMetaData` gives column names and types.
Connection pooling
Opening a connection is expensive; production systems use a pool (HikariCP, DBCP) that reuses connections.

JDBC से Java program database से जुड़ता है: driver load → connection → PreparedStatement → execute → ResultSet पढ़ना → close। SQL injection रोकने के लिए PreparedStatement इस्तेमाल करें।
Use PreparedStatement with ? placeholders, always.

qa.q: List the steps of JDBC programming.
qa.a: Load or register the driver, open a Connection, create a Statement or PreparedStatement, execute the SQL, process the ResultSet, and close the resources.

qa.q: Difference between Statement and PreparedStatement?
qa.a: PreparedStatement is precompiled with ? parameters, which prevents SQL injection and is faster when reused; Statement sends a plain SQL string every time.

qa.q: What does executeQuery return?
qa.a: A ResultSet for SELECT statements; executeUpdate returns the number of affected rows for INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

qa.q: Which JDBC driver type is common now?
qa.a: Type 4, the pure Java thin driver that talks to the database directly over the network.

qa.q: How do you make several updates atomic in JDBC?
qa.a: Turn off auto-commit, execute the statements, call commit() when all succeed, and rollback() on failure.

With string concatenation the input becomes WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1', which is always true. A PreparedStatement sends the SQL structure first and the value separately as data, so the whole input is treated as a literal name, not as SQL.

import java.sql.*;
public class StudentDao {
    private final String url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/college";
    public void add(int id, String name, double cgpa) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "INSERT INTO student(id, name, cgpa) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
        try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "root", "password");
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setInt(1, id); ps.setString(2, name); ps.setDouble(3, cgpa);
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
    public void printAll() throws SQLException {
        try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "root", "password");
             Statement st = con.createStatement();
             ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery("SELECT id, name, cgpa FROM student")) {
            while (rs.next())
                System.out.println(rs.getInt("id") + " " + rs.getString("name") + " " + rs.getDouble("cgpa"));
        }
    }
    public int updateCgpa(int id, double cgpa) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "root", "password");
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("UPDATE student SET cgpa = ? WHERE id = ?")) {
            ps.setDouble(1, cgpa); ps.setInt(2, id);
            return ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
}

blocks.x: How the web works
A browser sends an **HTTP request** (method, URL, headers, body); the server returns an **HTTP response** (status code, headers, body).

x: Methods: **GET** (read; parameters in the URL), **POST** (send data in the body), PUT, DELETE, HEAD.
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301/302 redirect, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.
HTTP is **stateless**, so sessions and cookies are added for memory.

blocks.x: Servlet

A **servlet** is a Java class that runs inside a **web container** (Apache Tomcat, Jetty) and handles requests. It extends `HttpServlet` (package `javax.servlet` in older versions, `jakarta.servlet` from Jakarta EE 9 / Tomcat 10+).
Life cycle

x: **Loading and instantiation** by the container.
**`init()`**: called once.
**`service()`** → `doGet()` / `doPost()`: called for each request (each in its own thread of one servlet instance).
**`destroy()`**: called once at unloading.

blocks.x: Example servlet (runs in Tomcat; shown for reference)
Visiting `/hello?name=Anil` shows "Hello, Anil!". Output must be escaped when it contains user input, to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS).
Request and response objects
`getParameter`, `getParameterValues`, `getHeader`, `getSession`, `getRequestDispatcher`; response: `setContentType`, `getWriter`, `sendRedirect`, `setStatus`, `addCookie`.
Deployment descriptor and annotations
Servlets can be mapped using `web.xml` (`<servlet>` and `<servlet-mapping>`) or the `@WebServlet` annotation.
forward versus redirect

x: `RequestDispatcher.forward()`: server-side, same request, URL does not change.
`response.sendRedirect()`: tells the browser to make a **new** request, URL changes.

blocks.x: Session management

x: **Cookies:** small data stored in the browser.
**HttpSession:** server-side object per user, identified by the `JSESSIONID` cookie: `session.setAttribute("user", name)`.
**URL rewriting** and **hidden form fields**.

blocks.x: Filters and listeners
Filters intercept requests (logging, authentication); listeners react to events such as application start or session creation.
Hindi saransh
Servlet एक Java class है जो Tomcat जैसे container में चलती है। Life cycle: init → service (doGet/doPost) → destroy। HTTP stateless है, इसलिए session और cookie इस्तेमाल होते हैं।
init once, service many times, destroy once.

qa.q: Explain the servlet life cycle.
qa.a: The container loads the servlet and calls init() once, then calls service() (doGet or doPost) for every request, and finally calls destroy() once before unloading it.

qa.q: Difference between doGet and doPost?
qa.a: doGet handles GET requests with parameters in the URL (visible, size-limited, idempotent); doPost handles POST requests with data in the body, used for forms and sensitive data.

qa.q: Difference between forward and sendRedirect?
qa.a: forward is handled inside the server with the same request and no URL change; sendRedirect sends a response asking the browser to make a new request to another URL.

qa.q: Why is HTTP called stateless and how is state kept?
qa.a: Each request is independent and the server does not remember earlier ones. Cookies, HttpSession and URL rewriting maintain state across requests.

qa.q: What is a web container?
qa.a: Server software such as Tomcat that manages servlets: it receives HTTP requests, creates request/response objects, calls servlets and manages their life cycle.

quiz.why: It initialises the servlet one time.

HttpSession is identified by the cookie
Which keeps the same URL in the browser?
quiz.why: Forward is internal to the server.

blocks.x: **JavaServer Pages (JSP)** let you write HTML with embedded Java. The container **translates a JSP into a servlet** on first request, compiles it and runs it.
JSP elements

x: **Directives:** `<%@ page import="java.util.*" %>`, `<%@ include file="header.jsp" %>`, `<%@ taglib ... %>`.
**Declaration:** `<%! int count = 0; %>`.
**Scriptlet:** `<% ... %>` Java code.
**Expression:** `<%= name %>` prints a value.
**Comments:** `<%-- hidden --%>`.
**Actions:** `<jsp:include>`, `<jsp:forward>`, `<jsp:useBean>`.

blocks.x: Implicit objects
`request`, `response`, `session`, `application` (ServletContext), `out`, `config`, `pageContext`, `page`, `exception`.
Example (reference)

<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> <% String name = request.getParameter("name"); %>

Welcome, <%= name == null ? "guest" : name %>
Scopes
Page, request, session and application: where an attribute lives. `request.setAttribute("students", list)` shares data with a JSP after a forward.
Expression Language and JSTL
**EL**: `${student.name}`. **JSTL** tags remove scriptlets:
${s.name}${s.cgpa} Distinction
JSP vs servlet
Servlets are best for logic; JSP is best for presentation. Mixing both leads to the MVC pattern.
MVC architecture

x: **Model:** data and business rules (Java beans, DAO classes using JDBC).
**View:** presentation (JSP).
**Controller:** servlet that receives the request, calls the model, picks the view.

blocks.x: Flow: Browser → Controller servlet → Model (DAO, database) → request attribute → forward to View JSP → HTML back to browser. Benefits: separation of concerns, easier testing, parallel work by designers and developers. Frameworks such as **Spring MVC** implement this pattern.
JavaBean
A reusable class with a no-argument constructor, private fields and getters/setters, usable by JSP via `jsp:useBean` or EL.
Security basics
Validate input, use PreparedStatement, escape output (`<c:out>`), store passwords hashed, use HTTPS, and set session timeout.
Hindi saransh
JSP में HTML के अंदर Java लिखी जाती है और container उसे servlet में बदल देता है। MVC में Model = data, View = JSP, Controller = servlet।
Controller decides, Model works with data, View displays it.

qa.q: How is a JSP executed?
qa.a: On the first request the container translates the JSP into a servlet, compiles it, loads it and then runs the servlet to produce HTML.

qa.q: Difference between scriptlet and expression?
qa.a: A scriptlet <% %> contains arbitrary Java statements; an expression <%= %> evaluates one expression and prints its value.

qa.q: What is MVC?
qa.a: A design pattern that splits an application into Model (data and logic), View (user interface) and Controller (request handling).

qa.q: Name four JSP implicit objects.
qa.a: request, response, session, out (also application, config, pageContext, page, exception).

qa.q: Why use JSTL and EL?
qa.a: They remove Java code from pages, making JSPs cleaner, safer and easier for designers to maintain.

quiz.q: In MVC the servlet usually acts as the
<%= x %> is a JSP
quiz.why: It prints the value of x.

quiz.q: A JSP is converted by the container into a
EL syntax for a bean property
Attribute that lives for the whole user session is in

problems.q: List the four main JSP element types with one example of each.
problems.a: Directive: <%@ page import="java.util.*" %>. Declaration: <%! int count = 0; %>. Scriptlet: <% int x = 5; %>. Expression: <%= x * 2 %> which prints a value. (Action tags such as <jsp:include> are also elements.)

problems.q: Explain the roles of Model, View and Controller using a student login example.
problems.a: Model: a Student JavaBean and a DAO that checks the database. View: login.jsp and welcome.jsp, which only display. Controller: a servlet that receives the form, calls the model and then forwards to welcome.jsp or back to login.jsp. This keeps logic and presentation separate.

problems.a: request, response, session, application, out (also config, pageContext, page, exception). EL gives simple access to data in scopes without Java code: ${user.name} reads the name property of the user object found in page, request, session or application scope.

  • Declaration: <%! int count = 0; %>.
  • Scriptlet: <% ... %> Java code.
  • Expression: <%= name %> prints a value.
Read the full explanation
  • Directives: <%@ page import="java.util.*" %>, <%@ include file="header.jsp" %>, <%@ taglib ... %>.
  • Declaration: <%! int count = 0; %>.
  • Scriptlet: <% ... %> Java code.
  • Expression: <%= name %> prints a value.
  • Comments: <%-- hidden --%>.
  • Actions: <jsp:include>, <jsp:forward>, <jsp:useBean>.
🧠

Implicit objects

  • Request, response, session, application (ServletContext), out, config, pageContext, page, exception
💡

Example (reference)

<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>
<html><body>
<% String name = request.getParameter("name"); %>
<h2>Welcome, <%= name == null ? "guest" : name %></h2>
</body></html>
🔬

Scopes

  • Page, request, session and application: where an attribute lives
  • Request.setAttribute("students", list) shares data with a JSP after a forward
📊

Expression Language and JSTL

  • EL: ${student.name}
  • JSTL tags remove scriptlets:
<c:forEach var="s" items="${students}">
  <tr><td>${s.name}</td><td>${s.cgpa}</td></tr>
</c:forEach>
<c:if test="${s.cgpa >= 8}">Distinction</c:if>
🔑

JSP vs servlet

  • Servlets are best for logic
  • JSP is best for presentation
  • Mixing both leads to the MVC pattern
📌

MVC architecture

  • Model: data and business rules (Java beans, DAO classes using JDBC).
  • View: presentation (JSP).
  • Controller: servlet that receives the request, calls the model, picks the view.
🧠

JavaBean

  • A reusable class with a no-argument constructor, private fields and getters/setters, usable by JSP via jsp:useBean or EL
📘

  • Validate input, use PreparedStatement, escape output (<c:out>), store passwords hashed, use HTTPS, and set session timeout
