🔑

Big idea

  • A graph G = (V, E) has vertices (nodes) and edges
  • Graphs model networks, maps, social links, circuits and dependencies
📌

Types

  • Undirected / directed (digraph); simple (no loops or parallel edges), multigraph, pseudograph.
  • Weighted graph: edges have weights (distance, cost).
  • Complete graph K_n: every pair joined; it has n(n−1)/2 edges (K_5 has 10).
  • Bipartite: vertices split into two sets with edges only between sets (no odd cycles). K_{m,n} has mn edges.
Read the full explanation
  • Undirected / directed (digraph); simple (no loops or parallel edges), multigraph, pseudograph.
  • Weighted graph: edges have weights (distance, cost).
  • Complete graph K_n: every pair joined; it has n(n−1)/2 edges (K_5 has 10).
  • Bipartite: vertices split into two sets with edges only between sets (no odd cycles). K_{m,n} has mn edges.
  • Regular, cycle C_n, path P_n, wheel W_n, hypercube Q_n.
🧠

Degree

  • Degree deg(v) = number of edges at v (a loop counts 2)
  • Handshaking lemma: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|, so the number of odd-degree vertices is even
  • In a directed graph Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|
  • Example: a graph with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 has (3+3+2+2+2)/2 = 6 edges
🌟

Representation

  • Adjacency matrix n × n (A[i][j] = 1 if edge): O(1) edge check, O(n²) space.
  • Adjacency list: each vertex has a list of neighbours: O(V + E) space, ideal for sparse graphs.
  • Incidence matrix (vertices × edges).
🔬

Subgraphs, connectivity

  • Walk, trail (no repeated edge), path (no repeated vertex), circuit, cycle
  • A graph is connected if a path exists between every pair
  • Components, cut vertices (articulation points) and bridges matter for reliability of networks
📊

Isomorphism

  • Graphs G1 and G2 are isomorphic if a bijection of vertices preserves adjacency
  • Invariants (must match): number of vertices, edges, degree sequence, number of cycles of each length
  • Matching invariants does not prove isomorphism
  • A mismatch proves non-isomorphism
🔑

Number of graphs

  • There are 2^(n(n−1)/2) labelled simple graphs on n vertices (for n = 4: 64)
  • The number of labelled trees on n vertices is n^(n−2) (Cayley's formula
  • 125 for n = 5)

blocks.x: Euler paths and circuits
An **Euler circuit** uses every **edge** exactly once and returns to the start (the Königsberg bridges problem, Euler 1736).

x: A connected graph has an Euler **circuit** iff **every vertex has even degree**.
It has an Euler **path** (not circuit) iff **exactly two vertices have odd degree**.

blocks.x: Königsberg: all four land masses had odd degree, so no walk existed. For directed graphs, in-degree must equal out-degree.
Hamilton paths and cycles
A **Hamilton cycle** visits every **vertex** exactly once and returns. No simple necessary-and-sufficient test is known (it is NP-complete).

x: **Dirac's theorem:** if n ≥ 3 and every vertex has degree ≥ n/2, a Hamilton cycle exists.
**Ore's theorem:** if deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every non-adjacent pair, a Hamilton cycle exists.

blocks.x: K_n has a Hamilton cycle. The Travelling Salesman Problem asks for the cheapest Hamilton cycle in a weighted graph.
Planar graphs

A graph is **planar** if it can be drawn without edge crossings. **Euler's formula** for connected planar graphs: **V − E + F = 2**. For simple connected planar graphs with V ≥ 3: **E ≤ 3V − 6**, and if bipartite E ≤ 2V − 4.

x: K_5 has E = 10 > 3·5 − 6 = 9, so it is **non-planar**.
K_{3,3} has E = 9 > 2·6 − 4 = 8, so it is **non-planar**.

blocks.x: **Kuratowski's theorem:** a graph is planar iff it has no subdivision of K_5 or K_{3,3}. Example: a cube has V = 8, E = 12, so F = 2 − 8 + 12 = 6 faces.
Graph colouring
A proper colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours. The **chromatic number χ(G)** is the minimum number of colours.

x: χ(K_n) = n; χ(bipartite) = 2 (if it has an edge); χ(odd cycle) = 3; χ(even cycle) = 2.
**Four colour theorem:** every planar graph is 4-colourable.
**Brooks:** χ ≤ Δ (max degree) except for complete graphs and odd cycles.

blocks.x: Applications: **timetable scheduling** (courses as vertices, an edge if they share a student; colours are time slots), register allocation in compilers, frequency assignment for mobile towers, map colouring.
Greedy colouring
Order the vertices and give each the smallest colour not used by its neighbours; not always optimal but fast.
Output:
Vertices 1, 2, 3 form a triangle, so 3 colours are needed and used.
Euler: edges once, check degrees. Hamilton: vertices once, no easy test.

blocks.x: A **tree** is a connected graph with no cycles. A **forest** is a set of trees.
Properties
For a tree with n vertices:

x: It has exactly **n − 1** edges.
Exactly one path between any two vertices.
Adding any edge creates exactly one cycle; removing any edge disconnects it.
Every tree with n ≥ 2 has at least two leaves.

blocks.x: A rooted tree has parent, child, leaf, height and level. An **m-ary tree** with i internal vertices has n = mi + 1 vertices; a full binary tree with i internal vertices has i + 1 leaves. A binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes and at most 2^h leaves.
Traversals of binary trees
Preorder (root, left, right), inorder (left, root, right), postorder (left, right, root), and level-order (breadth first). Inorder of a binary search tree is sorted.
Spanning trees
A **spanning tree** of a connected graph contains all its vertices and is a tree (n − 1 edges). A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** has least total weight.

x: **Kruskal's algorithm:** sort edges by weight; add the next edge if it does not form a cycle (union-find).
**Prim's algorithm:** grow a tree from a vertex, always adding the cheapest edge leaving the tree.

blocks.x: Both give MSTs, in O(E log V). The MST weight is unique even when the tree is not. Used for laying cables, pipelines, network design, clustering.
Shortest path: Dijkstra

For non-negative weights. Keep tentative distances; repeatedly settle the nearest unsettled vertex and relax its edges. O((V + E) log V) with a priority queue. For negative weights use Bellman-Ford; for all pairs, Floyd-Warshall.

Other tree facts
Cayley: n^(n−2) labelled trees. Prüfer sequences encode labelled trees. Huffman trees give optimal prefix codes.
A tree on n vertices always has exactly n − 1 edges.

import heapq
g = {'A': {'B': 4, 'C': 2}, 'B': {'D': 5}, 'C': {'B': 1, 'D': 8}, 'D': {}}
dist = {v: float('inf') for v in g}; dist['A'] = 0
pq = [(0, 'A')]
while pq:
    d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
    if d > dist[u]: continue
    for v, w in g[u].items():
        if d + w < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = d + w; heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
print(dist)
edges = sorted([(1,'A','B'),(3,'B','C'),(2,'A','C'),(4,'C','D'),(5,'B','D')])
parent = {x: x for x in 'ABCD'}
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x: x = parent[x]
    return x
total = 0
for w, u, v in edges:
    ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
    if ru != rv: parent[ru] = rv; total += w
print(total)

blocks.x: Divisibility
a | b means b = ka for some integer k. Division algorithm: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b.
Primes

A prime has exactly two positive divisors. The **fundamental theorem of arithmetic**: every integer > 1 is a unique product of primes (360 = 2³·3²·5). There are infinitely many primes (Euclid's proof by contradiction).
GCD and LCM

gcd(a, b) is the largest common divisor. **Euclid's algorithm:** gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b). gcd(240, 46): 240 = 5·46 + 10; 46 = 4·10 + 6; 10 = 1·6 + 4; 6 = 1·4 + 2; 4 = 2·2 + 0, so gcd = 2. Also gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = a·b.
Extended Euclid and Bézout
There exist integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b). For 240 and 46: 240(−9) + 46(47) = −2160 + 2162 = **2** (verified by program).
Modular arithmetic
a ≡ b (mod m) means m | (a − b). Operations respect congruence: addition, subtraction and multiplication work modulo m.

x: **Modular inverse** of a mod m exists iff gcd(a, m) = 1, found by extended Euclid. Example: inverse of 3 mod 11 is **4**, since 3·4 = 12 ≡ 1.
Units of Z_6 are {1, 5}.
Linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m) has a solution iff gcd(a, m) divides b.

blocks.x: Fermat and Euler

x: **Fermat's little theorem:** if p is prime and p ∤ a then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). So 7^128 mod 13: since 7^12 ≡ 1, 128 = 10·12 + 8, so 7^128 ≡ 7^8 ≡ 3 (mod 13) (verified).
**Euler's totient φ(n):** count of integers 1..n coprime with n. φ(p) = p − 1; φ(pq) = (p−1)(q−1); Euler: a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) if gcd(a,n)=1.

blocks.x: Chinese remainder theorem
If the moduli are pairwise coprime, the system x ≡ a_i (mod m_i) has a unique solution modulo the product. Example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5) gives x ≡ 8 (mod 15).
Application: RSA

x: Choose primes p, q; n = pq; φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1).
Choose e coprime to φ(n); compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n).
Public key (n, e), private key d. Encrypt c = m^e mod n; decrypt m = c^d mod n.

blocks.x: Security relies on the difficulty of factoring n. Toy example p=3, q=11: n = 33, φ = 20, e = 3, d = 7; message 4 gives c = 64 mod 33 = 31; decrypt 31^7 mod 33 = 4.

n, e, d = 33, 3, 7
c = pow(4, e, n); print(c, pow(c, d, n))
Output:
Other uses: hashing, checksums (ISBN, Aadhaar-type check digits), pseudo-random number generators, hash table sizes.
Modular inverse exists only when the number is coprime to the modulus.

gcd(a, b) is the largest common divisor. Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b). gcd(240, 46): 240 = 5·46 + 10; 46 = 4·10 + 6; 10 = 1·6 + 4; 6 = 1·4 + 2; 4 = 2·2 + 0, so gcd = 2. Also gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = a·b.

🌟

Extended Euclid and Bézout

  • There exist integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b)
  • For 240 and 46: 240(−9) + 46(47) = −2160 + 2162 = 2 (verified by program)
🔬

Modular arithmetic

  • Modular inverse of a mod m exists iff gcd(a, m) = 1, found by extended Euclid. Example: inverse of 3 mod 11 is 4, since 3·4 = 12 ≡ 1.
  • Units of Z_6 are {1, 5}.
  • Linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m) has a solution iff gcd(a, m) divides b.
📊

Fermat and Euler

  • Fermat's little theorem: if p is prime and p ∤ a then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). So 7128 mod 13: since 712 ≡ 1, 128 = 10·12 + 8, so 7128 ≡ 78 ≡ 3 (mod…
  • Euler's totient φ(n): count of integers 1..n coprime with n. φ(p) = p − 1; φ(pq) = (p−1)(q−1); Euler: a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) if gcd(a,n)=1.
⚖️

Chinese remainder theorem

  • If the moduli are pairwise coprime, the system x ≡ a_i (mod m_i) has a unique solution modulo the product
  • Example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5) gives x ≡ 8 (mod 15)
💡

Application: RSA

  • Choose primes p, q; n = pq; φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1).
  • Choose e coprime to φ(n); compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n).
  • Public key (n, e), private key d. Encrypt c = m^e mod n; decrypt m = c^d mod n.

lessons.title: Algebraic structures: groups, rings, fields and Boolean algebra
yt: group theory basics discrete mathematics subgroup cyclic

blocks.x: An **algebraic structure** is a set with operations obeying certain laws.
Groups
A **group (G, ∗)** satisfies:

x: **Closure:** a ∗ b ∈ G.
**Associativity.**
**Identity** e: a ∗ e = e ∗ a = a.
**Inverse** a⁻¹ for every a.

blocks.x: An **abelian** group is also commutative. Examples: (ℤ, +), (ℚ − {0}, ×), (Z_n, +_n), non-zero residues mod a prime under multiplication, symmetric group S_n (permutations; order n!, non-abelian for n ≥ 3). Weaker structures: **semigroup** (closure + associativity), **monoid** (+ identity). (ℕ, +) is a monoid but not a group; strings with concatenation form a monoid.
Subgroups, cosets, Lagrange

A subgroup H ≤ G is a subset that is itself a group. **Lagrange's theorem:** |H| divides |G|. So a group of order 7 (prime) has only trivial subgroups and is cyclic. The **order of an element** a is the smallest n with aⁿ = e. A **cyclic group** is generated by one element, such as Z_6 = ⟨1⟩. Z_6 under + has subgroups of orders 1, 2, 3, 6.
Homomorphism and isomorphism
f(a ∗ b) = f(a) ∘ f(b). Isomorphic groups have identical structure. Example: (ℝ, +) ≅ (ℝ⁺, ×) via the exponential function.
Rings and fields

x: **Ring:** abelian group under + and a monoid (semigroup) under ×, with distributive laws. (ℤ, +, ×), matrices.
**Field:** a commutative ring where every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse: ℚ, ℝ, ℂ and Z_p for prime p. Z_6 is not a field (2 has no inverse).
**Finite fields** (Galois fields) are used in error-correcting codes and AES.

blocks.x: Coding theory (brief)
Hamming distance and parity checks detect and correct errors; a code with minimum distance d detects d − 1 errors and corrects ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋.
Boolean algebra
A Boolean algebra has ∧, ∨ and complement obeying the laws of sets and logic: identity, complement, commutative, distributive, De Morgan, absorption. Variables take 0/1.

x: Boolean functions are written as sums of **minterms** (SOP) or products of **maxterms** (POS).
**Karnaugh maps** simplify functions by grouping adjacent 1s in powers of two.

blocks.x: Example: F = x'y + xy' + xy simplifies to x + y (since xy' + xy = x, and x'y + x = x + y).

x: n variables give 2^(2^n) distinct Boolean functions (16 for n = 2).

blocks.x: Gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR (NAND and NOR are universal), XOR.
Group = closure, associativity, identity, inverse. Field = a ring where division by non-zero is possible.

qa.q: List the group axioms.
qa.a: Closure, associativity, an identity element, and an inverse for every element.

qa.q: What does Lagrange's theorem state?
qa.a: The order of a subgroup divides the order of the finite group.

qa.q: Is (ℕ, +) a group?
qa.a: No. It has an identity 0 but elements other than 0 have no additive inverse in ℕ, so it is a monoid.

qa.q: Why is Z_6 not a field while Z_7 is?
qa.a: In Z_6, elements such as 2 and 3 have no multiplicative inverse (they share factors with 6). 7 is prime, so every non-zero element of Z_7 has an inverse.

qa.q: Simplify xy' + xy.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a group axiom?
quiz.why: Commutativity is required only for abelian groups.

quiz.q: If a group has order 12, a subgroup cannot have order
Z_7 under multiplication of non-zero elements forms
quiz.why: Every non-zero residue has an inverse because 7 is prime.

quiz.q: Number of Boolean functions of 2 variables
NAND is called universal because
o: every Boolean function can be built from NAND gates alone
quiz.why: NAND can create NOT, AND and OR.

visuals.data: A + A.B = A ; A + A'.B = A + B ; (A.B)' = A' + B' and (A + B)' = A'.B'

problems.q: List the group axioms and check whether (Z5, +) with elements {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} under addition mod 5 is a group.
problems.a: Axioms: closure, associativity, identity and inverses. Closure: the sum mod 5 is in the set. Associativity holds. Identity: 0. Inverses: 0 to 0, 1 to 4, 2 to 3, 3 to 2, 4 to 1. So it is a group (also abelian).

problems.q: Show that {1, 3, 5, 7} under multiplication modulo 8 is a group. What is its order and does every element satisfy x * x = 1?
problems.a: 3 x 5 = 15 = 7, 3 x 7 = 21 = 5, 5 x 7 = 35 = 3 (mod 8), so the set is closed. Identity is 1. Each element is its own inverse: 3 x 3 = 9 = 1, 5 x 5 = 25 = 1, 7 x 7 = 49 = 1. Order is 4. Yes, every element squares to 1 (the Klein four-group).

problems.q: Simplify F = A.B + A.B' + A'.B, naming the laws used. Then give the dual of A + 0 = A.
problems.a: A.B + A.B' = A.(B + B') = A. So F = A + A'.B = A + B (absorption law A + A'.B = A + B). The dual of A + 0 = A is A.1 = A.

indian-knowledge-system.title: Indian Knowledge System
indian-knowledge-system.tagline: India's heritage in science, maths, medicine and arts.

lessons.title: Introduction to Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS)
yt: indian knowledge system introduction NEP 2020 IKS

blocks.x: **Indian Knowledge System (IKS)** is the body of knowledge developed in the Indian subcontinent over thousands of years, covering philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, language, arts, architecture, metallurgy, agriculture, water management and ethics, passed down through texts, teachers (guru–shishya parampara) and practice.
Why study it?

x: To understand the roots of science and culture.
To connect traditional ideas with modern disciplines (for example Panini's grammar and computer science).
To value sustainability and community knowledge.
The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 encourages including IKS in higher education; AICTE has an IKS Division and the Ministry of Education supports IKS research.

blocks.x: Study critically: separate documented evidence from legend, and acknowledge sources.
Sources of knowledge (pramanas)
Indian philosophy recognises means of valid knowledge:

x: **Pratyaksha:** direct perception.
**Anumana:** inference.
**Shabda:** reliable testimony (texts, experts).
Others used by some schools: upamana (analogy), arthapatti, anupalabdhi.

blocks.x: This resembles observation, logical inference and evidence in modern science.
The literature

x: **Vedas:** Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda; each has Samhita, Brahmana, Aranyaka and Upanishad parts.
**Vedangas** (auxiliary sciences): Shiksha (phonetics), Chandas (metre), Vyakarana (grammar), Nirukta (etymology), Kalpa (rituals), Jyotisha (astronomy).
**Upanishads, Itihasa (Ramayana, Mahabharata), Puranas, Smritis, Arthashastra.**
Sutra style: very short, memorable aphorisms, supported by commentaries (bhashya).
Preservation: oral transmission with strict recitation methods, then manuscripts on palm leaf and birch bark; Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit, Tamil and other languages.

blocks.x: Knowledge traditions
Chatur-Vidya, 14 vidyas and 64 kalas (arts) in classical lists; Ayurveda, Yoga, Jyotisha, Ganita (mathematics), Vastu, Natya, Sangita, Krishi.
Features of the Indian approach
Holistic (body–mind–nature), emphasis on dialogue and debate (shastrartha), practical application, and respect for diversity of schools of thought.
Time periods (rough)

Indus (Harappan) civilisation (about 3300–1300 BCE), Vedic period, Mauryan and Gupta ages (classical science), medieval Kerala school, Mughal–Rajput era observatories, and modern scientists such as Ramanujan, C. V. Raman, J. C. Bose.
IKS is a living heritage: learn it with curiosity and evidence.

qa.q: What is the Indian Knowledge System?
qa.a: The accumulated knowledge of India in fields such as philosophy, science, mathematics, medicine, arts, language and ecology, transmitted through texts and teacher–student traditions.

qa.q: Name the four Vedas.
What are the Vedangas?
qa.a: Six auxiliary disciplines: Shiksha, Chandas, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Kalpa and Jyotisha.

qa.q: What are pramanas?
qa.a: The accepted means of valid knowledge, mainly perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana) and testimony (shabda).

qa.q: Why is IKS included in modern curricula?
qa.a: To connect students with India's intellectual heritage, encourage interdisciplinary and sustainable thinking, and follow NEP 2020's vision.

visuals.data: Indian Knowledge Systems; Mathematics and astronomy; Language and logic; Medicine and yoga; Metallurgy and architecture; Arts and music; Philosophy and ethics

problems.q: What is meant by Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS)? Name five areas in which India has a traditional knowledge heritage.
problems.a: IKS is the body of knowledge, practices and ways of learning developed in the Indian subcontinent over thousands of years and passed on through texts, teachers and traditions. Areas: mathematics and astronomy, medicine (Ayurveda) and yoga, language and grammar (Panini), philosophy and logic, metallurgy, architecture, water management, and arts such as music and drama.

problems.q: Name three ancient Indian texts or scholars and the field of each. Why is it important for engineering students to study IKS?
problems.a:
Examples: Aryabhatiya (mathematics and astronomy), Sushruta Samhita (surgery), Ashtadhyayi by Panini (grammar), Arthashastra (administration and economics), Natyashastra (performing arts), Charaka Samhita (internal medicine).
IKS builds cultural roots, shows sustainable and low-resource solutions, inspires innovation (for example water harvesting, medicine, algorithms) and gives a broader view of knowledge beyond a single tradition.

rubric.t: Three texts or scholars with fields

problems.q: Explain how knowledge was preserved and passed on in the Gurukul tradition. How does it compare with modern education, and what does NEP 2020 say about IKS?
problems.a: Knowledge was passed on orally and through manuscripts: students lived with the teacher, learned by listening, memorising, repeating and practising (shruti and smriti), with personal mentoring. Modern education is institutional, written, examination-based and scalable, but it can lose personal mentoring and practice. NEP 2020 encourages integrating Indian knowledge, languages and traditions into curricula in a scientific, relevant way.

lessons.title: Indian mathematics: from Sulba Sutras to the Kerala school
yt: ancient indian mathematics aryabhata brahmagupta madhava

blocks.x: India made major contributions to number systems, algebra, trigonometry and infinite series.
Early foundations

x: **Indus civilisation:** standardised bricks (ratio 4:2:1), weights and town planning.

**Sulba Sutras** (Baudhayana, Apastamba; roughly the first millennium BCE): geometry for altar construction, including a statement of the Pythagorean relation, Pythagorean triples, and an approximation of √2:

blocks.x: √2 ≈ 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3·4) − 1/(3·4·34) = **1.4142156…** (true value 1.4142135…, correct to about 5 decimals; verified).
Decimal place-value and zero

The decimal place-value system with a symbol for zero was developed in India and later spread via the Arab world to Europe ("Hindu-Arabic numerals"). **Brahmagupta** (628 CE, *Brahmasphutasiddhanta*) gave rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers (debts and fortunes), and a general solution of quadratic equations. The Bakhshali manuscript (radiocarbon dated to centuries earlier than first thought) uses a dot as a zero placeholder.
Pingala (Chandahsastra, about 3rd–2nd century BCE)

Analysed poetic metres with short (laghu) and long (guru) syllables, which is equivalent to **binary patterns**. The number of patterns of n syllables is 2ⁿ (16 for 4 syllables). His method led to the **Meru Prastara** (Pascal's triangle): row 5 is 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. Combinations of metre related to what are now called **Fibonacci numbers** (Virahanka, then Hemachandra): 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 (verified).
Aryabhata (born 476 CE, *Aryabhatiya*)

x: Sine tables, place-value methods, algorithms for square and cube roots.
Proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, explained eclipses by shadows.
Gave sum formulas for series.

blocks.x: Bhaskara II (1114 CE, *Lilavati*, *Bijaganita*, *Siddhanta Shiromani*)

Problems in arithmetic and algebra, often written as poems; concepts close to calculus (instantaneous motion of planets). The **chakravala (cyclic) method** for Pell's equation x² − N y² = 1: for N = 61 the smallest solution is x = 1,766,319,049 and y = 226,153,980; Python confirms x² − 61y² = 1. Europeans solved this in the 17th century.
Kerala school (Madhava of Sangamagrama, about 1340–1425)
Infinite series centuries before Newton and Leibniz:

x: **π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + …** (known as the Madhava–Leibniz series).
Series for sine, cosine and arctangent. Taking terms to x⁷/5040, sin(30°) = 0.5 (computed to six decimals).

blocks.x:
import math
x = math.pi / 6
print(round(x - x**3 / 6 + x**5 / 120 - x**7 / 5040, 6))
print(round(4 * sum((-1) ** k / (2 * k + 1) for k in range(10)), 4))
Output:

The first line is the Madhava sine series; the second shows the slow Madhava–Leibniz series needs many terms (Madhava used correction terms to get π to 11 decimals). Successors: Nilakantha Somayaji, Jyeshthadeva (*Yuktibhasha*, in Malayalam, with proofs).
Modern: Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920)
Self-taught genius: infinite series for π, partitions, mock theta functions, the Hardy–Ramanujan number 1729 (the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two ways: 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³).
Links with computer science
Binary (Pingala), algorithms (square root, chakravala), series approximation (numerical methods), combinatorics.
Zero, decimal place value, binary patterns and infinite series all have Indian roots.

qa.q: What is Brahmagupta's contribution regarding zero?
qa.a: In 628 CE he gave explicit rules for operations with zero and negative numbers and treated them as numbers in their own right.

qa.q: What value of π did Aryabhata give?
How did Pingala's work anticipate binary numbers?
qa.a: He represented metres as sequences of short and long syllables, equivalent to 0/1 patterns, counting 2ⁿ possibilities for n syllables.

qa.q: What is the chakravala method?
qa.a: A cyclic algorithm described by Brahmagupta and perfected by Bhaskara II for solving Pell-type equations x² − N y² = 1.

qa.q: What did the Kerala school achieve?
qa.a: Madhava and his followers discovered infinite series for π, sine, cosine and arctangent about two centuries before European mathematicians.

visuals.title: Some milestones of Indian mathematics (approximate dates)
visuals.data: c. 800 BCE=Sulba Sutras give geometry for altars; c. 200 BCE=Pingala describes binary-like patterns; 476 CE=Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya; 628 CE=Brahmagupta states rules for zero; 1114 CE=Bhaskaracharya II writes Lilavati; c. 1400=Madhava and the Kerala school

problems.q: State two contributions each of Aryabhata and Brahmagupta.
problems.a: Aryabhata (476 CE): a value of pi about 3.1416 (62832 / 20000), the sine table, place-value notation in verse, and the idea that the Earth rotates. Brahmagupta (628 CE): rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers, and methods for solving quadratic and Diophantine equations.

problems.q: What do the Sulba Sutras say about the right triangle? Verify with a 3-4-5 triangle. What did Pingala contribute that is relevant to computer science?
problems.a:
The Baudhayana Sulba Sutra states that the square on the diagonal of a rectangle equals the sum of the squares on its sides (the Pythagorean theorem). Check: 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2.
Pingala (Chandahshastra) described poetic metres using short and long syllables, a binary pattern, and listed all combinations, an early idea of binary numbers and combinatorics.

problems.q: The Madhava series states pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ... Compute the estimate of pi from the first four terms. Why is this series slow, and what was Madhava's contribution?
problems.a:
Four terms: 1 - 0.3333 + 0.2 - 0.1429 = 0.7238, so pi is about 4 x 0.7238 = 2.895, which is far from 3.1416. The series converges slowly because the terms shrink only like 1/n, so thousands of terms are needed for few correct digits (Madhava used correction terms to speed it up).
Madhava of Sangamagrama (Kerala school, about 1340 to 1425) discovered infinite series for sine, cosine, arctangent and pi, about two centuries before similar work in Europe.

lessons.title: Astronomy, calendar and observatories

blocks.x: Jyotisha and Siddhantas

Early Indian astronomy (*Vedanga Jyotisha*) was tied to calendars and rituals. The classical **Siddhanta** texts (Surya Siddhanta, Aryabhatiya, Brahmasphutasiddhanta, Siddhanta Shiromani) calculate planetary positions, eclipses and time.
Key ideas

x: **Aryabhata:** Earth rotates on its axis (apparent motion of stars due to Earth's rotation); eclipses are due to shadows of Earth and Moon; length of the sidereal year about 365.2587 days (365 days 6 h 12 min 30 s).
Use of sine (jya) in astronomical computation; words *sine* and *cosine* trace back through Arabic from the Sanskrit jya.
Lunar and solar motion models, epicycles, and tables (karanas) for computation.

blocks.x: The Panchang

The traditional almanac with five elements: **tithi** (lunar day), **vara** (weekday), **nakshatra** (lunar mansion; 27), **yoga**, **karana** (half tithi). India uses many regional calendars: lunisolar (Vikrama Samvat, Shaka Samvat) and solar (Tamil, Bengali, Malayalam). The Indian national calendar based on the Shaka era was adopted in 1957. Festivals follow lunisolar dates, with an extra month (adhika masa) inserted about every three years to align with the solar year.
Units
Time units from the tiny truti to the large yuga cycles; the day was divided into 60 ghatis.
Observatories

**Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II** (1688–1743) built five observatories (Jantar Mantar) in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura in the early 18th century. The Jaipur one, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, includes the **Samrat Yantra**, a giant sundial that tells time to about two seconds accuracy, and instruments for finding the position of stars and the zodiac.
Modern achievements

ISRO's Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013–14, first Asian mission to reach Mars orbit and the first to do so on the first attempt), Aditya-L1 (Sun), and the work of Indian astrophysicists such as S. Chandrasekhar (Chandrasekhar limit, Nobel 1983) and Meghnad Saha.
Sundial idea
A gnomon's shadow length changes with the Sun's altitude. At noon on an equinox at latitude φ, shadow length/gnomon height = tan φ. For Dehradun (about 30.3° N): tan 30.3° ≈ 0.58.
Indian astronomy blended careful observation, mathematics and calendar-making.

visuals.title: Why an extra month is added to the Hindu calendar
visuals.data: 12 lunar months = about 354 days ; 1 solar year = about 365 days ; The gap of about 11 days a year adds up to one extra month (Adhika Masa) roughly every 2.7 years

problems.q: Name the five limbs (elements) of the Panchang and say what each measures.
problems.a: Tithi (lunar day), Vara (weekday), Nakshatra (the lunar star mansion, one of 27), Yoga (a combination of sun and moon longitudes) and Karana (half of a tithi).

problems.q: Why is the Hindu calendar called lunisolar? A lunar month is 29.53 days and a solar year is 365.24 days. Find the length of 12 lunar months, the yearly gap and how often an extra month is needed.
problems.a: Months follow the Moon (lunar), while the year is kept in step with the seasons using the Sun, so it is lunisolar. 12 x 29.53 = 354.4 days. Gap = 365.24 - 354.37 = about 10.9 days per year. An extra month (Adhika Masa) is needed after 29.53 / 10.9 = about 2.7 years, so roughly 7 times in 19 years.

problems.q: Describe the Jantar Mantar observatories: who built them, what is the Samrat Yantra and how does a sundial of that kind tell time? Give two astronomical ideas of Aryabhata.
problems.a:
Jantar Mantar observatories were built in the early 1700s by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. The Samrat Yantra is a huge stone sundial: a triangular gnomon points to the celestial pole, its shadow falls on a calibrated quadrant scale and gives local time to a precision of seconds.
Aryabhata proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, causing the apparent motion of stars, and explained eclipses as shadows of the Earth and the Moon.

lessons.title: Panini, Sanskrit grammar and computing

blocks.x: Panini's Ashtadhyayi

Panini (around the 4th century BCE) composed the *Ashtadhyayi* ("eight chapters") with roughly 4,000 concise rules (sutras) describing Sanskrit completely. It is a famous early example of a **formal, generative grammar**.
Features resembling computing

x: **Rule-based system:** rules apply in an order, with a conflict-resolution principle (a later rule can override an earlier one in certain cases).
**Meta-rules and metalanguage:** technical labels (*pratyahara* abbreviations, *it* markers) used to refer to groups of sounds compactly, similar to variables and macros.
**Compactness:** extreme economy, like compression.
**Context-sensitive rules** and operations such as substitution, deletion and insertion.

Comparison with **Backus–Naur Form (BNF)**: scholars have noted similarities, and some call it the Panini–Backus Form. This is an analogy in methods, not a claim that modern languages were derived from it.

blocks.x: Phonetics: Shiksha
Sounds are arranged scientifically by place of articulation (guttural, palatal, retroflex, dental, labial) in the **varnamala**, which is why Devanagari order is systematic.
Pratyahara example
The Shiva Sutras list sounds in a fixed order with marker letters; a pratyahara like **ac** denotes all vowels from a to the marker c. This is like specifying a range (a..c) in a list.
Sanskrit and technology

x: Sanskrit's regular grammar and rich morphology attract natural language processing (NLP) research: tokenisation, sandhi splitting, parsing, machine translation.
Tools: Sanskrit Heritage platform, the Digital Corpus of Sanskrit, Bhashini (India's language translation mission).
The claim that Sanskrit is "the best language for computers" is popular but not proven; what is accurate is that its formal grammar is a rich subject for computational linguistics.

blocks.x: Other traditions
*Nirukta* (Yaska, etymology), Tolkappiyam (Tamil grammar), Prakrit and Pali grammars, Kannada, Telugu and Bengali literary traditions. India has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule.

problems.q: Who was Panini, what is the Ashtadhyayi and how is it organised?
problems.a: Panini was an ancient Sanskrit grammarian (around the 4th century BCE). The Ashtadhyayi ("eight chapters") is his grammar of Sanskrit with roughly 4000 very short rules (sutras) arranged in eight chapters. It describes word formation and sound changes in a precise, rule-based way.

problems.q: What are the Maheshwara Sutras and a pratyahara? Give an example.
problems.a: The Maheshwara (Shiva) Sutras are 14 short sound lists that arrange the Sanskrit sounds. A pratyahara is a short label formed by taking the first sound and the end marker of a stretch of the list to mean every sound in between. Example: "ac" stands for all vowels, which makes rules very compact (like a variable that stands for a set).

rubric.t: Example such as ac for vowels

problems.q: Relate Panini's grammar to formal grammars and computing. Give two ideas that resemble programming practice.
problems.a:
Panini's rules generate correct words from roots and suffixes, like a production system in a formal grammar; the 20th-century BNF notation for programming languages has been compared with his method. Ideas: (1) abbreviation (pratyahara) is like defining a name for a set of values; (2) anuvritti, carrying a word forward from earlier sutras to avoid repeating it, is like reuse of code; (3) ordering of rules with general rules and exceptions resembles priority of rules in a parser.
Sanskrit's precise structure is studied for natural language processing.

lessons.title: Indian philosophy, logic and ethics
yt: six schools of indian philosophy darshana nyaya vaisheshika

blocks.x: Darshanas (viewpoints)
**Astika** (accept the authority of the Vedas): Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Purva Mimamsa, Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta). **Nastika** (do not): Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka (Lokayata, materialist).

head: School
Core idea
rows: Atomism (Kanada): matter made of paramanu; categories of reality
Discipline of body and mind (Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, eight limbs)
Ritual duty and interpretation of Vedic texts
Nature of Brahman and self (Advaita by Shankara, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita)
Four noble truths, eight-fold path, impermanence
Perception as the only valid knowledge

blocks.x: Nyaya logic

A syllogism with five members (**pancha-avayava**): pratijna (claim), hetu (reason), udaharana (example), upanaya (application), nigamana (conclusion). Example: "There is fire on the hill (claim), because there is smoke (reason); wherever smoke is, there is fire, as in a kitchen (example); this hill has smoke (application); therefore it has fire (conclusion)." Compare with modus ponens and the Western syllogism, which uses three parts. Navya-Nyaya (14th century onwards) developed a precise formal language for relations and qualifiers. **Jain syadvada** lists seven predications for a statement ("in some respects it is…"), related to many-valued logic. **Buddhist logic** (Dignaga, Dharmakirti) refined theories of inference.
Atomism
Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutra describes indivisible atoms (paramanu) that combine to make matter, with qualities such as weight, motion and contact.
Yoga

Patanjali's eight limbs (ashtanga): yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi. International Yoga Day is observed on 21 June (declared by the UN in 2014). Modern studies show benefits for stress and flexibility, but yoga is not a substitute for medical treatment.
Ethics and values

Ahimsa (non-violence), satya (truth), dharma (duty), karma (action and consequence), seva (service), vasudhaiva kutumbakam (the world is one family), aparigraha (non-possessiveness). Gandhi applied ahimsa and satyagraha to politics.
Education and debate
Shastrartha (formal debate) trained reasoning. **Takshashila**, **Nalanda** (5th–12th century CE) and **Vikramashila** were great centres of learning attracting students from across Asia.
Relevance today
Logic (AI reasoning), ethics (responsible technology), mindfulness (well-being), plural thinking (anekantavada supports tolerance in teams).
Indian philosophy valued reasoned debate; logic was a tool to test claims.

visuals.data: Six darshanas; Nyaya (logic); Vaisheshika (atoms and categories); Samkhya (matter and consciousness); Yoga (discipline); Mimamsa (ritual and interpretation); Vedanta (ultimate reality)

problems.q: List the six orthodox (astika) schools of Indian philosophy and name two heterodox (nastika) schools.
problems.a: Orthodox: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta. Heterodox: Charvaka (materialism), Buddhism and Jainism.

problems.q: Name the four pramanas (means of valid knowledge) in Nyaya with an example of each.
problems.a: Pratyaksha (perception): seeing a tree. Anumana (inference): seeing smoke and inferring fire. Upamana (comparison): recognising a wild ox because it resembles a cow. Shabda (testimony): trusting a reliable expert or text.

problems.q: Write the five steps of a Nyaya syllogism for "the hill has fire". How does it compare with Western logic, and what is the Jain idea of syadvada?
problems.a:
1) Pratijna (proposition): the hill has fire. 2) Hetu (reason): because it has smoke. 3) Udaharana (example): wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen. 4) Upanaya (application): this hill has smoke. 5) Nigamana (conclusion): therefore the hill has fire. It includes a concrete example, unlike the three-step Aristotelian syllogism.
Syadvada (saptabhangi): a statement can be true from one standpoint, so judgements are qualified with "in some sense" (seven-fold predication), supporting non-absolutism.

blocks.x: Ayurveda
"Science of life" (ayus = life, veda = knowledge). Classical texts:

x: **Charaka Samhita:** internal medicine, diagnosis, diet, ethics of the physician.
**Sushruta Samhita:** surgery (shalya tantra), instruments, anatomy, training by practice on models; the traditions of reconstructive (rhinoplasty) surgery are described.
**Ashtanga Hridaya (Vagbhata).**

blocks.x: These texts were compiled over centuries (dates are debated; roughly from the first millennium BCE to early centuries CE).
Core concepts

x: **Tridosha:** vata, pitta, kapha; health is balance and disease is imbalance.
**Dhatus** (tissues), **agni** (digestion/metabolism), **prakriti** (constitution).
Emphasis on **diet, daily routine (dinacharya), seasonal routine, sleep, exercise and mental health**.
Treatment: herbs and formulations, panchakarma cleansing, diet, yoga.

blocks.x: Plants and medicines

Examples: turmeric (curcumin: studied for anti-inflammatory effects), neem, tulsi, ashwagandha, amla, giloy. Many modern drugs derive from plants (for example aspirin from salicin in willow, reserpine from Rauvolfia serpentina used in Indian practice). Evidence levels differ: some remedies have trials, many need more research, and some preparations have contained harmful metals, so quality control matters.
Other Indian systems (AYUSH)

**A**yurveda, **Y**oga and naturopathy, **U**nani, **S**iddha, **H**omoeopathy. The Ministry of AYUSH regulates education, research and standards. Patients should not replace modern emergency or serious-disease treatment with unproven remedies; integrative approaches work with qualified doctors.
Protecting traditional knowledge
**Biopiracy** is patenting traditional knowledge without credit.

x: **Turmeric patent (US, 1995):** granted for wound healing; revoked in 1997 after India (CSIR) showed ancient texts.
**Neem patent (European Patent Office):** revoked in 2005 after challenge by India and others.
**Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL):** India's database of traditional formulations in several languages, used by patent examiners worldwide.
**GI (Geographical Indication) tags:** Darjeeling tea was India's first GI-tagged product (registered in the early 2000s); others include Basmati, Kanchipuram silk and Mysore silk.

blocks.x: Medicine and technology
IoT wearables measure pulse and sleep; digital Ayurveda records; AI-based herb identification; telemedicine (e-Sanjeevani).
Public health traditions
Yoga and pranayama for stress, community nutrition (millets), and hygiene customs.
Respect the tradition, test it with evidence, protect it from misuse.

qa.q: What are the major classical Ayurvedic texts?
qa.a: Charaka Samhita (internal medicine), Sushruta Samhita (surgery) and Ashtanga Hridaya (Vagbhata).

qa.q: What is tridosha?
qa.a: The concept of three bodily humours or principles, vata, pitta and kapha, whose balance is considered the basis of health in Ayurveda.

qa.q: What does AYUSH stand for?
qa.a: Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy.

qa.q: What is TKDL?
qa.a: The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library, a database of documented traditional knowledge used to prevent wrongful patents.

qa.q: Why was the turmeric patent revoked?
qa.a: India showed that the wound-healing use of turmeric was already documented in traditional knowledge, so it lacked novelty.

visuals.data: Ashtanga yoga; Yama (restraints); Niyama (observances); Asana (posture); Pranayama (breath control); Pratyahara (withdrawing the senses); Dharana (concentration); Dhyana (meditation); Samadhi (absorption)

problems.q: Name the three doshas of Ayurveda and the main quality of each.
problems.a: Vata (air and space; movement, dryness, lightness), Pitta (fire and water; heat, digestion, metabolism) and Kapha (earth and water; structure, stability, lubrication). Ayurveda aims at balance among them.

problems.q: List the eight limbs of Ashtanga yoga in order. Who compiled the Yoga Sutras and why was 21 June chosen as the International Day of Yoga?
problems.a: Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi. The Yoga Sutras were compiled by Patanjali. The International Day of Yoga is on 21 June, the summer solstice, the longest day in the northern hemisphere; it was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2014 and first observed in 2015.

problems.q: Compare the Charaka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita. What is TKDL and why was it created (turmeric patent example)?
problems.a:
Charaka Samhita is mainly about internal medicine, diagnosis, diet and physician ethics; Sushruta Samhita is mainly about surgery, instruments, anatomy and training.
TKDL (Traditional Knowledge Digital Library) is an Indian database of traditional medicine knowledge in languages and formats patent examiners understand. It was created to prevent wrong patents on traditional knowledge, as in the turmeric wound-healing patent granted in the US in the 1990s and revoked after India proved prior knowledge.

blocks.x: Metallurgy

x: **Wootz steel:** high-carbon crucible steel made in South India (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana); source of the famed "Damascus" blades.

**Iron Pillar of Delhi** (Mehrauli; Gupta period, around the 4th–5th century CE): about 7 m tall and weighing over 6 tonnes, it shows remarkable corrosion resistance, attributed to a thin protective layer rich in iron-hydrogen-phosphate formed because of the high phosphorus content and the local climate.
**Zinc distillation at Zawar (Rajasthan):** one of the earliest large-scale production of metallic zinc (from about the 12th century CE or earlier).
Bronze casting: the dancing-girl statue (Mohenjo-daro) and Chola bronzes using the lost-wax method.

blocks.x: Town planning and architecture

x: **Indus cities** (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal): grid streets, covered drains, standard bricks, the Great Bath, the dockyard at Lothal.

**Vastu Shastra** and **Shilpa Shastra**: guidelines on layout, orientation to light and wind, proportions. Scientific proof of all claims is limited, but passive-design ideas (ventilation, sunlight) are sound.
Temple architecture styles: Nagara (north), Dravida (south), Vesara; examples Konark, Khajuraho, Brihadeeswara (Thanjavur).
Stone and cave structures: Ajanta, Ellora (Kailasa temple carved from one rock).

blocks.x: Water management
Different regions evolved different systems:

head: Region
System
rows: Vav (stepwell, e.g. Rani ki Vav, Patan)
Kuls and naulas (Uttarakhand/Himachal channels and springs)
Eris (tank systems in Tamil Nadu), temple tanks

blocks.x: Cholas built the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) across the Kaveri, still in use. Dholavira had a sophisticated reservoir system. Modern revival: Rajendra Singh's johad work in Alwar (Rajasthan), rooftop rainwater harvesting.
Agriculture

Kautilya's *Arthashastra* and *Krishi-Parashara* describe seasons, soil, seeds, crop rotation and irrigation. Traditional practices: mixed cropping, millets (now promoted as "Shree Anna"; the UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets), organic manure, and seed saving.
Ecology and sustainability

Sacred groves, worship of rivers and trees, **Bishnoi** community's protection of trees and wildlife (the 1730 Khejarli sacrifice), **Chipko movement** (1970s Uttarakhand, led by villagers including Gaura Devi, with Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt). These show community-based conservation and relate to the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
IoT and traditional wisdom
Soil-moisture sensors with drip irrigation, smart water meters for stepwell-style conservation, and weather stations for traditional crop calendars link IKS to modern engineering.

visuals.title: Examples of Indian engineering heritage (approximate dates)
visuals.data: c. 2500 BCE=Dholavira builds a water conservation system; c. 2nd century CE=Grand Anicut (Kallanai) built on the Kaveri; c. 4th to 5th century=Delhi Iron Pillar erected; 11th century=Rani ki Vav stepwell at Patan; 13th century=Konark Sun Temple

problems.q: Name three examples of ancient Indian metallurgy or engineering and say what makes each remarkable.
problems.a: The Delhi Iron Pillar (about 1600 years old) has hardly rusted. Wootz steel from south India was famous for very high-quality blades. Zinc was produced by distillation at Zawar in Rajasthan, a very early large-scale zinc production. Also valid: the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) dam, still in use.

problems.q: Roof area is 100 square metres, annual rainfall 800 mm and the runoff coefficient is 0.8. Find the yearly rainwater harvest in cubic metres and litres. Name two traditional water systems of India.
problems.a: Harvest = area x rainfall x coefficient = 100 x 0.8 x 0.8 = 64 cubic metres = 64,000 litres per year. Traditional systems: stepwells (vav or baoli) in Gujarat and Rajasthan, tanks (eri) in Tamil Nadu, and Dholavira's reservoirs.

problems.q: Explain how traditional water and building practices show sustainability, and how IoT sensors could help one of them today.
problems.a:
Stepwells and tanks stored monsoon water for dry months and recharged groundwater; buildings used local materials, ventilation and shade suited to the climate; Vastu and temple design used orientation and light. They are sustainable because they use local resources, low energy and long-term planning.
IoT: water-level sensors and flow meters in a stepwell or tank give real-time storage data and alert when levels are low; soil moisture sensors guide drip irrigation.

lessons.title: Arts, music, Natyashastra and IKS in the modern world
yt: raga tala indian classical music basics

blocks.x: Natyashastra

Attributed to **Bharata Muni** (traditionally dated between about 200 BCE and 200 CE), it is a treatise on performing arts covering drama, dance, music, stage design and aesthetics. **Rasa theory:** the aesthetic experience of an audience. Nine rasas (navarasa): shringara (love), hasya (laughter), karuna (compassion), raudra (anger), veera (heroism), bhayanaka (fear), bibhatsa (disgust), adbhuta (wonder), shanta (peace). Bhava (emotion) shown by the performer becomes rasa in the audience.
Classical dance forms (recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi)
Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Sattriya.
Music

Two main systems: **Hindustani** (north) and **Carnatic** (south). Core ideas: **swara** (notes: sa re ga ma pa dha ni), **raga** (melodic framework with rules, mood and time of day), **tala** (rhythmic cycle, e.g. teentaal has 16 beats), improvisation. The seven notes relate to a scale; microtones are called **shruti**. Instruments: sitar, sarod, tabla, veena, flute (bansuri), mridangam, violin. Mathematics in music: tala cycles (16 beats = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4) and permutations of rhythm.
Folk and visual arts
Madhubani, Warli, Pattachitra, Kalamkari, Gond; textiles (Banarasi, Pochampally ikat), crafts (Channapatna toys), and regional theatre (Nautanki, Yakshagana, Therukoothu).
Gurukul and apprenticeship
Learning by listening, imitation, practice and personal guidance: a model modern internships and mentoring echo.
IKS and the modern world

x: **Technology:** the data of Ayurveda or astronomy tables in digital libraries; AI for manuscripts (OCR for palm leaf), Bhashini.
**Management:** *Arthashastra* on administration and strategy; Bhagavad Gita on duty, balance and decision-making under pressure (karma yoga: act without anxiety about results).
**Sustainability:** traditional crop and water practices.
**Wellness:** yoga, meditation, dietary diversity.
**Entrepreneurship:** GI-tagged crafts, handloom, AYUSH start-ups.
**Heritage protection:** UNESCO sites, manuscripts mission (National Mission for Manuscripts).

blocks.x: Critical thinking about IKS

Good scholarship: cite sources and dates, avoid exaggerated or unverified claims ("everything was invented in ancient India"), compare with other civilisations fairly, and be open to testing traditional ideas scientifically. IKS and modern science can complement each other.
Project ideas for students
Document a local craft or oral tradition with interviews; build an app map of stepwells; digitise a family recipe book; analyse a raga with audio software; measure the Sun's shadow to find latitude.
Learn from tradition, test with science, and apply it responsibly.

qa.q: What is rasa theory?
qa.a: A theory from the Natyashastra explaining how the emotions (bhava) portrayed by performers evoke aesthetic experiences (rasa) such as love, humour or compassion in the audience.

qa.q: Name the nine rasas.
qa.a: Shringara, hasya, karuna, raudra, veera, bhayanaka, bibhatsa, adbhuta and shanta.

qa.q: Difference between Hindustani and Carnatic music?
qa.a: Hindustani is the north Indian tradition with more emphasis on elaboration of ragas and often Persian-influenced forms; Carnatic is the south Indian tradition with a strong compositional repertoire (kritis). Both use raga and tala.

qa.q: What is a tala?
qa.a: A rhythmic cycle of beats that structures a piece of music, such as teentaal of 16 beats.

qa.q: Why is critical thinking needed when studying IKS?
qa.a: To distinguish documented evidence from legend, avoid exaggeration and ensure that claims are supported by sources and, where possible, tested.

visuals.title: The nine rasas (Natyashastra)
visuals.data: Navarasa; Shringara (love); Hasya (laughter); Karuna (compassion); Raudra (anger); Veera (heroism); Bhayanaka (fear); Bibhatsa (disgust); Adbhuta (wonder); Shanta (peace)

problems.q: List the nine rasas and name the text that describes rasa theory.
problems.a: Shringara (love), Hasya (laughter), Karuna (compassion), Raudra (anger), Veera (heroism), Bhayanaka (fear), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder) and Shanta (peace). Rasa theory comes from the Natyashastra attributed to Bharata Muni.

problems.q: Name the seven swaras of Indian music, define raga and tala, and show how a 16-beat tala (teental) is divided.
problems.a: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni. A raga is a melodic framework with rules for notes and phrases that expresses a mood (and traditionally a time of day). A tala is a rhythmic cycle of beats. Teental has 16 beats in 4 groups of 4 (4 + 4 + 4 + 4).

problems.q: Suggest three ways in which IKS can be applied in the modern world (technology, management, sustainability, wellness), each with a concrete example.
problems.a: Technology: OCR and AI to digitise palm-leaf manuscripts and the Bhashini language platform for Indian languages. Management: Arthashastra ideas on administration and the Gita's idea of acting with focus without anxiety about results. Sustainability: traditional rainwater harvesting and mixed cropping. Wellness: yoga and meditation for stress and health. GI-tagged crafts and AYUSH start-ups are examples of entrepreneurship.

blocks.x: **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** is the science of making machines do tasks that normally need human intelligence: perceiving, reasoning, learning, deciding and using language.
Four views of AI
The **Turing test** (1950): a machine passes if a human interrogator cannot tell its answers from a human's.
Short history

1943 artificial neuron model; 1950 Turing's paper; **1956 Dartmouth workshop** coins "Artificial Intelligence"; 1960s–70s early optimism, then the first **AI winter**; 1980s expert systems; 1997 Deep Blue beats Kasparov; 2012 deep learning wins ImageNet; 2016 AlphaGo; 2017 Transformer architecture; 2020s large language models and generative AI.
Types

x: **Narrow (weak) AI:** one task (spam filter, face unlock, chess). All AI today.
**General AI (AGI):** human-level across tasks (not yet achieved).
**Super-intelligence:** beyond humans (hypothetical).

blocks.x: By function: reactive machines, limited memory, theory of mind, self-aware (the last two are research ideas).
Intelligent agents

An **agent** perceives its environment through **sensors** and acts through **actuators**. A **rational agent** picks the action expected to maximise its performance measure. Describe a task with **PEAS**: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. Example, self-driving car: P = safety, speed, comfort; E = roads, traffic, pedestrians; A = steering, brake, horn; S = cameras, lidar, GPS.
Agent types (increasing sophistication)

x: **Simple reflex:** condition–action rules.
**Model-based reflex:** keeps internal state.
**Goal-based:** plans to reach goals.
**Utility-based:** chooses the best among many ways using a utility function.
**Learning agent:** improves with experience.

blocks.x: Environment properties

Fully vs partially observable; deterministic vs stochastic; episodic vs sequential; static vs dynamic; discrete vs continuous; single vs multi-agent. Chess: fully observable, deterministic, discrete. Taxi driving: partially observable, stochastic, dynamic, continuous.
AI applications
Healthcare imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, voice assistants, robotics, agriculture, smart cities and IoT analytics.
Responsible AI
Bias in data, privacy, transparency (explainability), accountability, job impact, and safety.
A rational agent does the right thing given what it knows.

qa.q: What is artificial intelligence?
qa.a: The field of building machines or software that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence such as learning, reasoning, perception and language understanding.

qa.q: What is the Turing test?
qa.a: A test proposed by Alan Turing in which a machine is considered intelligent if a human judge cannot reliably tell its conversation apart from a human's.

qa.q: What does PEAS stand for?
qa.a: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors, used to specify an agent's task.

qa.q: Difference between a simple reflex agent and a goal-based agent?
qa.a: A simple reflex agent reacts to the current percept using fixed rules; a goal-based agent considers future consequences and plans actions to reach a goal.

qa.q: What is narrow AI?
qa.a: AI designed for a specific task, such as image recognition or translation; all current systems are narrow.

quiz.why: John McCarthy and colleagues named the field in 1956.

quiz.why: It tracks unobserved aspects of the world.

visuals.data: 1950=Turing proposes the imitation game; 1956=Dartmouth workshop names the field; 1997=Deep Blue beats the chess champion; 2012=Deep learning wins the ImageNet contest; 2017=Transformer architecture introduced

problems.q: Define Artificial Intelligence and list four approaches (thinking or acting, humanly or rationally).
problems.a: AI is the study and design of machines that perceive their environment and take actions to achieve goals, behaving intelligently. Four approaches: thinking humanly (cognitive modelling), thinking rationally (laws of thought, logic), acting humanly (the Turing test) and acting rationally (rational agents), which is the most common modern view.

problems.q: Write the PEAS description for an automatic vacuum cleaner robot.
problems.a: Performance measure: amount of dirt cleaned, time and energy used, safety. Environment: rooms, floor, furniture, people and pets. Actuators: wheels, brushes, vacuum motor. Sensors: dirt sensor, bump sensor, cliff sensor, camera or lidar.

problems.q: Compare simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based and learning agents using the vacuum cleaner as the example.
problems.a: Simple reflex: if the square is dirty then clean, based only on the current percept. Model-based: remembers which rooms are already cleaned. Goal-based: plans a route to reach the goal of all rooms clean. Utility-based: chooses the plan that balances cleanliness, battery and speed (higher utility). Learning agent: improves its behaviour from experience, for example learns where dirt appears most.

lessons.title: Problem solving by search: BFS, DFS, UCS and A*
yt: uninformed search BFS DFS uniform cost search AI

blocks.x: Many AI problems (route finding, puzzles, planning) are solved by **searching** a space of states.
Problem formulation
Initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, path cost. The **search tree** expands states from the start.
Uninformed (blind) search
b = branching factor, d = depth of shallowest goal, m = max depth.
Worked BFS example (verified by code)
Graph: S→A, B; A→C; B→C, D; C→G; D→G. BFS from S finds the path **S → A → C → G** (3 steps); the first goal found in level order is a shortest path in steps.
Informed (heuristic) search
A **heuristic h(n)** estimates the cost from n to the goal.

x: **Greedy best-first:** expand lowest h(n); fast but not optimal.
**A\*:** expand lowest **f(n) = g(n) + h(n)** where g is the cost so far. A\* is complete and **optimal** if h is **admissible** (never overestimates) and, for graph search, **consistent**.

blocks.x: Example: 8-puzzle heuristics — misplaced tiles, or total Manhattan distance (better because it is closer to the true cost).
Worked A* example
Output:
The cheapest path costs 6 (1 + 2 + 3), better than S→A→G (7) or S→B→G (7).
Local search and optimisation
**Hill climbing** (moves to a better neighbour; can get stuck in local maxima), **simulated annealing** (sometimes accepts worse moves), **genetic algorithms** (selection, crossover, mutation).
Adversarial search (games)
**Minimax** assumes the opponent plays optimally; **alpha–beta pruning** skips branches that cannot affect the result, giving the same answer with far fewer nodes.
Constraint satisfaction
Variables, domains, constraints (Sudoku, map colouring, timetabling) solved by backtracking with forward checking.
A* = cost so far + estimated cost to go; keep the heuristic admissible.

qa.q: Compare BFS and DFS.
qa.a: BFS explores level by level with a queue, is complete and finds the shallowest goal but needs much memory. DFS goes deep first with a stack, uses little memory, but may not find the shortest path and can loop in infinite spaces.

qa.q: What is an admissible heuristic?
qa.a: A heuristic that never overestimates the true cost to reach the goal, which guarantees A* finds an optimal solution.

qa.q: What is f(n) in A*?
qa.a: f(n) = g(n) + h(n), the cost from the start to n plus the estimated cost from n to the goal.

qa.q: Why can hill climbing fail?
qa.a: It can get stuck at a local maximum, a plateau or a ridge where no neighbour is better, although a better solution exists elsewhere.

qa.q: What does alpha-beta pruning do?
qa.a: It prunes branches of the minimax tree that cannot influence the final decision, reducing the number of nodes evaluated without changing the result.

A* chooses the node with the lowest

problems.q: Differentiate BFS and DFS: data structure, completeness and optimality (equal step costs).
problems.a: BFS uses a queue (first in, first out) and explores level by level; it is complete and finds the shallowest (optimal for equal costs) solution but needs a lot of memory. DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and goes deep first; it needs little memory but is not optimal and can loop forever in infinite or cyclic spaces unless a visited set is used.

problems.q: Tree: A has children B and C; B has children D and E; C has child F. Give the order in which nodes are visited by BFS and by DFS (left child first).
problems.a: BFS: A, B, C, D, E, F (level by level). DFS: A, B, D, E, C, F (go deep before moving to the sibling).

lessons.title: Knowledge representation, logic and probabilistic reasoning
yt: knowledge representation propositional logic first order logic AI

blocks.x: Knowledge-based agents

A **knowledge base (KB)** stores facts and rules; an **inference engine** derives new facts. Representations: propositional logic, first-order logic (FOL), semantic networks, frames, production rules (IF–THEN).
Logic recap

x: **Propositional logic** uses true/false statements. Rule: `Rain → WetGround`. Inference rules: **modus ponens** (from P and P → Q, conclude Q), modus tollens, resolution.
**First-order logic** adds objects, predicates, quantifiers: ∀x (Human(x) → Mortal(x)), Human(Socrates) ⊢ Mortal(Socrates).
**Forward chaining** (data-driven) and **backward chaining** (goal-driven, used in Prolog).

blocks.x: Expert systems

Knowledge base + inference engine + user interface (+ explanation facility). Examples: MYCIN (medical diagnosis), early troubleshooting systems. Weakness: knowledge acquisition is hard and rules are brittle.
Uncertainty
Real data is noisy, so we use probability.

x: **Conditional probability:** P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B).
**Bayes' theorem:** P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E).

blocks.x: Worked example

A disease affects 1% of people. A test is positive for 90% of sick people (sensitivity) and falsely positive for 5% of healthy people. P(positive) = 0.9·0.01 + 0.05·0.99 = 0.0585. P(disease | positive) = 0.009 / 0.0585 ≈ **0.154 (15.4%)**. Even after a positive test the chance of disease is only about 15%, because the disease is rare. This is the **base-rate effect**.

pd, sens, fpr = 0.01, 0.90, 0.05
p_pos = sens * pd + fpr * (1 - pd)
print(round(sens * pd / p_pos, 4))
Output:
Naive Bayes idea
Assume features are independent given the class: P(C | x1..xn) ∝ P(C)·ΠP(xi | C). Works well for spam filtering and text.
Bayesian networks
A directed acyclic graph where nodes are random variables and edges show direct influence; each node has a conditional probability table. Used in diagnosis and risk models.
Fuzzy logic
Truth values between 0 and 1 ("fairly hot = 0.7"), used in washing machines, AC controllers.
Natural language and vision (preview)
Tokenisation, embeddings, transformers for text; convolutional networks for images.
Bayes' rule updates belief using evidence; rare events stay unlikely even after a positive test.

qa.q: What is modus ponens?
qa.a: An inference rule: from P and P → Q, infer Q.

qa.q: Difference between forward and backward chaining?
qa.a: Forward chaining starts with known facts and applies rules to derive new facts; backward chaining starts from a goal and works back to find supporting facts.

qa.q: State Bayes' theorem.
Why is the probability of disease only about 15% after a positive test in the example?
qa.a: The disease is rare (1%), so most positive results come from the large healthy group with false positives. This is the base-rate effect.

qa.q: What is the naive assumption in Naive Bayes?
qa.a: That all features are conditionally independent given the class.

quiz.q: In the disease example, P(disease | positive) is about
Forward chaining is
Which is used by spam filters?
quiz.why: It multiplies word likelihoods per class.

quiz.q: First-order logic adds to propositional logic
Fuzzy logic uses truth values

visuals.title: Bayes' theorem
visuals.data: P(H|E) = P(E|H) x P(H) / P(E) ; posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence

problems.q: Give one example each of a propositional logic sentence and a first-order logic sentence for "All students who study pass". Why is first-order logic more expressive?
problems.a: Propositional: StudiesHard implies Passes (it talks about one fixed case). First-order: for all x (Student(x) AND Studies(x) implies Passes(x)). First-order logic has objects, predicates and quantifiers, so it can talk about all or some members of a group instead of one fixed fact.

problems.q: A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it 95% of the time when present and gives a false positive 5% of the time. If a person tests positive, what is the probability of having the disease?
problems.a: P(+) = 0.95 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059. P(D | +) = 0.0095 / 0.059 = 0.161, about 16.1%. Most positive results are false positives because the disease is rare.

rubric.t: Explanation about the low base rate

problems.q: The same person takes a second independent test and it is also positive. Update the probability. Explain why the prior matters.
problems.a:
The new prior is 0.161, so the odds are 0.161 / 0.839 = 0.192. Each positive result multiplies the odds by the likelihood ratio 0.95 / 0.05 = 19, so the odds become 0.192 x 19 = 3.65 and the probability is 3.65 / 4.65 = about 0.785 (78.5%).
The prior matters because a rare condition needs strong evidence; ignoring it (the base rate fallacy) makes a positive test look far more convincing than it is.

lessons.title: Machine learning: concepts, types and workflow
yt: machine learning introduction supervised unsupervised reinforcement
overfitting underfitting bias variance train test split

blocks.x: **Machine learning (ML)** lets computers learn patterns from data instead of being programmed with explicit rules. Tom Mitchell's definition: a program learns from experience E for task T with performance P if its performance on T improves with E.
Types of learning

x: **Supervised:** labelled data (input → known output). *Classification* (predict a category: spam/not spam) and *regression* (predict a number: house price).
**Unsupervised:** no labels; find structure: *clustering* (customer groups), dimensionality reduction (PCA), association rules.
**Semi-supervised:** few labels, many unlabelled.
**Reinforcement learning:** an agent learns by **rewards** from actions in an environment (game playing, robots).

blocks.x: Data terms
Features (inputs, columns), label/target, sample (row), dataset, training set, validation set, test set. Typical split 70/15/15 or 80/20.
ML workflow

x: Define the problem and metric.
Collect data.
Clean data (missing values, duplicates, outliers).
Explore and engineer features; encode categories; **scale** numeric features.
Split into train/test (never tune on the test set).
Train a model.
Evaluate with proper metrics and cross-validation.
Tune hyper-parameters.
Deploy and monitor (data drift).

blocks.x: Generalisation

x: **Underfitting:** model too simple; high error on both train and test (high **bias**).
**Overfitting:** model memorises training data; low train error but high test error (high **variance**).

blocks.x: Remedies for overfitting: more data, simpler model, **regularisation** (L1/L2), early stopping, dropout, cross-validation. For underfitting: richer model, more features.
Bias–variance trade-off
Total error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance.
Cross-validation
**k-fold:** split data into k parts, train on k−1, test on the remaining one, repeat k times and average. Gives a more reliable estimate than one split.
Feature scaling
Min–max: x' = (x − min)/(max − min). Standardisation: z = (x − μ)/σ. Distance-based models (KNN, SVM, K-means) need scaling.
Libraries
Python: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Matplotlib; deep learning: TensorFlow, PyTorch.
Learn from training data, judge on unseen data.

qa.q: Difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
qa.a: Supervised learning uses labelled examples to predict outputs; unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data, such as clusters.

qa.q: What is overfitting and how can it be reduced?
qa.a: Overfitting is when a model fits noise in the training data and performs poorly on new data. It is reduced by more data, simpler models, regularisation, early stopping and cross-validation.

qa.q: What is the purpose of a test set?
qa.a: To estimate how well the final model performs on unseen data; it must not be used for training or tuning.

qa.q: What is k-fold cross-validation?
qa.a: The data is split into k folds; the model is trained on k−1 folds and tested on the remaining fold, repeating k times and averaging the scores.

qa.q: Why scale features?
qa.a: Algorithms that use distances or gradients are dominated by features with large ranges unless all features are brought to comparable scales.

quiz.why: The target is a continuous number.

quiz.q: A model with low training error but high test error is
Which uses rewards?
quiz.why: The agent learns from reward signals.

The test set should be used

problems.q: Differentiate between supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning with an example of each.
problems.a: Supervised: learns from labelled data (email spam or not spam). Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (grouping customers by behaviour). Reinforcement: an agent learns by trial and error with rewards (a program learning to play a game).

problems.q: Model A has 2% training error and 20% test error. Model B has 25% training error and 26% test error. Diagnose each and suggest one fix.
problems.a: Model A overfits (low bias, high variance): it memorised training data. Fixes: more data, regularisation, a simpler model, early stopping. Model B underfits (high bias): it is too simple to capture the pattern. Fixes: a more complex model, better features, longer training.

rubric.t: Model A overfitting with a fix
Model B underfitting with a fix

problems.q: Explain why the test set must stay untouched and give an example of data leakage. How does 5-fold cross-validation work for 100 samples?
problems.a:
The test set simulates unseen data; if it influences training or tuning, the measured score is too optimistic. Leakage example: scaling the whole dataset (using the test data's mean) before splitting.
5-fold cross-validation splits the data into 5 folds of 20 samples. In each of 5 rounds the model trains on 80 and tests on the remaining 20, and the 5 scores are averaged.

rubric.t: Why the test set is kept separate

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Machine learning: concepts, types and workflow

Machine learning (ML) lets computers learn patterns from data instead of being programmed with explicit rules

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Types of learning›3Data terms›4ML workflow›5Generalisation›6Bias–variance trade-off›7Cross-validation›8Feature scaling›9Libraries
🔑

Big idea

  • Machine learning (ML) lets computers learn patterns from data instead of being programmed with explicit rules
  • Tom Mitchell's definition: a program learns from experience E for task T with performance P if its performance on T improves with E
📌

Types of learning

  • Supervised: labelled data (input → known output). *Classification* (predict a category: spam/not spam) and *regression* (predict a number: house…
  • Unsupervised: no labels; find structure: *clustering* (customer groups), dimensionality reduction (PCA), association rules.
  • Semi-supervised: few labels, many unlabelled.
  • Reinforcement learning: an agent learns by rewards from actions in an environment (game playing, robots).
🧠

Data terms

  • Features (inputs, columns), label/target, sample (row), dataset, training set, validation set, test set
  • Typical split 70/15/15 or 80/20
🔄

ML workflow

  • Define the problem and metric.
  • Collect data.
  • Clean data (missing values, duplicates, outliers).
  • Explore and engineer features; encode categories; scale numeric features.
Read the full explanation
  1. Define the problem and metric.
  2. Collect data.
  3. Clean data (missing values, duplicates, outliers).
  4. Explore and engineer features; encode categories; scale numeric features.
  5. Split into train/test (never tune on the test set).
  6. Train a model.
  7. Evaluate with proper metrics and cross-validation.
  8. Tune hyper-parameters.
  9. Deploy and monitor (data drift).
🧬

Generalisation

  • Underfitting: model too simple; high error on both train and test (high bias).
  • Overfitting: model memorises training data; low train error but high test error (high variance).
📊

Bias–variance trade-off

  • Total error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise
  • Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance
🔑

Cross-validation

  • K-fold: split data into k parts, train on k−1, test on the remaining one, repeat k times and average
  • Gives a more reliable estimate than one split
📌

Feature scaling

  • Min–max: x' = (x − min)/(max − min)
  • Standardisation: z = (x − μ)/σ
  • Distance-based models (KNN, SVM, K-means) need scaling
🧠

Libraries

  • Python: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Matplotlib
  • Deep learning: TensorFlow, PyTorch
🎯 Remember Learn from training data, judge on unseen data.

lessons.title: Linear regression and gradient descent

blocks.x: **Regression** predicts a continuous value. **Simple linear regression** fits y = a + b·x.
Least squares
Choose a and b to minimise the sum of squared errors Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². b = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Worked example

import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5.]); y = np.array([2, 4, 5, 4, 5.])
b = ((x - x.mean()) * (y - y.mean())).sum() / ((x - x.mean()) ** 2).sum()
a = y.mean() - b * x.mean()
print(round(b, 3), round(a, 3), round(a + b * 6, 3))
Output:
Multiple and polynomial regression
y = w0 + w1x1 + … + wnxn. Adding powers (x², x³) fits curves; too high a degree overfits. **Regularisation:** Ridge (L2) shrinks weights, Lasso (L1) can set weights to zero (feature selection).
Evaluation metrics
MAE (mean absolute error), MSE, RMSE, and **R²** (fraction of variance explained, 1 is perfect).
Gradient descent
An iterative way to minimise a loss: repeatedly move opposite to the gradient. **w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w**, where η is the **learning rate**.

x: Too small η: slow. Too large η: overshoots or diverges.
Variants: batch (all data), **stochastic (one sample)**, mini-batch (small groups, most common).

blocks.x: Worked example
Minimise L(w) = (w − 3)², gradient 2(w − 3), start w = 0, η = 0.1: w₁ = 0.6, w₂ = 1.08, w₃ = 1.464, w₄ = 1.7712, w₅ = 2.017. The values approach the minimum at w = 3.

w = 0.0
for _ in range(5):
    w -= 0.1 * 2 * (w - 3)
    print(round(w, 4), end=" ")
Output:
Logistic regression (classification)
Uses the **sigmoid** σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) to turn a linear score into a probability between 0 and 1; classify as 1 if probability ≥ 0.5. Loss: cross-entropy.
Gradient descent walks downhill on the loss surface; the learning rate is the step size.

qa.q: What does least squares minimise?
qa.a: The sum of squared differences between actual and predicted values.

qa.q: Why is the learning rate important?
qa.a: It sets the step size of gradient descent. If too small, training is very slow; if too large, the updates overshoot or diverge.

qa.q: Difference between Ridge and Lasso regression?
qa.a: Ridge adds an L2 penalty that shrinks weights; Lasso adds an L1 penalty that can reduce some weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection.

qa.q: What does R-squared measure?
qa.a: The proportion of the variance in the target explained by the model; 1 means a perfect fit.

qa.q: Why is logistic regression used for classification though called regression?
qa.a: It models the probability of a class using the sigmoid of a linear function and then thresholds that probability.

quiz.q: In the worked example the slope b equals
Gradient descent update rule
quiz.why: Move against the gradient to reduce loss.

quiz.q: Which regularisation can zero out coefficients?
Sigmoid outputs values in
quiz.why: This is why it models probabilities.

quiz.q: Mini-batch gradient descent uses
o: a small subset of samples per update
quiz.why: A compromise between batch and stochastic.

visuals.title: A loss function with one minimum at w = 3 (gradient descent walks downhill)
visuals.data: y = (x-3)^2 ; xmin=-1 ; xmax=7

problems.q: For hours studied x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and marks y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5 the fitted line is y = 2.2 + 0.6x. Predict the mark for 6 hours and explain what the slope means.
problems.a: y = 2.2 + 0.6 x 6 = 5.8. The slope 0.6 means each extra hour of study adds 0.6 marks (out of 10) on average.

problems.q: The predictions of the line for x = 1 to 5 are 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2. Compute the sum of squared errors and R squared. The mean of y is 4.
problems.a: Errors (y - prediction): -0.8, 0.6, 1.0, -0.6, -0.2. Squares: 0.64, 0.36, 1.00, 0.36, 0.04, so SSE = 2.4. Total variation SST = sum of (y - 4)^2 = 4 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 6. R squared = 1 - 2.4 / 6 = 0.6, meaning the line explains 60% of the variation.

problems.q: Minimise L(w) = (w - 3)^2 by gradient descent from w = 0 with learning rate 0.1. Give w after two steps. What happens with learning rate 1.1?
problems.a:
Gradient = 2(w - 3). Step 1: gradient at 0 is -6, w = 0 - 0.1 x (-6) = 0.6. Step 2: gradient at 0.6 is -4.8, w = 0.6 + 0.48 = 1.08. It moves towards 3.
With rate 1.1: w1 = 0 + 6.6 = 6.6, then gradient 7.2 gives w2 = 6.6 - 7.92 = -1.32. Each step overshoots further (distance from 3 grows 3, 3.6, 4.32), so it diverges.
