ML mein model data se seekhta hai. Supervised mein labels hote hain (regression, classification), unsupervised mein nahi (clustering). Underfitting = high bias, overfitting = high variance. Test set ko sirf aakhri mein use karo.

lessons.title: Linear regression and gradient descent
yt: linear regression gradient descent from scratch

blocks.x: **Linear regression** fits a straight line y = w x + b to data. For many features: y = w1 x1 + ... + wn xn + b.
Loss function
**Mean squared error (MSE)** = (1/m) sum (prediction - actual)^2. Training means finding w and b that minimise MSE.
Gradient descent
Repeat: w = w - alpha dL/dw and b = b - alpha dL/db, where **alpha** is the **learning rate**. For MSE with y_hat = w x + b:

x: dL/dw = (2/m) sum (y_hat - y) x
dL/db = (2/m) sum (y_hat - y)

blocks.x: Worked example
Data (1,3), (2,5), (3,7) (true line y = 2x + 1). Start w = 0, b = 0, alpha = 0.1.
The loss collapses quickly and the parameters approach w = 2 and b = 1.

import numpy as np
X = np.array([1, 2, 3.]); Y = np.array([3, 5, 7.]); w = b = 0.0; lr = 0.1
for i in range(3):
    e = w * X + b - Y
    print(i, round((e ** 2).mean(), 4))
    w -= lr * (2 * e * X).mean(); b -= lr * 2 * e.mean()
print(round(w, 4), round(b, 4))   # 2.0439 0.9076
Choosing the learning rate
Too small: slow. Too large: overshoots and diverges. Common variants: batch, **stochastic (SGD)** (one sample at a time), **mini-batch**.
Normal equation
w = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y gives the answer directly but is expensive for many features.
R-squared
R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot. 1 is perfect; 0 means no better than predicting the mean.
Hindi saransh

Linear regression y = wx + b ko MSE minimise karke seekhte hain. Gradient descent mein parameters ko gradient ki ulti disha mein alpha step se badalte hain. Alpha bahut bada ho to diverge, bahut chhota ho to dheere.
Gradient points uphill, so we subtract it to go downhill.

qa.q: What is the loss function used in linear regression?
qa.a: Mean squared error, the average of squared differences between predictions and true values.

qa.q: Write the gradient descent update rule.
qa.a: parameter = parameter - alpha x (gradient of the loss with respect to that parameter).

qa.q: What happens if the learning rate is too large?
qa.a: Steps overshoot the minimum, so the loss may oscillate or diverge.

qa.q: What is the difference between batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent?
qa.a: Batch uses all samples for each update, stochastic uses one sample, and mini-batch uses a small group (for example 32), balancing speed and stability.

qa.q: What does R-squared measure?
qa.a: The fraction of variance in the target explained by the model.

lessons.title: Logistic regression and classification metrics
yt: precision recall f1 score confusion matrix

blocks.x: **Logistic regression** is a classifier. It computes a linear score z = w.x + b and squeezes it with the **sigmoid** function: p = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)), a probability between 0 and 1. If p >= 0.5 predict class 1.
Properties of sigmoid
sigmoid(0) = 0.5, large positive z gives about 1, large negative z gives about 0, and the derivative is p(1 - p).
Loss: binary cross-entropy
L = -[ y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p) ]. It punishes confident wrong answers heavily. Training uses gradient descent.
Confusion matrix
Metrics

x: **Accuracy** = (TP + TN) / total
**Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) (of predicted positives, how many are right)
**Recall** = TP / (TP + FN) (of real positives, how many found)

blocks.x: Worked example
When accuracy misleads
With 99% healthy patients, a model that always says "healthy" has 99% accuracy but 0% recall for disease. Use recall, precision or F1 on **imbalanced data**.
Threshold

Raising the threshold increases precision and lowers recall; lowering it does the opposite. The **ROC curve** plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate for all thresholds; the area under it (AUC) summarises ranking quality.
Multi-class
Softmax turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1.
Hindi saransh
Logistic regression sigmoid se probability deta hai. Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN). Imbalanced data mein accuracy dhokha deti hai, F1 use karo.
Precision asks "of my alarms, how many were real?" Recall asks "of the real events, how many did I catch?"

qa.q: What does the sigmoid function do?
qa.a: It maps any real number to the range (0, 1) so the output can be read as a probability.

qa.q: Why is accuracy a poor metric for imbalanced data?
qa.a: A model that always predicts the majority class gets high accuracy while missing every minority case.

qa.q: Define precision and recall.
qa.a: Precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN).

qa.q: What is the effect of raising the classification threshold?
qa.a: Fewer positives are predicted, so precision usually rises and recall falls.

qa.q: What is AUC?
qa.a: The area under the ROC curve; 1.0 is perfect ranking and 0.5 is random.

lessons.title: Decision trees: entropy and information gain
yt: decision tree entropy information gain example

blocks.x: A **decision tree** classifies by asking a series of questions. Each internal node tests a feature, each branch is an outcome, and each leaf gives a class.
Entropy
For classes with proportions p_i: **Entropy = - sum p_i log2 p_i**. It is 0 for a pure node and 1 for a 50/50 split of two classes.
Information gain
Gain(S, A) = Entropy(S) - sum (|S_v| / |S|) Entropy(S_v). At each node choose the feature with the highest gain (ID3). **Gini impurity** = 1 - sum p_i^2 is used by CART.
Worked example (play tennis, 14 days: 9 Yes, 5 No)

Entropy(S) = -(9/14) log2(9/14) - (5/14) log2(5/14) = **0.940**. Splitting by Outlook gives Sunny (2 Yes, 3 No) entropy 0.971, Overcast (4 Yes, 0 No) entropy 0, Rain (3 Yes, 2 No) entropy 0.971. Weighted entropy = (5/14)(0.971) + (4/14)(0) + (5/14)(0.971) = 0.694. **Gain(Outlook) = 0.940 - 0.694 = 0.247**, the largest among the features, so Outlook becomes the root.

from math import log2
H = lambda a, b: -sum(x/(a+b) * log2(x/(a+b)) for x in (a, b) if x)
print(round(H(9, 5), 3))                                          # 0.94
print(round(H(9, 5) - (5/14*H(2, 3) + 4/14*H(4, 0) + 5/14*H(3, 2)), 3))   # 0.247
Overfitting and pruning
A very deep tree memorises training data. Limit depth, require a minimum samples per leaf, or prune after training.
Ensembles

x: **Random forest:** many trees on random subsets of data and features; predictions are averaged or voted. Reduces variance.
**Gradient boosting** (XGBoost): trees added one after another, each correcting the previous errors.

blocks.x: Hindi saransh

Decision tree har node par ek feature ke hisaab se sawaal poochta hai. Entropy impurity naapti hai (9 Yes, 5 No ke liye 0.940). Information gain sabse zyada wala feature root banta hai (Outlook = 0.247). Random forest kai trees ka vote hai.
Pure node means entropy 0. The best split is the one that gets us closest to pure children.

qa.q: What is entropy in a decision tree?
qa.a: A measure of impurity: -sum p_i log2 p_i. It is 0 when all samples are in one class and highest when classes are evenly mixed.

qa.q: How does the tree choose the splitting feature?
qa.a: It picks the feature with the highest information gain (or lowest Gini impurity for CART).

qa.q: Why do deep trees overfit and how do we limit them?
qa.a: They can create a leaf for every training point. Limit the depth, set a minimum leaf size or prune the tree.

qa.q: What is a random forest?
qa.a: An ensemble of many decision trees trained on random samples of rows and features, combining their votes to reduce variance.

qa.q: What is the Gini impurity of a 50/50 node?

lessons.title: Neural networks and backpropagation

blocks.x: A **neuron** computes z = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + b and applies an **activation function** a = f(z). A **neural network** stacks layers of neurons: input layer, one or more hidden layers, output layer. Without a non-linear activation, many layers collapse into a single linear model.
Activation functions
Training loop

x: **Forward pass:** compute outputs and the loss.
**Backward pass (backpropagation):** apply the chain rule to get the gradient of the loss for each weight.
**Update:** w = w - alpha dL/dw.

blocks.x: Worked example: one sigmoid neuron
Inputs x = (1, 2), weights w = (0.5, -0.3), bias b = 0.1, target y = 1, loss L = (a - y)^2 / 2.
The negative gradients mean increasing the weights will reduce the loss.

import math
x = [1, 2]; w = [0.5, -0.3]; b = 0.1; y = 1
z = sum(i * j for i, j in zip(x, w)) + b; a = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))
dz = (a - y) * a * (1 - a)
print(z, a, round((a - y) ** 2 / 2, 3), dz, [dz * i for i in x])   # 0.0 0.5 0.125 -0.125 [-0.125, -0.25]
Problems in deep networks

x: **Vanishing gradient:** sigmoid/tanh shrink gradients across many layers; ReLU and good initialisation help.
**Overfitting:** use dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, early stopping.

blocks.x: Optimisers
SGD, momentum, RMSprop and **Adam** (adaptive learning rates; the common default).
Hindi saransh
Neuron weighted sum nikal kar activation lagata hai. Backpropagation chain rule se har weight ka gradient nikalta hai. ReLU hidden layers ke liye default hai. Example: z = 0, a = 0.5, loss 0.125.
Backprop is just the chain rule applied layer by layer, from output to input.

qa.q: Why do we need non-linear activation functions?
qa.a: Without them any stack of layers is equivalent to one linear transformation, so the network could not learn non-linear patterns.

qa.q: What is backpropagation?
qa.a: An efficient use of the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, moving from the output layer backwards.

qa.q: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
qa.a: In deep networks with sigmoid or tanh, gradients get multiplied by small numbers layer after layer and become almost zero in early layers, so they stop learning. ReLU reduces this.

qa.q: What does softmax do?
qa.a: It converts a vector of scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1, for multi-class output.

qa.q: Name two ways to reduce overfitting in neural networks.
qa.a: Dropout and weight decay (L2); also data augmentation or early stopping.

lessons.title: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) basics
yt: CNN output size formula padding stride

blocks.x: Images have too many pixels for a fully connected layer (a 224x224 colour image has 150,528 inputs). A **CNN** uses small shared filters that slide over the image, exploiting that nearby pixels are related.
Convolution layer

A **kernel** (for example 3x3) slides across the input; at each position it multiplies and sums to produce one output value. The same weights are reused everywhere (**weight sharing**), so there are few parameters and the layer detects a pattern wherever it occurs (translation equivariance). Early layers learn edges, deeper layers learn shapes and objects.
Output size
Output = floor( (N - F + 2P) / S ) + 1, where N is input size, F kernel size, P padding, S stride.
Parameters
Parameters = (F x F x C_in + 1) x C_out. A 5x5 kernel on 3 channels with 6 filters: (5 x 5 x 3 + 1) x 6 = **456**.
Pooling
**Max pooling** (2x2, stride 2) keeps the largest value in each window, halving height and width and giving small translation tolerance. It has no learnable parameters.
Typical architecture
Input, [Conv, ReLU, Pool] repeated, flatten, fully connected layers, softmax. Examples: LeNet-5, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet (skip connections that let very deep networks train).
Training tricks
Data augmentation (flips, crops), batch normalisation, dropout, and **transfer learning**: reuse a network pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tune it on your small dataset.

CNN chhote filters image par slide karke features nikalta hai. Output size = floor((N - F + 2P)/S) + 1. 32 aur 5x5 kernel se 28 milta hai. Max pooling size aadhi kar deta hai. Transfer learning mein pretrained network reuse karte hain.

lessons.title: Phases of a compiler and lexical analysis

blocks.x: A **compiler** translates source code to target code. Phases: **lexical analysis** (tokens), **syntax analysis** (parse tree), **semantic analysis** (type checking), **intermediate code generation**, **code optimisation**, **code generation**; the symbol table and error handler are used throughout. Front end (analysis) and back end (synthesis).
Lexical analysis

The lexer groups characters into **tokens** (identifier, keyword, number, operator) using regular expressions and finite automata. For `int x = a + 10;` the tokens are: int, x, =, a, +, 10, ; : **7 tokens**. Identifier: letter (letter | digit)*; integer: digit+.
Syntax analysis

Grammars (context-free) and parsers. **Top-down** (LL(1), recursive descent) and **bottom-up** (LR, SLR, LALR). FIRST and FOLLOW sets build the LL(1) table. Ambiguous grammars have more than one parse tree.
Intermediate code
Three-address code: `t1 = b * c; t2 = a + t1` for a + b * c. Optimisations: constant folding (2 + 3 becomes 5), dead-code elimination, common sub-expression elimination, loop-invariant motion.
Hindi saransh
Compiler ke phases: lexical, syntax, semantic, intermediate code, optimisation, code generation. Lexer tokens banata hai.
The lexer is built from regular expressions; the parser from context-free grammars.

qa.a: Evaluating constant expressions at compile time, such as 2 + 3 to 5.

lessons.title: Line drawing (Bresenham) and 2D transformations

blocks.x: **Bresenham's line algorithm** draws a line using only integer arithmetic. For a line with 0 < slope < 1 from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1): dx = x1 - x0, dy = y1 - y0, initial decision p = 2 dy - dx. At each x step: if p < 0 plot (x + 1, y) and p += 2 dy; otherwise plot (x + 1, y + 1) and p += 2 dy - 2 dx. Example: (0, 0) to (5, 2): dx = 5, dy = 2, p0 = -1. Points: **(0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (3,1), (4,2), (5,2)**.
2D transformations (homogeneous matrices)

x: Translation by (tx, ty); scaling by (sx, sy); rotation by t: x' = x cos t - y sin t, y' = x sin t + y cos t.
Rotating (3, 4) by 90 degrees about the origin gives **(-4, 3)**.
Composite transformations are matrix products; order matters (rotate then translate differs from translate then rotate).

blocks.x: Other topics
Viewport and clipping (Cohen-Sutherland, Sutherland-Hodgman), 3D projection (parallel and perspective), hidden-surface removal (z-buffer), shading models (flat, Gouraud, Phong).

lessons.title: Classical ciphers and RSA

blocks.x: **Goals of security (CIA):** confidentiality, integrity, availability; plus authentication and non-repudiation.
Classical ciphers

**Caesar cipher:** shift every letter by k. With k = 3, HELLO becomes **KHOOR**. Only 25 keys, so brute force breaks it. Others: Vigenere (repeating key), Playfair, Hill, rail fence, one-time pad (unbreakable if the key is random, as long as the message and never reused).
Symmetric and asymmetric

Symmetric (AES, DES): one shared key; fast. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public and private keys; slower; solves key distribution and enables digital signatures. AES uses 128-bit blocks and 128, 192 or 256-bit keys.
RSA worked example

Choose primes p = 61 and q = 53. n = p q = **3233**; phi = (p - 1)(q - 1) = **3120**. Choose e = 17 (coprime with phi). Then d = e^-1 mod phi = **2753**. Public key (17, 3233); private key (2753, 3233). Encrypt m = 65: c = 65^17 mod 3233 = **2790**. Decrypt: 2790^2753 mod 3233 = **65**.
Real RSA uses 2048-bit or larger n and padding (OAEP); textbook RSA as shown is insecure.
Hashing and signatures
A hash (SHA-256) maps data to a fixed-size digest: one-way, collision resistant. A digital signature is the hash encrypted with the private key; anyone can verify it with the public key.
Hindi saransh
Caesar cipher mein har letter k jagah shift hota hai. RSA mein n = pq, d = e^-1 mod phi; public key se encrypt, private key se decrypt.
Never use textbook RSA or a Caesar cipher to protect real data.

lessons.title: Text processing, TF-IDF and n-grams
yt: tf idf and n gram language model

blocks.x: **NLP pipeline:** tokenisation, lower-casing, stop-word removal, stemming (cut suffixes) or lemmatisation (dictionary form), part-of-speech tagging, parsing. **Bag of words** counts words and ignores order. **TF-IDF** weighs a word by how often it appears in a document (TF) and how rare it is across documents: idf = ln(N / df). Example: 3 documents, "cat" in 2 of them, TF in a 3-word document = 1/3; idf = ln(3/2) = 0.405; TF-IDF = **0.135**. A word in every document gets idf = 0. **Cosine similarity** = A.B / (|A||B|): vectors [1,1,0] and [1,0,1] give **0.5**. **N-gram language model:** P(w2 | w1) = count(w1 w2) / count(w1). In "the cat sat the cat ran the dog sat": count("the cat") = 2 and count("the") = 3, so P(cat | the) = **2/3**. Smoothing (add-one) handles unseen n-grams. Perplexity measures model quality (lower is better). **Modern NLP:** word embeddings (word2vec), transformers, BERT and GPT-style models using attention.

TF-IDF = word ki frequency x rarity. Bigram probability = count(w1 w2) / count(w1).
A word present in all documents carries no discriminating power.

lessons.title: Association rules (Apriori) and k-means clustering
yt: apriori algorithm support confidence k means

blocks.x: **Association rules** find items bought together. For rule A -> B: **support** = P(A and B); **confidence** = P(B | A) = support(A and B) / support(A); **lift** = confidence / support(B) (lift above 1 means a positive association). Apriori principle: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, so we prune candidates. Example with 5 baskets: {bread, milk}, {bread, butter}, {bread, milk, butter}, {milk, butter}, {bread, milk, butter}. support(bread) = 4/5 = 0.8; support(milk) = 0.8; support(bread, milk) = 3/5 = 0.6; confidence(bread -> milk) = 0.6/0.8 = **0.75**; lift = 0.75/0.8 = **0.94** (slightly below 1, so no useful positive association).
k-means

x: Choose k centres. 2. Assign each point to the nearest centre. 3. Recompute the centres as means. 4. Repeat until no change. Example: points 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12 with k = 2 and initial centres 1 and 10 converge to centres **2** and **11**. Limitations: choose k beforehand, sensitive to initial centres and outliers; elbow method and silhouette score help choose k.

blocks.x: **Other methods:** decision trees, naive Bayes, DBSCAN (density-based), hierarchical clustering.
Hindi saransh
Support, confidence aur lift se association rules judge karte hain. k-means mein centres ko mean se update karte hain.
Lift above 1 means the items occur together more often than by chance.

qa.a: All subsets of a frequent itemset must also be frequent.

qa.a: k must be given in advance and results depend on the initial centres.

Visual lesson

Association rules (Apriori) and k-means clustering

Association rules find items bought together

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
1Big idea›2K-means
🔑

Big idea

  • Association rules find items bought together
  • For rule A -> B: support = P(A and B)
  • Confidence = P(B | A) = support(A and B) / support(A)
  • Lift = confidence / support(B) (lift above 1 means a positive association)
Read the full explanation

Association rules find items bought together. For rule A -> B: support = P(A and B); confidence = P(B | A) = support(A and B) / support(A); lift = confidence / support(B) (lift above 1 means a positive association). Apriori principle: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, so we prune candidates. Example with 5 baskets: {bread, milk}, {bread, butter}, {bread, milk, butter}, {milk, butter}, {bread, milk, butter}. support(bread) = 4/5 = 0.8; support(milk) = 0.8; support(bread, milk) = 3/5 = 0.6; confidence(bread -> milk) = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75; lift = 0.75/0.8 = 0.94 (slightly below 1, so no useful positive association).

📌

K-means

  • Choose k centres. 2. Assign each point to the nearest centre. 3. Recompute the centres as means. 4. Repeat until no change. Example: points 1, 2, 3…
🎯 Remember Lift above 1 means the items occur together more often than by chance.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

Support, confidence aur lift se association rules judge karte hain. k-means mein centres ko mean se update karte hain.

lessons.title: Communication skills

blocks.x: Communication is the exchange of information, ideas or feelings between a sender and a receiver. The process has a sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding and feedback; noise can block it. It can be verbal (spoken or written) or non-verbal (body language, gestures, eye contact). The 7 Cs are clear, concise, correct, complete, courteous, concrete and considerate. Good listening, clear writing and polite behaviour make communication effective.
Deep dive: the communication process

Communication needs a sender who has an idea, a message put into words or signs (encoding), a channel (speech, phone, e-mail, letter), a receiver who decodes the message and feedback that tells the sender it was understood. Noise (a loud room, poor network, unclear words) can distort the message at any step. Two-way communication has feedback; one-way communication (a TV broadcast) does not.
Deep dive: verbal and non-verbal communication

Verbal communication uses words: oral (face to face, phone call, meeting) or written (letter, e-mail, report, text message). Non-verbal communication uses body language: posture, facial expression, eye contact, gestures, tone of voice and personal space. Formal communication follows rules and a chain of command (office memo); informal communication is casual (chat with friends). Communication also flows upward, downward and sideways in an organisation.
Deep dive: the 7 Cs and barriers

Clear: one idea in simple words. Concise: short without losing meaning. Correct: right facts and grammar. Complete: all needed information. Courteous: polite and respectful. Concrete: specific facts and figures. Considerate: keeps the receiver in mind. Barriers are physical (noise, distance), language (jargon, accents), emotional (anger, fear), cultural (different customs), and attitude (not listening). They are overcome by active listening, simple language, checking understanding and respecting differences.
Deep dive: listening, speaking and writing

Active listening means giving full attention, not interrupting, nodding, asking questions and summarising what was said. Good speaking uses clear voice, correct pace, and eye contact. Good writing has a greeting, a clear body in short paragraphs and a polite closing; an e-mail also needs a meaningful subject line. A telephone call should begin with a greeting and name, speak clearly and end politely.
Hindi saransh
Communication = bhejne wala, sandesh, madhyam, prapt karne wala aur feedback. 7 Cs yaad rakhein.
Barriers: physical, language, emotional, cultural and attitude. Feedback completes the cycle.

Visual lesson

Communication skills

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2The communication process›3Verbal and non-verbal…›4The 7 Cs and barriers›5Listening, speaking and…
🔑

Big idea

  • Communication is the exchange of information, ideas or feelings between a sender and a receiver
  • The process has a sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding and feedback
  • Noise can block it
  • It can be verbal (spoken or written) or non-verbal (body language, gestures, eye contact)
Read the full explanation

Communication is the exchange of information, ideas or feelings between a sender and a receiver. The process has a sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding and feedback; noise can block it. It can be verbal (spoken or written) or non-verbal (body language, gestures, eye contact). The 7 Cs are clear, concise, correct, complete, courteous, concrete and considerate. Good listening, clear writing and polite behaviour make communication effective.

🔄

The communication process

  • Communication needs a sender who has an idea, a message put into words or signs (encoding), a channel (speech, phone, e-mail, letter), a receiver who…
  • Noise (a loud room, poor network, unclear words) can distort the message at any step
  • Two-way communication has feedback
  • One-way communication (a TV broadcast) does not
Read the full explanation

Communication needs a sender who has an idea, a message put into words or signs (encoding), a channel (speech, phone, e-mail, letter), a receiver who decodes the message and feedback that tells the sender it was understood. Noise (a loud room, poor network, unclear words) can distort the message at any step. Two-way communication has feedback; one-way communication (a TV broadcast) does not.

🧠

Verbal and non-verbal communication

  • Verbal communication uses words: oral (face to face, phone call, meeting) or written (letter, e-mail, report, text message)
  • Non-verbal communication uses body language: posture, facial expression, eye contact, gestures, tone of voice and personal space
  • Formal communication follows rules and a chain of command (office memo)
  • Informal communication is casual (chat with friends)
Read the full explanation

Verbal communication uses words: oral (face to face, phone call, meeting) or written (letter, e-mail, report, text message). Non-verbal communication uses body language: posture, facial expression, eye contact, gestures, tone of voice and personal space. Formal communication follows rules and a chain of command (office memo); informal communication is casual (chat with friends). Communication also flows upward, downward and sideways in an organisation.

🌟

The 7 Cs and barriers

  • Clear: one idea in simple words
  • Concise: short without losing meaning
  • Correct: right facts and grammar
  • Complete: all needed information
Read the full explanation

Clear: one idea in simple words. Concise: short without losing meaning. Correct: right facts and grammar. Complete: all needed information. Courteous: polite and respectful. Concrete: specific facts and figures. Considerate: keeps the receiver in mind. Barriers are physical (noise, distance), language (jargon, accents), emotional (anger, fear), cultural (different customs), and attitude (not listening). They are overcome by active listening, simple language, checking understanding and respecting differences.

✍️

Listening, speaking and writing

  • Active listening means giving full attention, not interrupting, nodding, asking questions and summarising what was said
  • Good speaking uses clear voice, correct pace, and eye contact
  • Good writing has a greeting, a clear body in short paragraphs and a polite closing
  • An e-mail also needs a meaningful subject line
Read the full explanation

Active listening means giving full attention, not interrupting, nodding, asking questions and summarising what was said. Good speaking uses clear voice, correct pace, and eye contact. Good writing has a greeting, a clear body in short paragraphs and a polite closing; an e-mail also needs a meaningful subject line. A telephone call should begin with a greeting and name, speak clearly and end politely.

lessons.title: Self-management skills

blocks.x: Self-management is the ability to manage your own thoughts, feelings, time and actions to reach goals. It includes knowing your strengths and weaknesses, positive attitude, self-confidence, self-motivation, good grooming and hygiene, time management, stress management, goal setting (SMART goals) and working well with others. Self-awareness is the base; SWOT analysis helps list strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
Deep dive: self-awareness and SWOT

Self-awareness means knowing your own strengths, weaknesses, values, interests and habits. A SWOT analysis lists Strengths and Weaknesses (inside you) and Opportunities and Threats (outside you). Knowing them helps you pick a career and improve. Strengths are things you do well; weaknesses are areas to improve; opportunities are chances you can use; threats are things that may harm your progress.
Deep dive: attitude, confidence and motivation

Attitude is the way you think and react. A positive attitude looks for solutions; a negative one sees only problems. Self-confidence is belief in your own abilities and grows with practice and success. Self-motivation is the inner drive to do work without being pushed; it comes from clear goals, rewards, interest and positive self-talk. Habits of positive people: they smile, thank others, learn from failure and keep trying.
Deep dive: time and stress management

Time management means planning and using time wisely: make a to-do list, set priorities (urgent and important first), avoid procrastination and keep a timetable. A priority matrix has four boxes: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, and neither. Stress is the body's response to pressure; healthy ways to manage it are exercise, enough sleep, hobbies, deep breathing, talking to someone and a balanced diet.
Deep dive: grooming, hygiene and working with others

Grooming is taking care of your appearance: clean neat clothes, combed hair, clean nails and polished shoes. Personal hygiene includes bathing daily, brushing teeth, washing hands and wearing clean clothes. Teamwork means working together for a common goal: respect others, listen, share work, communicate openly and accept feedback. Good etiquette includes punctuality, politeness and honesty.

🔑

Big idea

  • Self-management is the ability to manage your own thoughts, feelings, time and actions to reach goals
  • It includes knowing your strengths and weaknesses, positive attitude, self-confidence, self-motivation, good grooming and hygiene, time management…
  • Self-awareness is the base

Read the full explanation

Self-management is the ability to manage your own thoughts, feelings, time and actions to reach goals. It includes knowing your strengths and weaknesses, positive attitude, self-confidence, self-motivation, good grooming and hygiene, time management, stress management, goal setting (SMART goals) and working well with others. Self-awareness is the base; SWOT analysis helps list strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.

🕰️

Self-awareness and SWOT

  • Self-awareness means knowing your own strengths, weaknesses, values, interests and habits
  • A SWOT analysis lists Strengths and Weaknesses (inside you) and Opportunities and Threats (outside you)
  • Knowing them helps you pick a career and improve
  • Strengths are things you do well
Read the full explanation

Self-awareness means knowing your own strengths, weaknesses, values, interests and habits. A SWOT analysis lists Strengths and Weaknesses (inside you) and Opportunities and Threats (outside you). Knowing them helps you pick a career and improve. Strengths are things you do well; weaknesses are areas to improve; opportunities are chances you can use; threats are things that may harm your progress.

🧠

Attitude, confidence and motivation

  • Attitude is the way you think and react
  • A positive attitude looks for solutions
  • A negative one sees only problems
  • Self-confidence is belief in your own abilities and grows with practice and success
Read the full explanation

Attitude is the way you think and react. A positive attitude looks for solutions; a negative one sees only problems. Self-confidence is belief in your own abilities and grows with practice and success. Self-motivation is the inner drive to do work without being pushed; it comes from clear goals, rewards, interest and positive self-talk. Habits of positive people: they smile, thank others, learn from failure and keep trying.

🌟

Time and stress management

  • Time management means planning and using time wisely: make a to-do list, set priorities (urgent and important first), avoid procrastination and keep…
  • A priority matrix has four boxes: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, and neither
  • Stress is the body's response to pressure
  • Healthy ways to manage it are exercise, enough sleep, hobbies, deep breathing, talking to someone and a balanced diet
Read the full explanation

Time management means planning and using time wisely: make a to-do list, set priorities (urgent and important first), avoid procrastination and keep a timetable. A priority matrix has four boxes: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, and neither. Stress is the body's response to pressure; healthy ways to manage it are exercise, enough sleep, hobbies, deep breathing, talking to someone and a balanced diet.

🚀

Grooming, hygiene and working with others

  • Grooming is taking care of your appearance: clean neat clothes, combed hair, clean nails and polished shoes
  • Personal hygiene includes bathing daily, brushing teeth, washing hands and wearing clean clothes
  • Teamwork means working together for a common goal: respect others, listen, share work, communicate openly and accept feedback
  • Good etiquette includes punctuality, politeness and honesty
Read the full explanation

Grooming is taking care of your appearance: clean neat clothes, combed hair, clean nails and polished shoes. Personal hygiene includes bathing daily, brushing teeth, washing hands and wearing clean clothes. Teamwork means working together for a common goal: respect others, listen, share work, communicate openly and accept feedback. Good etiquette includes punctuality, politeness and honesty.

🧮

SWOTStrengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
Priority matrixurgent and important first
Stress reliefexercise, sleep, hobbies, breathing
🎯 Remember A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound.

lessons.title: ICT skills

blocks.x: ICT (Information and Communication Technology) covers devices and tools used to store, process and share information: computers, phones, the internet and software. Basic ICT skills include using a keyboard and mouse, word processing, spreadsheets, e-mail, browsing and online safety. Hardware is the physical part of a computer; software is the set of programs. Input devices (keyboard, mouse) send data in; output devices (monitor, printer) show results; the CPU processes data; memory and storage hold it.
Deep dive: computer hardware

A computer has input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam), a processing unit (CPU, the brain), memory (RAM is temporary and fast; ROM is permanent), storage (hard disk, SSD, pen drive) and output devices (monitor, printer, speakers). The CPU has an ALU for arithmetic and logic and a control unit that directs operations. Data size: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB.
Deep dive: software and operating systems

Software is of two kinds: system software (operating system such as Windows, Linux, Android; utilities; drivers) and application software (word processor, spreadsheet, browser, games). The operating system manages hardware, files, memory and programs and provides the user interface. A file has a name and an extension (.docx, .xlsx, .jpg, .pdf, .mp3) that shows its type. Folders organise files.
Deep dive: the internet and e-mail

The internet is a global network of computers. The World Wide Web is a collection of web pages reached with a browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) using a URL. A search engine (Google, Bing) finds information. E-mail has an address (name@domain), fields To, Cc, Bcc, Subject and Attachment. Safe use: strong passwords, no sharing of personal data, avoiding unknown links, logging out of shared computers.
Deep dive: digital citizenship

Cyber safety means using technology responsibly. Cyberbullying is harassing others online; plagiarism is copying work without credit; copyright protects an author's work. Phishing tricks people into giving passwords. A strong password has upper and lower case letters, digits and symbols. Antivirus software protects against viruses and malware. Backing up data avoids loss.
Hindi saransh
ICT = computer, phone aur internet se jaankari bhejna aur sambhalna. Hardware chhoo sakte hain, software nahi.
Hardware is touched; software is not. 1 byte = 8 bits.

Read the full explanation

ICT (Information and Communication Technology) covers devices and tools used to store, process and share information: computers, phones, the internet and software. Basic ICT skills include using a keyboard and mouse, word processing, spreadsheets, e-mail, browsing and online safety. Hardware is the physical part of a computer; software is the set of programs. Input devices (keyboard, mouse) send data in; output devices (monitor, printer) show results; the CPU processes data; memory and storage hold it.

🕰️

Computer hardware

  • A computer has input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam), a processing unit (CPU, the brain), memory (RAM is temporary and fast
  • ROM is permanent), storage (hard disk, SSD, pen drive) and output devices (monitor, printer, speakers)
  • The CPU has an ALU for arithmetic and logic and a control unit that directs operations
  • Data size: 1 byte = 8 bits

A computer has input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam), a processing unit (CPU, the brain), memory (RAM is temporary and fast; ROM is permanent), storage (hard disk, SSD, pen drive) and output devices (monitor, printer, speakers). lessons.title: Entrepreneurial skills

blocks.x: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business, taking risks to earn profit and create jobs. Entrepreneurship needs ideas, planning, resources and risk-taking. Qualities: creativity, leadership, risk-taking, decision-making, hard work and communication. Profit = selling price - cost price; loss when cost price is more. Sectors: primary, secondary and tertiary; businesses can be small, medium or large. Government schemes such as Startup India and Make in India support entrepreneurs.
Deep dive: who is an entrepreneur

An entrepreneur sees a need, develops an idea, arranges resources (money, people, materials) and starts a business, accepting the risk of loss for the chance of profit. Entrepreneurs create jobs, bring new products and help the economy grow. Famous examples include Dhirubhai Ambani, Ratan Tata, Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw and Falguni Nayar. An intrapreneur creates new ideas inside an existing company.
Deep dive: qualities and the business idea

Qualities: creativity, risk-taking, leadership, self-confidence, hard work, decision-making, communication, problem solving and willingness to learn from failure. A business idea comes from a need or problem in the market. Market research asks who the customers are, what they need and what competitors offer. A business plan describes the product, target customers, costs, price, marketing and expected profit.
Deep dive: types and sectors of business

Businesses may be sole proprietorship (one owner), partnership (two or more owners), company or cooperative. By size: micro, small, medium and large. By sector: primary (farming, mining), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services such as banking, transport and teaching). Sources of money: own savings, family, loans from banks, investors and government schemes.
Deep dive: profit, loss and marketing

Profit = selling price - cost price (when SP is more than CP). Loss = cost price - selling price. Profit percent = profit/CP x 100 and loss percent = loss/CP x 100. Marketing is promoting and selling products; the 4 Ps are product, price, place and promotion. Customer satisfaction, quality and honest dealing build a brand. Entrepreneurs must keep accounts of income and expenses.

Profit = SP - CP; Profit % = (Profit/CP) x 100.

lessons.title: Green skills

blocks.x: Green skills are the knowledge and abilities needed to live and work in a way that protects the environment. They support sustainable development: meeting present needs without harming future generations. Key ideas are the 3 Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), saving energy and water, renewable energy, waste management and green jobs. Pollution, global warming and loss of biodiversity are major environmental problems.
Deep dive: environment and sustainable development

The environment is everything around us: air, water, soil, plants and animals. Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It balances economic growth, social well-being and environmental protection. India has set targets for clean energy, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (17 goals) guide the world.
Deep dive: pollution and climate change

Air pollution comes from vehicles, factories and burning waste; water pollution from sewage, chemicals and plastics; soil pollution from pesticides and garbage; noise pollution from traffic and loudspeakers. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat and causes global warming and climate change. The ozone layer protects us from ultraviolet rays and is damaged by CFCs.
Deep dive: saving resources and energy

Save water by fixing leaks, harvesting rainwater and using drip irrigation. Save electricity by using LED bulbs, switching off unused devices and using star-rated appliances. Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal) are replaced naturally; non-renewable sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas) are limited. Public transport, cycling and carpooling reduce fuel use.
Deep dive: waste management and green jobs

Waste is biodegradable (food, paper, leaves) or non-biodegradable (plastic, glass, metal). Segregation into wet and dry waste helps recycling; composting turns wet waste into manure. E-waste from old electronics needs safe disposal. Green jobs include solar panel technician, wind turbine technician, waste manager, water conservation expert, organic farmer and environmental consultant.

Green skills

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Green skills are the knowledge and abilities needed to live and work in a way that protects the environment. They support sustainable development: meeting present needs without harming future generations. Key ideas are the 3 Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), saving energy and water, renewable energy, waste management and green jobs. Pollution, global warming and loss of biodiversity are major environmental problems.

📌

Environment and sustainable development

  • The environment is everything around us: air, water, soil, plants and animals
  • Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
  • It balances economic growth, social well-being and environmental protection
  • India has set targets for clean energy, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (17 goals) guide the world
Read the full explanation

The environment is everything around us: air, water, soil, plants and animals. Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It balances economic growth, social well-being and environmental protection. India has set targets for clean energy, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (17 goals) guide the world.

🗺️

Pollution and climate change

  • Air pollution comes from vehicles, factories and burning waste
  • Water pollution from sewage, chemicals and plastics
  • Soil pollution from pesticides and garbage
  • Noise pollution from traffic and loudspeakers
Read the full explanation

Air pollution comes from vehicles, factories and burning waste; water pollution from sewage, chemicals and plastics; soil pollution from pesticides and garbage; noise pollution from traffic and loudspeakers. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat and causes global warming and climate change. The ozone layer protects us from ultraviolet rays and is damaged by CFCs.

🗺️

Saving resources and energy

  • Save water by fixing leaks, harvesting rainwater and using drip irrigation
  • Save electricity by using LED bulbs, switching off unused devices and using star-rated appliances
  • Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal) are replaced naturally
  • Non-renewable sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas) are limited
Read the full explanation

Save water by fixing leaks, harvesting rainwater and using drip irrigation. Save electricity by using LED bulbs, switching off unused devices and using star-rated appliances. Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal) are replaced naturally; non-renewable sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas) are limited. Public transport, cycling and carpooling reduce fuel use.

🔬

Waste management and green jobs

  • Waste is biodegradable (food, paper, leaves) or non-biodegradable (plastic, glass, metal)
  • Segregation into wet and dry waste helps recycling
  • Composting turns wet waste into manure
  • E-waste from old electronics needs safe disposal
Read the full explanation

Waste is biodegradable (food, paper, leaves) or non-biodegradable (plastic, glass, metal). Segregation into wet and dry waste helps recycling; composting turns wet waste into manure. E-waste from old electronics needs safe disposal. Green jobs include solar panel technician, wind turbine technician, waste manager, water conservation expert, organic farmer and environmental consultant.

lessons.title: Introduction to artificial intelligence

blocks.x: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a machine to do tasks that normally need human intelligence: learning, reasoning, understanding language and recognising images. AI is a broad idea, Machine Learning (ML) is a way of achieving it by learning from data, and Deep Learning (DL) is ML using neural networks. The three main AI domains are Data Science, Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing. AI must be used ethically, avoiding bias and protecting privacy.
Deep dive: what is AI

Intelligence is the ability to learn, understand, reason, solve problems and adapt. Artificial intelligence is intelligence shown by machines. The term was coined by John McCarthy in 1956. Examples: voice assistants (Alexa, Siri, Google Assistant), recommendation systems (YouTube, Netflix), face unlock, self-driving cars, spam filters, chess programs and chatbots. Not every smart-looking machine is AI: a washing machine that follows fixed steps is automated, but an AI system learns from data and improves.
Deep dive: AI, ML and DL

AI is the wider goal. Machine learning is a subset of AI in which machines learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed for each case. Deep learning is a subset of ML that uses multi-layer artificial neural networks to learn from large amounts of data such as images and speech. Types of machine learning: supervised (labelled data), unsupervised (unlabelled data, finds groups) and reinforcement learning (learning by reward and penalty).
Deep dive: domains of AI

Data Science works with numbers and data to find patterns and make predictions (sales forecasting, price prediction). Computer Vision lets machines see and understand images and videos (face recognition, medical scans, self-driving). Natural Language Processing (NLP) lets machines understand human language (translation, chatbots, voice assistants, sentiment analysis). Other related fields are robotics and expert systems.
Deep dive: AI ethics, bias and society

AI ethics asks that AI be fair, transparent, safe and respect privacy. Bias occurs when training data is unfair or incomplete, so the AI treats some groups unfairly (a hiring tool preferring one gender). Privacy means protecting personal data. Other issues are job changes, deepfakes, safety and accountability: humans must remain responsible. Good practice: use diverse data, test for bias, keep humans in the loop and be honest about what AI can do.

qa.a: An AI that suggests products or videos based on your past choices.

qa.a: Identifying a person from a picture of the face.

qa.a: A vehicle that drives itself using AI and sensors.

qa.a: An AI that detects and blocks unwanted e-mail.

qa.a: Automatic conversion of text from one language to another.

qa.a: Finding whether a text is positive, negative or neutral.

qa.q: What is meant by Speech recognition?

qa.a: The field that builds machines that can move and act.

qa.q: What is meant by Expert system?
qa.a: An AI program that gives advice like a human expert.

qa.a: Learning from data that has labels or correct answers.

qa.q: What is meant by Unsupervised learning?
qa.a: Learning to find groups in data without labels.

qa.q: What is meant by Reinforcement learning?
qa.a: Learning by getting rewards and penalties.

qa.a: The data used to teach an AI model.

qa.q: What is meant by Testing data?
qa.a: The data used to check how well a model works.

qa.q: What is meant by Label?
qa.a: The correct answer attached to a data example.

qa.q: What is meant by Algorithm?
qa.a: A set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem.

qa.q: What is meant by Model?
qa.a: The result of training an algorithm on data.

qa.q: What is meant by Prediction?
qa.a: The output a model gives for new input.

qa.q: What is meant by Bias?
qa.a: Unfair results caused by unfair or incomplete data.

qa.q: What is meant by AI ethics?
qa.a: Principles that make sure AI is fair, safe and respects privacy.

qa.q: What is meant by Privacy?
What is meant by Transparency?
qa.a: Being open about how an AI makes decisions.

qa.q: What is meant by Accountability?
qa.a: Humans being responsible for the actions of an AI.

qa.q: What is meant by Deepfake?
qa.a: A fake video or audio made by AI to look real.

qa.q: What is meant by Turing test?
qa.a: A test of whether a machine can imitate human conversation.

qa.q: What is meant by Automation?
qa.a: Machines doing fixed tasks without human help.

qa.q: What is meant by Big data?
qa.a: Extremely large sets of data that are hard to process normally.

qa.q: What is meant by Data?
qa.a: Raw facts and figures used by AI.

qa.q: What is meant by Pattern?
qa.a: A repeated feature or trend found in data.

qa.q: What is meant by Narrow AI?
qa.a: AI that can do only one specific task.

qa.q: What is meant by General AI?
qa.a: AI that could do any intellectual task a human can.

qa.q: What is meant by Smart speaker?
qa.a: A device with a voice assistant that answers questions.

qa.q: What is meant by Sensor?
qa.a: A device that collects data from the surroundings.

qa.q: What is meant by Digital twin?
qa.a: A virtual copy of a real object used for testing.

qa.q: What is meant by Autonomous?
qa.a: Able to work without human control.

qa.q: What is meant by Human in the loop?
qa.a: Keeping a person involved to check AI decisions.

qa.q: What is meant by Explainable AI?
qa.a: AI whose decisions can be understood by humans.

Read the full explanation

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a machine to do tasks that normally need human intelligence: learning, reasoning, understanding language and recognising images. AI is a broad idea, Machine Learning (ML) is a way of achieving it by learning from data, and Deep Learning (DL) is ML using neural networks. The three main AI domains are Data Science, Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing. AI must be used ethically, avoiding bias and protecting privacy.

📘

What is AI

  • Intelligence is the ability to learn, understand, reason, solve problems and adapt
  • Artificial intelligence is intelligence shown by machines
  • The term was coined by John McCarthy in 1956
  • Examples: voice assistants (Alexa, Siri, Google Assistant), recommendation systems (YouTube, Netflix), face unlock, self-driving cars, spam filters…
Read the full explanation

Intelligence is the ability to learn, understand, reason, solve problems and adapt. Artificial intelligence is intelligence shown by machines. The term was coined by John McCarthy in 1956. Examples: voice assistants (Alexa, Siri, Google Assistant), recommendation systems (YouTube, Netflix), face unlock, self-driving cars, spam filters, chess programs and chatbots. Not every smart-looking machine is AI: a washing machine that follows fixed steps is automated, but an AI system learns from data and improves.

🧠

  • AI is the wider goal
  • Machine learning is a subset of AI in which machines learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed for each case

Read the full explanation

AI is the wider goal. Machine learning is a subset of AI in which machines learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed for each case. Deep learning is a subset of ML that uses multi-layer artificial neural networks to learn from large amounts of data such as images and speech. Types of machine learning: supervised (labelled data), unsupervised (unlabelled data, finds groups) and reinforcement learning (learning by reward and penalty).

🌟

Domains of AI

  • Data Science works with numbers and data to find patterns and make predictions (sales forecasting, price prediction)
  • Computer Vision lets machines see and understand images and videos (face recognition, medical scans, self-driving)
  • Natural Language Processing (NLP) lets machines understand human language (translation, chatbots, voice assistants, sentiment analysis)
  • Other related fields are robotics and expert systems
Read the full explanation

Data Science works with numbers and data to find patterns and make predictions (sales forecasting, price prediction). Computer Vision lets machines see and understand images and videos (face recognition, medical scans, self-driving). Natural Language Processing (NLP) lets machines understand human language (translation, chatbots, voice assistants, sentiment analysis). Other related fields are robotics and expert systems.

AI ethics, bias and society

  • AI ethics asks that AI be fair, transparent, safe and respect privacy
  • Bias occurs when training data is unfair or incomplete, so the AI treats some groups unfairly (a hiring tool preferring one gender)
  • Privacy means protecting personal data
  • Other issues are job changes, deepfakes, safety and accountability: humans must remain responsible
Read the full explanation

AI ethics asks that AI be fair, transparent, safe and respect privacy. Bias occurs when training data is unfair or incomplete, so the AI treats some groups unfairly (a hiring tool preferring one gender). Privacy means protecting personal data. Other issues are job changes, deepfakes, safety and accountability: humans must remain responsible. Good practice: use diverse data, test for bias, keep humans in the loop and be honest about what AI can do.

lessons.title: AI project cycle

blocks.x: The AI project cycle has five stages: problem scoping, data acquisition, data exploration, modelling and evaluation. Problem scoping uses the 4Ws canvas (Who, What, Where, Why). Data is collected, then explored with charts. Modelling can be rule-based or learning-based. Evaluation tests the model on unseen data using accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score from the confusion matrix.
Deep dive: problem scoping

Problem scoping means understanding clearly the problem to be solved. The 4Ws canvas asks Who (the stakeholders affected), What (the problem and its nature), Where (the context or situation) and Why (the benefit of solving it). The result is the problem statement template: "Our <stakeholder> has a problem of <issue> when <context>. An ideal solution would <benefit>." Linking the problem to the UN Sustainable Development Goals is common.
Deep dive: data acquisition and exploration

Data acquisition collects accurate and reliable data for training and testing. Sources: surveys, web scraping, sensors, cameras, observations, APIs and open government data. Data may be structured (tables) or unstructured (images, audio). Data exploration finds patterns by visualising: bar graphs, line graphs, pie charts, scatter plots and histograms. Clean data (no missing or wrong values) gives a better model.
Deep dive: modelling

Modelling is choosing and training an algorithm. A rule-based approach has rules written by the developer; it cannot learn. A learning-based approach lets the machine find rules from data. Learning-based models include supervised learning (classification gives categories, regression gives numbers), unsupervised learning (clustering groups similar items; association finds items that go together) and reinforcement learning. Data is split into training and testing sets (for example 80 percent and 20 percent).
Deep dive: evaluation

Evaluation checks the model with unseen data. The confusion matrix compares predicted and actual values: TP (true positive), TN (true negative), FP (false positive), FN (false negative). Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN). Precision = TP/(TP + FP). Recall = TP/(TP + FN). F1 score = 2 x precision x recall/(precision + recall). Overfitting means the model memorises training data and fails on new data; underfitting means it is too simple to learn the pattern.

Visual lesson

AI project cycle

The AI project cycle has five stages: problem scoping, data acquisition, data exploration, modelling and evaluation

Big idea

  • The AI project cycle has five stages: problem scoping, data acquisition, data exploration, modelling and evaluation
  • Problem scoping uses the 4Ws canvas (Who, What, Where, Why)
  • Data is collected, then explored with charts
  • Modelling can be rule-based or learning-based
Read the full explanation

The AI project cycle has five stages: problem scoping, data acquisition, data exploration, modelling and evaluation. Problem scoping uses the 4Ws canvas (Who, What, Where, Why). Data is collected, then explored with charts. Modelling can be rule-based or learning-based. Evaluation tests the model on unseen data using accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score from the confusion matrix.

📌

Problem scoping

  • Problem scoping means understanding clearly the problem to be solved
  • The 4Ws canvas asks Who (the stakeholders affected), What (the problem and its nature), Where (the context or situation) and Why (the benefit of…
  • The result is the problem statement template: "Our <stakeholder> has a problem of <issue> when <context>
  • An ideal solution would <benefit>." Linking the problem to the UN Sustainable Development Goals is common
Read the full explanation

Problem scoping means understanding clearly the problem to be solved. The 4Ws canvas asks Who (the stakeholders affected), What (the problem and its nature), Where (the context or situation) and Why (the benefit of solving it). The result is the problem statement template: "Our <stakeholder> has a problem of <issue> when <context>. An ideal solution would <benefit>." Linking the problem to the UN Sustainable Development Goals is common.

🧠

Data acquisition and exploration

  • Data acquisition collects accurate and reliable data for training and testing
  • Sources: surveys, web scraping, sensors, cameras, observations, APIs and open government data
  • Data may be structured (tables) or unstructured (images, audio)
  • Data exploration finds patterns by visualising: bar graphs, line graphs, pie charts, scatter plots and histograms
Read the full explanation

Data acquisition collects accurate and reliable data for training and testing. Sources: surveys, web scraping, sensors, cameras, observations, APIs and open government data. Data may be structured (tables) or unstructured (images, audio). Data exploration finds patterns by visualising: bar graphs, line graphs, pie charts, scatter plots and histograms. Clean data (no missing or wrong values) gives a better model.

🌟

Modelling

  • Modelling is choosing and training an algorithm
  • A rule-based approach has rules written by the developer
  • It cannot learn
  • A learning-based approach lets the machine find rules from data
Read the full explanation

Modelling is choosing and training an algorithm. A rule-based approach has rules written by the developer; it cannot learn. A learning-based approach lets the machine find rules from data. Learning-based models include supervised learning (classification gives categories, regression gives numbers), unsupervised learning (clustering groups similar items; association finds items that go together) and reinforcement learning. Data is split into training and testing sets (for example 80 percent and 20 percent).

🔬

Evaluation

  • Evaluation checks the model with unseen data
  • The confusion matrix compares predicted and actual values: TP (true positive), TN (true negative), FP (false positive), FN (false negative)
  • Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN)
  • Precision = TP/(TP + FP)
Read the full explanation

Evaluation checks the model with unseen data. The confusion matrix compares predicted and actual values: TP (true positive), TN (true negative), FP (false positive), FN (false negative). Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN). Precision = TP/(TP + FP). Recall = TP/(TP + FN). F1 score = 2 x precision x recall/(precision + recall). Overfitting means the model memorises training data and fails on new data; underfitting means it is too simple to learn the pattern.

🧮

lessons.title: Neural networks basics

blocks.x: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a model inspired by the human brain, made of connected artificial neurons arranged in layers: input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each connection has a weight; a neuron adds the weighted inputs plus a bias and passes the result through an activation function. Training adjusts weights to reduce error. Networks with many hidden layers are called deep neural networks.
Deep dive: from the brain to the artificial neuron

A biological neuron has dendrites (receive signals), a cell body (processes), an axon (sends the signal) and synapses (junctions). An artificial neuron copies this: inputs (x), weights (w), a bias (b), a summation and an activation function that gives the output. Net input = x1 w1 + x2 w2 + ... + b. A larger weight means that input has more influence.
Deep dive: layers and architecture

The input layer receives the data (pixels, numbers). Hidden layers do the calculations and find features. The output layer gives the result (a class or number). A network with more than one hidden layer is a deep neural network, which is why this is called deep learning. In a fully connected layer every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.
Deep dive: activation and learning

An activation function decides whether and how strongly a neuron fires: step (0 or 1), sigmoid (between 0 and 1), tanh (between -1 and 1) and ReLU (output = max(0, x)). Learning means adjusting weights: the network predicts, the loss (error) is measured, and backpropagation sends the error backwards to update weights using gradient descent. One full pass over the training data is an epoch. The learning rate controls the size of each weight update.
Deep dive: applications and limits

Neural networks power image recognition, speech recognition, language translation, medical diagnosis, self-driving cars and recommendation systems. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are used for images; recurrent neural networks (RNN) and transformers for text and speech. Limits: they need large data and computing power, can inherit bias, and are often a black box whose decisions are hard to explain.

qa.q: What is meant by Neural network?

qa.a: A number that shows how important an input is.

qa.a: An extra number added to the weighted sum.

qa.a: The sum of each input multiplied by its weight.

qa.a: A function that decides the output of a neuron.

qa.a: An activation that gives a value between 0 and 1.

qa.a: An activation that gives zero for negative values and x otherwise.

qa.a: A neural network with many hidden layers.

qa.a: A layer where every neuron connects to all neurons of the next layer.

qa.a: A number that shows how wrong the predictions are.

Visual lesson

Neural networks basics

An artificial neural network (ANN) is a model inspired by the human brain, made of connected artificial neurons arranged in layers: input layer, one or more hidden…

🔑

Big idea

  • An artificial neural network (ANN) is a model inspired by the human brain, made of connected artificial neurons arranged in layers: input layer, one…
  • Each connection has a weight
  • A neuron adds the weighted inputs plus a bias and passes the result through an activation function
  • Training adjusts weights to reduce error
Read the full explanation

An artificial neural network (ANN) is a model inspired by the human brain, made of connected artificial neurons arranged in layers: input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each connection has a weight; a neuron adds the weighted inputs plus a bias and passes the result through an activation function. Training adjusts weights to reduce error. Networks with many hidden layers are called deep neural networks.

📌

From the brain to the artificial neuron

  • A biological neuron has dendrites (receive signals), a cell body (processes), an axon (sends the signal) and synapses (junctions)
  • An artificial neuron copies this: inputs (x), weights (w), a bias (b), a summation and an activation function that gives the output
  • Net input = x1 w1 + x2 w2 +
  • A larger weight means that input has more influence
🧠

Layers and architecture

  • The input layer receives the data (pixels, numbers)
  • Hidden layers do the calculations and find features
  • The output layer gives the result (a class or number)
  • A network with more than one hidden layer is a deep neural network, which is why this is called deep learning
Read the full explanation

The input layer receives the data (pixels, numbers). Hidden layers do the calculations and find features. The output layer gives the result (a class or number). A network with more than one hidden layer is a deep neural network, which is why this is called deep learning. In a fully connected layer every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

🌟

Activation and learning

  • An activation function decides whether and how strongly a neuron fires: step (0 or 1), sigmoid (between 0 and 1), tanh (between -1 and 1) and ReLU…
  • Learning means adjusting weights: the network predicts, the loss (error) is measured, and backpropagation sends the error backwards to update weights…
  • One full pass over the training data is an epoch
  • The learning rate controls the size of each weight update
Read the full explanation

An activation function decides whether and how strongly a neuron fires: step (0 or 1), sigmoid (between 0 and 1), tanh (between -1 and 1) and ReLU (output = max(0, x)). Learning means adjusting weights: the network predicts, the loss (error) is measured, and backpropagation sends the error backwards to update weights using gradient descent. One full pass over the training data is an epoch. The learning rate controls the size of each weight update.

💡

Applications and limits

  • Neural networks power image recognition, speech recognition, language translation, medical diagnosis, self-driving cars and recommendation systems
  • Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are used for images
  • Recurrent neural networks (RNN) and transformers for text and speech
  • Limits: they need large data and computing power, can inherit bias, and are often a black box whose decisions are hard to explain
Read the full explanation

Neural networks power image recognition, speech recognition, language translation, medical diagnosis, self-driving cars and recommendation systems. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are used for images; recurrent neural networks (RNN) and transformers for text and speech. Limits: they need large data and computing power, can inherit bias, and are often a black box whose decisions are hard to explain.

lessons.title: Digital documentation (word processing)

blocks.x: A word processor (MS Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs) is software to create, edit, format, save and print documents. Basic steps: type text, select, cut, copy, paste, format (font, size, bold, italic, underline, alignment), insert pictures, tables and page numbers, check spelling, save and print. Useful shortcuts: Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+B bold, Ctrl+I italic, Ctrl+U underline.
Deep dive: creating and saving a document

Open the word processor, a blank document appears with a title bar, menu bar, toolbars, ruler, the typing area and the status bar. Type the text; the blinking cursor shows the place of typing. Save with File > Save (Ctrl+S) giving a file name and location; Save As makes a copy under a new name or format (.docx, .odt, .pdf). Print with File > Print (Ctrl+P) after Print Preview.
Deep dive: editing and formatting text

Select text by dragging or Shift with arrow keys; double click selects a word, triple click a line or paragraph, Ctrl+A selects all. Edit with Cut, Copy, Paste, Undo, Redo and Find and Replace. Character formatting: font name, font size, bold, italic, underline, strike-through, subscript, superscript, colour and highlight. Paragraph formatting: left, centre, right, justify alignment, line spacing, indent, bullets and numbering.
Deep dive: inserting objects and page layout

Insert pictures, shapes, tables (rows and columns), hyperlinks, page numbers, headers and footers, date and symbols. A table cell is the box where a row and column meet; cells can be merged or split. Page setup: margins, orientation (portrait or landscape), paper size, columns and page borders. Styles such as Heading 1 give a consistent look and help make a table of contents.
Deep dive: reviewing and sharing

Spelling and grammar check shows errors with a red or green wavy line. Word count shows words and characters. Mail merge makes many letters from one template and a list of names. Documents can be shared as PDF, printed, e-mailed or stored in cloud services such as Google Docs, where several people can edit together. Protect important files with passwords and keep backups.

Visual lesson

Digital documentation (word processing)

A word processor (MS Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs) is software to create, edit, format, save and print documents

1Big idea›2Creating and saving a…›3Editing and formatting text›4Inserting objects and page…›5Reviewing and sharing
🔑

Big idea

  • A word processor (MS Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs) is software to create, edit, format, save and print documents
  • Basic steps: type text, select, cut, copy, paste, format (font, size, bold, italic, underline, alignment), insert pictures, tables and page numbers…
  • Useful shortcuts: Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+B bold, Ctrl+I italic, Ctrl+U underline
Read the full explanation

A word processor (MS Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs) is software to create, edit, format, save and print documents. Basic steps: type text, select, cut, copy, paste, format (font, size, bold, italic, underline, alignment), insert pictures, tables and page numbers, check spelling, save and print. Useful shortcuts: Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+B bold, Ctrl+I italic, Ctrl+U underline.

📌

Creating and saving a document

  • Open the word processor, a blank document appears with a title bar, menu bar, toolbars, ruler, the typing area and the status bar
  • Type the text
  • The blinking cursor shows the place of typing
  • Save with File > Save (Ctrl+S) giving a file name and location
Read the full explanation

Open the word processor, a blank document appears with a title bar, menu bar, toolbars, ruler, the typing area and the status bar. Type the text; the blinking cursor shows the place of typing. Save with File > Save (Ctrl+S) giving a file name and location; Save As makes a copy under a new name or format (.docx, .odt, .pdf). Print with File > Print (Ctrl+P) after Print Preview.

🧠

Editing and formatting text

  • Select text by dragging or Shift with arrow keys
  • Double click selects a word, triple click a line or paragraph, Ctrl+A selects all
  • Edit with Cut, Copy, Paste, Undo, Redo and Find and Replace
  • Character formatting: font name, font size, bold, italic, underline, strike-through, subscript, superscript, colour and highlight
Read the full explanation

Select text by dragging or Shift with arrow keys; double click selects a word, triple click a line or paragraph, Ctrl+A selects all. Edit with Cut, Copy, Paste, Undo, Redo and Find and Replace. Character formatting: font name, font size, bold, italic, underline, strike-through, subscript, superscript, colour and highlight. Paragraph formatting: left, centre, right, justify alignment, line spacing, indent, bullets and numbering.

🌟

Inserting objects and page layout

  • Insert pictures, shapes, tables (rows and columns), hyperlinks, page numbers, headers and footers, date and symbols
  • A table cell is the box where a row and column meet
  • Cells can be merged or split
  • Page setup: margins, orientation (portrait or landscape), paper size, columns and page borders
Read the full explanation

Insert pictures, shapes, tables (rows and columns), hyperlinks, page numbers, headers and footers, date and symbols. A table cell is the box where a row and column meet; cells can be merged or split. Page setup: margins, orientation (portrait or landscape), paper size, columns and page borders. Styles such as Heading 1 give a consistent look and help make a table of contents.

🔬

Reviewing and sharing

  • Spelling and grammar check shows errors with a red or green wavy line
  • Word count shows words and characters
  • Mail merge makes many letters from one template and a list of names
  • Documents can be shared as PDF, printed, e-mailed or stored in cloud services such as Google Docs, where several people can edit together
Read the full explanation

Spelling and grammar check shows errors with a red or green wavy line. Word count shows words and characters. Mail merge makes many letters from one template and a list of names. Documents can be shared as PDF, printed, e-mailed or stored in cloud services such as Google Docs, where several people can edit together. Protect important files with passwords and keep backups.

lessons.title: Electronic spreadsheet

blocks.x: An electronic spreadsheet (MS Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets) arranges data in rows and columns. Rows are numbered, columns are lettered and a cell address such as B3 joins them. A formula starts with = and uses cell references and operators. Common functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT and IF. Cell references can be relative (A1), absolute ($A$1) or mixed. Charts show data visually.
Deep dive: the spreadsheet window

A workbook contains worksheets (sheets). A sheet has rows (1, 2, 3 ...) and columns (A, B, C ...). The intersection of a row and column is a cell with an address such as C5. The active cell is the one selected. The name box shows the address and the formula bar shows the content. A range is a group of cells written as first:last, for example A1:C4 (3 columns x 4 rows = 12 cells). Data types: text, number, date and formula.
Deep dive: formulas and operators

Every formula starts with =. Arithmetic operators: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division and ^ power. Brackets change the order: BODMAS applies. Example: =B2*C2 multiplies two cells; =(A1+A2)/2 finds an average. Cell references in formulas update automatically when data changes. A relative reference changes when the formula is copied; an absolute reference ($A$1) does not; a mixed reference ($A1 or A$1) fixes only the column or row.
Deep dive: functions

SUM(range) adds numbers; AVERAGE(range) gives the mean; MAX(range) the largest; MIN(range) the smallest; COUNT(range) the number of numeric cells; COUNTA counts non-empty cells; IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) makes a decision, for example =IF(B2>=33,"Pass","Fail"). ROUND(number, digits) rounds a value. Errors: #DIV/0! (division by zero), #NAME? (wrong function name), #REF! (invalid reference), #VALUE! (wrong type of value).
Deep dive: formatting, sorting and charts

Format cells: number formats (currency, percent, date), fonts, borders, colours, merge and centre. Sort data ascending (A to Z, small to large) or descending. Filter shows only rows that match a condition. Charts: column or bar (compare), line (trend over time), pie (parts of a whole). A chart has a title, axes, labels, legend and data series. Freeze panes keep headings visible while scrolling.
Hindi saransh
Spreadsheet: rows, columns, cells. Formula = se shuru hota hai. =SUM(A1:A5).
A formula always starts with =. A range is written like A1:A5.

qa.q: What is meant by Spreadsheet?

qa.q: What is meant by Workbook?
qa.a: A spreadsheet file that contains one or more sheets.

qa.a: A single page of rows and columns in a workbook.

qa.a: A horizontal line of cells identified by a number.

qa.a: A vertical line of cells identified by a letter.

qa.q: What is meant by Cell?
