qa.a: The column letter and row number of a cell such as B3.

qa.q: What is meant by Active cell?
qa.a: The cell that is currently selected.

qa.q: What is meant by Range?
qa.a: A group of cells such as A1:A5.

qa.q: What is meant by Name box?
qa.a: The box that shows the address of the active cell.

qa.q: What is meant by Formula bar?
qa.a: The bar that shows the content of the active cell.

qa.q: What is meant by Formula?
qa.a: An expression that starts with = and calculates a value.

qa.q: What is meant by Function?
qa.a: A ready-made formula such as SUM.

qa.q: What is meant by SUM?
qa.a: The function that adds the numbers in a range.

qa.q: What is meant by AVERAGE?
qa.a: The function that finds the mean of the numbers in a range.

qa.q: What is meant by MAX?
qa.a: The function that returns the largest value in a range.

qa.q: What is meant by MIN?
qa.a: The function that returns the smallest value in a range.

qa.q: What is meant by COUNT?
qa.a: The function that counts the cells containing numbers.

qa.q: What is meant by COUNTA?
qa.a: The function that counts the cells that are not empty.

qa.q: What is meant by IF?
qa.a: The function that returns one value if a condition is true and another if false.

qa.q: What is meant by ROUND?
qa.a: The function that rounds a number to the given digits.

qa.q: What is meant by Relative reference?
qa.a: A cell reference that changes when a formula is copied.

qa.q: What is meant by Absolute reference?
qa.a: A cell reference that stays fixed and uses the $ sign.

qa.q: What is meant by Mixed reference?
qa.a: A reference in which only the row or the column is fixed.

qa.q: What is meant by Operator?
qa.a: A symbol such as + or * that tells what calculation to do.

qa.q: What is meant by Sort?
qa.a: Arranging data in ascending or descending order.

qa.q: What is meant by Ascending order?
qa.a: Arranging from smallest to largest or A to Z.

qa.q: What is meant by Descending order?
qa.a: Arranging from largest to smallest or Z to A.

qa.q: What is meant by Filter?
qa.a: Showing only the rows that meet a condition.

qa.q: What is meant by Chart?
qa.a: A picture that shows data visually.

qa.q: What is meant by Column chart?
qa.a: A chart that compares values using vertical bars.

qa.q: What is meant by Line chart?
qa.a: A chart that shows how values change over time.

qa.q: What is meant by Pie chart?
qa.a: A chart that shows parts of a whole.

qa.q: What is meant by Legend?
qa.a: The key that explains the colours in a chart.

qa.q: What is meant by Axis?
qa.a: The line along which values or categories are shown in a chart.

qa.q: What is meant by Merge and centre?
qa.a: Joining selected cells and centring the content.

qa.q: What is meant by Freeze panes?
qa.a: Keeping rows or columns visible while scrolling.

qa.q: What is meant by Autofill?
qa.a: Filling cells automatically by dragging the fill handle.

qa.q: What is meant by Fill handle?
qa.a: The small square at the corner of the active cell.

qa.q: What is meant by Currency format?
qa.a: A number format that shows a money symbol.

qa.q: What is meant by Percent format?
qa.a: A number format that shows a value with the % sign.

qa.q: What is meant by #DIV/0!?
qa.a: The error shown when a number is divided by zero.

qa.q: What is meant by #NAME??
qa.a: The error shown when a function name is wrong.

qa.q: What is meant by #REF!?
qa.a: The error shown when a cell reference is not valid.

qa.q: What is meant by #VALUE!?
qa.a: The error shown when the wrong type of value is used.

qa.q: What is meant by Data validation?
qa.a: A rule that limits what can be typed in a cell.

qa.q: What is meant by Conditional formatting?
qa.a: Formatting that changes automatically when a condition is met.

Visual lesson

Electronic spreadsheet

An electronic spreadsheet (MS Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets) arranges data in rows and columns

Absolute$A$1
Mixed$A1 or A$1
🔑

Big idea

  • An electronic spreadsheet (MS Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets) arranges data in rows and columns
  • Rows are numbered, columns are lettered and a cell address such as B3 joins them
  • A formula starts with = and uses cell references and operators
  • Common functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT and IF
Read the full explanation

An electronic spreadsheet (MS Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets) arranges data in rows and columns. Rows are numbered, columns are lettered and a cell address such as B3 joins them. A formula starts with = and uses cell references and operators. Common functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT and IF. Cell references can be relative (A1), absolute ($A$1) or mixed. Charts show data visually.

📌

The spreadsheet window

  • A workbook contains worksheets (sheets)
  • A sheet has rows (1, 2, 3 ...) and columns (A, B, C ...)
  • The intersection of a row and column is a cell with an address such as C5
  • The active cell is the one selected
Read the full explanation

A workbook contains worksheets (sheets). A sheet has rows (1, 2, 3 ...) and columns (A, B, C ...). The intersection of a row and column is a cell with an address such as C5. The active cell is the one selected. The name box shows the address and the formula bar shows the content. A range is a group of cells written as first:last, for example A1:C4 (3 columns x 4 rows = 12 cells). Data types: text, number, date and formula.

🧮

Formulas and operators

  • Every formula starts with =
  • Arithmetic operators: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division and ^ power
  • Brackets change the order: BODMAS applies
  • Example: =B2*C2 multiplies two cells
Read the full explanation

Every formula starts with =. Arithmetic operators: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division and ^ power. Brackets change the order: BODMAS applies. Example: =B2*C2 multiplies two cells; =(A1+A2)/2 finds an average. Cell references in formulas update automatically when data changes. A relative reference changes when the formula is copied; an absolute reference ($A$1) does not; a mixed reference ($A1 or A$1) fixes only the column or row.

🌟

Functions

  • SUM(range) adds numbers
  • AVERAGE(range) gives the mean
  • MAX(range) the largest
  • MIN(range) the smallest
Read the full explanation

SUM(range) adds numbers; AVERAGE(range) gives the mean; MAX(range) the largest; MIN(range) the smallest; COUNT(range) the number of numeric cells; COUNTA counts non-empty cells; IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) makes a decision, for example =IF(B2>=33,"Pass","Fail"). ROUND(number, digits) rounds a value. Errors: #DIV/0! (division by zero), #NAME? (wrong function name), #REF! (invalid reference), #VALUE! (wrong type of value).

🔬

Formatting, sorting and charts

  • Format cells: number formats (currency, percent, date), fonts, borders, colours, merge and centre
  • Sort data ascending (A to Z, small to large) or descending
  • Filter shows only rows that match a condition
  • Charts: column or bar (compare), line (trend over time), pie (parts of a whole)
Read the full explanation

Format cells: number formats (currency, percent, date), fonts, borders, colours, merge and centre. Sort data ascending (A to Z, small to large) or descending. Filter shows only rows that match a condition. Charts: column or bar (compare), line (trend over time), pie (parts of a whole). A chart has a title, axes, labels, legend and data series. Freeze panes keep headings visible while scrolling.

lessons.title: Database management system

blocks.x: A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS (Database Management System) such as LibreOffice Base, MySQL or MS Access creates, stores, retrieves and protects the data. A table has fields (columns) and records (rows). A primary key uniquely identifies each record. Objects in a database: tables, forms (enter data), queries (ask questions), and reports (print results). Data types include text, integer, decimal, date and Yes/No.
Deep dive: data, database and DBMS

Data is raw facts; information is processed data. A database stores data in an organised way so it can be found easily (a school database holds student, class and marks data). A DBMS is the software that manages it: it creates tables, stores and updates data, searches it quickly, controls access, avoids duplication and protects it from loss. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, MS Access, LibreOffice Base, PostgreSQL. A file system keeps separate files with repeated data; a DBMS reduces redundancy and keeps data consistent.
Deep dive: tables, fields, records and keys

A table is a grid. Each column is a field (attribute) such as RollNo, Name or Marks; each row is a record (tuple). A relational database links tables through common fields. A primary key is a field whose value is unique and never empty for every record (RollNo, Aadhaar number). A foreign key is a field that refers to the primary key of another table. Data types: Text (VARCHAR), Integer, Decimal, Date and Boolean (Yes/No). Field size and format limit what can be entered.
Deep dive: forms, queries and reports

A form is a friendly screen for entering and viewing one record at a time. A query asks a question of the data, for example students with marks above 80, and shows the matching records; it can sort and filter. A report presents selected data in a neat printable format with titles, groups and totals. These objects work on the same stored tables, so changes in a table show everywhere.
Deep dive: advantages and care of a database

Advantages: less duplication, accurate and consistent data, fast searching, data sharing, security and easy backup. Examples of use: bank accounts, railway reservation, library records, hospital patient records, online shopping and school results. Good practice: choose meaningful field names, pick correct data types, always set a primary key, enter data carefully, keep backups and protect with passwords. A database administrator (DBA) looks after the system.

Visual lesson

Database management system

A database is an organised collection of related data

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Data, database and DBMS›3Tables, fields, records and…›4Forms, queries and reports›5Advantages and care of a…
🔑

Big idea

  • A database is an organised collection of related data
  • A DBMS (Database Management System) such as LibreOffice Base, MySQL or MS Access creates, stores, retrieves and protects the data
  • A table has fields (columns) and records (rows)
  • A primary key uniquely identifies each record
Read the full explanation

A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS (Database Management System) such as LibreOffice Base, MySQL or MS Access creates, stores, retrieves and protects the data. A table has fields (columns) and records (rows). A primary key uniquely identifies each record. Objects in a database: tables, forms (enter data), queries (ask questions), and reports (print results). Data types include text, integer, decimal, date and Yes/No.

⚗️

Data, database and DBMS

  • Data is raw facts
  • Information is processed data
  • A database stores data in an organised way so it can be found easily (a school database holds student, class and marks data)
  • A DBMS is the software that manages it: it creates tables, stores and updates data, searches it quickly, controls access, avoids duplication and…
Read the full explanation

Data is raw facts; information is processed data. A database stores data in an organised way so it can be found easily (a school database holds student, class and marks data). A DBMS is the software that manages it: it creates tables, stores and updates data, searches it quickly, controls access, avoids duplication and protects it from loss. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, MS Access, LibreOffice Base, PostgreSQL. A file system keeps separate files with repeated data; a DBMS reduces redundancy and keeps data consistent.

🧠

Tables, fields, records and keys

  • A table is a grid
  • Each column is a field (attribute) such as RollNo, Name or Marks
  • Each row is a record (tuple)
  • A relational database links tables through common fields
Read the full explanation

A table is a grid. Each column is a field (attribute) such as RollNo, Name or Marks; each row is a record (tuple). A relational database links tables through common fields. A primary key is a field whose value is unique and never empty for every record (RollNo, Aadhaar number). A foreign key is a field that refers to the primary key of another table. Data types: Text (VARCHAR), Integer, Decimal, Date and Boolean (Yes/No). Field size and format limit what can be entered.

🌟

Forms, queries and reports

  • A form is a friendly screen for entering and viewing one record at a time
  • A query asks a question of the data, for example students with marks above 80, and shows the matching records
  • It can sort and filter
  • A report presents selected data in a neat printable format with titles, groups and totals
Read the full explanation

A form is a friendly screen for entering and viewing one record at a time. A query asks a question of the data, for example students with marks above 80, and shows the matching records; it can sort and filter. A report presents selected data in a neat printable format with titles, groups and totals. These objects work on the same stored tables, so changes in a table show everywhere.

⚗️

Advantages and care of a database

  • Advantages: less duplication, accurate and consistent data, fast searching, data sharing, security and easy backup
  • Examples of use: bank accounts, railway reservation, library records, hospital patient records, online shopping and school results
  • Good practice: choose meaningful field names, pick correct data types, always set a primary key, enter data carefully, keep backups and protect with…
  • A database administrator (DBA) looks after the system

Advantages: less duplication, accurate and consistent data, fast searching, data sharing, security and easy backup. Examples of use: bank accounts, railway reservation, library records, hospital patient records, online shopping and school results. Good practice: choose meaningful field names, pick correct data types, always set a primary key, enter data carefully, keep backups and protect with passwords. A database administrator (DBA) looks after the system.

lessons.title: Web applications and security

blocks.x: A web application runs in a browser and uses the internet (Gmail, Google Docs, online banking, e-commerce). A web page has a URL, is written in HTML and is served by a web server. Security protects users: strong passwords, antivirus, firewall, updates, safe browsing (https) and care with personal data. Threats include viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, ransomware, phishing and hacking.
Deep dive: the web and web applications

The internet is the global network; the World Wide Web (WWW) is the service of linked web pages. A web page is written in HTML and may use CSS (style) and JavaScript (action). A website is a set of related pages with a home page. A URL (https://www.example.com/page) has a protocol, domain name and path. A web server stores sites and sends pages to a browser (client). A web application (web app) is software used through a browser: e-mail, online forms, maps, e-commerce, net banking, online classes and cloud documents. Cloud computing stores and processes data on internet servers.
Deep dive: e-mail, social media and online services

E-mail uses addresses of the form name@domain. Social media (Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp) lets people share content; think before you post because posts can stay forever. E-commerce is buying and selling online (Amazon, Flipkart); e-governance gives government services online (DigiLocker, UMANG); online payment uses UPI, cards or net banking and needs extra care. A blog is a website of regularly posted articles.
Deep dive: threats to security

Malware is harmful software. A virus attaches to files and spreads when they are opened; a worm spreads by itself through networks; a trojan pretends to be useful software; spyware secretly watches your activity; ransomware locks files and demands money; adware shows unwanted advertisements. Phishing tricks people with fake messages or sites. Hacking is unauthorised access to a system. Identity theft is stealing personal details. Cyberbullying and online fraud are other risks.
Deep dive: staying safe

Use a strong, unique password (long, with upper and lower case letters, digits and symbols) and two-factor authentication (OTP). Install antivirus and a firewall, keep software updated, download only from trusted sources and avoid public Wi-Fi for banking. Check that a site uses https with a padlock. Do not share OTP, PIN, passwords or personal information. Report cyber crime at cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930. Respect copyright and do not plagiarise. Be kind online.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Web applications and security

A web application runs in a browser and uses the internet (Gmail, Google Docs, online banking, e-commerce)

formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2The web and web applications›3E-mail, social media and…›4Threats to security›5Staying safe
Report cyber crimehelpline 1930
🔑

Big idea

  • A web application runs in a browser and uses the internet (Gmail, Google Docs, online banking, e-commerce)

A web application runs in a browser and uses the internet (Gmail, Google Docs, online banking, e-commerce). A web page has a URL, is written in HTML and is served by a web server. Security protects users: strong passwords, antivirus, firewall, updates, safe browsing (https) and care with personal data. Threats include viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, ransomware, phishing and hacking.

The web and web applications

The internet is the global network; the World Wide Web (WWW) is the service of linked web pages. A web page is written in HTML and may use CSS (style) and JavaScript (action). A website is a set of related pages with a home page. A URL (https://www.example.com/page) has a protocol, domain name and path. A web server stores sites and sends pages to a browser (client). A web application (web app) is software used through a browser: e-mail, online forms, maps, e-commerce, net banking, online classes and cloud documents. Cloud computing stores and processes data on internet servers.

🧠

E-mail, social media and online services

E-mail uses addresses of the form name@domain. Social media (Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp) lets people share content; think before you post because posts can stay forever. E-commerce is buying and selling online (Amazon, Flipkart); e-governance gives government services online (DigiLocker, UMANG); online payment uses UPI, cards or net banking and needs extra care. A blog is a website of regularly posted articles.

🌟

Threats to security

  • Malware is harmful software
  • A virus attaches to files and spreads when they are opened
  • A worm spreads by itself through networks
  • A trojan pretends to be useful software
Read the full explanation

Malware is harmful software. A virus attaches to files and spreads when they are opened; a worm spreads by itself through networks; a trojan pretends to be useful software; spyware secretly watches your activity; ransomware locks files and demands money; adware shows unwanted advertisements. Phishing tricks people with fake messages or sites. Hacking is unauthorised access to a system. Identity theft is stealing personal details. Cyberbullying and online fraud are other risks.

lessons.title: The story of village Palampur
yt: class 9 economics story of village palampur

blocks.x: Palampur is a model village in western Uttar Pradesh used to explain production. Production needs four factors: land, labour, physical capital and human capital. Land is fixed, so farmers use multiple cropping and modern methods (Green Revolution: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation) to raise output. Farming is the main activity; non-farm activities are dairy, small manufacturing, shopkeeping and transport. Wages of farm labourers are low and many families own little or no land.
Deep dive: the village and its farming

Palampur is well connected by road to the nearby village Raiganj and the small town Shahpur, has electricity, a primary and a high school, a primary health centre and a private dispensary. Of about 450 families, 150 have no land for cultivation (mostly dalits); 240 families cultivate small plots of less than 2 hectares; 60 medium and large farmers cultivate more than 2 hectares and some own 10 hectares or more. Land area is fixed, so the same land must produce more. Farmers grow two or more crops a year (multiple cropping): jowar and bajra in the rainy season, potato in between and wheat in winter, with sugarcane harvested for jaggery.
Deep dive: the Green Revolution and its effects

Traditional farming used cow-dung manure, local seeds and rain. In the late 1960s the Green Revolution introduced high yielding varieties (HYV) of seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation (tubewells, electricity). Wheat yield in Palampur rose from about 1300 kg per hectare to 3200 kg per hectare. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained the most. Drawbacks: chemical fertilisers reduce soil fertility, over-use of groundwater lowers the water table, and the cost of cultivation rises, hurting small farmers. Sustainable farming protects land and water.
Deep dive: factors of production

Land includes soil, water, forests and minerals; labour is the physical and mental effort of workers; physical capital includes fixed capital (tools, machines, buildings) and working capital (raw materials and cash). Human capital is the knowledge and enterprise needed to combine land, labour and capital to produce output. Capital is needed in large amounts and small farmers often borrow from moneylenders at high interest, while large farmers use their own savings.
Deep dive: non-farm activities and farm labour

Only about a fourth of the workers in a village are in non-farm work. Examples in Palampur: dairy (buffaloes, selling milk in Raiganj), small-scale manufacturing using simple methods and family labour (such as jaggery making), shopkeeping, and transport (rickshaws, tongas, jeeps, tractors, bullock carts). Farm labourers are landless and earn wages in cash or kind; they are poor because there is more labour than work and wages are often below the minimum set by the government. Better irrigation, roads, markets and credit can create more non-farm jobs.

Visual lesson

The story of village Palampur

Palampur is a model village in western Uttar Pradesh used to explain production

🔑

Big idea

  • Palampur is a model village in western Uttar Pradesh used to explain production
  • Production needs four factors: land, labour, physical capital and human capital
  • Land is fixed, so farmers use multiple cropping and modern methods (Green Revolution: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation) to raise output
  • Farming is the main activity
Read the full explanation

Palampur is a model village in western Uttar Pradesh used to explain production. Production needs four factors: land, labour, physical capital and human capital. Land is fixed, so farmers use multiple cropping and modern methods (Green Revolution: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation) to raise output. Farming is the main activity; non-farm activities are dairy, small manufacturing, shopkeeping and transport. Wages of farm labourers are low and many families own little or no land.

📌

The village and its farming

  • Palampur is well connected by road to the nearby village Raiganj and the small town Shahpur, has electricity, a primary and a high school, a primary…
  • Of about 450 families, 150 have no land for cultivation (mostly dalits)
  • 240 families cultivate small plots of less than 2 hectares
  • 60 medium and large farmers cultivate more than 2 hectares and some own 10 hectares or more
Read the full explanation

Palampur is well connected by road to the nearby village Raiganj and the small town Shahpur, has electricity, a primary and a high school, a primary health centre and a private dispensary. Of about 450 families, 150 have no land for cultivation (mostly dalits); 240 families cultivate small plots of less than 2 hectares; 60 medium and large farmers cultivate more than 2 hectares and some own 10 hectares or more. Land area is fixed, so the same land must produce more. Farmers grow two or more crops a year (multiple cropping): jowar and bajra in the rainy season, potato in between and wheat in winter, with sugarcane harvested for jaggery.

🕰️

The Green Revolution and its effects

  • Traditional farming used cow-dung manure, local seeds and rain
  • In the late 1960s the Green Revolution introduced high yielding varieties (HYV) of seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation…
  • Wheat yield in Palampur rose from about 1300 kg per hectare to 3200 kg per hectare
  • Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained the most
Read the full explanation

Traditional farming used cow-dung manure, local seeds and rain. In the late 1960s the Green Revolution introduced high yielding varieties (HYV) of seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation (tubewells, electricity). Wheat yield in Palampur rose from about 1300 kg per hectare to 3200 kg per hectare. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained the most. Drawbacks: chemical fertilisers reduce soil fertility, over-use of groundwater lowers the water table, and the cost of cultivation rises, hurting small farmers. Sustainable farming protects land and water.

🌟

Factors of production

  • Land includes soil, water, forests and minerals
  • Labour is the physical and mental effort of workers
  • Physical capital includes fixed capital (tools, machines, buildings) and working capital (raw materials and cash)
  • Human capital is the knowledge and enterprise needed to combine land, labour and capital to produce output
Read the full explanation

Land includes soil, water, forests and minerals; labour is the physical and mental effort of workers; physical capital includes fixed capital (tools, machines, buildings) and working capital (raw materials and cash). Human capital is the knowledge and enterprise needed to combine land, labour and capital to produce output. Capital is needed in large amounts and small farmers often borrow from moneylenders at high interest, while large farmers use their own savings.

🔬

Non-farm activities and farm labour

  • Only about a fourth of the workers in a village are in non-farm work
  • Examples in Palampur: dairy (buffaloes, selling milk in Raiganj), small-scale manufacturing using simple methods and family labour (such as jaggery…
  • Farm labourers are landless and earn wages in cash or kind
  • They are poor because there is more labour than work and wages are often below the minimum set by the government
Read the full explanation

Only about a fourth of the workers in a village are in non-farm work. Examples in Palampur: dairy (buffaloes, selling milk in Raiganj), small-scale manufacturing using simple methods and family labour (such as jaggery making), shopkeeping, and transport (rickshaws, tongas, jeeps, tractors, bullock carts). Farm labourers are landless and earn wages in cash or kind; they are poor because there is more labour than work and wages are often below the minimum set by the government. Better irrigation, roads, markets and credit can create more non-farm jobs.

lessons.title: People as resource

blocks.x: People are a resource when they are educated, healthy and skilled; this is human capital formation. Economic activities are primary (agriculture, fishing), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services). Education and health raise productivity and income. Unemployment is when people willing to work at the going wage cannot find jobs: seasonal, disguised and educated unemployment. Government programmes include Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the mid-day meal.
Deep dive: population as an asset

A large population becomes an asset when invested in education, training and health, turning people into human capital. The story of Sakal (a farmer) and Vilas shows how an educated and skilled person earns more than an unskilled one. Land and physical capital are productive only when human beings use them. Japan has few natural resources but invested in people and became rich. Human capital adds more value than land or physical capital because it can use them well and create new knowledge.
Deep dive: economic activities

Economic activities add value to the national income and are of three sectors: primary (agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, poultry farming), secondary (manufacturing of goods by factories and small units) and tertiary or services (trade, transport, communication, banking, education, health, tourism, insurance). Non-economic activities are done for self-satisfaction without pay (cooking for the family). Market activities are done for pay or profit; non-market activities include production for self-consumption. Women's household work is often not counted though it is valuable.
Deep dive: education, health and training

Education raises skills and income. Literacy rate in India was about 74 percent in the 2011 census, with a gap between men and women and between states. Schemes: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (universal elementary education, 2001), mid-day meal (to raise enrolment and nutrition) and National Education Policy. Health includes the ability to work to full potential: measured by life expectancy, infant mortality rate and nutrition. Training makes workers skilled, and migration for better jobs also forms human capital when people earn more.
Deep dive: unemployment

Unemployment exists when people willing to work at the going wage cannot find work. The working age is 15 to 59 years. Seasonal unemployment occurs in months when there is no farm work. Disguised unemployment occurs when more people work on a farm than needed; removing some does not reduce output. Educated unemployment affects matriculates, graduates and postgraduates who cannot find suitable jobs. Unemployment wastes human resources, lowers income and increases poverty and dependence. Employment generation, skill training and growth of the service sector help to reduce it.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

People as resource

People are a resource when they are educated, healthy and skilled

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Population as an asset›3Economic activities›4Education, health and…›5Unemployment
Working age15 to 59 years
🔑

Big idea

  • People are a resource when they are educated, healthy and skilled
  • This is human capital formation
  • Economic activities are primary (agriculture, fishing), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services)
  • Education and health raise productivity and income
Read the full explanation

People are a resource when they are educated, healthy and skilled; this is human capital formation. Economic activities are primary (agriculture, fishing), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services). Education and health raise productivity and income. Unemployment is when people willing to work at the going wage cannot find jobs: seasonal, disguised and educated unemployment. Government programmes include Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the mid-day meal.

📌

Population as an asset

  • A large population becomes an asset when invested in education, training and health, turning people into human capital
  • The story of Sakal (a farmer) and Vilas shows how an educated and skilled person earns more than an unskilled one
  • Land and physical capital are productive only when human beings use them
  • Japan has few natural resources but invested in people and became rich
Read the full explanation

A large population becomes an asset when invested in education, training and health, turning people into human capital. The story of Sakal (a farmer) and Vilas shows how an educated and skilled person earns more than an unskilled one. Land and physical capital are productive only when human beings use them. Japan has few natural resources but invested in people and became rich. Human capital adds more value than land or physical capital because it can use them well and create new knowledge.

🏛️

Economic activities

  • Economic activities add value to the national income and are of three sectors: primary (agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, poultry farming)…
  • Non-economic activities are done for self-satisfaction without pay (cooking for the family)
  • Market activities are done for pay or profit
  • Non-market activities include production for self-consumption
Read the full explanation

Economic activities add value to the national income and are of three sectors: primary (agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, poultry farming), secondary (manufacturing of goods by factories and small units) and tertiary or services (trade, transport, communication, banking, education, health, tourism, insurance). Non-economic activities are done for self-satisfaction without pay (cooking for the family). Market activities are done for pay or profit; non-market activities include production for self-consumption. Women's household work is often not counted though it is valuable.

🌟

Education, health and training

  • Education raises skills and income
  • Literacy rate in India was about 74 percent in the 2011 census, with a gap between men and women and between states
  • Schemes: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (universal elementary education, 2001), mid-day meal (to raise enrolment and nutrition) and National Education Policy
  • Health includes the ability to work to full potential: measured by life expectancy, infant mortality rate and nutrition
Read the full explanation

Education raises skills and income. Literacy rate in India was about 74 percent in the 2011 census, with a gap between men and women and between states. Schemes: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (universal elementary education, 2001), mid-day meal (to raise enrolment and nutrition) and National Education Policy. Health includes the ability to work to full potential: measured by life expectancy, infant mortality rate and nutrition. Training makes workers skilled, and migration for better jobs also forms human capital when people earn more.

🔬

Unemployment

  • Unemployment exists when people willing to work at the going wage cannot find work
  • The working age is 15 to 59 years
  • Seasonal unemployment occurs in months when there is no farm work
  • Disguised unemployment occurs when more people work on a farm than needed
Read the full explanation

Unemployment exists when people willing to work at the going wage cannot find work. The working age is 15 to 59 years. Seasonal unemployment occurs in months when there is no farm work. Disguised unemployment occurs when more people work on a farm than needed; removing some does not reduce output. Educated unemployment affects matriculates, graduates and postgraduates who cannot find suitable jobs. Unemployment wastes human resources, lowers income and increases poverty and dependence. Employment generation, skill training and growth of the service sector help to reduce it.

🧮

blocks.x: Poverty means being unable to meet basic needs of food, clothing, shelter, health and education. The poverty line separates the poor from the non-poor using the money needed for a minimum calorie intake: 2400 calories a day in rural areas and 2100 in urban areas. Causes: low growth, population, inequality, illiteracy and unemployment. Vulnerability, social exclusion and inequality worsen poverty. Anti-poverty measures include MGNREGA, PMRY, SGSY and the Antyodaya Anna Yojana.
Deep dive: what poverty means

Poverty is a multi-dimensional problem: hunger, lack of shelter, no safe water, illiteracy, poor health, child labour, no job security and a feeling of helplessness. Poor people live in overcrowded huts, often have no land, work as casual or bonded labour and cannot send children to school. Social scientists look at poverty through the poverty line, social exclusion (being kept out of facilities enjoyed by others, such as through caste), vulnerability (the greater chance of becoming or staying poor in bad times) and inequality.
Deep dive: the poverty line

The poverty line is a common measure. It is based on the money needed to buy food for a minimum calorie intake (2400 calories per person per day for rural areas and 2100 for urban areas) plus basic clothing, shoes, fuel, light, education and health. Rural people need more calories as they do heavier work, but the money value of the line is higher in towns because of higher prices. The line is updated by the government using the Consumer Price Index; for 2011-12 it was about Rs 816 per person per month in rural and Rs 1000 in urban areas. The Planning Commission earlier, and now NITI Aayog and the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), measure it from household surveys.
Deep dive: who is poor and why

Poverty is highest among scheduled tribe and scheduled caste households and among casual agricultural labour and urban casual labour households. Poor households are larger, with more children, and women, children and the elderly suffer most. States such as Bihar, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh have more poor people; Kerala, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat have reduced poverty through land reform, growth and food distribution. The proportion of poor in India fell from about 55 percent in 1973 to about 22 percent in 2011-12, but absolute numbers remain large. Globally, poverty fell sharply in China and Southeast Asia, while it remained high in sub-Saharan Africa.
Deep dive: causes and anti-poverty measures

Causes: colonial rule that destroyed handicrafts, slow growth and population increase, unequal land distribution, unequal income, illiteracy, unemployment, social customs (spending on marriages and festivals leading to debt) and low productivity. Measures: economic growth with jobs, and targeted programmes. MGNREGA 2005 gives 100 days of guaranteed wage employment per rural household. PMRY (1993) helps educated unemployed youth to start businesses, REGP and SGSY support self-employment, PMGSY builds rural roads, and the Antyodaya Anna Yojana gives cheap grain to the poorest. The Midday meal, ICDS and health schemes support the poor. Future challenge: educated, healthy and well-paid for all.

Causes: low growth, population, inequality, illiteracy and unemployment. Vulnerability, social exclusion and inequality worsen poverty. Anti-poverty measures include MGNREGA, PMRY, SGSY and the Antyodaya Anna Yojana.

Read the full explanation

Poverty is a multi-dimensional problem: hunger, lack of shelter, no safe water, illiteracy, poor health, child labour, no job security and a feeling of helplessness. Poor people live in overcrowded huts, often have no land, work as casual or bonded labour and cannot send children to school. Social scientists look at poverty through the poverty line, social exclusion (being kept out of facilities enjoyed by others, such as through caste), vulnerability (the greater chance of becoming or staying poor in bad times) and inequality.

🧠

The poverty line

  • The poverty line is a common measure
  • It is based on the money needed to buy food for a minimum calorie intake (2400 calories per person per day for rural areas and 2100 for urban areas)…
  • Rural people need more calories as they do heavier work, but the money value of the line is higher in towns because of higher prices
  • The line is updated by the government using the Consumer Price Index
Read the full explanation

The poverty line is a common measure. It is based on the money needed to buy food for a minimum calorie intake (2400 calories per person per day for rural areas and 2100 for urban areas) plus basic clothing, shoes, fuel, light, education and health. Rural people need more calories as they do heavier work, but the money value of the line is higher in towns because of higher prices. The line is updated by the government using the Consumer Price Index; for 2011-12 it was about Rs 816 per person per month in rural and Rs 1000 in urban areas. The Planning Commission earlier, and now NITI Aayog and the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), measure it from household surveys.

🌟

Who is poor and why

  • Poverty is highest among scheduled tribe and scheduled caste households and among casual agricultural labour and urban casual labour households
  • Poor households are larger, with more children, and women, children and the elderly suffer most
  • States such as Bihar, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh have more poor people
  • Kerala, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat have reduced poverty through land reform, growth and food distribution
Read the full explanation

States such as Bihar, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh have more poor people; Kerala, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat have reduced poverty through land reform, growth and food distribution. The proportion of poor in India fell from about 55 percent in 1973 to about 22 percent in 2011-12, but absolute numbers remain large. Globally, poverty fell sharply in China and Southeast Asia, while it remained high in sub-Saharan Africa.

lessons.title: Food security in India
yt: class 9 economics food security in india

blocks.x: Food security means availability, accessibility and affordability of food to all people at all times. India achieved self-sufficiency in foodgrains after the Green Revolution. The government keeps a buffer stock through the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and distributes grain through the Public Distribution System (PDS) with ration shops at subsidised prices. Minimum support price (MSP) is announced for farmers. The National Food Security Act 2013 gives legal rights to subsidised grain.
Deep dive: what is food security

Food security means that food is available (produced within the country, imported and in government stocks), accessible (within reach of every person) and affordable (people have money to buy enough safe and nutritious food). It also means a balanced diet. Food insecurity can be chronic (a continuing lack of food because of low income) or seasonal (related to harvests and the farming cycle). The most food insecure are the landless, small farmers, artisans, casual labourers, the destitute, and women and children; regions such as Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh are worst affected. Famines such as the Bengal famine of 1943, which killed about 30 lakh people, showed the danger.
Deep dive: the Green Revolution and self-sufficiency

After independence, India aimed at self-sufficiency in foodgrains. The Green Revolution of the late 1960s (HYV seeds of wheat and rice, fertilisers, irrigation) made India self-sufficient, mostly in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. Foodgrain production rose from about 50 million tonnes in 1950-51 to over 250 million tonnes. Yet some people remain hungry because of poor purchasing power. The White Revolution of Amul and the cooperative milk movement raised milk supply.
Deep dive: buffer stock, MSP and PDS

The Food Corporation of India (FCI, set up in 1965) buys wheat and rice from farmers at a Minimum Support Price (MSP) announced before the sowing season. The grain forms the buffer stock, which is kept to be used in shortage and to stabilise prices. It is distributed through the Public Distribution System (PDS) in ration shops (fair price shops) at a price lower than the market price, the issue price. Card types: Antyodaya cards for the poorest, BPL (below poverty line) and APL (above poverty line). Rationing began during the 1940s Bengal famine. The Revamped PDS (1992) and Targeted PDS (1997) improved delivery; the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (2000) provides cheap grain to the poorest.
Deep dive: current schemes and problems

National Food Security Act 2013 gives subsidised food grain to about two-thirds of the population: 5 kg per person per month, with the poorest AAY households getting 35 kg per family. Other schemes: Mid-day Meal, ICDS, Food for Work and the Annapurna Scheme for senior citizens. Problems of PDS: ration shop dealers divert grain to the open market, poor quality of grain, irregular opening, and growing stocks with high storage costs. Cooperatives such as Amul and Mother Dairy and NGOs help; grain banks and Academy of Development Science work in Maharashtra. Reforms include technology for tracking and direct benefit transfer.

Visual lesson

Food security in India

Food security means availability, accessibility and affordability of food to all people at all times

Big idea

  • Food security means availability, accessibility and affordability of food to all people at all times
  • India achieved self-sufficiency in foodgrains after the Green Revolution
  • The government keeps a buffer stock through the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and distributes grain through the Public Distribution System (PDS)…

Food security means that food is available (produced within the country, imported and in government stocks), accessible (within reach of every person) and affordable (people have money to buy enough safe and nutritious food). It also means a balanced diet. Food insecurity can be chronic (a continuing lack of food because of low income) or seasonal (related to harvests and the farming cycle). The most food insecure are the landless, small farmers, artisans, casual labourers, the destitute, and women and children; regions such as Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh are worst affected. Famines such as the Bengal famine of 1943, which killed about 30 lakh people, showed the danger.

After independence, India aimed at self-sufficiency in foodgrains. The Green Revolution of the late 1960s (HYV seeds of wheat and rice, fertilisers, irrigation) made India self-sufficient, mostly in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. Foodgrain production rose from about 50 million tonnes in 1950-51 to over 250 million tonnes. Yet some people remain hungry because of poor purchasing power. The White Revolution of Amul and the cooperative milk movement raised milk supply.

The Food Corporation of India (FCI, set up in 1965) buys wheat and rice from farmers at a Minimum Support Price (MSP) announced before the sowing season. The grain forms the buffer stock, which is kept to be used in shortage and to stabilise prices. It is distributed through the Public Distribution System (PDS) in ration shops (fair price shops) at a price lower than the market price, the issue price. Card types: Antyodaya cards for the poorest, BPL (below poverty line) and APL (above poverty line). Rationing began during the 1940s Bengal famine. The Revamped PDS (1992) and Targeted PDS (1997) improved delivery; the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (2000) provides cheap grain to the poorest.

National Food Security Act 2013 gives subsidised food grain to about two-thirds of the population: 5 kg per person per month, with the poorest AAY households getting 35 kg per family. Other schemes: Mid-day Meal, ICDS, Food for Work and the Annapurna Scheme for senior citizens. Problems of PDS: ration shop dealers divert grain to the open market, poor quality of grain, irregular opening, and growing stocks with high storage costs. Cooperatives such as Amul and Mother Dairy and NGOs help; grain banks and Academy of Development Science work in Maharashtra. Reforms include technology for tracking and direct benefit transfer.

lessons.title: Tenses

blocks.x: A tense shows the time of an action: present, past or future. Each has four forms: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous, making 12 tenses. Simple present: V1 or V1+s for habits and facts. Present continuous: am/is/are + V-ing. Present perfect: has/have + V3. Simple past: V2. Past continuous: was/were + V-ing. Past perfect: had + V3. Simple future: will + V1. Always match the verb with the subject.
Deep dive: present tenses

Simple present: habits, general truths and fixed facts: The sun rises in the east. He plays cricket. With he, she, it add s or es to the verb. Present continuous: action happening now or around now: She is reading. Present perfect: action finished but linked to the present, or experience: I have seen the film. It uses since (point of time) and for (period of time). Present perfect continuous: action started in the past and still going on: He has been studying since morning.
Deep dive: past tenses

Simple past: finished action at a definite past time: They went to Agra last year. Past continuous: action in progress at a past moment: I was sleeping when you called. Past perfect: the earlier of two past actions: The train had left before we reached. Past perfect continuous: continuous action before a past moment: She had been waiting for an hour when he came.
Deep dive: future tenses

Simple future: will/shall + V1 for promises and predictions: I will help you. Future continuous: will be + V-ing, an action in progress at a future time: This time tomorrow I will be flying. Future perfect: will have + V3, completed before a future time: By June I will have finished the course. Future perfect continuous: will have been + V-ing: By May she will have been working here for ten years.
Deep dive: signal words and common errors

Signal words: always, usually, every day (simple present); now, at present, look! (present continuous); already, just, yet, ever, never, since, for (present perfect); yesterday, ago, last week (simple past); tomorrow, next week (future). Never use will after if or when in the condition: If it rains, we will stay (not will rain). Use did + V1 in questions and negatives of the simple past. Verbs of state (know, like, want, belong) are not normally used in continuous form.
Hindi saransh
Tense = kaam ka samay. Present, past, future, har ek ke chaar roop.
Present perfect: has/have + V3. Past perfect: had + V3. Future: will + V1.

qa.q: What is meant by Tense?
qa.a: The form of a verb that shows the time of an action.

qa.q: What is meant by Present tense?
qa.a: The tense that shows an action happening now or habitually.

qa.q: What is meant by Past tense?
qa.a: The tense that shows an action that has already happened.

qa.q: What is meant by Future tense?
qa.a: The tense that shows an action that will happen later.

qa.q: What is meant by Simple present?
qa.a: The tense for habits, general truths and facts.

qa.q: What is meant by Present continuous?
qa.a: The tense for an action happening at the moment of speaking.

qa.q: What is meant by Present perfect?
qa.a: The tense for a finished action linked to the present.

qa.q: What is meant by Present perfect continuous?
qa.a: The tense for an action that began earlier and is still going on.

qa.q: What is meant by Simple past?
qa.a: The tense for an action finished at a definite time in the past.

qa.q: What is meant by Past continuous?
qa.a: The tense for an action in progress at a moment in the past.

qa.q: What is meant by Past perfect?
qa.a: The tense for the earlier of two actions in the past.

qa.q: What is meant by Past perfect continuous?
qa.a: The tense for a continuous action that went on up to a past moment.

qa.q: What is meant by Simple future?
qa.a: The tense for promises, predictions and decisions about the future.

qa.q: What is meant by Future continuous?
qa.a: The tense for an action that will be in progress at a future time.

qa.q: What is meant by Future perfect?
qa.a: The tense for an action that will be completed before a future time.

qa.q: What is meant by Future perfect continuous?
qa.a: The tense for an action that will have been going on up to a future time.

qa.q: What is meant by Verb?
qa.a: A word that shows an action or a state.

qa.q: What is meant by Base form?
qa.a: The first form of a verb such as eat.

qa.q: What is meant by Past participle?
qa.a: The third form of a verb used with has, have and had.

qa.q: What is meant by Present participle?
qa.a: The verb form ending in ing.

qa.q: What is meant by Auxiliary verb?
qa.a: A helping verb such as is, has or will.

qa.q: What is meant by Since?
qa.a: The word used with a point of time in the present perfect.

qa.q: What is meant by For?
qa.a: The word used with a period of time in the present perfect.

qa.q: What is meant by Already?
qa.a: An adverb used with the present perfect to show something has happened earlier than expected.

qa.q: What is meant by Yet?
qa.a: An adverb used in questions and negatives with the present perfect.

qa.q: What is meant by Ago?
qa.a: A word used with the simple past to show how long before now.

qa.q: What is meant by Irregular verb?
qa.a: A verb that does not form its past with ed.

qa.q: What is meant by Regular verb?
qa.a: A verb that forms its past and past participle with ed.

qa.q: What is meant by Stative verb?
qa.a: A verb of state such as know that is not used in continuous tenses.

qa.q: What is meant by Subject-verb agreement?
qa.a: The verb matching its subject in number.

Visual lesson

Tenses

A tense shows the time of an action: present, past or future

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Present tenses›3Past tenses›4Future tenses›5Signal words and common…
Simple presentV1 / V1 + s
Present perfecthas/have + V3
Simple pastV2
Past perfecthad + V3
Simple futurewill + V1
Future perfectwill have + V3
🔑

Big idea

  • A tense shows the time of an action: present, past or future
  • Each has four forms: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous, making 12 tenses
  • Simple present: V1 or V1+s for habits and facts
  • Present continuous: am/is/are + V-ing
Read the full explanation

A tense shows the time of an action: present, past or future. Each has four forms: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous, making 12 tenses. Simple present: V1 or V1+s for habits and facts. Present continuous: am/is/are + V-ing. Present perfect: has/have + V3. Simple past: V2. Past continuous: was/were + V-ing. Past perfect: had + V3. Simple future: will + V1. Always match the verb with the subject.

📌

Present tenses

  • Simple present: habits, general truths and fixed facts: The sun rises in the east
  • He plays cricket
  • With he, she, it add s or es to the verb
  • Present continuous: action happening now or around now: She is reading
Read the full explanation

Simple present: habits, general truths and fixed facts: The sun rises in the east. He plays cricket. With he, she, it add s or es to the verb. Present continuous: action happening now or around now: She is reading. Present perfect: action finished but linked to the present, or experience: I have seen the film. It uses since (point of time) and for (period of time). Present perfect continuous: action started in the past and still going on: He has been studying since morning.

🧠

Past tenses

  • Simple past: finished action at a definite past time: They went to Agra last year
  • Past continuous: action in progress at a past moment: I was sleeping when you called
  • Past perfect: the earlier of two past actions: The train had left before we reached
  • Past perfect continuous: continuous action before a past moment: She had been waiting for an hour when he came
Read the full explanation

Simple past: finished action at a definite past time: They went to Agra last year. Past continuous: action in progress at a past moment: I was sleeping when you called. Past perfect: the earlier of two past actions: The train had left before we reached. Past perfect continuous: continuous action before a past moment: She had been waiting for an hour when he came.

🌟

Future tenses

  • Simple future: will/shall + V1 for promises and predictions: I will help you
  • Future continuous: will be + V-ing, an action in progress at a future time: This time tomorrow I will be flying
  • Future perfect: will have + V3, completed before a future time: By June I will have finished the course
  • Future perfect continuous: will have been + V-ing: By May she will have been working here for ten years
Read the full explanation

Simple future: will/shall + V1 for promises and predictions: I will help you. Future continuous: will be + V-ing, an action in progress at a future time: This time tomorrow I will be flying. Future perfect: will have + V3, completed before a future time: By June I will have finished the course. Future perfect continuous: will have been + V-ing: By May she will have been working here for ten years.

✍️

Signal words and common errors

  • Signal words: always, usually, every day (simple present)
  • Now, at present, look!
  • (present continuous)
  • Already, just, yet, ever, never, since, for (present perfect)
Read the full explanation

Signal words: always, usually, every day (simple present); now, at present, look! (present continuous); already, just, yet, ever, never, since, for (present perfect); yesterday, ago, last week (simple past); tomorrow, next week (future). Never use will after if or when in the condition: If it rains, we will stay (not will rain). Use did + V1 in questions and negatives of the simple past. Verbs of state (know, like, want, belong) are not normally used in continuous form.

🧮

lessons.title: Modals

blocks.x: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need, dare) help the main verb to show ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice and requests. They are followed by the base form of the verb, have no s in the third person and do not take do or does in questions. Can shows ability; may shows permission or possibility; must shows strong obligation; should shows advice; would is the past of will and is used for polite requests.
Deep dive: what modals are

Modals are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need and dare. They do not change form for the subject (no s or ing), are followed by the bare infinitive (the base form without to, except ought to), and form questions by moving the modal before the subject: Can you help? Negatives add not: cannot, should not, must not.
Deep dive: meanings and uses

Can: ability (She can sing), permission (informal) and possibility. Could: past ability (I could swim at six), polite request (Could you help?) and weak possibility. May: permission (May I go?) and possibility (It may rain). Might: weaker possibility. Must: strong obligation (You must wear a helmet), logical certainty and, in the negative, prohibition (You must not smoke). Should and ought to: advice and duty. Shall: offers and suggestions with I and we (Shall I open the window?). Will: promises, predictions and decisions. Would: polite request and habits in the past.
Deep dive: need, dare and have to

Need and dare can act as modals in negatives and questions (He need not go; Dare you say that?). Need not means no obligation (you do not have to), while must not means prohibition. Have to shows external obligation (I have to wake up early), and had to is its past; must has no past form. Used to describes past habits. Modal perfect forms: should have + V3 (a past duty not done), could have + V3, might have + V3 and must have + V3 (certainty about the past).
Deep dive: common errors

Do not add to after a modal (except ought to): wrong "She can to swim". Do not use a modal after another modal: wrong "He will can come". Avoid the s form: wrong "He musts go". Do not use did with could or should. Use "may I" for formal permission and "can I" for casual speech. Choose must for the speaker's own sense of duty and have to for rules from outside.
Hindi saransh
Modals ke baad hamesha verb ka base form aata hai. Can = kshamta, may = anumati, must = zaroorat, should = salah.
After a modal always use V1: She can swim, not She can swims.

Big idea

Read the full explanation

Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need, dare) help the main verb to show ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice and requests. They are followed by the base form of the verb, have no s in the third person and do not take do or does in questions. Can shows ability; may shows permission or possibility; must shows strong obligation; should shows advice; would is the past of will and is used for polite requests.

📌

What modals are

  • Modals are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need and dare
  • They do not change form for the subject (no s or ing), are followed by the bare infinitive (the base form without to, except ought to), and form…
  • Negatives add not: cannot, should not, must not
Read the full explanation

Modals are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need and dare. They do not change form for the subject (no s or ing), are followed by the bare infinitive (the base form without to, except ought to), and form questions by moving the modal before the subject: Can you help? Negatives add not: cannot, should not, must not.

📘

Meanings and uses

  • Can: ability (She can sing), permission (informal) and possibility
  • Could: past ability (I could swim at six), polite request (Could you help?) and weak possibility
  • May: permission (May I go?) and possibility (It may rain)
  • Might: weaker possibility
Read the full explanation

Can: ability (She can sing), permission (informal) and possibility. Could: past ability (I could swim at six), polite request (Could you help?) and weak possibility. May: permission (May I go?) and possibility (It may rain). Might: weaker possibility. Must: strong obligation (You must wear a helmet), logical certainty and, in the negative, prohibition (You must not smoke). Should and ought to: advice and duty. Shall: offers and suggestions with I and we (Shall I open the window?). Will: promises, predictions and decisions. Would: polite request and habits in the past.

🌟

Need, dare and have to

  • Need and dare can act as modals in negatives and questions (He need not go
  • Dare you say that?)
  • Need not means no obligation (you do not have to), while must not means prohibition
  • Have to shows external obligation (I have to wake up early), and had to is its past
Read the full explanation

Need and dare can act as modals in negatives and questions (He need not go; Dare you say that?). Need not means no obligation (you do not have to), while must not means prohibition. Have to shows external obligation (I have to wake up early), and had to is its past; must has no past form. Used to describes past habits. Modal perfect forms: should have + V3 (a past duty not done), could have + V3, might have + V3 and must have + V3 (certainty about the past).

🔬

Common errors

  • Do not add to after a modal (except ought to): wrong "She can to swim"
  • Do not use a modal after another modal: wrong "He will can come"
  • Avoid the s form: wrong "He musts go"
  • Do not use did with could or should
Read the full explanation

Do not add to after a modal (except ought to): wrong "She can to swim". Do not use a modal after another modal: wrong "He will can come". Avoid the s form: wrong "He musts go". Do not use did with could or should. Use "may I" for formal permission and "can I" for casual speech. Choose must for the speaker's own sense of duty and have to for rules from outside.

lessons.title: Subject-verb agreement

blocks.x: The verb must agree with its subject in number and person. A singular subject takes a singular verb (She plays), a plural subject takes a plural verb (They play). Either, neither, each, every, everyone, someone and nobody take singular verbs. Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb unless they are one unit. With either-or and neither-nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Words such as news, mathematics and physics are singular.
Deep dive: the basic rule

A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Singular present verbs end in s (He runs); plural verbs do not (They run). Be forms: I am, he/she/it is, we/you/they are; was for I/he/she/it and were for we/you/they. Have forms: has with he, she, it; have with I, we, you, they. Do not be misled by words between the subject and the verb: The box of apples is heavy; the real subject is box.
Deep dive: singular subjects

Each, every, either, neither, one, everyone, everybody, someone, anybody, nobody and no one take a singular verb: Each of the girls has finished. Many a + singular noun takes a singular verb. Subjects ending in s but singular: news, mathematics, physics, economics, mumps, measles, the United States, and book titles such as Gulliver's Travels. Amounts of money, distance, time and weight taken as one unit are singular: Ten kilometres is far. A number of takes a plural verb; The number of takes a singular verb.
Deep dive: plural subjects and joined subjects

Scissors, trousers, spectacles, glasses, clothes, police, cattle, people and the poor are plural: The police are here. Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Ram and Shyam are friends; but when the two form one idea the verb is singular: Bread and butter is my breakfast. With or, nor, either-or and neither-nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the teacher nor the students were present. With as well as, along with, together with, and with, the verb agrees with the first subject: The captain, with his players, is arriving.
Deep dive: collective nouns and there is

A collective noun (committee, jury, team, class, family) takes a singular verb when it acts as one unit (The committee has decided) and a plural verb when members act separately (The committee are arguing). In sentences beginning with there, the verb agrees with the noun that follows: There are three books on the shelf; There is a pen and a book on the table (nearer noun). In questions, find the real subject: Where are my glasses?

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Subject-verb agreement

The verb must agree with its subject in number and person

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2The basic rule›3Singular subjects›4Plural subjects and joined…›5Collective nouns and there…
🔑

Big idea

  • The verb must agree with its subject in number and person
  • A singular subject takes a singular verb (She plays), a plural subject takes a plural verb (They play)
  • Either, neither, each, every, everyone, someone and nobody take singular verbs
  • Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb unless they are one unit
Read the full explanation

The verb must agree with its subject in number and person. A singular subject takes a singular verb (She plays), a plural subject takes a plural verb (They play). Either, neither, each, every, everyone, someone and nobody take singular verbs. Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb unless they are one unit. With either-or and neither-nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Words such as news, mathematics and physics are singular.

📘

The basic rule

  • A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb
  • Singular present verbs end in s (He runs)
  • Plural verbs do not (They run)
  • Be forms: I am, he/she/it is, we/you/they are
Read the full explanation

A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Singular present verbs end in s (He runs); plural verbs do not (They run). Be forms: I am, he/she/it is, we/you/they are; was for I/he/she/it and were for we/you/they. Have forms: has with he, she, it; have with I, we, you, they. Do not be misled by words between the subject and the verb: The box of apples is heavy; the real subject is box.

🧠

Singular subjects

  • Each, every, either, neither, one, everyone, everybody, someone, anybody, nobody and no one take a singular verb: Each of the girls has finished
  • Many a + singular noun takes a singular verb
  • Subjects ending in s but singular: news, mathematics, physics, economics, mumps, measles, the United States, and book titles such as Gulliver's…
  • Amounts of money, distance, time and weight taken as one unit are singular: Ten kilometres is far
Read the full explanation

Each, every, either, neither, one, everyone, everybody, someone, anybody, nobody and no one take a singular verb: Each of the girls has finished. Many a + singular noun takes a singular verb. Subjects ending in s but singular: news, mathematics, physics, economics, mumps, measles, the United States, and book titles such as Gulliver's Travels. Amounts of money, distance, time and weight taken as one unit are singular: Ten kilometres is far. A number of takes a plural verb; The number of takes a singular verb.

🌟

Plural subjects and joined subjects

  • Scissors, trousers, spectacles, glasses, clothes, police, cattle, people and the poor are plural: The police are here
  • Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Ram and Shyam are friends
  • But when the two form one idea the verb is singular: Bread and butter is my breakfast
  • With or, nor, either-or and neither-nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the teacher nor the students were present
Read the full explanation

Scissors, trousers, spectacles, glasses, clothes, police, cattle, people and the poor are plural: The police are here. Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Ram and Shyam are friends; but when the two form one idea the verb is singular: Bread and butter is my breakfast. With or, nor, either-or and neither-nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the teacher nor the students were present. With as well as, along with, together with, and with, the verb agrees with the first subject: The captain, with his players, is arriving.

🔬

Collective nouns and there is

  • A collective noun (committee, jury, team, class, family) takes a singular verb when it acts as one unit (The committee has decided) and a plural verb…
  • In sentences beginning with there, the verb agrees with the noun that follows: There are three books on the shelf
  • There is a pen and a book on the table (nearer noun)
  • In questions, find the real subject: Where are my glasses?
Read the full explanation

A collective noun (committee, jury, team, class, family) takes a singular verb when it acts as one unit (The committee has decided) and a plural verb when members act separately (The committee are arguing). In sentences beginning with there, the verb agrees with the noun that follows: There are three books on the shelf; There is a pen and a book on the table (nearer noun). In questions, find the real subject: Where are my glasses?

🧮

lessons.title: Determiners

blocks.x: A determiner is a word placed before a noun to show which one or how many. Types: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), quantifiers (some, any, much, many, few, little, all, enough, several), distributives (each, every, either, neither) and numbers. Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds. Use much with uncountable nouns and many with countable nouns.
Deep dive: articles

The indefinite articles a and an are used for a single, non-specific countable noun: a pen, an egg. The choice depends on sound, not spelling: a university (y sound), a one-rupee note (w sound), an hour (silent h), an honest man, an MBA. The definite article the is used for something known or unique (the sun, the moon), the same thing mentioned earlier, rivers, seas, mountain ranges, holy books, musical instruments, superlatives (the best), ordinals (the first) and the only of its kind. Do not use the before names of people, most countries, languages, meals, subjects, or plural nouns used in general: I like music.
Deep dive: demonstratives and possessives

This and these point to near things; that and those point to distant things: this book, that book, these books, those books. Possessive determiners show ownership and come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their; they differ from possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs), which stand alone: This is my pen; the pen is mine.
Deep dive: quantifiers

Some is used in positive sentences and offers (some milk), any in negatives and questions (I do not have any money). Much goes with uncountable nouns (much time), many with countable (many friends); both are mainly used in negatives and questions, while a lot of is common in positive sentences. Few means not many (almost none); a few means some. Little means not much; a little means some. Fewer is for countable nouns and less for uncountable. Enough, all, most, several, both, half and plenty of also quantify nouns.
Deep dive: distributives and numbers

Each means every one of two or more taken separately; every means all, seen as a group (every student). Either means one or the other of two; neither means not one and not the other of two. All of these take singular verbs. Numbers: cardinal (one, two) and ordinal (first, second). Other determiners include which, what, whose, another and other: Which book do you want?
Hindi saransh
Determiner noun se pehle aata hai. A/an: awaz ke hisab se. Much = uncountable, many = countable.
A before a consonant sound; an before a vowel sound. Much + uncountable; many + countable.

Visual lesson

Determiners

A determiner is a word placed before a noun to show which one or how many

🔑

Big idea

  • A determiner is a word placed before a noun to show which one or how many
  • Types: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), quantifiers (some, any…
  • Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds
  • Use much with uncountable nouns and many with countable nouns
Read the full explanation

A determiner is a word placed before a noun to show which one or how many. Types: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), quantifiers (some, any, much, many, few, little, all, enough, several), distributives (each, every, either, neither) and numbers. Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds. Use much with uncountable nouns and many with countable nouns.

📌

Articles

  • The indefinite articles a and an are used for a single, non-specific countable noun: a pen, an egg
  • The choice depends on sound, not spelling: a university (y sound), a one-rupee note (w sound), an hour (silent h), an honest man, an MBA
  • The definite article the is used for something known or unique (the sun, the moon), the same thing mentioned earlier, rivers, seas, mountain ranges…
  • Do not use the before names of people, most countries, languages, meals, subjects, or plural nouns used in general: I like music
Read the full explanation

The indefinite articles a and an are used for a single, non-specific countable noun: a pen, an egg. The choice depends on sound, not spelling: a university (y sound), a one-rupee note (w sound), an hour (silent h), an honest man, an MBA. The definite article the is used for something known or unique (the sun, the moon), the same thing mentioned earlier, rivers, seas, mountain ranges, holy books, musical instruments, superlatives (the best), ordinals (the first) and the only of its kind. Do not use the before names of people, most countries, languages, meals, subjects, or plural nouns used in general: I like music.

🧠

Demonstratives and possessives

  • This and these point to near things
  • That and those point to distant things: this book, that book, these books, those books
  • Possessive determiners show ownership and come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
  • They differ from possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs), which stand alone: This is my pen
Read the full explanation

This and these point to near things; that and those point to distant things: this book, that book, these books, those books. Possessive determiners show ownership and come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their; they differ from possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs), which stand alone: This is my pen; the pen is mine.

🌟

Quantifiers

  • Some is used in positive sentences and offers (some milk), any in negatives and questions (I do not have any money)
  • Much goes with uncountable nouns (much time), many with countable (many friends)
  • Both are mainly used in negatives and questions, while a lot of is common in positive sentences
  • Few means not many (almost none)
Read the full explanation

Some is used in positive sentences and offers (some milk), any in negatives and questions (I do not have any money). Much goes with uncountable nouns (much time), many with countable (many friends); both are mainly used in negatives and questions, while a lot of is common in positive sentences. Few means not many (almost none); a few means some. Little means not much; a little means some. Fewer is for countable nouns and less for uncountable. Enough, all, most, several, both, half and plenty of also quantify nouns.

🔬

Distributives and numbers

  • Each means every one of two or more taken separately
  • Every means all, seen as a group (every student)
  • Either means one or the other of two
  • Neither means not one and not the other of two
Read the full explanation

Each means every one of two or more taken separately; every means all, seen as a group (every student). Either means one or the other of two; neither means not one and not the other of two. All of these take singular verbs. Numbers: cardinal (one, two) and ordinal (first, second). Other determiners include which, what, whose, another and other: Which book do you want?

🧮
