lessons.title: Reported speech

blocks.x: In direct speech we give the exact words of the speaker inside quotation marks; in indirect (reported) speech we report the meaning using that, if, whether or to. Changes: the reporting verb in the past tense moves the tense back (am/is to was; do to did; will to would; can to could; have to had), pronouns change by sense, and words of time and place change (now to then; today to that day; tomorrow to the next day; here to there; this to that). Questions use if or whether (yes/no) or the wh-word with normal order; commands use to + verb.
Deep dive: statements

Direct: Meena said, "I like mangoes." Indirect: Meena said that she liked mangoes. The conjunction that joins the clauses, the pronoun changes from I to she according to the speaker, and simple present changes to simple past. When the reporting verb is in the present or future (She says, She will say) or when the statement is a universal truth, the tense does not change: He said that the earth moves round the sun.
Deep dive: tense changes

Simple present becomes simple past; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect and simple past become past perfect; will becomes would; can becomes could; may becomes might; must stays must or becomes had to. Past continuous and past perfect usually stay unchanged or shift to past perfect continuous. Time and place words shift: now to then, today to that day, tonight to that night, yesterday to the day before, tomorrow to the next day, ago to before, here to there, this to that, these to those, come to go.
Deep dive: questions, commands and exclamations

Yes/no questions: use if or whether, and the order becomes subject then verb with no question mark: He asked me, "Are you tired?" becomes He asked me if I was tired. Wh-questions keep the wh-word: She asked, "Where do you live?" becomes She asked where I lived. Commands and requests use to + verb: The teacher said, "Open your books" becomes The teacher told us to open our books; a negative command uses not to. Exclamations use exclaimed with joy or sorrow: She said, "Hurray! We won" becomes She exclaimed with joy that they had won.
Deep dive: reporting verbs and pronoun rules

Use said (statement), told (with an object), asked (question), ordered, advised, requested, suggested, warned, promised, exclaimed, replied. Pronoun rule: first person pronouns follow the subject of the reporting verb, second person pronouns follow its object, and third person pronouns do not change. So He said to me, "You are late" becomes He told me that I was late. Note: say to becomes tell; said to in questions becomes asked.

Visual lesson

Reported speech

In direct speech we give the exact words of the speaker inside quotation marks

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Statements›3Tense changes›4Questions, commands and…›5Reporting verbs and pronoun…
🔑

Big idea

  • In direct speech we give the exact words of the speaker inside quotation marks
  • In indirect (reported) speech we report the meaning using that, if, whether or to
  • Changes: the reporting verb in the past tense moves the tense back (am/is to was
  • Will to would
Read the full explanation

In direct speech we give the exact words of the speaker inside quotation marks; in indirect (reported) speech we report the meaning using that, if, whether or to. Changes: the reporting verb in the past tense moves the tense back (am/is to was; do to did; will to would; can to could; have to had), pronouns change by sense, and words of time and place change (now to then; today to that day; tomorrow to the next day; here to there; this to that). Questions use if or whether (yes/no) or the wh-word with normal order; commands use to + verb.

📌

Statements

  • Direct: Meena said, "I like mangoes." Indirect: Meena said that she liked mangoes
  • The conjunction that joins the clauses, the pronoun changes from I to she according to the speaker, and simple present changes to simple past
  • When the reporting verb is in the present or future (She says, She will say) or when the statement is a universal truth, the tense does not change:…
Read the full explanation

Direct: Meena said, "I like mangoes." Indirect: Meena said that she liked mangoes. The conjunction that joins the clauses, the pronoun changes from I to she according to the speaker, and simple present changes to simple past. When the reporting verb is in the present or future (She says, She will say) or when the statement is a universal truth, the tense does not change: He said that the earth moves round the sun.

🧠

Tense changes

  • Simple present becomes simple past
  • Present continuous becomes past continuous
  • Present perfect and simple past become past perfect
  • Will becomes would
Read the full explanation

Simple present becomes simple past; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect and simple past become past perfect; will becomes would; can becomes could; may becomes might; must stays must or becomes had to. Past continuous and past perfect usually stay unchanged or shift to past perfect continuous. Time and place words shift: now to then, today to that day, tonight to that night, yesterday to the day before, tomorrow to the next day, ago to before, here to there, this to that, these to those, come to go.

🌟

Questions, commands and exclamations

  • Yes/no questions: use if or whether, and the order becomes subject then verb with no question mark: He asked me, "Are you tired?" becomes He asked me…
  • Wh-questions keep the wh-word: She asked, "Where do you live?" becomes She asked where I lived
  • Commands and requests use to + verb: The teacher said, "Open your books" becomes The teacher told us to open our books
  • A negative command uses not to
Read the full explanation

Yes/no questions: use if or whether, and the order becomes subject then verb with no question mark: He asked me, "Are you tired?" becomes He asked me if I was tired. Wh-questions keep the wh-word: She asked, "Where do you live?" becomes She asked where I lived. Commands and requests use to + verb: The teacher said, "Open your books" becomes The teacher told us to open our books; a negative command uses not to. Exclamations use exclaimed with joy or sorrow: She said, "Hurray! We won" becomes She exclaimed with joy that they had won.

⚖️

Reporting verbs and pronoun rules

  • Use said (statement), told (with an object), asked (question), ordered, advised, requested, suggested, warned, promised, exclaimed, replied
  • Pronoun rule: first person pronouns follow the subject of the reporting verb, second person pronouns follow its object, and third person pronouns do…
  • So He said to me, "You are late" becomes He told me that I was late
  • Note: say to becomes tell
Read the full explanation

Use said (statement), told (with an object), asked (question), ordered, advised, requested, suggested, warned, promised, exclaimed, replied. Pronoun rule: first person pronouns follow the subject of the reporting verb, second person pronouns follow its object, and third person pronouns do not change. So He said to me, "You are late" becomes He told me that I was late. Note: say to becomes tell; said to in questions becomes asked.

lessons.title: Active and passive voice
yt: class 9 english active and passive voice

blocks.x: In the active voice the subject does the action (Ravi writes a letter); in the passive voice the object becomes the subject and the action is done to it (A letter is written by Ravi). Passive = object + be form + past participle (V3) + by + agent. The tense stays the same: only the be form changes (is/are, was/were, has been, will be). Intransitive verbs have no passive. Use the passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious.
Deep dive: what voice means

Voice shows whether the subject performs or receives the action. Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be turned into the passive. The agent (doer) is introduced by by and is often omitted: The window was broken (by someone). Pronouns change case: I to me, he to him, she to her, we to us and they to them in the by-phrase: The cake was eaten by him.
Deep dive: forming the passive

Steps: (1) find the subject, verb and object; (2) make the object the new subject; (3) choose the be form in the same tense as the active verb, matching the new subject; (4) add the past participle of the main verb; (5) add by + the old subject. Simple present: is/are + V3. Present continuous: is/are being + V3. Simple past: was/were + V3. Past continuous: was/were being + V3. Present perfect: has/have been + V3. Past perfect: had been + V3. Simple future: will be + V3. With modals: can/may/must/should + be + V3.
Deep dive: special cases

Questions: Who wrote this letter? becomes By whom was this letter written? Imperatives use let: Open the door becomes Let the door be opened. Verbs with two objects: He gave me a book becomes I was given a book (or A book was given to me). Verbs such as sleep, come, go, arrive, die have no object and have no passive. Perfect continuous tenses and the future continuous are rarely used in the passive.
Deep dive: when to use the passive

Use the passive when the doer is unknown (My bike was stolen), unimportant or obvious (The thief was arrested), when we want to stress the action or result, in news, science and formal writing (Water is boiled at 100 degrees), and in notices and rules (Smoking is prohibited). Avoid the passive where it makes writing dull or hides who is responsible.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Active and passive voice

In the active voice the subject does the action (Ravi writes a letter)

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2What voice means›3Forming the passive›4Special cases›5When to use the passive
Simple presentis/are + V3
Present continuousis/are being + V3
Simple pastwas/were + V3
Past continuouswas/were being + V3
Present perfecthas/have been + V3
Past perfecthad been + V3
Simple futurewill be + V3
Modalcan/may/must/should be + V3
🔑

Big idea

  • In the active voice the subject does the action (Ravi writes a letter)
  • In the passive voice the object becomes the subject and the action is done to it (A letter is written by Ravi)
  • Passive = object + be form + past participle (V3) + by + agent
  • The tense stays the same: only the be form changes (is/are, was/were, has been, will be)
Read the full explanation

In the active voice the subject does the action (Ravi writes a letter); in the passive voice the object becomes the subject and the action is done to it (A letter is written by Ravi). Passive = object + be form + past participle (V3) + by + agent. The tense stays the same: only the be form changes (is/are, was/were, has been, will be). Intransitive verbs have no passive. Use the passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious.

📌

What voice means

  • Voice shows whether the subject performs or receives the action
  • Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be turned into the passive
  • The agent (doer) is introduced by by and is often omitted: The window was broken (by someone)
  • Pronouns change case: I to me, he to him, she to her, we to us and they to them in the by-phrase: The cake was eaten by him
Read the full explanation

Voice shows whether the subject performs or receives the action. Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be turned into the passive. The agent (doer) is introduced by by and is often omitted: The window was broken (by someone). Pronouns change case: I to me, he to him, she to her, we to us and they to them in the by-phrase: The cake was eaten by him.

🧠

Forming the passive

  • Steps: (1) find the subject, verb and object
  • (2) make the object the new subject
  • (3) choose the be form in the same tense as the active verb, matching the new subject
  • (4) add the past participle of the main verb
Read the full explanation

Steps: (1) find the subject, verb and object; (2) make the object the new subject; (3) choose the be form in the same tense as the active verb, matching the new subject; (4) add the past participle of the main verb; (5) add by + the old subject. Simple present: is/are + V3. Present continuous: is/are being + V3. Simple past: was/were + V3. Past continuous: was/were being + V3. Present perfect: has/have been + V3. Past perfect: had been + V3. Simple future: will be + V3. With modals: can/may/must/should + be + V3.

🌟

Special cases

  • Questions: Who wrote this letter?
  • Becomes By whom was this letter written?
  • Imperatives use let: Open the door becomes Let the door be opened
  • Verbs with two objects: He gave me a book becomes I was given a book (or A book was given to me)
Read the full explanation

Questions: Who wrote this letter? becomes By whom was this letter written? Imperatives use let: Open the door becomes Let the door be opened. Verbs with two objects: He gave me a book becomes I was given a book (or A book was given to me). Verbs such as sleep, come, go, arrive, die have no object and have no passive. Perfect continuous tenses and the future continuous are rarely used in the passive.

💡

When to use the passive

  • Use the passive when the doer is unknown (My bike was stolen), unimportant or obvious (The thief was arrested), when we want to stress the action or…
  • Avoid the passive where it makes writing dull or hides who is responsible
🧮

Formula tiles

Simple presentis/are + V3A letter is written
Present continuousis/are being + V3A letter is being written
Simple pastwas/were + V3A letter was written
Past continuouswas/were being + V3A letter was being written
Present perfecthas/have been + V3A letter has been written
Past perfecthad been + V3A letter had been written
Simple futurewill be + V3A letter will be written
Modalcan/may/must/should be + V3A letter can be written
🎯 Remember Passive = be form + V3. The tense of the be form matches the active tense.
🇮🇳

Active me kartta kaam karta hai, passive me karm par kaam hota hai. Passive = be + V3.

lessons.title: Clauses

blocks.x: A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb. A main (independent) clause makes complete sense; a subordinate (dependent) clause does not. Subordinate clauses are of three kinds: noun clauses (do the work of a noun, often begin with that, what, whether), adjective clauses (describe a noun, begin with who, which, that, whose) and adverb clauses (tell time, place, reason, condition, purpose, result, concession or comparison).
Deep dive: phrase and clause

A phrase is a group of words without a subject and verb (in the garden). A clause has a subject and a finite verb. A sentence with one clause is simple; a sentence with a main clause and subordinate clause(s) is complex; two or more main clauses joined by and, but, or, so form a compound sentence. A main clause: The boy won. A subordinate clause: who studied hard.
Deep dive: noun clauses

A noun clause does the work of a noun. It can be the subject (What he said is true), object (I know that he is honest), complement (The truth is that he lied) or object of a preposition (I am sure of what I saw). It starts with that, what, whether, if, who, why, how, when, where. Test: replace it with something or it and the sentence still makes sense.
Deep dive: adjective clauses

An adjective (relative) clause describes a noun or pronoun and follows it directly. Relative pronouns: who (people), whom, whose, which (things), that (people and things); relative adverbs: where, when, why. Example: The boy who won the prize is my cousin. Defining clauses are essential to the meaning; non-defining ones add extra information within commas: My brother, who lives in Pune, is a doctor.
Deep dive: adverb clauses

An adverb clause tells how, when, where, why, or on what condition the action takes place. Time: when, while, before, after, until, as soon as. Place: where, wherever. Reason: because, since, as. Condition: if, unless, provided that. Purpose: so that, in order that. Result: so...that, such...that. Concession: although, though, even if. Comparison: than, as...as. Example: She was absent because she was ill. Do not use a comma before because clauses that follow the main clause.
Hindi saransh
Clause = subject + verb wala shabd samuh. Subordinate clause akele poora arth nahi deti.
Noun clause = noun, adjective clause = describes a noun, adverb clause = tells time, place, reason.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause?
qa.a: A group of words that has its own subject and verb.

qa.q: What is meant by Phrase?
qa.a: A group of words without a subject and verb.

qa.q: What is meant by Main clause?
qa.a: A clause that makes complete sense by itself.

qa.q: What is meant by Independent clause?
qa.a: Another name for a main clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Subordinate clause?
qa.a: A clause that depends on a main clause for its meaning.

qa.q: What is meant by Dependent clause?
qa.a: Another name for a subordinate clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Noun clause?
qa.a: A subordinate clause that does the work of a noun.

qa.q: What is meant by Adjective clause?
qa.a: A subordinate clause that describes a noun or pronoun.

qa.q: What is meant by Relative clause?
qa.a: Another name for an adjective clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Adverb clause?
qa.a: A subordinate clause that does the work of an adverb.

qa.q: What is meant by Relative pronoun?
qa.a: A word such as who or which that begins an adjective clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Relative adverb?
qa.a: The words where, when or why that begin an adjective clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Conjunction?
qa.a: A word that joins words, phrases or clauses.

qa.q: What is meant by Subordinating conjunction?
qa.a: A conjunction that begins a subordinate clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Coordinating conjunction?
qa.a: A conjunction that joins two equal clauses such as and, but, or.

qa.q: What is meant by Simple sentence?
qa.a: A sentence with one main clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Compound sentence?
qa.a: A sentence with two or more main clauses.

qa.q: What is meant by Complex sentence?
qa.a: A sentence with a main clause and a subordinate clause.

qa.q: What is meant by Defining clause?
qa.a: An adjective clause that is essential to the meaning of the noun.

qa.q: What is meant by Non-defining clause?
qa.a: An adjective clause that adds extra information inside commas.

qa.q: What is meant by Finite verb?
qa.a: A verb that shows tense and agrees with its subject.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of time?
qa.a: An adverb clause that tells when something happens.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of reason?
qa.a: An adverb clause that tells why something happens.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of condition?
qa.a: An adverb clause that begins with if or unless.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of purpose?
qa.a: An adverb clause that tells why an action is done.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of result?
qa.a: An adverb clause that shows the effect of the action.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of concession?
qa.a: An adverb clause that shows a contrast and begins with although.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of comparison?
qa.a: An adverb clause that compares things using than or as.

qa.q: What is meant by Clause of place?
qa.a: An adverb clause that tells where something happens.

qa.q: What is meant by Object clause?
qa.a: A noun clause that follows a verb as its object.

Visual lesson

Clauses

A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb

Flat concept map (2D)

🔑

Big idea

  • A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb
  • A main (independent) clause makes complete sense
  • A subordinate (dependent) clause does not
  • Subordinate clauses are of three kinds: noun clauses (do the work of a noun, often begin with that, what, whether), adjective clauses (describe a…
Read the full explanation

A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb. A main (independent) clause makes complete sense; a subordinate (dependent) clause does not. Subordinate clauses are of three kinds: noun clauses (do the work of a noun, often begin with that, what, whether), adjective clauses (describe a noun, begin with who, which, that, whose) and adverb clauses (tell time, place, reason, condition, purpose, result, concession or comparison).

💡

Phrase and clause

  • A phrase is a group of words without a subject and verb (in the garden)
  • A clause has a subject and a finite verb
  • A sentence with one clause is simple
  • A sentence with a main clause and subordinate clause(s) is complex
Read the full explanation

A phrase is a group of words without a subject and verb (in the garden). A clause has a subject and a finite verb. A sentence with one clause is simple; a sentence with a main clause and subordinate clause(s) is complex; two or more main clauses joined by and, but, or, so form a compound sentence. A main clause: The boy won. A subordinate clause: who studied hard.

💡

Noun clauses

  • A noun clause does the work of a noun
  • It can be the subject (What he said is true), object (I know that he is honest), complement (The truth is that he lied) or object of a preposition (I…
  • It starts with that, what, whether, if, who, why, how, when, where
  • Test: replace it with something or it and the sentence still makes sense
💡

Adjective clauses

  • An adjective (relative) clause describes a noun or pronoun and follows it directly
  • Relative pronouns: who (people), whom, whose, which (things), that (people and things)
  • Relative adverbs: where, when, why
  • Example: The boy who won the prize is my cousin
Read the full explanation

An adjective (relative) clause describes a noun or pronoun and follows it directly. Relative pronouns: who (people), whom, whose, which (things), that (people and things); relative adverbs: where, when, why. Example: The boy who won the prize is my cousin. Defining clauses are essential to the meaning; non-defining ones add extra information within commas: My brother, who lives in Pune, is a doctor.

💡

Adverb clauses

  • An adverb clause tells how, when, where, why, or on what condition the action takes place
  • Time: when, while, before, after, until, as soon as
  • Place: where, wherever
  • Reason: because, since, as
Read the full explanation

An adverb clause tells how, when, where, why, or on what condition the action takes place. Time: when, while, before, after, until, as soon as. Place: where, wherever. Reason: because, since, as. Condition: if, unless, provided that. Purpose: so that, in order that. Result: so...that, such...that. Concession: although, though, even if. Comparison: than, as...as. Example: She was absent because she was ill. Do not use a comma before because clauses that follow the main clause.

lessons.title: Notice and message writing
yt: class 9 english notice and message writing

blocks.x: A notice gives public information about an event, change or request, in a box with the name of the issuer, the heading NOTICE, a date, a title, the body in 50 words or fewer, and the name, designation and signature of the writer. A message is a short note for a person who is absent, with the date, time, a salutation, the body and the sender. Both are brief and clear, give the 5Ws (what, who, when, where, why) and use polite words.
Deep dive: notice writing

A notice is a formal written announcement for a group of people on a notice board. Format: (1) the name of the school or organisation at the top; (2) the word NOTICE as the heading; (3) the date; (4) a short title that states the subject in capital letters; (5) the body in the third person; (6) the name and designation of the writer, with signature. Write within a box in about 50 words. Use the passive voice and a formal tone: Students are informed that... Include the 5Ws: what event, who may attend, when, where, and whom to contact.
Deep dive: types of notices

Common notices are of events (annual day, sports day, debate, quiz), of lost and found items, of meetings, of changes in timing, of cancellations, of admissions, of sale, and of public warnings. A lost-and-found notice gives a description of the item, where and when it was lost, and a contact number. An invitation to an event states the programme, chief guest, date and venue. A cancellation notice gives the reason and a new date if any.
Deep dive: message writing

A message is a short note left for a person who is not available. Format: date and time at the top, salutation (Dear Sir, Hi Riya), the body in two or three lines, and the sender's name at the end. Write in the first person for the sender and refer to the receiver as you. Include only the essential details: who called, what is to be done, by when, and a contact number. A telephone message begins with While you were out, or a similar line and uses simple words.
Deep dive: tips for good writing

Keep the language simple and direct. Do not add extra details or personal feelings in a notice. Check the date, time and venue; repeated details cause confusion. Use correct spelling and punctuation, begin sentences with capitals and use the present or future tense for events. Respect the word limit; examiners check content, format, accuracy and fluency.

Format: (1) the name of the school or organisation at the top; (2) the word NOTICE as the heading; (3) the date; (4) a short title that states the subject in capital letters; (5) the body in the third person; (6) the name and designation of the writer, with signature. Write within a box in about 50 words. Use the passive voice and a formal tone: Students are informed that... Include the 5Ws: what event, who may attend, when, where, and whom to contact.

🧠

Types of notices

  • Common notices are of events (annual day, sports day, debate, quiz), of lost and found items, of meetings, of changes in timing, of cancellations, of…
  • A lost-and-found notice gives a description of the item, where and when it was lost, and a contact number
  • An invitation to an event states the programme, chief guest, date and venue
  • A cancellation notice gives the reason and a new date if any
Read the full explanation

Common notices are of events (annual day, sports day, debate, quiz), of lost and found items, of meetings, of changes in timing, of cancellations, of admissions, of sale, and of public warnings. A lost-and-found notice gives a description of the item, where and when it was lost, and a contact number. An invitation to an event states the programme, chief guest, date and venue. A cancellation notice gives the reason and a new date if any.

✍️

Message writing

  • A message is a short note left for a person who is not available
  • Format: date and time at the top, salutation (Dear Sir, Hi Riya), the body in two or three lines, and the sender's name at the end
  • Write in the first person for the sender and refer to the receiver as you
  • Include only the essential details: who called, what is to be done, by when, and a contact number
Read the full explanation

A message is a short note left for a person who is not available. Format: date and time at the top, salutation (Dear Sir, Hi Riya), the body in two or three lines, and the sender's name at the end. Write in the first person for the sender and refer to the receiver as you. Include only the essential details: who called, what is to be done, by when, and a contact number. A telephone message begins with While you were out, or a similar line and uses simple words.

✍️

Tips for good writing

  • Keep the language simple and direct
  • Do not add extra details or personal feelings in a notice
  • Check the date, time and venue
  • Repeated details cause confusion
Read the full explanation

Keep the language simple and direct. Do not add extra details or personal feelings in a notice. Check the date, time and venue; repeated details cause confusion. Use correct spelling and punctuation, begin sentences with capitals and use the present or future tense for events. Respect the word limit; examiners check content, format, accuracy and fluency.

blocks.x: Letters are formal (to an editor, principal or officer) or informal (to friends and family). A formal letter has the sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, and complimentary close (Yours faithfully) with name. An informal letter has an address, date, Dear friend, a friendly body and Yours lovingly. An e-mail has To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, a greeting, a short body and a closing with the name.
Deep dive: formal letters

Formal letters include letters to the editor, complaints, requests, applications and enquiries. Layout: sender's address (top right), date, receiver's designation and address (left), subject line (short and clear, underlined), salutation (Sir/Madam), body in three paragraphs (introduction stating the purpose, details, request or action asked), a polite close (Thanking you / I shall be grateful), complimentary close (Yours faithfully) and the signature with name. Use a respectful, impersonal tone, no slang, and keep the length to about 120 words.
Deep dive: informal letters

An informal letter is a personal letter to a friend or relative. Layout: sender address and date, salutation (Dear Aman), a friendly opening (Hope you are fine), the body in two or three paragraphs, a warm closing (Write soon) and Yours affectionately/lovingly/sincerely with the sender's first name. Contractions and a friendly tone are allowed, but avoid slang and errors. Topics: an invitation, congratulating a friend, describing a trip, giving advice or thanking someone.
Deep dive: letter to the editor and complaints

A letter to the editor states a public issue (noise, garbage, traffic, pollution), its cause and effect, and a suggestion. A complaint letter states the problem, the date and the action expected. Give facts and avoid blaming people. A request or application clearly states what is asked and why. Add enclosures if documents are attached.
Deep dive: writing an e-mail

An e-mail has a recipient address (To), copy (Cc) and blind copy (Bcc), a clear subject line, a greeting (Dear Sir/Hello), a short body, a closing (Regards, Thank you) and your name. Keep paragraphs short, check the address, attach files only when needed, and use a polite tone. Avoid capital letters (they look like shouting) and text abbreviations in formal e-mails. Re-read before sending.

Lengthabout 120 words
🔑

Big idea

  • Letters are formal (to an editor, principal or officer) or informal (to friends and family)
  • A formal letter has the sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, and complimentary close (Yours faithfully)…
  • An informal letter has an address, date, Dear friend, a friendly body and Yours lovingly

Read the full explanation

Letters are formal (to an editor, principal or officer) or informal (to friends and family). A formal letter has the sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, and complimentary close (Yours faithfully) with name. An informal letter has an address, date, Dear friend, a friendly body and Yours lovingly. An e-mail has To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, a greeting, a short body and a closing with the name.

📌

Formal letters

  • Formal letters include letters to the editor, complaints, requests, applications and enquiries
  • Layout: sender's address (top right), date, receiver's designation and address (left), subject line (short and clear, underlined), salutation…
  • Use a respectful, impersonal tone, no slang, and keep the length to about 120 words
Read the full explanation

Formal letters include letters to the editor, complaints, requests, applications and enquiries. Layout: sender's address (top right), date, receiver's designation and address (left), subject line (short and clear, underlined), salutation (Sir/Madam), body in three paragraphs (introduction stating the purpose, details, request or action asked), a polite close (Thanking you / I shall be grateful), complimentary close (Yours faithfully) and the signature with name. Use a respectful, impersonal tone, no slang, and keep the length to about 120 words.

🧠

Informal letters

  • An informal letter is a personal letter to a friend or relative
  • Layout: sender address and date, salutation (Dear Aman), a friendly opening (Hope you are fine), the body in two or three paragraphs, a warm closing…
  • Contractions and a friendly tone are allowed, but avoid slang and errors
  • Topics: an invitation, congratulating a friend, describing a trip, giving advice or thanking someone
Read the full explanation

An informal letter is a personal letter to a friend or relative. Layout: sender address and date, salutation (Dear Aman), a friendly opening (Hope you are fine), the body in two or three paragraphs, a warm closing (Write soon) and Yours affectionately/lovingly/sincerely with the sender's first name. Contractions and a friendly tone are allowed, but avoid slang and errors. Topics: an invitation, congratulating a friend, describing a trip, giving advice or thanking someone.

🌟

Letter to the editor and complaints

  • A letter to the editor states a public issue (noise, garbage, traffic, pollution), its cause and effect, and a suggestion
  • A complaint letter states the problem, the date and the action expected
  • Give facts and avoid blaming people
  • A request or application clearly states what is asked and why
Read the full explanation

A letter to the editor states a public issue (noise, garbage, traffic, pollution), its cause and effect, and a suggestion. A complaint letter states the problem, the date and the action expected. Give facts and avoid blaming people. A request or application clearly states what is asked and why. Add enclosures if documents are attached.

✍️

Writing an e-mail

  • An e-mail has a recipient address (To), copy (Cc) and blind copy (Bcc), a clear subject line, a greeting (Dear Sir/Hello), a short body, a closing…
  • Keep paragraphs short, check the address, attach files only when needed, and use a polite tone
  • Avoid capital letters (they look like shouting) and text abbreviations in formal e-mails
  • Re-read before sending
Read the full explanation

An e-mail has a recipient address (To), copy (Cc) and blind copy (Bcc), a clear subject line, a greeting (Dear Sir/Hello), a short body, a closing (Regards, Thank you) and your name. Keep paragraphs short, check the address, attach files only when needed, and use a polite tone. Avoid capital letters (they look like shouting) and text abbreviations in formal e-mails. Re-read before sending.

lessons.title: Paragraph, story and article writing
yt: class 9 english paragraph story article writing

blocks.x: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea, with a topic sentence, supporting sentences and a concluding sentence. A story has a title, a beginning, middle and end, characters, setting, conflict and a moral. An article has a catchy title, the writer's name (by-line), an introduction, two or three body paragraphs and a conclusion. Use linking words, correct tenses and about 100 to 150 words.
Deep dive: writing a paragraph

A good paragraph has unity: one main idea. The topic sentence at the start states the idea; two to four supporting sentences give reasons, facts and examples; the concluding sentence repeats the idea or gives a result. Use linking words (first, besides, for example, therefore, in conclusion). A descriptive paragraph uses the senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) and adjectives; a narrative paragraph tells events in order; an argumentative paragraph gives reasons.
Deep dive: writing a story

Story writing is often based on given outlines or a first line. Plan the characters, setting, plot and ending. Structure: a title, an opening that sets the scene, rising action with a problem or conflict, a climax (the most exciting point), a resolution and, in many cases, a moral. Use the past tense, direct speech for liveliness, adjectives and adverbs and a variety of sentences. Keep the story within the word limit and end with a moral if asked (Honesty is the best policy).
Deep dive: writing an article

An article presents ideas on a topic for readers of a magazine or newspaper. Parts: a catchy title; the writer's name (by-line); an introduction that states the topic and draws interest; the body in two or three paragraphs with causes, effects, facts and examples; and a conclusion with a suggestion or a thought for readers. Use a formal but lively style. Topics: pollution, road safety, importance of sports, use of mobile phones, plastic ban, digital India. Use facts, not rumours.
Deep dive: skills and common errors

Plan before writing: brainstorm points and arrange them. Use connectors, a variety of sentence beginnings and the right tense. Avoid repetition, slang and run-on sentences. Check spelling and punctuation; read the final copy once. Marking looks at content, expression, format and accuracy. A word limit is about 100 to 120 words for a paragraph and 150 to 200 for a story or article, unless the question states otherwise.

Visual lesson

Paragraph, story and article writing

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea, with a topic sentence, supporting sentences and a concluding sentence

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Writing a paragraph›3Writing a story›4Writing an article›5Skills and common errors
🔑

Big idea

  • A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea, with a topic sentence, supporting sentences and a concluding sentence
  • A story has a title, a beginning, middle and end, characters, setting, conflict and a moral
  • An article has a catchy title, the writer's name (by-line), an introduction, two or three body paragraphs and a conclusion
  • Use linking words, correct tenses and about 100 to 150 words
Read the full explanation

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea, with a topic sentence, supporting sentences and a concluding sentence. A story has a title, a beginning, middle and end, characters, setting, conflict and a moral. An article has a catchy title, the writer's name (by-line), an introduction, two or three body paragraphs and a conclusion. Use linking words, correct tenses and about 100 to 150 words.

✍️

Writing a paragraph

  • A good paragraph has unity: one main idea
  • The topic sentence at the start states the idea
  • Two to four supporting sentences give reasons, facts and examples
  • The concluding sentence repeats the idea or gives a result
Read the full explanation

A good paragraph has unity: one main idea. The topic sentence at the start states the idea; two to four supporting sentences give reasons, facts and examples; the concluding sentence repeats the idea or gives a result. Use linking words (first, besides, for example, therefore, in conclusion). A descriptive paragraph uses the senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) and adjectives; a narrative paragraph tells events in order; an argumentative paragraph gives reasons.

✍️

Writing a story

  • Story writing is often based on given outlines or a first line
  • Plan the characters, setting, plot and ending
  • Structure: a title, an opening that sets the scene, rising action with a problem or conflict, a climax (the most exciting point), a resolution and…
  • Use the past tense, direct speech for liveliness, adjectives and adverbs and a variety of sentences
Read the full explanation

Story writing is often based on given outlines or a first line. Plan the characters, setting, plot and ending. Structure: a title, an opening that sets the scene, rising action with a problem or conflict, a climax (the most exciting point), a resolution and, in many cases, a moral. Use the past tense, direct speech for liveliness, adjectives and adverbs and a variety of sentences. Keep the story within the word limit and end with a moral if asked (Honesty is the best policy).

✍️

Writing an article

  • An article presents ideas on a topic for readers of a magazine or newspaper
  • Parts: a catchy title
  • The writer's name (by-line)
  • An introduction that states the topic and draws interest
Read the full explanation

An article presents ideas on a topic for readers of a magazine or newspaper. Parts: a catchy title; the writer's name (by-line); an introduction that states the topic and draws interest; the body in two or three paragraphs with causes, effects, facts and examples; and a conclusion with a suggestion or a thought for readers. Use a formal but lively style. Topics: pollution, road safety, importance of sports, use of mobile phones, plastic ban, digital India. Use facts, not rumours.

🔬

Skills and common errors

  • Plan before writing: brainstorm points and arrange them
  • Use connectors, a variety of sentence beginnings and the right tense
  • Avoid repetition, slang and run-on sentences
  • Check spelling and punctuation
Read the full explanation

Plan before writing: brainstorm points and arrange them. Use connectors, a variety of sentence beginnings and the right tense. Avoid repetition, slang and run-on sentences. Check spelling and punctuation; read the final copy once. Marking looks at content, expression, format and accuracy. A word limit is about 100 to 120 words for a paragraph and 150 to 200 for a story or article, unless the question states otherwise.

lessons.title: Reading comprehension and vocabulary
yt: class 9 english reading comprehension and vocabulary

blocks.x: Reading comprehension is understanding a passage: read it once for the gist, then read the questions, find the answers in the text and write in your own words. Types of passage: factual, discursive and literary. Skills: skimming (quick overview), scanning (finding facts), inferring (reading between the lines) and finding the main idea. Vocabulary: synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutes, idioms, phrasal verbs and the meaning of words in context.
Deep dive: reading strategies

Skimming means reading quickly to get the main idea. Scanning means searching for a particular word, name or number. Inferring means using clues to understand what is not stated directly. Look at the title, the first and last sentences of paragraphs and the connectors. Underline key words. Answer in complete sentences using your own words; avoid copying large chunks. Multiple-choice items need the best answer from the text, not general knowledge.
Deep dive: kinds of passages and questions

Factual passages (news, reports, notices, advertisements) give information; discursive passages (articles, opinion) give views and arguments; literary passages (stories, poems) express feelings and use figures of speech. Questions ask for the main idea, details, reasons, the writer's attitude, the meaning of a word in the passage, references (what does it refer to), and inferences. For vocabulary-in-context questions, read the sentence around the word and replace the word with each option.
Deep dive: building vocabulary

A synonym is a word of similar meaning (happy and glad); an antonym has an opposite meaning (happy and sad). One-word substitutes replace a phrase (a person who loves books is a bibliophile). Idioms are phrases whose meaning is not the sum of the words (a piece of cake means very easy). Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (give up means stop). Prefixes (un-, dis-, re-) and suffixes (-ness, -ful, -less) change the meaning of root words. Learn words in context and use a dictionary.
Deep dive: comprehension practice

Time yourself, mark the lines where answers appear and check spelling and grammar. For summary questions, write in the present tense, in your own words, and cover only the main points. For poetry, identify the speaker, theme, tone, imagery and poetic devices such as simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration and rhyme. Revise regularly with unseen passages.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Reading comprehension and vocabulary

Reading comprehension is understanding a passage: read it once for the gist, then read the questions, find the answers in the text and write in your own words

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Reading strategies›3Kinds of passages and…›4Building vocabulary›5Comprehension practice
🔑

Big idea

  • Reading comprehension is understanding a passage: read it once for the gist, then read the questions, find the answers in the text and write in your…
  • Types of passage: factual, discursive and literary
  • Skills: skimming (quick overview), scanning (finding facts), inferring (reading between the lines) and finding the main idea
  • Vocabulary: synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutes, idioms, phrasal verbs and the meaning of words in context
Read the full explanation

Reading comprehension is understanding a passage: read it once for the gist, then read the questions, find the answers in the text and write in your own words. Types of passage: factual, discursive and literary. Skills: skimming (quick overview), scanning (finding facts), inferring (reading between the lines) and finding the main idea. Vocabulary: synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutes, idioms, phrasal verbs and the meaning of words in context.

📌

Reading strategies

  • Skimming means reading quickly to get the main idea
  • Scanning means searching for a particular word, name or number
  • Inferring means using clues to understand what is not stated directly
  • Look at the title, the first and last sentences of paragraphs and the connectors
Read the full explanation

Skimming means reading quickly to get the main idea. Scanning means searching for a particular word, name or number. Inferring means using clues to understand what is not stated directly. Look at the title, the first and last sentences of paragraphs and the connectors. Underline key words. Answer in complete sentences using your own words; avoid copying large chunks. Multiple-choice items need the best answer from the text, not general knowledge.

🧠

Kinds of passages and questions

  • Factual passages (news, reports, notices, advertisements) give information
  • Discursive passages (articles, opinion) give views and arguments
  • Literary passages (stories, poems) express feelings and use figures of speech
  • Questions ask for the main idea, details, reasons, the writer's attitude, the meaning of a word in the passage, references (what does it refer to)…
Read the full explanation

Factual passages (news, reports, notices, advertisements) give information; discursive passages (articles, opinion) give views and arguments; literary passages (stories, poems) express feelings and use figures of speech. Questions ask for the main idea, details, reasons, the writer's attitude, the meaning of a word in the passage, references (what does it refer to), and inferences. For vocabulary-in-context questions, read the sentence around the word and replace the word with each option.

🌟

Building vocabulary

  • A synonym is a word of similar meaning (happy and glad)
  • An antonym has an opposite meaning (happy and sad)
  • One-word substitutes replace a phrase (a person who loves books is a bibliophile)
  • Idioms are phrases whose meaning is not the sum of the words (a piece of cake means very easy)
Read the full explanation

A synonym is a word of similar meaning (happy and glad); an antonym has an opposite meaning (happy and sad). One-word substitutes replace a phrase (a person who loves books is a bibliophile). Idioms are phrases whose meaning is not the sum of the words (a piece of cake means very easy). Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (give up means stop). Prefixes (un-, dis-, re-) and suffixes (-ness, -ful, -less) change the meaning of root words. Learn words in context and use a dictionary.

🔬

Comprehension practice

  • Time yourself, mark the lines where answers appear and check spelling and grammar
  • For summary questions, write in the present tense, in your own words, and cover only the main points
  • For poetry, identify the speaker, theme, tone, imagery and poetic devices such as simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration and rhyme
  • Revise regularly with unseen passages
Read the full explanation

Time yourself, mark the lines where answers appear and check spelling and grammar. For summary questions, write in the present tense, in your own words, and cover only the main points. For poetry, identify the speaker, theme, tone, imagery and poetic devices such as simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration and rhyme. Revise regularly with unseen passages.

🧮

Antonymopposite meaningbig, small

Phrasal verbverb + particlegive up

🎯 Remember Skim for the gist, scan for facts, infer for hidden meaning.

yt: class 9 english the fun they had

blocks.x: A science fiction story by Isaac Asimov set in the year 2157. Eleven-year-old Margie and thirteen-year-old Tommy live in a world where children are taught alone at home by mechanical teachers. Tommy finds a real paper book about school in the old days and they wonder at a time when children studied together with a human teacher. Margie feels that those children had fun.
Deep dive: plot

The story opens with Margie writing in her diary on 17 May 2157 that Tommy found a real book. It was very old, its pages yellow and crinkly, and the words stood still instead of moving on a screen. They talk about how, long ago, books were printed on paper and could be thrown away after reading. Margie has had trouble with her geography lessons, so her mother called the County Inspector, who adjusted the mechanical teacher and said that it was set too fast. Margie then reads about a school in which children studied together and had a human teacher, and she imagines how much fun they had. The story ends with her thinking about those happy children.
Deep dive: setting and characters

The year is 2157. Margie is lonely and bored with lessons. Tommy is older and more interested in the real book. The mechanical teacher is a machine with a screen and slot for homework. Mrs Jones is a concerned mother who relies on technology. The Inspector is calm and practical. Margie, a child of her time, finds old schooling strange and wonderful.
Deep dive: themes and literary devices

Themes: the loss of human contact in a technological world, the joy of shared learning, change and nostalgia. The author uses irony (the children find a printed book strange while we find it ordinary), contrast between old and new schools, and a simple child's viewpoint. The story warns that machines may help but cannot replace teachers and friends.

Margie aur Tommy 2157 me mashini shikshak se padhte hain. Purane school unhe maze ka lagta hai.
Theme: technology cannot replace the human touch and joy of learning together.

A science fiction story by Isaac Asimov set in the year 2157. Eleven-year-old Margie and thirteen-year-old Tommy live in a world where children are taught alone at home by mechanical teachers. Tommy finds a real paper book about school in the old days and they wonder at a time when children studied together with a human teacher. Margie feels that those children had fun.

📌

Plot

Read the full explanation

The story opens with Margie writing in her diary on 17 May 2157 that Tommy found a real book. It was very old, its pages yellow and crinkly, and the words stood still instead of moving on a screen. They talk about how, long ago, books were printed on paper and could be thrown away after reading. Margie has had trouble with her geography lessons, so her mother called the County Inspector, who adjusted the mechanical teacher and said that it was set too fast. Margie then reads about a school in which children studied together and had a human teacher, and she imagines how much fun they had. The story ends with her thinking about those happy children.

🧠

Setting and characters

  • The year is 2157
  • Margie is lonely and bored with lessons
  • Tommy is older and more interested in the real book
  • The mechanical teacher is a machine with a screen and slot for homework
Read the full explanation

The year is 2157. Margie is lonely and bored with lessons. Tommy is older and more interested in the real book. The mechanical teacher is a machine with a screen and slot for homework. Mrs Jones is a concerned mother who relies on technology. The Inspector is calm and practical. Margie, a child of her time, finds old schooling strange and wonderful.

🌟

Themes and literary devices

  • Themes: the loss of human contact in a technological world, the joy of shared learning, change and nostalgia
  • The author uses irony (the children find a printed book strange while we find it ordinary), contrast between old and new schools, and a simple…
  • The story warns that machines may help but cannot replace teachers and friends

lessons.title: The sound of music
yt: class 9 english the sound of music

blocks.x: The chapter has two parts. Part I: Evelyn Glennie, a Scottish percussionist who became deaf by the age of eleven yet became a world-famous solo percussionist; she hears music by feeling vibrations, often performing barefoot. Part II: Ustad Bismillah Khan, the shehnai maestro from Dumraon in Bihar, who raised the shehnai to the concert stage and played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947.
Deep dive: Evelyn Glennie

Evelyn Glennie was born in Scotland. She gradually lost her hearing and was almost deaf by eleven. Her parents and teachers encouraged her. Her teacher Ron Forbes asked her to place her hands on the wall of the room while he beat the drum, and she learned to feel the sound; he taught her that low notes could be felt in the legs and feet and high notes in the face or upper body. She chose percussion and was admitted to the Royal Academy of Music in London despite her deafness. She became the first full-time solo percussionist in the world, playing barefoot to feel the music.
Deep dive: Bismillah Khan

Long ago the pungi, a reed instrument, was played by snake charmers, and it was forbidden in the royal courts because its sound was shrill. A barber from a family of professional musicians who had access to the court improved it: he made a pipe with a natural hollow stem with seven holes, and it produced a soft sound and came to be called the shehnai. Bismillah Khan, born in Dumraon in Bihar, became its greatest player. He played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947 at the first Independence Day. He loved Varanasi and the Ganga and refused to settle abroad. He was given the Bharat Ratna in 2001.
Deep dive: themes
Both parts show that talent, hard work and love for music matter more than difficulty. The chapter links music to dedication, humility and national pride.

Courage and practice can overcome any disability.

Read the full explanation

The chapter has two parts. Part I: Evelyn Glennie, a Scottish percussionist who became deaf by the age of eleven yet became a world-famous solo percussionist; she hears music by feeling vibrations, often performing barefoot. Part II: Ustad Bismillah Khan, the shehnai maestro from Dumraon in Bihar, who raised the shehnai to the concert stage and played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947.

📌

Evelyn Glennie

  • Evelyn Glennie was born in Scotland
  • She gradually lost her hearing and was almost deaf by eleven
  • Her parents and teachers encouraged her
  • Her teacher Ron Forbes asked her to place her hands on the wall of the room while he beat the drum, and she learned to feel the sound
Read the full explanation

Evelyn Glennie was born in Scotland. She gradually lost her hearing and was almost deaf by eleven. Her parents and teachers encouraged her. Her teacher Ron Forbes asked her to place her hands on the wall of the room while he beat the drum, and she learned to feel the sound; he taught her that low notes could be felt in the legs and feet and high notes in the face or upper body. She chose percussion and was admitted to the Royal Academy of Music in London despite her deafness. She became the first full-time solo percussionist in the world, playing barefoot to feel the music.

🧠

Bismillah Khan

  • Long ago the pungi, a reed instrument, was played by snake charmers, and it was forbidden in the royal courts because its sound was shrill
  • A barber from a family of professional musicians who had access to the court improved it: he made a pipe with a natural hollow stem with seven holes…
  • Bismillah Khan, born in Dumraon in Bihar, became its greatest player
  • He played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947 at the first Independence Day
Read the full explanation

Long ago the pungi, a reed instrument, was played by snake charmers, and it was forbidden in the royal courts because its sound was shrill. A barber from a family of professional musicians who had access to the court improved it: he made a pipe with a natural hollow stem with seven holes, and it produced a soft sound and came to be called the shehnai. Bismillah Khan, born in Dumraon in Bihar, became its greatest player. He played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947 at the first Independence Day. He loved Varanasi and the Ganga and refused to settle abroad. He was given the Bharat Ratna in 2001.

🌟

Themes

  • Both parts show that talent, hard work and love for music matter more than difficulty
  • The chapter links music to dedication, humility and national pride

lessons.title: The little girl

blocks.x: A short story by Katherine Mansfield. Kezia is afraid of her stern father, who she thinks does not love her, and she finds comfort in her grandmother. After she tears the pages of his speech to make a pincushion as a birthday present, he scolds and punishes her. Later her mother is ill, and one night, when she has a bad dream, her father comforts her, and she learns that he loves her.
Deep dive: plot

Kezia, a small girl, feels her father is a frightening figure: he is stern, busy and does not smile. Her grandmother is her comfort. On the day of her father's birthday she wants to make a present: a pincushion. She stuffs it with paper, which turns out to be the pages of her father's speech for the Port Authority. When he learns this he is angry and strikes her. She is terrified and sad. Soon her mother is ill and Kezia must sleep alone. At night a nightmare wakes her, and her father takes her into his bed and comforts her. She realises how much he loves her.
Deep dive: characters
Kezia is sensitive and innocent. Her father is the strict head of the family who feels deeply but does not show it. The grandmother is gentle. The mother plays a small role.
Deep dive: themes

Misunderstanding between parent and child, the need for love and reassurance, and how a moment of tenderness can change a relationship. The story is told in a simple style from the child's point of view.
Hindi saransh
Kezia apne pita se darti hai. Ek raat pita use gale lagate hain aur uska darr door ho jata hai.
Parents may seem strict but may love their children deeply.

Read the full explanation

A short story by Katherine Mansfield. Kezia is afraid of her stern father, who she thinks does not love her, and she finds comfort in her grandmother. After she tears the pages of his speech to make a pincushion as a birthday present, he scolds and punishes her. Later her mother is ill, and one night, when she has a bad dream, her father comforts her, and she learns that he loves her.

📌

Plot

  • Kezia, a small girl, feels her father is a frightening figure: he is stern, busy and does not smile
  • Her grandmother is her comfort
  • On the day of her father's birthday she wants to make a present: a pincushion
  • She stuffs it with paper, which turns out to be the pages of her father's speech for the Port Authority
Read the full explanation

Kezia, a small girl, feels her father is a frightening figure: he is stern, busy and does not smile. Her grandmother is her comfort. On the day of her father's birthday she wants to make a present: a pincushion. She stuffs it with paper, which turns out to be the pages of her father's speech for the Port Authority. When he learns this he is angry and strikes her. She is terrified and sad. Soon her mother is ill and Kezia must sleep alone. At night a nightmare wakes her, and her father takes her into his bed and comforts her. She realises how much he loves her.

🧠

Characters

  • Kezia is sensitive and innocent
  • Her father is the strict head of the family who feels deeply but does not show it
  • The grandmother is gentle
  • The mother plays a small role
🌟

Themes

  • Misunderstanding between parent and child, the need for love and reassurance, and how a moment of tenderness can change a relationship
  • The story is told in a simple style from the child's point of view

blocks.x: A short biography of Albert Einstein (1879 to 1955). He was born in Ulm, Germany, was slow to speak, hated rote learning and was fascinated by a compass and geometry. He was a pacifist who left Germany when the Nazis came to power, settled in the USA, won the Nobel Prize in 1921 for the photoelectric effect and developed the theory of relativity. Later he regretted that his equation led to the atom bomb.
Deep dive: childhood and education

Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, on 14 March 1879. His family later moved to Munich. His father had an electrical business and his mother taught him the violin. He was slow to speak, and some thought him dull, but he was very curious. At five his father showed him a compass, and he was amazed that the needle pointed north without being touched. He disliked rote learning and strict schooling. He loved Euclid's geometry. He left school in Germany at fifteen and went to Switzerland to finish school and study at the Zurich Polytechnic.
Deep dive: career and achievements

He worked as a clerk in the patent office in Bern and, in 1905, published papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and the special theory of relativity. These made him famous. He later developed the general theory of relativity. For his work on the photoelectric effect he received the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921. He became a professor and travelled widely.
Deep dive: peace and later life

Einstein was a pacifist. When the Nazis took power in Germany in 1933 he left for the United States and worked at Princeton. He wrote to President Roosevelt warning that Germany might build an atom bomb, but later regretted that his work led to nuclear weapons. He supported world peace, civil rights and humanitarian causes, declined the presidency of Israel and died on 18 April 1955. The chapter shows that a truly beautiful mind combines great intelligence with kindness and courage.

Visual lesson

A truly beautiful mind

A short biography of Albert Einstein (1879 to 1955)

🔑

Big idea

  • A short biography of Albert Einstein (1879 to 1955)
  • He was born in Ulm, Germany, was slow to speak, hated rote learning and was fascinated by a compass and geometry
  • He was a pacifist who left Germany when the Nazis came to power, settled in the USA, won the Nobel Prize in 1921 for the photoelectric effect and…
  • Later he regretted that his equation led to the atom bomb
Read the full explanation

A short biography of Albert Einstein (1879 to 1955). He was born in Ulm, Germany, was slow to speak, hated rote learning and was fascinated by a compass and geometry. He was a pacifist who left Germany when the Nazis came to power, settled in the USA, won the Nobel Prize in 1921 for the photoelectric effect and developed the theory of relativity. Later he regretted that his equation led to the atom bomb.

📌

Childhood and education

  • Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, on 14 March 1879
  • His family later moved to Munich
  • His father had an electrical business and his mother taught him the violin
  • He was slow to speak, and some thought him dull, but he was very curious
Read the full explanation

Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, on 14 March 1879. His family later moved to Munich. His father had an electrical business and his mother taught him the violin. He was slow to speak, and some thought him dull, but he was very curious. At five his father showed him a compass, and he was amazed that the needle pointed north without being touched. He disliked rote learning and strict schooling. He loved Euclid's geometry. He left school in Germany at fifteen and went to Switzerland to finish school and study at the Zurich Polytechnic.

🧠

Career and achievements

  • He worked as a clerk in the patent office in Bern and, in 1905, published papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and the special theory…
  • These made him famous
  • He later developed the general theory of relativity
  • For his work on the photoelectric effect he received the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921
Read the full explanation

He worked as a clerk in the patent office in Bern and, in 1905, published papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and the special theory of relativity. These made him famous. He later developed the general theory of relativity. For his work on the photoelectric effect he received the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921. He became a professor and travelled widely.

🌟

Peace and later life

  • Einstein was a pacifist
  • When the Nazis took power in Germany in 1933 he left for the United States and worked at Princeton
  • He wrote to President Roosevelt warning that Germany might build an atom bomb, but later regretted that his work led to nuclear weapons
  • He supported world peace, civil rights and humanitarian causes, declined the presidency of Israel and died on 18 April 1955
Read the full explanation

Einstein was a pacifist. When the Nazis took power in Germany in 1933 he left for the United States and worked at Princeton. He wrote to President Roosevelt warning that Germany might build an atom bomb, but later regretted that his work led to nuclear weapons. He supported world peace, civil rights and humanitarian causes, declined the presidency of Israel and died on 18 April 1955. The chapter shows that a truly beautiful mind combines great intelligence with kindness and courage.

🎯 Remember Einstein was a great scientist and a lover of peace.

lessons.title: The snake and the mirror
yt: class 9 english the snake and the mirror

blocks.x: A humorous story by Vaikom Muhammad Basheer. A vain homoeopathic doctor, who dreams of marrying a rich and beautiful woman doctor, sits in his small rented room on a hot night. A snake drops onto his arm, he is frozen with fear and thinks it is a punishment for his pride. The snake becomes distracted by its own reflection in the large mirror, and the doctor slips away to safety.
Deep dive: story

The narrator, a homoeopathic doctor, tells a story from his youth. After dinner at a cafeteria he returns to his rented room, takes off his suit and shirt, and opens two windows because of the heat. He sits with a medical book, then looks at himself in the large mirror and daydreams about marrying a rich and beautiful woman doctor. The rats stop their noise, and he hears a plunging sound. A snake falls on his arm. He is frozen and thinks it is God's punishment for his arrogance. Then the snake sees its own reflection in the mirror and moves toward it; the doctor slips out of the room and escapes.
Deep dive: devices

Humour comes from the contrast between the doctor's pride and his helplessness. The author uses irony (a vain doctor saved by a mirror), suspense in the silence of the rats and a first-person narration. The snake's own vanity mirrors the doctor's.
Deep dive: themes
Vanity and pride; the unpredictable nature of life and fate; helplessness before danger; and how humour can make a serious event enjoyable.

Ek ghamandi doctor ko saanp aa jata hai; darpan me apni parchhai dekh saanp use chhod deta hai.
Vanity is foolish; fear and humour mix in this story.

Visual lesson

The snake and the mirror

A humorous story by Vaikom Muhammad Basheer

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Story›3Devices›4Themes
🔑

Big idea

  • A humorous story by Vaikom Muhammad Basheer
  • A vain homoeopathic doctor, who dreams of marrying a rich and beautiful woman doctor, sits in his small rented room on a hot night
  • A snake drops onto his arm, he is frozen with fear and thinks it is a punishment for his pride
  • The snake becomes distracted by its own reflection in the large mirror, and the doctor slips away to safety
Read the full explanation

A humorous story by Vaikom Muhammad Basheer. A vain homoeopathic doctor, who dreams of marrying a rich and beautiful woman doctor, sits in his small rented room on a hot night. A snake drops onto his arm, he is frozen with fear and thinks it is a punishment for his pride. The snake becomes distracted by its own reflection in the large mirror, and the doctor slips away to safety.

✍️

Story

  • The narrator, a homoeopathic doctor, tells a story from his youth
  • After dinner at a cafeteria he returns to his rented room, takes off his suit and shirt, and opens two windows because of the heat
  • He sits with a medical book, then looks at himself in the large mirror and daydreams about marrying a rich and beautiful woman doctor
  • The rats stop their noise, and he hears a plunging sound
Read the full explanation

The narrator, a homoeopathic doctor, tells a story from his youth. After dinner at a cafeteria he returns to his rented room, takes off his suit and shirt, and opens two windows because of the heat. He sits with a medical book, then looks at himself in the large mirror and daydreams about marrying a rich and beautiful woman doctor. The rats stop their noise, and he hears a plunging sound. A snake falls on his arm. He is frozen and thinks it is God's punishment for his arrogance. Then the snake sees its own reflection in the mirror and moves toward it; the doctor slips out of the room and escapes.

🧠

Devices

  • Humour comes from the contrast between the doctor's pride and his helplessness
  • The author uses irony (a vain doctor saved by a mirror), suspense in the silence of the rats and a first-person narration
  • The snake's own vanity mirrors the doctor's
🌟

Themes

  • Vanity and pride
  • The unpredictable nature of life and fate
  • Helplessness before danger
  • And how humour can make a serious event enjoyable
🧮

lessons.title: My childhood

blocks.x: An extract from the autobiography Wings of Fire by Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam. He describes his childhood in Rameswaram, his loving but strict family, his friends Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan, a teacher who refused to let a Hindu boy sit with a Muslim, and how his science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer invited him home. He also worked for his cousin Samsuddin to deliver newspapers and earned his first wages.
Deep dive: family and friends

A. P. J. Abdul Kalam was born into a middle-class Muslim family in Rameswaram. His father, Jainulabdeen, had little formal education or wealth, but he was generous and wise and taught him honesty, self-discipline and simplicity; his mother Ashiamma fed many people daily. Kalam had three close friends, Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan, all Hindus, and no one in the group felt any difference of religion. Ahmed Jallaluddin, his friend and later his brother-in-law, spoke to him about spiritual matters.
Deep dive: the teacher and the lesson

When Kalam was in the fifth class a new teacher saw him sitting with Ramanadha Sastry, the son of the temple's chief priest, and sent him to the back bench. The two boys were hurt and told their parents. Ramanadha's father, Lakshmana Sastry, summoned the teacher and said that he must not spread social inequality and communal intolerance, or else leave the village. The teacher apologised and changed. Another teacher, Sivasubramania Iyer, invited Kalam to his home for a meal even though his wife refused at first to serve a Muslim boy; he served Kalam himself and sat beside him. Kalam later returned and found the same wife serving him with her own hands.
Deep dive: first earnings

During the war the demand for newspapers rose. As the trains stopped at Rameswaram, the bundles of papers were thrown from the moving train and Kalam's cousin Samsuddin needed help catching them. Kalam did so and earned his first wages. The chapter shows how childhood experiences shaped his belief in unity and service.
Hindi saransh
Kalam ka bachpan Rameswaram me bita. Unke dost alag dharm ke the par unme koi bhed nahi tha.
Respect for all religions and hard work shaped Kalam's character.

🔑

Big idea

  • An extract from the autobiography Wings of Fire by Dr A
  • He describes his childhood in Rameswaram, his loving but strict family, his friends Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan, a teacher who…
  • He also worked for his cousin Samsuddin to deliver newspapers and earned his first wages
Read the full explanation

An extract from the autobiography Wings of Fire by Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam. He describes his childhood in Rameswaram, his loving but strict family, his friends Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan, a teacher who refused to let a Hindu boy sit with a Muslim, and how his science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer invited him home. He also worked for his cousin Samsuddin to deliver newspapers and earned his first wages.

📌

Family and friends

  • Abdul Kalam was born into a middle-class Muslim family in Rameswaram
  • His father, Jainulabdeen, had little formal education or wealth, but he was generous and wise and taught him honesty, self-discipline and simplicity
  • His mother Ashiamma fed many people daily
  • Kalam had three close friends, Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan, all Hindus, and no one in the group felt any difference of religion
Read the full explanation

A. P. J. Abdul Kalam was born into a middle-class Muslim family in Rameswaram. His father, Jainulabdeen, had little formal education or wealth, but he was generous and wise and taught him honesty, self-discipline and simplicity; his mother Ashiamma fed many people daily. Kalam had three close friends, Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan, all Hindus, and no one in the group felt any difference of religion. Ahmed Jallaluddin, his friend and later his brother-in-law, spoke to him about spiritual matters.

🧠

The teacher and the lesson

  • When Kalam was in the fifth class a new teacher saw him sitting with Ramanadha Sastry, the son of the temple's chief priest, and sent him to the back…
  • The two boys were hurt and told their parents
  • Ramanadha's father, Lakshmana Sastry, summoned the teacher and said that he must not spread social inequality and communal intolerance, or else leave…
  • The teacher apologised and changed
Read the full explanation

When Kalam was in the fifth class a new teacher saw him sitting with Ramanadha Sastry, the son of the temple's chief priest, and sent him to the back bench. The two boys were hurt and told their parents. Ramanadha's father, Lakshmana Sastry, summoned the teacher and said that he must not spread social inequality and communal intolerance, or else leave the village. The teacher apologised and changed. Another teacher, Sivasubramania Iyer, invited Kalam to his home for a meal even though his wife refused at first to serve a Muslim boy; he served Kalam himself and sat beside him. Kalam later returned and found the same wife serving him with her own hands.

🌟

First earnings

  • During the war the demand for newspapers rose
  • As the trains stopped at Rameswaram, the bundles of papers were thrown from the moving train and Kalam's cousin Samsuddin needed help catching them
  • Kalam did so and earned his first wages
  • The chapter shows how childhood experiences shaped his belief in unity and service
🧮

lessons.title: Packing

blocks.x: A humorous extract from Three Men in a Boat by Jerome K. Jerome. The narrator, J., with his friends George and Harris and the dog Montmorency, plans a boat trip on the Thames. The narrator boasts that he is an excellent packer and takes charge, while George and Harris lounge. The packing turns into a comic disaster: things are lost, broken and re-packed again.
Deep dive: story

The narrator J. announces that he will pack for the boating trip and says he is an expert. George and Harris sit back and let him do all the work. As he packs, he forgets some things, packs others in the wrong place and has to open everything again. Montmorency helps by getting in the way. The comic effect comes from the narrator's exaggerated claim and his repeated failure.
Deep dive: devices
Jerome uses humour, exaggeration, irony and self-mockery. The narrator is the butt of his own joke. The language is light, simple and conversational.
Deep dive: lesson
Boasting about one's skill can lead to embarrassment, and a task is best done with the help of others.
Hindi saransh
Teen dost naav yatra ke liye saaman pack karte hain aur sab kuch gadbad ho jata hai.
Boasting before doing invites trouble; the humour comes from the narrator's overconfidence.

Visual lesson

Packing

A humorous extract from Three Men in a Boat by Jerome K

minutes
formulas
Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Story›3Devices›4Lesson
🔑

Big idea

  • A humorous extract from Three Men in a Boat by Jerome K
  • The narrator, J., with his friends George and Harris and the dog Montmorency, plans a boat trip on the Thames
  • The narrator boasts that he is an excellent packer and takes charge, while George and Harris lounge
  • The packing turns into a comic disaster: things are lost, broken and re-packed again
Read the full explanation

A humorous extract from Three Men in a Boat by Jerome K. Jerome. The narrator, J., with his friends George and Harris and the dog Montmorency, plans a boat trip on the Thames. The narrator boasts that he is an excellent packer and takes charge, while George and Harris lounge. The packing turns into a comic disaster: things are lost, broken and re-packed again.

✍️

Story

  • The narrator J
  • Announces that he will pack for the boating trip and says he is an expert
  • George and Harris sit back and let him do all the work
  • As he packs, he forgets some things, packs others in the wrong place and has to open everything again
Read the full explanation

The narrator J. announces that he will pack for the boating trip and says he is an expert. George and Harris sit back and let him do all the work. As he packs, he forgets some things, packs others in the wrong place and has to open everything again. Montmorency helps by getting in the way. The comic effect comes from the narrator's exaggerated claim and his repeated failure.

🧠

Devices

  • Jerome uses humour, exaggeration, irony and self-mockery
  • The narrator is the butt of his own joke
  • The language is light, simple and conversational
🌟

Lesson

  • Boasting about one's skill can lead to embarrassment, and a task is best done with the help of others
🧮

🎯 Remember Boasting before doing invites trouble; the humour comes from the narrator's overconfidence.
