lessons.title: प्रेमचंद के फटे जूते
yt: class 9 hindi प्रेमचंद के फटे जूते

blocks.x: हरिशंकर परसाई का यह व्यंग्य प्रेमचंद के एक चित्र पर आधारित है जिसमें उनके जूते फटे हैं और उँगली बाहर झाँक रही है। लेखक इस बहाने दिखावे और सादगी, साहित्यकार की गरीबी और समाज की विडंबना पर व्यंग्य करते हैं।
गहराई से समझें: व्यंग्य
परसाई प्रेमचंद के फटे जूते को देखकर कहते हैं कि वे जूते की चिंता नहीं करते थे। लेखक अपने जूते से तुलना करते हैं जो बाहर से ठीक पर अंदर से फटा है। इस प्रकार समाज के दिखावे पर चोट होती है।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
पाठ बताता है कि सच्चा साहित्यकार सादगी से जीता है और दिखावे में नहीं पड़ता।
Hindi saransh
फटे जूते वाले प्रेमचंद सादगी और संघर्ष के प्रतीक हैं।
व्यंग्य में कही गई बात के पीछे गंभीर आशय होता है।

lessons.title: मेरे बचपन के दिन
yt: class 9 hindi मेरे बचपन के दिन

blocks.x: महादेवी वर्मा के इस संस्मरण में उनके बचपन की स्मृतियाँ हैं। वे बताती हैं कि उनके परिवार में सैकड़ों वर्षों बाद कन्या का जन्म हुआ था, इसलिए उनका स्वागत हुआ। साथ ही हिंदू-मुस्लिम एकता के सुंदर चित्र भी इसमें हैं।
गहराई से समझें: बचपन
लेखिका के परिवार में कन्या के जन्म पर उल्लास हुआ। उन्हें पढ़ाई और संस्कार दोनों मिले। पड़ोस के मुस्लिम परिवार से स्नेह का संबंध था और धर्म के बँटवारे का भाव नहीं था।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
पाठ सांप्रदायिक सौहार्द और बेटियों के सम्मान की शिक्षा देता है।
Hindi saransh
लेखिका के बचपन की मधुर यादें और सांप्रदायिक सौहार्द का चित्रण।
महादेवी वर्मा छायावाद की प्रमुख कवयित्री हैं।

blocks.x: हज़ारीप्रसाद द्विवेदी का यह निबंध शांतिनिकेतन के गुरुदेव रवींद्रनाथ टैगोर से जुड़ा है। एक कुत्ता गुरुदेव का भक्त था, और एक लँगड़ी मैना शांतिनिकेतन में रहती थी। लेखक ने पशु-पक्षियों की संवेदना और प्रेम को दिखाया है।
गहराई से समझें: विषय
निबंध में गुरुदेव का प्रिय स्थान शांतिनिकेतन है। एक कुत्ता उनका भक्त था और एक लँगड़ी मैना का वर्णन है। लेखक पशु-पक्षियों की संवेदना को मनुष्य के लिए शिक्षाप्रद बताते हैं।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
प्राणियों के प्रति दया और प्रेम रखना ही सच्ची मनुष्यता है।
Hindi saransh
पशु-पक्षी भी प्रेम और भक्ति को समझते हैं।
गुरुदेव के प्रति कुत्ते की निष्ठा मनुष्य को भी सिखाती है।

lessons.title: रैदास के पद

blocks.x: रैदास (रविदास) भक्तिकाल की निर्गुण संत धारा के कवि थे। पहले पद में भक्त और भगवान की घनिष्ठता को चंदन-पानी, घन-मोर, चाँद-चकोर, दीपक-बाती, मोती-धागा और सोना-सुहागा जैसे उदाहरणों से बताया गया है। दूसरे पद में प्रभु की कृपा और गरीबों पर दया का वर्णन है।
गहराई से समझें: पहला पद
कवि कहता है कि राम नाम की रट लग गई है और वह अब कैसे छूटे। प्रभु चंदन हैं और भक्त पानी, जिसकी सुगंध अंग-अंग में बसती है। प्रभु घन हैं तो भक्त मोर; प्रभु चाँद हैं तो भक्त चकोर।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
रैदास जाति-पाँति के भेद को नहीं मानते और ईश्वर की कृपा को सब पर समान मानते हैं।
Hindi saransh
रैदास भक्त और भगवान को अभिन्न मानते हैं।
भगवान चंदन हैं और भक्त पानी; दोनों का संग अटूट है।

Visual lesson

रैदास के पद

रैदास (रविदास) भक्तिकाल की निर्गुण संत धारा के कवि थे। पहले पद में भक्त और भगवान की घनिष्ठता को चंदन-पानी, घन-मोर, चाँद-चकोर, दीपक-बाती, मोती-धागा और सोना-सुहागा जैसे…

Big idea

  • रैदास (रविदास) भक्तिकाल की निर्गुण संत धारा के कवि थे। पहले पद में भक्त और भगवान की घनिष्ठता को चंदन-पानी, घन-मोर, चाँद-चकोर, दीपक-बाती, मोती-धागा और…
📌

गहराई से समझें: पहला पद

  • कवि कहता है कि राम नाम की रट लग गई है और वह अब कैसे छूटे। प्रभु चंदन हैं और भक्त पानी, जिसकी सुगंध अंग-अंग में बसती है। प्रभु घन हैं तो भक्त मोर
  • प्रभु चाँद हैं तो भक्त चकोर।
🧠

गहराई से समझें: संदेश

  • रैदास जाति-पाँति के भेद को नहीं मानते और ईश्वर की कृपा को सब पर समान मानते हैं।

lessons.title: रसखान के सवैये

blocks.x: रसखान का मूल नाम सैयद इब्राहीम था। वे कृष्णभक्त कवि थे। इन सवैयों में वे कहते हैं कि अगले जन्म में मैं ब्रज में ग्वाला, गाय, पत्थर या पक्षी बनूँ ताकि कृष्ण के निकट रह सकूँ।
गहराई से समझें: भाव

रसखान कहते हैं कि अगले जन्म में मनुष्य बनूँ तो गोकुल का ग्वाला, पशु बनूँ तो नंद की गाय, पत्थर बनूँ तो गोवर्धन का और पक्षी बनूँ तो यमुना के तट पर कदंब की डाल पर। उन्हें कृष्ण की लाठी-कंबल पर तीनों लोकों का राज्य निछावर है।
गहराई से समझें: कलात्मकता
ब्रजभाषा, सवैया छंद, अनुप्रास, माधुर्य और अनन्य भक्ति इनकी विशेषताएँ हैं।
Hindi saransh
रसखान कृष्ण और ब्रजभूमि के प्रति अनन्य प्रेम प्रकट करते हैं।
जन्म कोई भी हो, ब्रज और कृष्ण के पास रहने की इच्छा।

lessons.title: कैदी और कोकिला

blocks.x: माखनलाल चतुर्वेदी की यह कविता जेल में बंद स्वतंत्रता सेनानी और कोकिला के संवाद के रूप में है। रात के सन्नाटे में कोकिल गाती है तो कैदी उससे पूछता है कि वह क्या संदेश लाई है। कविता अंग्रेज़ी शासन के अत्याचारों का चित्रण करती है।
गहराई से समझें: कथ्य
रात के घने अँधेरे में कोकिला का स्वर गूँजता है। कैदी को यह स्वर आज़ादी का संदेश लगता है। वह जेल की यातनाओं का वर्णन करता है और कोकिला से जानना चाहता है कि वह क्या कहने आई है।
गहराई से समझें: प्रतीक
कोकिला स्वतंत्रता और आशा की प्रतीक है, जबकि जेल गुलामी और अत्याचार की।
Hindi saransh
कैदी जेल में कोकिला की आवाज़ से आज़ादी का संदेश खोजता है।
कोकिला का स्वर जेल के अँधेरे में आशा का प्रतीक है।

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

कैदी और कोकिला

माखनलाल चतुर्वेदी की यह कविता जेल में बंद स्वतंत्रता सेनानी और कोकिला के संवाद के रूप में है। रात के सन्नाटे में कोकिल गाती है तो कैदी उससे पूछता है कि वह क्या संदेश लाई…

lessons.title: ग्राम श्री

blocks.x: सुमित्रानंदन पंत की इस कविता में ग्रामीण प्रकृति का सुंदर चित्रण है। खेतों की हरियाली, फसलों की सुनहरी बालियाँ, फूलों की रंगत और आकाश की शोभा का वर्णन इसमें मिलता है। पंत छायावाद के प्रकृति-प्रेमी कवि हैं।
गहराई से समझें: वर्णन
कविता में खेतों की हरियाली, फसलों की चमक, फूलों की रंगीनी और गाँव की सुंदरता का चित्रण है। प्रकृति सजीव-सी प्रतीत होती है।
गहराई से समझें: शिल्प
पंत ने मानवीकरण, बिंब और कोमल शब्दावली से कविता को मधुर बनाया है।
Hindi saransh
पंत ने गाँव की हरी-भरी शोभा का मनोहर वर्णन किया है।
पंत को प्रकृति का सुकुमार कवि कहा जाता है।

blocks.x: केदारनाथ अग्रवाल की यह कविता प्रगतिवादी चेतना की कविता है। कवि खेत की मेड़ पर बैठकर चने, अलसी, सरसों और प्रकृति के बीच अपनी अनुभूतियाँ व्यक्त करता है। यहाँ प्रकृति और मनुष्य का आत्मीय संबंध है।
गहराई से समझें: दृश्य
कवि खेत की मेड़ पर बैठा है। सामने चने का पौधा सिर पर गुलाबी फूल की मुरेठा बाँधे दूल्हे-सा खड़ा है, अलसी नीले फूलों से सजी है और सरसों पीली दिखाई देती है। कवि प्रकृति से बात करता है।
गहराई से समझें: दृष्टि
कविता प्रगतिवादी है जिसमें प्रकृति के साथ मनुष्य के संबंध और श्रम की गरिमा झलकती है।
Hindi saransh
कवि खेत और प्रकृति के बीच अपनेपन का अनुभव करता है।
चना, अलसी और सरसों के दृश्यों में कवि जीवन की सुंदरता देखता है।

lessons.title: मेघ आए

blocks.x: सर्वेश्वर दयाल सक्सेना की इस कविता में बादलों के आने को गाँव में दामाद के आगमन की तरह चित्रित किया गया है। हवा, पेड़, धूल, नदी, तालाब आदि सब उनका स्वागत करते हैं। मानवीकरण इस कविता का मुख्य अलंकार है।
गहराई से समझें: चित्रण

कविता में बादल सजे-धजे दामाद की तरह आते हैं और पूरा गाँव उनका स्वागत करता है। हवा नाचती-गाती आगे चलती है, पेड़ गर्दन उचकाकर झाँकते हैं, आँधी में धूल घाघरा उठाए भागती है और नदी ठिठककर घूँघट सरकाकर देखती है।
गहराई से समझें: शिल्प
मानवीकरण और ग्रामीण संस्कृति के प्रतीक इसकी विशेषता हैं।
Hindi saransh
बादल बन-ठनकर गाँव में आए मेहमान की तरह लगते हैं।
कविता में हवा, पेड़, नदी आदि मेहमान का स्वागत करने वाले परिजन हैं।

lessons.title: यमराज की दिशा

blocks.x: चंद्रकांत देवताले की यह कविता बताती है कि माँ कहती थी कि यमराज दक्षिण दिशा में रहता है, इसलिए दक्षिण की ओर पैर करके नहीं सोना चाहिए। परंतु आज यमराज की कोई एक दिशा नहीं रही, शोषण और अत्याचार हर तरफ़ हैं।
गहराई से समझें: कथ्य
माँ की सीख थी कि दक्षिण की ओर पैर करके नहीं सोना क्योंकि वहाँ यमराज रहता है। कवि कहता है कि आज हर दिशा में, हर जगह शोषण और अत्याचार मौजूद हैं इसलिए यमराज की कोई निश्चित दिशा नहीं रही।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
समाज में बढ़ते शोषण से सावधान रहने का संदेश।
Hindi saransh
आज हर दिशा में यमराज के रूप में शोषण और अत्याचार मौजूद हैं।
पुरानी मान्यता बदल गई है; खतरा अब हर दिशा में है।

lessons.title: बच्चे काम पर जा रहे हैं
yt: class 9 hindi बच्चे काम पर जा रहे हैं

blocks.x: राजेश जोशी की यह कविता बाल श्रम की समस्या पर चोट करती है। कोहरे से ढकी सड़क पर बच्चे काम पर जा रहे हैं, यह दृश्य कवि को भयानक लगता है। कवि प्रश्न करता है कि क्या खेलने की गेंदें, किताबें और खिलौने खत्म हो गए हैं।
गहराई से समझें: विषय
सर्द कोहरे में बच्चे काम पर जा रहे हैं। कवि के लिए यह दृश्य भयावह है। वह सोचता है कि क्या उनकी गेंदें और किताबें खो गई हैं या हमारा समय बच्चों के लिए जगह ही नहीं रखता।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
बाल श्रम रोककर बच्चों को शिक्षा और खेल का अवसर देना ज़रूरी है।
Hindi saransh
बच्चों का काम पर जाना समाज के लिए चिंता की बात है।
बच्चों का बचपन छीनना अन्याय है।

lessons.title: ल्लद्यद के वाख

blocks.x: ल्लद्यद (लल देद) कश्मीरी भाषा की प्रसिद्ध शैव संत कवयित्री थीं, जो चौदहवीं शताब्दी में हुईं। उनके चार-चार पंक्तियों वाले छंद वाख कहलाते हैं। इनमें ईश्वर की प्राप्ति के लिए बाहरी आडंबर छोड़कर आत्मज्ञान, संयम और समभाव पर बल दिया गया है।
गहराई से समझें: वाख
ल्लद्यद के वाख बताते हैं कि भोग और त्याग दोनों की अति से बचना चाहिए। ईश्वर आत्मा में है, उसे जानने के लिए बाहरी दिखावे की ज़रूरत नहीं।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
समभाव, संयम और आत्मज्ञान ही मुक्ति का मार्ग हैं।
Hindi saransh
ईश्वर बाहर नहीं, भीतर है; उसे आत्मज्ञान से पाया जा सकता है।
अति भोग और अति त्याग दोनों से बचकर बीच का रास्ता अपनाओ।

blocks.x: फणीश्वरनाथ रेणु का यह रिपोर्ताज 1975 की पटना की भीषण बाढ़ का आँखों देखा वर्णन है। लेखक ने बाढ़ के बीच लोगों की स्थिति, अपनी बेचैनी और जीवन की जटिलताओं का सजीव चित्रण किया है। रिपोर्ताज में तथ्य और साहित्यिक भाषा का मेल होता है।
गहराई से समझें: बाढ़
रेणु ने पटना की बाढ़ को स्वयं देखा। पानी गलियों में भर गया और जन-जीवन ठप हो गया। रेणु मानवीय पीड़ा के साथ बाढ़ के विनोदपूर्ण और मार्मिक दृश्यों को भी जोड़ते हैं।
गहराई से समझें: शिल्प
रिपोर्ताज में पत्रकारिता और साहित्य दोनों के गुण होते हैं।
Hindi saransh
रेणु ने बाढ़ की विभीषिका को रिपोर्ताज के रूप में प्रस्तुत किया है।
रिपोर्ताज = घटना का साहित्यिक रिपोर्ट रूप।

lessons.title: मेरे संग की औरतें
yt: class 9 hindi मेरे संग की औरतें

blocks.x: मृदुला गर्ग का यह संस्मरण उनकी नानी, दादी और माँ जैसी स्त्रियों के साहस, स्वतंत्र विचार और अलग-अलग स्वभाव का चित्रण करता है। इसमें स्त्रियों की भूमिका, उनके संघर्ष और उनके जीवन-मूल्यों का सजीव वर्णन है।
गहराई से समझें: पाठ
लेखिका अपने संग रहने वाली स्त्रियों के जीवन का वर्णन करती हैं। हर स्त्री का स्वभाव अलग है, पर सब में साहस और अपनी सोच है। पाठ स्त्रियों के योगदान को सम्मान देता है।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
हर स्त्री के भीतर शक्ति और स्वतंत्र सोच होती है, जिसे सम्मान मिलना चाहिए।
Hindi saransh
लेखिका अपने परिवार की स्त्रियों के व्यक्तित्व का वर्णन करती हैं।
स्त्रियाँ हर पीढ़ी में सोच और साहस से अलग मिसाल बनीं।

lessons.title: रीढ़ की हड्डी

blocks.x: जगदीशचंद्र माथुर का यह एकांकी विवाह में दहेज और लड़की की पढ़ाई की परख जैसी रूढ़ियों पर व्यंग्य करता है। एकांकी में उमा नामक शिक्षित युवती है, जो आत्मसम्मान के साथ अपनी बात रखती है। शीर्षक का अर्थ है सीधी रीढ़, यानी स्वाभिमान।
गहराई से समझें: एकांकी
एकांकी में विवाह के प्रसंग में लड़की से अनावश्यक प्रश्न पूछे जाते हैं और दहेज की चर्चा होती है। उमा की शिक्षा और साहस इस रूढ़िवादी सोच के सामने खड़े होते हैं।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
बिना स्वाभिमान के मनुष्य रीढ़ रहित है; दहेज और भेदभाव का विरोध ज़रूरी है।
Hindi saransh
एकांकी में दहेज प्रथा और रूढ़ियों का विरोध है।
रीढ़ की हड्डी = स्वाभिमान और दृढ़ता का प्रतीक।

lessons.title: दुख का अधिकार

blocks.x: यशपाल की इस कहानी में एक गरीब बुढ़िया का वर्णन है जिसका जवान बेटा साँप के काटने से मर जाता है, फिर भी उसे अगले ही दिन खरबूजे बेचने बाज़ार जाना पड़ता है। लेखक दिखाते हैं कि दुख मनाने का अधिकार भी गरीबों को नहीं मिल पाता।
गहराई से समझें: कथा
बुढ़िया का जवान बेटा भगवाना खेत से खरबूजे तोड़ते समय साँप के काटने से मर जाता है। घर की मजबूरी के कारण वह दुख में भी खरबूजे बेचने बैठ जाती है। लोग उसकी निंदा करते हैं पर कोई उसका दुख नहीं समझता।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
कहानी हमें गरीबों की मजबूरी को समझने और संवेदनशील बनने की सीख देती है।
Hindi saransh
गरीब को दुख मनाने का भी अवसर नहीं मिलता।
अमीर शोक मना सकता है, गरीब मजबूरी में काम पर जाता है।

blocks.x: बचेंद्री पाल का यह यात्रा-वृत्तांत उनकी एवरेस्ट चढ़ाई का वर्णन है। वे एवरेस्ट पर चढ़ने वाली पहली भारतीय महिला थीं। पाठ में दल के साथ कठिनाइयाँ, हिमस्खलन, अदम्य साहस और दृढ़ संकल्प का चित्रण है।
गहराई से समझें: अभियान
बचेंद्री पाल एवरेस्ट अभियान दल की सदस्य थीं। शिविर तीन पर हिमस्खलन में वे बर्फ़ में दब गईं पर उन्होंने हिम्मत नहीं हारी। आगे बढ़ते हुए 23 मई 1984 को वे एवरेस्ट के शिखर पर पहुँचीं।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
दृढ़ संकल्प और साहस से बड़ी से बड़ी चुनौती पार की जा सकती है।
Hindi saransh
बचेंद्री पाल ने साहस और संकल्प से एवरेस्ट पर विजय पाई।
जहाँ चाह वहाँ राह: दृढ़ संकल्प से शिखर तक पहुँचा जा सकता है।

yt: class 9 hindi तुम कब जाओगे, अतिथि

blocks.x: शरद जोशी का यह व्यंग्य उस अतिथि पर है जो चार दिन से घर में टिका हुआ है। लेखक और उसकी पत्नी पहले उसका स्वागत करते हैं पर धीरे-धीरे उसका ठहरना बोझ बन जाता है। लेखक व्यंग्य के माध्यम से मेहमाननवाज़ी की सीमाओं और बदलती मानसिकता को दिखाते हैं।
गहराई से समझें: व्यंग्य
पाठ में लेखक अतिथि के लंबे ठहराव को हास्य और व्यंग्य से दिखाते हैं। पहले दिन का स्वागत धीरे-धीरे परेशानी में बदलता है।
गहराई से समझें: संदेश
मेहमान और मेज़बान दोनों को एक-दूसरे की सुविधा का ध्यान रखना चाहिए।
Hindi saransh
मेहमान का लंबा ठहराव मेज़बान पर बोझ बन जाता है।
अतिथि देवता है, पर सीमा में।

lessons.title: The French Revolution

blocks.x: The French Revolution began in 1789 when the people of France rose against the absolute monarchy of Louis XVI. Heavy taxes on the Third Estate, a financial crisis, food shortages and new ideas of liberty and equality led to the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789. France became a constitutional monarchy, then a republic, and passed through the Reign of Terror before Napoleon came to power.
Deep dive: causes

Louis XVI inherited an empty treasury. The wars and the support to the American War of Independence added debt. The privileged First and Second Estates paid no direct taxes, while the Third Estate paid taille, tithe and indirect taxes. Population growth raised the demand for grain and bread prices rose, causing a subsistence crisis. Thinkers such as Locke, Rousseau and Montesquieu spread ideas of equality, liberty and separation of powers.
Deep dive: the events

The Estates General met on 5 May 1789 but voting by estate left the Third Estate powerless; they declared themselves the National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath. On 14 July 1789 the people stormed the Bastille. Peasants attacked manors in the Great Fear and feudal dues were abolished. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen followed, and the Constitution of 1791 made France a constitutional monarchy with active and passive citizens.
Deep dive: republic, terror and Napoleon

War with Austria in 1792 led to the fall of the monarchy; France became a republic, and Louis XVI was executed in 1793. Under Robespierre the Reign of Terror killed thousands. After his fall the Directory ruled, and Napoleon seized power in 1799, becoming emperor in 1804. The Revolution spread ideas of liberty and equality worldwide. Women like Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights, and slavery was abolished in 1794 but restored by Napoleon.

Fransisi kranti 1789 me shuru hui. Swatantrata, samanta aur bandhutva uske naare the.

Visual lesson

The French Revolution

The French Revolution began in 1789 when the people of France rose against the absolute monarchy of Louis XVI

Flat concept map (2D)

Bastille14 July 1789

Louis XVI executed21 January 1793

🔑

Big idea

  • The French Revolution began in 1789 when the people of France rose against the absolute monarchy of Louis XVI
  • Heavy taxes on the Third Estate, a financial crisis, food shortages and new ideas of liberty and equality led to the storming of the Bastille on 14…
  • France became a constitutional monarchy, then a republic, and passed through the Reign of Terror before Napoleon came to power
Read the full explanation

The French Revolution began in 1789 when the people of France rose against the absolute monarchy of Louis XVI. Heavy taxes on the Third Estate, a financial crisis, food shortages and new ideas of liberty and equality led to the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789. France became a constitutional monarchy, then a republic, and passed through the Reign of Terror before Napoleon came to power.

💡

Causes

  • Louis XVI inherited an empty treasury
  • The wars and the support to the American War of Independence added debt
  • The privileged First and Second Estates paid no direct taxes, while the Third Estate paid taille, tithe and indirect taxes
  • Population growth raised the demand for grain and bread prices rose, causing a subsistence crisis
Read the full explanation

Louis XVI inherited an empty treasury. The wars and the support to the American War of Independence added debt. The privileged First and Second Estates paid no direct taxes, while the Third Estate paid taille, tithe and indirect taxes. Population growth raised the demand for grain and bread prices rose, causing a subsistence crisis. Thinkers such as Locke, Rousseau and Montesquieu spread ideas of equality, liberty and separation of powers.

🧠

The events

  • The Estates General met on 5 May 1789 but voting by estate left the Third Estate powerless
  • They declared themselves the National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath
  • On 14 July 1789 the people stormed the Bastille
  • Peasants attacked manors in the Great Fear and feudal dues were abolished
Read the full explanation

The Estates General met on 5 May 1789 but voting by estate left the Third Estate powerless; they declared themselves the National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath. On 14 July 1789 the people stormed the Bastille. Peasants attacked manors in the Great Fear and feudal dues were abolished. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen followed, and the Constitution of 1791 made France a constitutional monarchy with active and passive citizens.

🌟

Republic, terror and Napoleon

  • War with Austria in 1792 led to the fall of the monarchy
  • France became a republic, and Louis XVI was executed in 1793
  • Under Robespierre the Reign of Terror killed thousands
  • After his fall the Directory ruled, and Napoleon seized power in 1799, becoming emperor in 1804
Read the full explanation

War with Austria in 1792 led to the fall of the monarchy; France became a republic, and Louis XVI was executed in 1793. Under Robespierre the Reign of Terror killed thousands. After his fall the Directory ruled, and Napoleon seized power in 1799, becoming emperor in 1804. The Revolution spread ideas of liberty and equality worldwide. Women like Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights, and slavery was abolished in 1794 but restored by Napoleon.

🧮

yt: class 9 history socialism in europe and the russian revolution

blocks.x: The Russian Revolution of 1917 overthrew the Tsar and led to the first socialist state. Russia was an autocracy under Tsar Nicholas II with a poor peasantry and an industrial working class. The February Revolution of 1917 ended Tsarist rule, and the Bolsheviks under Lenin took power in the October Revolution. Stalin later built a planned socialist economy with collectivisation and Five Year Plans.
Deep dive: Russia before 1914

Russia was an empire stretching over Eurasia ruled by Tsar Nicholas II. Peasants formed most of the population and lived in poverty; landlords held the land. Industry grew late, with long working hours in factories. Socialists organised workers; the Russian Social Democratic Party split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks. In 1905 Bloody Sunday sparked a revolution, and the Tsar allowed a Duma but soon curbed it.
Deep dive: 1917

World War I brought heavy losses, food and fuel shortages and anger. In February 1917 workers and women in Petrograd rose, the Tsar abdicated and a Provisional Government took charge. Lenin returned and issued the April Theses. In October 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power. The new government ended the war by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, nationalised land and banks and fought a civil war against the Whites.
Deep dive: after the revolution

The USSR was formed in 1922. Under Stalin, farms were collectivised and Five Year Plans built heavy industry; critics and kulaks were harshly treated. The USSR became a major power and inspired socialist movements worldwide.

Visual lesson

Socialism in Europe and the Russian Revolution

The Russian Revolution of 1917 overthrew the Tsar and led to the first socialist state

February Revolution1917

🔑

Big idea

  • The Russian Revolution of 1917 overthrew the Tsar and led to the first socialist state
  • Russia was an autocracy under Tsar Nicholas II with a poor peasantry and an industrial working class
  • The February Revolution of 1917 ended Tsarist rule, and the Bolsheviks under Lenin took power in the October Revolution
  • Stalin later built a planned socialist economy with collectivisation and Five Year Plans
Read the full explanation

The Russian Revolution of 1917 overthrew the Tsar and led to the first socialist state. Russia was an autocracy under Tsar Nicholas II with a poor peasantry and an industrial working class. The February Revolution of 1917 ended Tsarist rule, and the Bolsheviks under Lenin took power in the October Revolution. Stalin later built a planned socialist economy with collectivisation and Five Year Plans.

📌

Russia before 1914

  • Russia was an empire stretching over Eurasia ruled by Tsar Nicholas II
  • Peasants formed most of the population and lived in poverty
  • Landlords held the land
  • Industry grew late, with long working hours in factories
Read the full explanation

Russia was an empire stretching over Eurasia ruled by Tsar Nicholas II. Peasants formed most of the population and lived in poverty; landlords held the land. Industry grew late, with long working hours in factories. Socialists organised workers; the Russian Social Democratic Party split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks. In 1905 Bloody Sunday sparked a revolution, and the Tsar allowed a Duma but soon curbed it.

🧠

1917

  • World War I brought heavy losses, food and fuel shortages and anger
  • In February 1917 workers and women in Petrograd rose, the Tsar abdicated and a Provisional Government took charge
  • Lenin returned and issued the April Theses
  • In October 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power
Read the full explanation

World War I brought heavy losses, food and fuel shortages and anger. In February 1917 workers and women in Petrograd rose, the Tsar abdicated and a Provisional Government took charge. Lenin returned and issued the April Theses. In October 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power. The new government ended the war by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, nationalised land and banks and fought a civil war against the Whites.

🕰️

After the revolution

  • The USSR was formed in 1922
  • Under Stalin, farms were collectivised and Five Year Plans built heavy industry
  • Critics and kulaks were harshly treated
  • The USSR became a major power and inspired socialist movements worldwide

lessons.title: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
yt: class 9 history nazism and the rise of hitler

blocks.x: After Germany's defeat in World War I the Weimar Republic was weakened by the Treaty of Versailles, hyperinflation and the Great Depression. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party rose by promising to restore national pride and jobs. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, set up a dictatorship, persecuted Jews and others and led Germany into World War II. The Holocaust killed millions.
Deep dive: the Weimar Republic

After Germany's defeat, the Weimar Republic had a democratic constitution but was unpopular, associated with the harsh Treaty of Versailles. Germany lost territory and colonies, had to pay reparations and reduce its army. In 1923 hyperinflation ruined savings. The Great Depression from 1929 caused huge unemployment. People lost faith in democracy.
Deep dive: Hitler's rise

Hitler used propaganda, mass rallies and promises of jobs and national pride. The Nazis won votes among the middle class, farmers and the unemployed. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act removed civil rights and gave him dictatorial power. He banned other parties, controlled the press and set up the Gestapo and SS.
Deep dive: persecution and war

Nazi racist ideology treated Jews as enemies. The Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht and concentration camps followed. The Final Solution led to the Holocaust, killing about six million Jews and many others. Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, starting World War II. Hitler died in 1945 and the Nuremberg Trials punished leaders.

Hitler 1933 me Germany ka Chancellor bana aur tanashahi shuru ki.
Nazism = extreme nationalism, racism and dictatorship.

Nazism and the Rise of Hitler

After Germany's defeat in World War I the Weimar Republic was weakened by the Treaty of Versailles, hyperinflation and the Great Depression

Big idea

Read the full explanation

After Germany's defeat in World War I the Weimar Republic was weakened by the Treaty of Versailles, hyperinflation and the Great Depression. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party rose by promising to restore national pride and jobs. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, set up a dictatorship, persecuted Jews and others and led Germany into World War II. The Holocaust killed millions.

📌

The Weimar Republic

  • After Germany's defeat, the Weimar Republic had a democratic constitution but was unpopular, associated with the harsh Treaty of Versailles
  • Germany lost territory and colonies, had to pay reparations and reduce its army
  • In 1923 hyperinflation ruined savings
  • The Great Depression from 1929 caused huge unemployment
Read the full explanation

After Germany's defeat, the Weimar Republic had a democratic constitution but was unpopular, associated with the harsh Treaty of Versailles. Germany lost territory and colonies, had to pay reparations and reduce its army. In 1923 hyperinflation ruined savings. The Great Depression from 1929 caused huge unemployment. People lost faith in democracy.

🧠

Hitler's rise

  • Hitler used propaganda, mass rallies and promises of jobs and national pride
  • The Nazis won votes among the middle class, farmers and the unemployed
  • Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933
  • The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act removed civil rights and gave him dictatorial power
Read the full explanation

Hitler used propaganda, mass rallies and promises of jobs and national pride. The Nazis won votes among the middle class, farmers and the unemployed. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act removed civil rights and gave him dictatorial power. He banned other parties, controlled the press and set up the Gestapo and SS.

🕰️

Persecution and war

  • Nazi racist ideology treated Jews as enemies
  • The Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht and concentration camps followed
  • The Final Solution led to the Holocaust, killing about six million Jews and many others
  • Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, starting World War II
Read the full explanation

Nazi racist ideology treated Jews as enemies. The Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht and concentration camps followed. The Final Solution led to the Holocaust, killing about six million Jews and many others. Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, starting World War II. Hitler died in 1945 and the Nuremberg Trials punished leaders.

lessons.title: Forest Society and Colonialism
yt: class 9 history forest society and colonialism

blocks.x: Forests were exploited by colonial rulers for railways, shipbuilding and plantations. The Forest Acts restricted the rights of people who lived in forests, leading to protests such as the Bastar rebellion of 1910 in India and the Samin movement in Java. Scientific forestry replaced diverse forests with commercial species like teak and sal.
Deep dive: why forests were exploited

The British needed timber for the navy, railways and construction, and land for plantations of tea, coffee and rubber. Forest cover shrank as agriculture and plantations expanded. The government declared forests state property and started the Imperial Forest Service under Dietrich Brandis. The Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927 classified forests into reserved, protected and village forests.
Deep dive: effects on people

Villagers lost access to firewood, grazing, fruits, honey and hunting. Shifting cultivation was banned because it was unfit for timber growing. Many communities were forced to work in forests. Some got jobs as labour and as forest guards. Tribal rebellions grew.
Deep dive: revolts

In Bastar the Dhurwas rose in 1910 under Gunda Dhur after two-thirds of the forest was reserved. In Java, the Kalangs resisted the Dutch and the Samin movement refused to pay taxes. The Dutch enforced Blandongdiensten and later forest laws. Scientific forestry replaced diverse forests with a few species, which harmed biodiversity.

Aupniveshik shasan me jangal kate gaye aur adivasiyon ke adhikar chhine gaye.

Visual lesson

Forest Society and Colonialism

Forests were exploited by colonial rulers for railways, shipbuilding and plantations

formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Why forests were exploited›3Effects on people›4Revolts
Forest Acts1865, 1878, 1927
Bastar revolt1910
🔑

Big idea

  • Forests were exploited by colonial rulers for railways, shipbuilding and plantations
  • The Forest Acts restricted the rights of people who lived in forests, leading to protests such as the Bastar rebellion of 1910 in India and the Samin…
  • Scientific forestry replaced diverse forests with commercial species like teak and sal
📌

Why forests were exploited

  • The British needed timber for the navy, railways and construction, and land for plantations of tea, coffee and rubber
  • Forest cover shrank as agriculture and plantations expanded
  • The government declared forests state property and started the Imperial Forest Service under Dietrich Brandis
  • The Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927 classified forests into reserved, protected and village forests
Read the full explanation

The British needed timber for the navy, railways and construction, and land for plantations of tea, coffee and rubber. Forest cover shrank as agriculture and plantations expanded. The government declared forests state property and started the Imperial Forest Service under Dietrich Brandis. The Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927 classified forests into reserved, protected and village forests.

🧠

Effects on people

  • Villagers lost access to firewood, grazing, fruits, honey and hunting
  • Shifting cultivation was banned because it was unfit for timber growing
  • Many communities were forced to work in forests
  • Some got jobs as labour and as forest guards
Read the full explanation

Villagers lost access to firewood, grazing, fruits, honey and hunting. Shifting cultivation was banned because it was unfit for timber growing. Many communities were forced to work in forests. Some got jobs as labour and as forest guards. Tribal rebellions grew.

🌟

Revolts

  • In Bastar the Dhurwas rose in 1910 under Gunda Dhur after two-thirds of the forest was reserved
  • In Java, the Kalangs resisted the Dutch and the Samin movement refused to pay taxes
  • The Dutch enforced Blandongdiensten and later forest laws
  • Scientific forestry replaced diverse forests with a few species, which harmed biodiversity
🧮

lessons.title: Pastoralists in the Modern World
yt: class 9 history pastoralists in the modern world

blocks.x: Pastoralists are people who move with their herds in search of pasture. In India the Gujjar Bakarwals, Gaddis, Gollas, Kurumas, Dhangars, Banjaras and Raikas, and in Africa the Maasai, lived by herding. Colonial laws, forest reservations, taxes and loss of pastures changed their lives, forcing many to adapt, settle or move.
Deep dive: pastoralists in India

In the mountains of J&K, Gujjar Bakarwals move between winter lowlands (bhabar) and summer meadows (bugyal). Gaddis of Himachal do the same. Dhangars of Maharashtra rear sheep; Gollas, Kurumas and Kurubas of the south herd cattle and sheep. Raikas of Rajasthan combine farming with camel herding. Banjaras trade grain and cattle.
Deep dive: colonial effects

The Waste Land Rules turned pastures into farms. The Forest Acts barred grazing in reserved forests. The Criminal Tribes Act (1871) controlled wandering groups. Tax was levied on every animal. As pasture shrank, herders cut herd size, took labour jobs or settled.
Deep dive: the Maasai

Maasailand in East Africa was divided between British Kenya and German Tanganyika in 1885. Maasai lost much pasture to farms and game reserves like the Masai Mara and Serengeti. Droughts caused severe losses. Social change gave power to chiefs and traders, and young warriors lost their role.
Hindi saransh
Pashupalak apne jaanvaron ke saath charagah ki talash me ghoomte hain.
Pastoral nomads moved in seasonal cycles; colonial laws restricted this.

Visual lesson

Pastoralists in the Modern World

Pastoralists are people who move with their herds in search of pasture

formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Pastoralists in India›3Colonial effects›4The Maasai
Criminal Tribes Act1871
Maasailand split1885
🔑

Big idea

  • Pastoralists are people who move with their herds in search of pasture
  • In India the Gujjar Bakarwals, Gaddis, Gollas, Kurumas, Dhangars, Banjaras and Raikas, and in Africa the Maasai, lived by herding
  • Colonial laws, forest reservations, taxes and loss of pastures changed their lives, forcing many to adapt, settle or move
📌

Pastoralists in India

  • In the mountains of J&K, Gujjar Bakarwals move between winter lowlands (bhabar) and summer meadows (bugyal)
  • Gaddis of Himachal do the same
  • Dhangars of Maharashtra rear sheep
  • Gollas, Kurumas and Kurubas of the south herd cattle and sheep
Read the full explanation

In the mountains of J&K, Gujjar Bakarwals move between winter lowlands (bhabar) and summer meadows (bugyal). Gaddis of Himachal do the same. Dhangars of Maharashtra rear sheep; Gollas, Kurumas and Kurubas of the south herd cattle and sheep. Raikas of Rajasthan combine farming with camel herding. Banjaras trade grain and cattle.

🧠

Colonial effects

  • The Waste Land Rules turned pastures into farms
  • The Forest Acts barred grazing in reserved forests
  • The Criminal Tribes Act (1871) controlled wandering groups
  • Tax was levied on every animal
Read the full explanation

The Waste Land Rules turned pastures into farms. The Forest Acts barred grazing in reserved forests. The Criminal Tribes Act (1871) controlled wandering groups. Tax was levied on every animal. As pasture shrank, herders cut herd size, took labour jobs or settled.

🌟

The Maasai

  • Maasailand in East Africa was divided between British Kenya and German Tanganyika in 1885
  • Maasai lost much pasture to farms and game reserves like the Masai Mara and Serengeti
  • Droughts caused severe losses
  • Social change gave power to chiefs and traders, and young warriors lost their role
🧮

lessons.title: Number systems and polynomials

blocks.x: **Number systems:** natural, whole, integers, rational (p/q), irrational (non-terminating non-repeating, like sqrt 2 and pi), real. Every rational number has a terminating or repeating decimal. **Polynomials:** an expression like a x^n + ... + c. Degree is the highest power. **Remainder theorem:** the remainder when p(x) is divided by (x - a) is p(a). **Factor theorem:** (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if p(a) = 0. Identities: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b). Example: factorise x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3), because 2 + 3 = 5 and 2 x 3 = 6.
Deep dive: number systems

**Natural numbers** N = 1, 2, 3, ... **Whole numbers** W = 0, 1, 2, ... **Integers** Z = ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ... **Rational numbers** Q are numbers p/q with p, q integers and q not 0. **Irrational numbers** cannot be written as p/q; their decimals neither end nor repeat (sqrt 2, sqrt 3, pi). **Real numbers** R = rational + irrational; every real number is a point on the number line and every point is a real number. **Decimals.** A rational number has a terminating decimal (1/8 = 0.125) or a non-terminating repeating decimal (1/3 = 0.333..., 1/7 = 0.142857 repeating). A fraction in lowest terms terminates only when the denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. To convert 0.666... to p/q put x = 0.666..., 10x = 6.666..., subtract: 9x = 6, so x = 2/3. **Operations.** The sum or product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational. The sum or product of two irrationals may be rational (sqrt 2 x sqrt 2 = 2) or irrational. Rationalising the denominator: 1/(a + sqrt b) = (a - sqrt b)/(a^2 - b). **Laws of exponents.** a^m x a^n = a^(m+n); a^m / a^n = a^(m-n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); a^m b^m = (ab)^m; a^0 = 1; a^(-n) = 1/a^n; a^(1/n) is the nth root of a.
Deep dive: polynomials

**Definition.** A polynomial in x is a sum of terms a x^n with whole-number powers n. Its degree is the highest power. Types by degree: constant (0), linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3). By number of terms: monomial, binomial, trinomial. x + 1/x and sqrt x + 3 are NOT polynomials. **Zeroes.** A zero of p(x) is a number a with p(a) = 0. A linear polynomial a x + b has exactly one zero, -b/a. A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. Graphically, the zeroes are where the graph meets the x-axis. **Remainder theorem.** When p(x) is divided by (x - a) the remainder is p(a). When divided by (a x + b) the remainder is p(-b/a). **Factor theorem.** (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0. To factorise a cubic, guess a zero among the factors of the constant term (+/-1, +/-2, ...), divide, then factorise the quadratic. **Identities.** (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab; (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca; (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b); (a - b)^3 = a^3 - b^3 - 3ab(a - b); a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2); a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2); if a + b + c = 0 then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc.
Hindi saransh
Factor theorem: p(a) = 0 to (x - a) factor hai. a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b).
A polynomial of degree n has at most n roots.

Big idea

  • Number systems: natural, whole, integers, rational (p/q), irrational (non-terminating non-repeating, like sqrt 2 and pi), real
  • Every rational number has a terminating or repeating decimal
  • Polynomials: an expression like a x^n +

Read the full explanation

Number systems: natural, whole, integers, rational (p/q), irrational (non-terminating non-repeating, like sqrt 2 and pi), real. Every rational number has a terminating or repeating decimal. Polynomials: an expression like a x^n + ... + c. Degree is the highest power. Remainder theorem: the remainder when p(x) is divided by (x - a) is p(a). Factor theorem: (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if p(a) = 0. Identities: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b). Example: factorise x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3), because 2 + 3 = 5 and 2 x 3 = 6.

📌

Number systems

  • Natural numbers N = 1, 2, 3,
  • Whole numbers W = 0, 1, 2,
  • Integers Z = ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2,
  • Rational numbers Q are numbers p/q with p, q integers and q not 0
Read the full explanation

Natural numbers N = 1, 2, 3, ... Whole numbers W = 0, 1, 2, ... Integers Z = ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ... Rational numbers Q are numbers p/q with p, q integers and q not 0. Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q; their decimals neither end nor repeat (sqrt 2, sqrt 3, pi). Real numbers R = rational + irrational; every real number is a point on the number line and every point is a real number. Decimals. A rational number has a terminating decimal (1/8 = 0.125) or a non-terminating repeating decimal (1/3 = 0.333..., 1/7 = 0.142857 repeating). A fraction in lowest terms terminates only when the denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. To convert 0.666... to p/q put x = 0.666..., 10x = 6.666..., subtract: 9x = 6, so x = 2/3. Operations. The sum or product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational. The sum or product of two irrationals may be rational (sqrt 2 x sqrt 2 = 2) or irrational. Rationalising the denominator: 1/(a + sqrt b) = (a - sqrt b)/(a^2 - b). Laws of exponents. a^m x a^n = a^(m+n); a^m / a^n = a^(m-n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); a^m b^m = (ab)^m; a^0 = 1; a^(-n) = 1/a^n; a^(1/n) is the nth root of a.

🧠

Polynomials

  • A polynomial in x is a sum of terms a x^n with whole-number powers n
  • Its degree is the highest power
  • Types by degree: constant (0), linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3)
  • By number of terms: monomial, binomial, trinomial
Read the full explanation

Definition. A polynomial in x is a sum of terms a x^n with whole-number powers n. Its degree is the highest power. Types by degree: constant (0), linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3). By number of terms: monomial, binomial, trinomial. x + 1/x and sqrt x + 3 are NOT polynomials. Zeroes. A zero of p(x) is a number a with p(a) = 0. A linear polynomial a x + b has exactly one zero, -b/a. A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. Graphically, the zeroes are where the graph meets the x-axis. Remainder theorem. When p(x) is divided by (x - a) the remainder is p(a). When divided by (a x + b) the remainder is p(-b/a). Factor theorem. (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0. To factorise a cubic, guess a zero among the factors of the constant term (+/-1, +/-2, ...), divide, then factorise the quadratic. Identities. (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab; (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca; (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b); (a - b)^3 = a^3 - b^3 - 3ab(a - b); a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2); a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2); if a + b + c = 0 then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc.

lessons.title: Number Systems

blocks.x: Numbers are classified as natural, whole, integers, rational and irrational; together rational and irrational numbers form the real numbers. A rational number is p/q with q not zero and has a terminating or repeating decimal; an irrational number has a non-terminating non-repeating decimal. Real numbers fill the number line, and laws of exponents work for rational powers.
Deep dive: classification of numbers

Natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}; whole numbers W = N and 0; integers Z = {..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...}; rational numbers Q = {p/q : p, q in Z, q not 0}; irrational numbers are numbers that are not rational; real numbers R are the union of Q and the irrationals. Every real number has a unique point on the number line, and every point is a real number. There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two rational numbers, and infinitely many irrationals too.
Deep dive: decimal expansions

A rational number has a terminating decimal or a non-terminating repeating (recurring) decimal. p/q (lowest terms) terminates exactly when q = 2^m x 5^n. To convert 0.333... to a fraction put x = 0.333..., then 10x - x = 3, so x = 1/3. For two repeating digits use 100x - x. An irrational number has a decimal that neither ends nor repeats, such as sqrt 2 = 1.41421356... or pi = 3.14159265...
Deep dive: operations and exponents

Sum, difference, product and quotient of a non-zero rational and an irrational are irrational; but two irrationals can combine to give a rational. Rationalising: 1/(a + sqrt b) = (a - sqrt b)/(a^2 - b). Laws: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n), a^m/a^n = a^(m-n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), a^m b^m = (ab)^m, a^0 = 1, a^(-n) = 1/a^n, a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m. The square root of a non-perfect-square natural number is irrational and can be located on the number line by the square-root spiral.

Big idea

  • Numbers are classified as natural, whole, integers, rational and irrational
  • Together rational and irrational numbers form the real numbers
  • A rational number is p/q with q not zero and has a terminating or repeating decimal
  • An irrational number has a non-terminating non-repeating decimal
Read the full explanation

Numbers are classified as natural, whole, integers, rational and irrational; together rational and irrational numbers form the real numbers. A rational number is p/q with q not zero and has a terminating or repeating decimal; an irrational number has a non-terminating non-repeating decimal. Real numbers fill the number line, and laws of exponents work for rational powers.

📌

Classification of numbers

  • Natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}
  • Whole numbers W = N and 0
  • Integers Z = {..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...}
  • Rational numbers Q = {p/q : p, q in Z, q not 0}
Read the full explanation

Natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}; whole numbers W = N and 0; integers Z = {..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...}; rational numbers Q = {p/q : p, q in Z, q not 0}; irrational numbers are numbers that are not rational; real numbers R are the union of Q and the irrationals. Every real number has a unique point on the number line, and every point is a real number. There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two rational numbers, and infinitely many irrationals too.

🧠

Decimal expansions

  • A rational number has a terminating decimal or a non-terminating repeating (recurring) decimal
  • P/q (lowest terms) terminates exactly when q = 2^m x 5^n
  • To convert 0.333
  • To a fraction put x = 0.333..., then 10x - x = 3, so x = 1/3
Read the full explanation

A rational number has a terminating decimal or a non-terminating repeating (recurring) decimal. p/q (lowest terms) terminates exactly when q = 2^m x 5^n. To convert 0.333... to a fraction put x = 0.333..., then 10x - x = 3, so x = 1/3. For two repeating digits use 100x - x. An irrational number has a decimal that neither ends nor repeats, such as sqrt 2 = 1.41421356... or pi = 3.14159265...

🌟

Operations and exponents

  • Sum, difference, product and quotient of a non-zero rational and an irrational are irrational
  • But two irrationals can combine to give a rational
  • Rationalising: 1/(a + sqrt b) = (a - sqrt b)/(a2 - b)
  • Laws: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n), a^m/a^n = a^(m-n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), a^m b^m = (ab)^m, a0 = 1, a^(-n) = 1/a^n, a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m
Read the full explanation

Sum, difference, product and quotient of a non-zero rational and an irrational are irrational; but two irrationals can combine to give a rational. Rationalising: 1/(a + sqrt b) = (a - sqrt b)/(a^2 - b). Laws: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n), a^m/a^n = a^(m-n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), a^m b^m = (ab)^m, a^0 = 1, a^(-n) = 1/a^n, a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m. The square root of a non-perfect-square natural number is irrational and can be located on the number line by the square-root spiral.

lessons.title: Polynomials

blocks.x: A polynomial is an expression with whole-number powers of a variable. Its degree is the highest power. A zero is a value that makes the polynomial zero. By the remainder theorem p(x) divided by (x - a) leaves p(a), and by the factor theorem (x - a) is a factor if p(a) = 0. Algebraic identities help in expansion and factorising.
Deep dive: polynomials and their zeroes

A polynomial in x has the form a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0 with whole-number powers. The degree is the highest power; polynomials of degree 0, 1, 2, 3 are constant, linear, quadratic and cubic. A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. The zero of a x + b is -b/a. Graphically, zeroes are the x-intercepts.
Deep dive: remainder and factor theorems

When p(x) is divided by x - a, the remainder is p(a). So p(a) = 0 means x - a is a factor. To factorise a cubic, test small integer values that divide the constant term, divide to get a quadratic and factorise it by splitting the middle term.
Deep dive: identities

(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab; (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca; (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b); (a - b)^3 = a^3 - b^3 - 3ab(a - b); a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2); a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2). If a + b + c = 0 then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc. These identities speed up arithmetic, such as 103^2 = (100 + 3)^2.

Polynomials

A polynomial is an expression with whole-number powers of a variable

🔑

Big idea

  • A polynomial is an expression with whole-number powers of a variable
  • Its degree is the highest power
  • A zero is a value that makes the polynomial zero
  • By the remainder theorem p(x) divided by (x - a) leaves p(a), and by the factor theorem (x - a) is a factor if p(a) = 0
Read the full explanation

A polynomial is an expression with whole-number powers of a variable. Its degree is the highest power. A zero is a value that makes the polynomial zero. By the remainder theorem p(x) divided by (x - a) leaves p(a), and by the factor theorem (x - a) is a factor if p(a) = 0. Algebraic identities help in expansion and factorising.

📌

Polynomials and their zeroes

  • A polynomial in x has the form a_n x^n +
  • + a_1 x + a_0 with whole-number powers
  • The degree is the highest power
  • Polynomials of degree 0, 1, 2, 3 are constant, linear, quadratic and cubic
Read the full explanation

A polynomial in x has the form a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0 with whole-number powers. The degree is the highest power; polynomials of degree 0, 1, 2, 3 are constant, linear, quadratic and cubic. A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. The zero of a x + b is -b/a. Graphically, zeroes are the x-intercepts.

⚖️

Remainder and factor theorems

  • When p(x) is divided by x - a, the remainder is p(a)
  • So p(a) = 0 means x - a is a factor
  • To factorise a cubic, test small integer values that divide the constant term, divide to get a quadratic and factorise it by splitting the middle term
🌟

Identities

  • (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2
  • (a - b)2 = a2 - 2ab + b2
  • A2 - b2 = (a + b)(a - b)
  • (x + a)(x + b) = x2 + (a + b)x + ab
Read the full explanation

(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab; (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca; (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b); (a - b)^3 = a^3 - b^3 - 3ab(a - b); a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2); a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2). If a + b + c = 0 then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc. These identities speed up arithmetic, such as 103^2 = (100 + 3)^2.

lessons.title: Linear equations in two variables
yt: class 9 linear equations in two variables

blocks.x: An equation ax + by + c = 0 with a and b not both zero is a linear equation in two variables. It has infinitely many solutions; each solution is a point on its straight-line graph.
Deep dive: solutions and graph

The standard form is ax + by + c = 0. Every pair (x, y) that makes both sides equal is a solution, and there are infinitely many of them. To draw the graph, find at least two (preferably three) solutions, plot them and join with a straight line; the third point checks your work. Every point on the line is a solution and every solution is on the line.
Deep dive: special lines

y = 0 is the x-axis and x = 0 is the y-axis. x = k is a vertical line parallel to the y-axis at distance k; y = k is a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis. y = mx passes through the origin. In one variable, x = 3 has one solution (a point on the number line), but in two variables it represents a line.
Deep dive: making equations

To find k so that (a, b) lies on px + qy + k = 0, substitute x = a and y = b. Equations modelling cost, distance and age problems are written in two variables and have infinitely many solutions when no second condition is given.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Linear equations in two variables

An equation ax + by + c = 0 with a and b not both zero is a linear equation in two variables

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Solutions and graph›3Special lines›4Making equations
🔑

Big idea

  • An equation ax + by + c = 0 with a and b not both zero is a linear equation in two variables
  • It has infinitely many solutions
  • Each solution is a point on its straight-line graph
🧪

Solutions and graph

  • The standard form is ax + by + c = 0
  • Every pair (x, y) that makes both sides equal is a solution, and there are infinitely many of them
  • To draw the graph, find at least two (preferably three) solutions, plot them and join with a straight line
  • The third point checks your work
Read the full explanation

The standard form is ax + by + c = 0. Every pair (x, y) that makes both sides equal is a solution, and there are infinitely many of them. To draw the graph, find at least two (preferably three) solutions, plot them and join with a straight line; the third point checks your work. Every point on the line is a solution and every solution is on the line.

🧠

Special lines

  • Y = 0 is the x-axis and x = 0 is the y-axis
  • X = k is a vertical line parallel to the y-axis at distance k
  • Y = k is a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis
  • Y = mx passes through the origin
Read the full explanation

y = 0 is the x-axis and x = 0 is the y-axis. x = k is a vertical line parallel to the y-axis at distance k; y = k is a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis. y = mx passes through the origin. In one variable, x = 3 has one solution (a point on the number line), but in two variables it represents a line.

🧮

Making equations

  • To find k so that (a, b) lies on px + qy + k = 0, substitute x = a and y = b
  • Equations modelling cost, distance and age problems are written in two variables and have infinitely many solutions when no second condition is given
🧮

Formula tiles

Standard formax + by + c = 0a, b not both 0
Vertical linex = kparallel to the y-axis
Horizontal liney = kparallel to the x-axis
Line through originy = mx
Number of solutionsinfinitely many
x-interceptput y = 0
y-interceptput x = 0
🎯 Remember x = k is parallel to the y-axis; y = k is parallel to the x-axis.

lessons.title: Coordinate geometry

blocks.x: A point is located by its abscissa (x) and ordinate (y) from two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, which meet at the origin (0, 0) and split the plane into four quadrants.
Deep dive: Cartesian plane

The x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical) intersect at the origin O (0, 0). A point (a, b) has abscissa a (distance from the y-axis) and ordinate b (distance from the x-axis). Signs: Quadrant I (+, +), II (-, +), III (-, -), IV (+, -). A point on the x-axis is (a, 0) and a point on the y-axis is (0, b). (a, b) and (b, a) are different points unless a = b.
Deep dive: reflections and plotting

Reflection of (a, b) in the x-axis is (a, -b); in the y-axis (-a, b); in the origin (-a, -b). To plot, move a units along the x-axis (right if positive, left if negative) and b units parallel to the y-axis. Four quadrants and the axes together cover the whole plane. Joining plotted points in order forms shapes such as triangles and rectangles; the area of a rectangle with vertices (0,0), (a,0), (a,b), (0,b) is |a| x |b|.
Hindi saransh
x = abscissa, y = ordinate. Quadrant I (+,+), II (-,+), III (-,-), IV (+,-).
Points on x-axis have y = 0; on y-axis have x = 0.

Big idea

  • A point is located by its abscissa (x) and ordinate (y) from two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, which meet at the origin (0, 0)…
📌

Cartesian plane

  • The x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical) intersect at the origin O (0, 0)
  • A point (a, b) has abscissa a (distance from the y-axis) and ordinate b (distance from the x-axis)
  • Signs: Quadrant I (+, +), II (-, +), III (-, -), IV (+, -)
  • A point on the x-axis is (a, 0) and a point on the y-axis is (0, b)
Read the full explanation

The x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical) intersect at the origin O (0, 0). A point (a, b) has abscissa a (distance from the y-axis) and ordinate b (distance from the x-axis). Signs: Quadrant I (+, +), II (-, +), III (-, -), IV (+, -). A point on the x-axis is (a, 0) and a point on the y-axis is (0, b). (a, b) and (b, a) are different points unless a = b.

🧠

Reflections and plotting

  • Reflection of (a, b) in the x-axis is (a, -b)
  • In the y-axis (-a, b)
  • In the origin (-a, -b)
  • To plot, move a units along the x-axis (right if positive, left if negative) and b units parallel to the y-axis
Read the full explanation

Reflection of (a, b) in the x-axis is (a, -b); in the y-axis (-a, b); in the origin (-a, -b). To plot, move a units along the x-axis (right if positive, left if negative) and b units parallel to the y-axis. Four quadrants and the axes together cover the whole plane. Joining plotted points in order forms shapes such as triangles and rectangles; the area of a rectangle with vertices (0,0), (a,0), (a,b), (0,b) is |a| x |b|.

lessons.title: Introduction to Euclid's Geometry

blocks.x: Euclid, a Greek mathematician of Alexandria (about 300 BC), wrote the Elements in 13 books and built geometry from a few definitions, five postulates and some common notions (axioms). Axioms are universal truths; postulates are assumptions specific to geometry. The fifth postulate led to non-Euclidean geometries.
Deep dive: definitions, axioms and postulates

Euclid's Elements opens with 23 definitions such as a point being that which has no part and a line being breadthless length. Because some terms must remain undefined, modern geometry takes point, line and plane as undefined terms. Axioms (common notions) are general truths used throughout mathematics, while postulates are assumptions specific to geometry. Seven axioms are listed in the NCERT text.
Deep dive: the five postulates

Postulate 1: a line may be drawn from any point to any other point. Postulate 2: a terminated line can be extended indefinitely. Postulate 3: a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius. Postulate 4: all right angles are equal. Postulate 5: if a line meets two lines so that the interior angles on one side total less than two right angles, the two lines meet on that side when extended. Postulate 5 is equivalent to Playfair's axiom about a unique parallel through an external point.
Deep dive: consequences

Two distinct lines cannot have more than one common point, and through two points exactly one line passes. Euclid built theorems on these ideas. Doubts about the fifth postulate led mathematicians in the nineteenth century to non-Euclidean geometries, which describe curved surfaces such as the sphere.

Read the full explanation

Euclid's Elements opens with 23 definitions such as a point being that which has no part and a line being breadthless length. Because some terms must remain undefined, modern geometry takes point, line and plane as undefined terms. Axioms (common notions) are general truths used throughout mathematics, while postulates are assumptions specific to geometry. Seven axioms are listed in the NCERT text.

🧠

The five postulates

  • Postulate 1: a line may be drawn from any point to any other point
  • Postulate 2: a terminated line can be extended indefinitely
  • Postulate 3: a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius
  • Postulate 4: all right angles are equal
Read the full explanation

Postulate 1: a line may be drawn from any point to any other point. Postulate 2: a terminated line can be extended indefinitely. Postulate 3: a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius. Postulate 4: all right angles are equal. Postulate 5: if a line meets two lines so that the interior angles on one side total less than two right angles, the two lines meet on that side when extended. Postulate 5 is equivalent to Playfair's axiom about a unique parallel through an external point.

🌟

Consequences

  • Two distinct lines cannot have more than one common point, and through two points exactly one line passes
  • Euclid built theorems on these ideas
  • Doubts about the fifth postulate led mathematicians in the nineteenth century to non-Euclidean geometries, which describe curved surfaces such as the…

lessons.title: Triangles, Pythagoras and Heron's formula

blocks.x: Triangle congruence criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS. Angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees; exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. **Pythagoras:** in a right triangle c^2 = a^2 + b^2; e.g. 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triples. **Heron's formula:** area = sqrt(s (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)), s = (a + b + c)/2. For sides 13, 14, 15: s = 21 and area = sqrt(21 x 8 x 7 x 6) = **84 square units**. **Mensuration:** cylinder volume pi r^2 h, curved surface 2 pi r h, total 2 pi r (r + h); with r = 7 and h = 10 (pi = 22/7): V = **1540 cubic units**, total surface area **748 square units**. Sphere volume (4/3) pi r^3, surface 4 pi r^2.
Deep dive: triangles

**Angle sum.** The three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, and it is greater than either of them. In an equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees; in an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. **Congruence.** Two triangles are congruent when they have the same shape and size. Criteria: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them), AAS (two angles and any side), and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and one side). AAA and SSA are not criteria. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT). **Inequalities.** The sum of two sides of a triangle is greater than the third. The side opposite the larger angle is the longer side. The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. **Pythagoras.** In a right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c: c^2 = a^2 + b^2. The converse also holds. Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and their multiples. **Area.** Half base x height. For an equilateral triangle of side a: area = (sqrt 3 / 4) a^2. For a right triangle: half the product of the legs. **Heron's formula.** With s = (a + b + c) / 2, area = sqrt (s (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)). Use it when the three sides are given but the height is not. Quadrilaterals can be split into two triangles by a diagonal and their areas added.
Deep dive: surface areas and volumes

**Cuboid** (l, b, h): volume l b h; total surface area 2 (lb + bh + hl); lateral surface 2h (l + b); diagonal sqrt (l^2 + b^2 + h^2). **Cube** (side a): volume a^3; total surface 6a^2; lateral 4a^2; diagonal a sqrt 3. **Cylinder** (r, h): curved surface 2 pi r h; total 2 pi r (r + h); volume pi r^2 h. **Cone** (r, h, slant l): l = sqrt (r^2 + h^2); curved surface pi r l; total pi r (r + l); volume (1/3) pi r^2 h. **Sphere** (r): surface 4 pi r^2; volume (4/3) pi r^3. **Hemisphere**: curved surface 2 pi r^2; total 3 pi r^2; volume (2/3) pi r^3. **Units.** Area is in square units, volume in cubic units. 1 m^3 = 1000 litres. Always convert to the same unit first, and use pi = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7.

Big idea

  • Angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees

  • Pythagoras: in a right triangle c2 = a2 + b2
Read the full explanation

Triangle congruence criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS. Angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees; exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Pythagoras: in a right triangle c^2 = a^2 + b^2; e.g. 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triples. Heron's formula: area = sqrt(s (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)), s = (a + b + c)/2. For sides 13, 14, 15: s = 21 and area = sqrt(21 x 8 x 7 x 6) = 84 square units. Mensuration: cylinder volume pi r^2 h, curved surface 2 pi r h, total 2 pi r (r + h); with r = 7 and h = 10 (pi = 22/7): V = 1540 cubic units, total surface area 748 square units. Sphere volume (4/3) pi r^3, surface 4 pi r^2.

📐

Triangles

  • The three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees
  • The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, and it is greater than either of them
  • In an equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees
  • In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal
Read the full explanation

Angle sum. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, and it is greater than either of them. In an equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees; in an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Congruence. Two triangles are congruent when they have the same shape and size. Criteria: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them), AAS (two angles and any side), and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and one side). AAA and SSA are not criteria. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT). Inequalities. The sum of two sides of a triangle is greater than the third. The side opposite the larger angle is the longer side. The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. Pythagoras. In a right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c: c^2 = a^2 + b^2. The converse also holds. Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and their multiples. Area. Half base x height. For an equilateral triangle of side a: area = (sqrt 3 / 4) a^2. For a right triangle: half the product of the legs. Heron's formula. With s = (a + b + c) / 2, area = sqrt (s (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)). Use it when the three sides are given but the height is not. Quadrilaterals can be split into two triangles by a diagonal and their areas added.

📐

Surface areas and volumes

  • Cuboid (l, b, h): volume l b h
  • Total surface area 2 (lb + bh + hl)
  • Lateral surface 2h (l + b)
  • Diagonal sqrt (l2 + b2 + h2)
Read the full explanation

Cuboid (l, b, h): volume l b h; total surface area 2 (lb + bh + hl); lateral surface 2h (l + b); diagonal sqrt (l^2 + b^2 + h^2). Cube (side a): volume a^3; total surface 6a^2; lateral 4a^2; diagonal a sqrt 3. Cylinder (r, h): curved surface 2 pi r h; total 2 pi r (r + h); volume pi r^2 h. Cone (r, h, slant l): l = sqrt (r^2 + h^2); curved surface pi r l; total pi r (r + l); volume (1/3) pi r^2 h. Sphere (r): surface 4 pi r^2; volume (4/3) pi r^3. Hemisphere: curved surface 2 pi r^2; total 3 pi r^2; volume (2/3) pi r^3. Units. Area is in square units, volume in cubic units. 1 m^3 = 1000 litres. Always convert to the same unit first, and use pi = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7.

blocks.x: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees, supplementary to 180 degrees. A linear pair adds to 180 degrees; vertically opposite angles are equal. A transversal across parallel lines makes equal corresponding angles and equal alternate interior angles, and interior angles on the same side add to 180 degrees. The angle sum of a triangle is 180 degrees.
Deep dive: pairs of angles

Complementary angles add to 90 degrees; supplementary angles add to 180 degrees. A linear pair is two adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a line, so they are supplementary. Vertically opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines are equal. The sum of angles around a point is 360 degrees.
Deep dive: parallel lines and a transversal

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines: corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, and interior angles on the same side are supplementary. The converse is also true: if any one of these holds, the lines are parallel. Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.
Deep dive: triangle angle properties

The angle sum of a triangle is 180 degrees. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. In an equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees; in an isosceles triangle the angles opposite equal sides are equal. For a triangle with angles in the ratio a:b:c, the actual angles are 180 a/(a+b+c) and so on.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals

blocks.x: The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees. In a parallelogram opposite sides and angles are equal and diagonals bisect each other. A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if a pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel. A rectangle has equal diagonals; a rhombus has perpendicular diagonals; a square has both. The mid-point theorem: the line joining mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.
Deep dive: parallelogram properties

A parallelogram has: opposite sides equal; opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other; each diagonal divides it into two congruent triangles; consecutive angles are supplementary. Conversely a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if (i) opposite sides are equal, or (ii) opposite angles are equal, or (iii) diagonals bisect each other, or (iv) one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.
Deep dive: special parallelograms

Rectangle: a parallelogram with one right angle; all angles 90 degrees; diagonals equal. Rhombus: a parallelogram with equal sides; diagonals perpendicular bisectors; diagonals bisect the angles. Square: both rectangle and rhombus; diagonals equal and perpendicular and bisect each other at 90 degrees. Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; one diagonal bisects the other perpendicularly. Trapezium: one pair of parallel sides.
Deep dive: mid-point theorem

In triangle ABC, if D and E are the mid-points of AB and AC then DE is parallel to BC and DE = (1/2) BC. Converse: a line through the mid-point of one side parallel to another side bisects the third side. Joining mid-points of the sides of any quadrilateral in order gives a parallelogram. A diagonal of a rhombus of side a has d1^2 + d2^2 = 4a^2.
Deep dive: parallelogram properties

A parallelogram has: opposite sides equal; opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other; each diagonal divides it into two congruent triangles; consecutive angles are supplementary. Conversely a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if (i) opposite sides are equal, or (ii) opposite angles are equal, or (iii) diagonals bisect each other, or (iv) one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.
Deep dive: special parallelograms

Rectangle: a parallelogram with one right angle; all angles 90 degrees; diagonals equal. Rhombus: a parallelogram with equal sides; diagonals perpendicular bisectors; diagonals bisect the angles. Square: both rectangle and rhombus; diagonals equal and perpendicular and bisect each other at 90 degrees. Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; one diagonal bisects the other perpendicularly. lessons.title: Circles

blocks.x: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre; the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle at any point on the remaining part. Angles in the same segment are equal. The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
Deep dive: chords and the centre

Equal chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) subtend equal angles at the centre, and conversely. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord, and the line joining the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to it. The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended at any point on the remaining part of the circle. Angles in the same segment are equal. lessons.title: Triangles

blocks.x: Two triangles are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size. The congruence rules are SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS. In congruent triangles corresponding parts are equal (CPCT). Angles opposite equal sides of a triangle are equal and the sides opposite equal angles are equal. The sum of the angles of a triangle is 180° and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. In a triangle, the larger side has the larger angle opposite it, and the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side.
Deep dive: congruence

Triangles ABC and PQR are congruent (written ABC ≅ PQR) if all corresponding sides and angles are equal. Rules: SAS (two sides and included angle), ASA (two angles and included side), AAS, SSS and RHS. SSA and AAA do not ensure congruence. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT).
Deep dive: properties of triangles

Angles opposite equal sides are equal; sides opposite equal angles are equal. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. An equilateral triangle has all angles equal to 60°.
Deep dive: inequalities
The larger side has the larger angle opposite and vice versa. The sum of any two sides is greater than the third, so lengths 3, 4, 8 cannot form a triangle.

blocks.x: Cuboid: TSA 2(lb + bh + hl), volume lbh. Cube: TSA 6a^2, volume a^3. Cylinder: CSA 2 pi r h, TSA 2 pi r (r + h), volume pi r^2 h. Cone: CSA pi r l, TSA pi r (l + r), volume one-third pi r^2 h, with l^2 = r^2 + h^2. Sphere: 4 pi r^2 and (4/3) pi r^3. Hemisphere: CSA 2 pi r^2, TSA 3 pi r^2, volume (2/3) pi r^3.
Deep dive: cuboid and cube

For a cuboid with length l, breadth b, height h: lateral surface area 2h (l + b), total surface area 2(lb + bh + hl), volume lbh, diagonal sqrt (l^2 + b^2 + h^2). For a cube of edge a: lateral surface area 4a^2, total 6a^2, volume a^3, diagonal a sqrt 3. Volume is measured in cubic units; 1 litre = 1000 cubic cm and 1 cubic metre = 1000 litres.
Deep dive: cylinder and cone

Cylinder (radius r, height h): CSA = 2 pi r h, TSA = 2 pi r (r + h), volume = pi r^2 h. Cone: slant height l = sqrt (r^2 + h^2), CSA = pi r l, TSA = pi r (r + l), volume = (1/3) pi r^2 h. Hollow cylinder with radii R and r: volume = pi h (R^2 - r^2).
Deep dive: sphere and hemisphere

Sphere of radius r: surface area 4 pi r^2, volume (4/3) pi r^3. Hemisphere: CSA = 2 pi r^2, TSA = 3 pi r^2, volume (2/3) pi r^3. A spherical shell with outer R and inner r has volume (4/3) pi (R^3 - r^3). Doubling the radius of a sphere multiplies its surface area by 4 and its volume by 8.

lessons.title: Heron's Formula

blocks.x: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle when the lengths of all three sides a, b and c are known: Area = √[s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)], where s = (a + b + c)/2 is the semi-perimeter. It is useful when the height is not known. The area of an equilateral triangle of side a is (√3/4)a², of an isosceles triangle with equal sides a and base b is (b/4)√(4a² - b²). Heron's formula can be used for quadrilaterals by dividing them into two triangles.
Deep dive: the formula

Heron's formula finds the area of a triangle from its three sides. First compute s = (a + b + c)/2; then area = √[s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)]. Example: for sides 13, 14, 15, s = 21 and area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84.
Deep dive: special triangles
Equilateral: area = (√3/4)a². Isosceles with equal sides a and base b: area = (b/4)√(4a² - b²). Right triangle: area = (1/2) × product of legs; also Heron's formula agrees with it.
Deep dive: quadrilaterals
Split a quadrilateral by a diagonal into two triangles and add their areas. Parallelogram: base × height. Rhombus: (1/2) d1 d2. Trapezium: (1/2)(a + b)h.
Deep dive: word problems
In real-life problems (parks, signboards, cost of painting) compute the area first, then multiply by the rate per unit area. Keep units consistent.

In real-life problems (parks, signboards, cost of painting) compute the area first, then multiply by the rate per unit area. Keep units consistent.

s = (a + b + c)/2; Area = √[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)].

Read the full explanation

Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle when the lengths of all three sides a, b and c are known: Area = √[s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)], where s = (a + b + c)/2 is the semi-perimeter. It is useful when the height is not known. The area of an equilateral triangle of side a is (√3/4)a², of an isosceles triangle with equal sides a and base b is (b/4)√(4a² - b²). Heron's formula can be used for quadrilaterals by dividing them into two triangles.

🧮

The formula

  • Heron's formula finds the area of a triangle from its three sides
  • First compute s = (a + b + c)/2
  • Then area = √[s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)]
  • Example: for sides 13, 14, 15, s = 21 and area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84
📐

Special triangles

  • Equilateral: area = (√3/4)a²
  • Isosceles with equal sides a and base b: area = (b/4)√(4a² - b²)
  • Right triangle: area = (1/2) × product of legs
  • Also Heron's formula agrees with it
🌟

Quadrilaterals

  • Split a quadrilateral by a diagonal into two triangles and add their areas
  • Parallelogram: base × height
  • Rhombus: (1/2) d1 d2
  • Trapezium: (1/2)(a + b)h
✍️

Word problems

  • In real-life problems (parks, signboards, cost of painting) compute the area first, then multiply by the rate per unit area
  • Keep units consistent

lessons.title: Statistics

blocks.x: Raw data is organised into a frequency distribution table, grouped into classes of equal width for large data. It can be shown as a bar graph, histogram or frequency polygon. The mean is the sum of observations divided by their number, the median is the middle value of the ordered data, and the mode is the most frequent value.
Deep dive: collecting and presenting data

Data collected first-hand is primary data; from other sources, secondary data. Ungrouped data is arranged in a frequency table with tally marks. For large data, group into continuous classes of equal width (class size = upper limit - lower limit). Graphs: a bar graph has bars of equal width with gaps; a histogram has no gaps and bars in a continuous class; a frequency polygon joins the mid-points of tops of histogram bars (or class marks vs frequency).
Deep dive: mean, median and mode

Mean x = (sum of all observations)/(number of observations). For a frequency table, x = sum (f x)/sum f. Median: arrange in order; for n odd it is the ((n+1)/2)th value, for n even the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th values. Mode: the observation with the highest frequency. Mean = sum/ n so adding a constant to every value adds it to the mean; multiplying multiplies the mean.
Deep dive: choosing the measure

The mean uses all values and is affected by extreme values; the median is not affected by extreme values and is best for skewed data; the mode is best for the most popular size or choice (such as shoe size).

lessons.title: Probability

blocks.x: Probability measures how likely an event is to occur. In the experimental or empirical approach, the probability of an event E is P(E) = (number of trials in which E happens) / (total number of trials). The probability of a sure event is 1 and that of an impossible event is 0, so 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. The probabilities of all elementary events of an experiment add up to 1. P(E) + P(not E) = 1. Equally likely outcomes are assumed in simple examples such as coins, dice and cards.
Deep dive: experimental probability

Repeat an experiment many times and record how often the event occurs. P(E) = (trials with E)/(total trials). For a coin tossed 100 times with 55 heads, P(head) = 55/100 = 0.55. As the trials increase the value approaches 1/2.
Deep dive: properties
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(sure event) = 1; P(impossible event) = 0; the sum of probabilities of all elementary events is 1; P(not E) = 1 - P(E).
Deep dive: coins, dice and cards
Sample space for one coin: {H, T}; for a die: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; two coins: {HH, HT, TH, TT}. A pack has 52 cards in four suits of 13. P(even number on a die) = 3/6 = 1/2; P(ace) = 4/52 = 1/13.
