Visual lesson

Motion, force and gravitation (Class 9)

Speed = distance/time

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Motion›3Force and laws of motion›4Gravitation, work and energy
🔑

Big idea

  • Speed = distance/time
  • Velocity has direction
  • Acceleration = (v - u)/t
  • Equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + at2/2, v2 = u2 + 2as
Read the full explanation

Speed = distance/time; velocity has direction; acceleration = (v - u)/t. Equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + at^2/2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Newton's laws: inertia; F = ma; action-reaction. Force 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2. Example: 5 kg with a = 2 m/s^2 needs F = 10 N. Momentum p = mv. Gravitation: F = G m1 m2 / r^2; g = 9.8 m/s^2; weight W = m g; mass is constant, weight changes with place (about one-sixth on the Moon). Work, energy: W = F s; KE = mv^2/2; PE = mgh; power = work/time. Sound: v = f x wavelength: f = 170 Hz and speed 340 m/s give wavelength 2 m. Density = mass/volume: 54 g in 20 cm^3 is 2.7 g/cm^3 (aluminium).

🚀

Motion

  • Distance and displacement
  • Distance is the total path length (scalar, never negative)
  • Displacement is the shortest straight-line change of position with direction (vector, can be zero or negative)
  • For a full circle the distance is 2 pi r but the displacement is 0
Read the full explanation

Distance and displacement. Distance is the total path length (scalar, never negative). Displacement is the shortest straight-line change of position with direction (vector, can be zero or negative). For a full circle the distance is 2 pi r but the displacement is 0. Speed, velocity, acceleration. Speed = distance / time. Velocity = displacement / time. Average speed = total distance / total time. Acceleration a = (v - u) / t, unit m/s^2; negative acceleration is retardation. Uniform motion means equal distances in equal times; non-uniform motion does not. Graphs. On a distance-time graph the slope is the speed; a straight line means uniform speed, a horizontal line means rest. On a velocity-time graph the slope is the acceleration and the area under the graph is the displacement. Equations of uniformly accelerated motion. v = u + a t; s = u t + (1/2) a t^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s. Free fall uses a = g = 9.8 m/s^2 (take 10 for quick work). For an object thrown up, speed is zero at the top. Circular motion. At constant speed v in a circle of radius r, the velocity changes direction, so the motion is accelerated; v = 2 pi r / T.

⚖️

Force and laws of motion

  • Force changes the state of rest or motion, speed, direction or shape
  • Balanced forces do not change motion
  • Unbalanced forces do
  • Unit: newton (1 N = 1 kg m/s2)
Read the full explanation

Force changes the state of rest or motion, speed, direction or shape. Balanced forces do not change motion; unbalanced forces do. Unit: newton (1 N = 1 kg m/s^2). Newton's first law (inertia). A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts. Inertia depends on mass. Examples: passengers jerk forward when a bus stops; dust falls off a beaten carpet. Momentum p = m v (kg m/s). Second law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force: F = m a. Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, acting on different bodies (rocket, recoil of a gun, walking). Conservation of momentum: in an isolated system total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Friction opposes relative motion; it is needed for walking and braking and is reduced by lubrication and wheels.

🚀

Gravitation, work and energy

  • Universal law of gravitation
  • F = G m1 m2 / r2 with G = 6.67 x 10-11 N m2/kg2
  • Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter
  • Free fall acceleration g = G M / R2 = 9.8 m/s2 on Earth, independent of the mass of the falling body
Read the full explanation

Universal law of gravitation. F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter. Free fall acceleration g = G M / R^2 = 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth, independent of the mass of the falling body; on the Moon g is about one sixth. Mass is the amount of matter (kg, same everywhere); weight W = m g (newton, varies with place). Thrust and pressure. Thrust is force perpendicular to a surface; pressure = thrust / area (pascal). Buoyancy. An object in a fluid feels an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced (Archimedes). It floats when its density is less than the fluid's. Density = mass / volume; relative density = density of substance / density of water. Work and energy. Work W = F s cos(angle) (joule); no work when there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to the motion. Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2; potential energy = m g h. Energy changes form but the total is conserved. Power = work / time (watt); 1 hp = 746 W. Sound. A mechanical longitudinal wave needing a medium. v = f x lambda. Speed is greatest in solids, least in gases (about 340 m/s in air at room temperature). Echo needs a reflector at least 17 m away. Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency. Audible range 20 Hz to 20000 Hz.

lessons.title: Sound

blocks.x: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that needs a medium. Speed v = f lambda; in air about 343 m/s at 20 C. Frequency is heard as pitch and amplitude as loudness. Audible range is 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Echo needs a reflector at least 17 m away; reflection of sound follows the same laws as light. Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) is used in sonar and medical imaging.
Deep dive: production and propagation of sound

Sound is produced by vibrating bodies (vocal cords, a tuning fork, a stretched string). It travels as a longitudinal wave: particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave, forming alternate compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure). It needs a material medium - solid, liquid or gas - and cannot travel through a vacuum (the bell-jar experiment). The speed of sound is greatest in solids and least in gases (about 5000 m/s in iron, 1500 m/s in water, 343 m/s in air at 20 C) and increases with temperature.
Deep dive: characteristics of sound

Wavelength lambda is the distance between two consecutive compressions or rarefactions; frequency f is the number of vibrations per second (hertz); time period T = 1/f; amplitude is the maximum displacement. Speed v = f x lambda. Pitch depends on frequency (a high frequency gives a shrill sound); loudness depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels; quality or timbre distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness. Intensity is the sound energy passing per second per unit area. Humans hear 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; infrasound (below 20 Hz) is produced by earthquakes and heard by elephants and whales; ultrasound (above 20 000 Hz) is heard by dogs, bats and dolphins.
Deep dive: reflection, echo, reverberation and applications

Sound reflects from hard surfaces and obeys the laws of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, all in one plane). An echo is the repetition of sound heard after reflection; the persistence of hearing is 0.1 second, so for an echo the minimum distance to the reflector is d = v t/2 = 343 x 0.1/2 = about 17 m. Repeated reflections give reverberation, reduced in halls by absorbing materials, curved ceilings and soundboards. Applications: megaphones, stethoscopes, SONAR (distance = v t/2), ultrasound scanning, cleaning of delicate parts, and flaw detection in metals. The human ear has the outer ear (pinna), middle ear (three ossicles: hammer, anvil, stirrup) and the inner ear with the cochlea that converts vibrations to electrical signals sent to the brain.

The speed of sound is greatest in solids and least in gases (about 5000 m/s in iron, 1500 m/s in water, 343 m/s in air at 20 C) and increases with temperature.

🌊

Characteristics of sound

  • Wavelength lambda is the distance between two consecutive compressions or rarefactions
  • Frequency f is the number of vibrations per second (hertz)
  • Time period T = 1/f
  • Amplitude is the maximum displacement
Read the full explanation

Wavelength lambda is the distance between two consecutive compressions or rarefactions; frequency f is the number of vibrations per second (hertz); time period T = 1/f; amplitude is the maximum displacement. Speed v = f x lambda. Pitch depends on frequency (a high frequency gives a shrill sound); loudness depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels; quality or timbre distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness. Intensity is the sound energy passing per second per unit area. Humans hear 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; infrasound (below 20 Hz) is produced by earthquakes and heard by elephants and whales; ultrasound (above 20 000 Hz) is heard by dogs, bats and dolphins.

💡

Reflection, echo, reverberation and applications

  • Sound reflects from hard surfaces and obeys the laws of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, all in one plane)
  • An echo is the repetition of sound heard after reflection
  • The persistence of hearing is 0.1 second, so for an echo the minimum distance to the reflector is d = v t/2 = 343 x 0.1/2 = about 17 m
  • Repeated reflections give reverberation, reduced in halls by absorbing materials, curved ceilings and soundboards
Read the full explanation

Sound reflects from hard surfaces and obeys the laws of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, all in one plane). An echo is the repetition of sound heard after reflection; the persistence of hearing is 0.1 second, so for an echo the minimum distance to the reflector is d = v t/2 = 343 x 0.1/2 = about 17 m. Repeated reflections give reverberation, reduced in halls by absorbing materials, curved ceilings and soundboards. Applications: megaphones, stethoscopes, SONAR (distance = v t/2), ultrasound scanning, cleaning of delicate parts, and flaw detection in metals. The human ear has the outer ear (pinna), middle ear (three ossicles: hammer, anvil, stirrup) and the inner ear with the cochlea that converts vibrations to electrical signals sent to the brain.

lessons.title: Work and energy

blocks.x: Work done W = F s cos theta (joule). Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2; potential energy near the Earth = m g h; the sum is conserved. Power P = W/t (watt); 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Work done is zero when displacement is zero or perpendicular to the force.
Deep dive: work

Work is done when a force produces displacement in the direction of the force: W = F x s (for a force along the displacement) or W = F s cos theta. The SI unit is the joule (1 J = 1 N m). Work is positive when force and displacement are in the same direction (pushing a trolley), negative when opposite (friction on a sliding block, or gravity on an object being lifted), and zero when there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to the displacement (a satellite in circular orbit, a coolie carrying a load along a level road). Work is a scalar quantity.
Deep dive: kinetic and potential energy

Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules. Kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving at speed v is E_k = (1/2) m v^2; from the work-energy theorem the work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. Potential energy is stored energy because of position or configuration: gravitational potential energy E_p = m g h (g = 9.8 m/s^2, or 10 for simple work); elastic potential energy is stored in a stretched spring or bow. Forms of energy: mechanical, heat, light, sound, chemical, electrical, nuclear.
Deep dive: conservation of energy and power

Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another; the total energy before and after a transformation is the same. For a freely falling body the sum of kinetic and potential energies is constant: m g h = (1/2) m v^2 at the bottom, so v = sqrt (2 g h). Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t (unit watt, 1 W = 1 J/s; 1 horsepower = 746 W). Commercial unit of energy: 1 kilowatt-hour = 1 kW x 1 h = 3.6 x 10^6 J = 1 unit of electricity. Average power = total energy consumed/total time. The efficiency of a machine = useful output/total input.

lessons.title: Motion

blocks.x: Motion is the change of position of an object with time. Distance is the total path length (scalar); displacement is the shortest straight-line distance with direction (vector). Speed is distance per unit time; velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For uniform acceleration the three equations of motion are v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at² and v² = u² + 2as. Motion can be shown on distance-time and velocity-time graphs; the slope of a distance-time graph gives speed, the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration and the area under it gives distance.
Deep dive: describing motion

Position is described relative to a reference point. Distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector. A car travelling round a circular track and returning to the start has zero displacement but non-zero distance. Speed = distance/time, velocity = displacement/time and acceleration = (v - u)/t.
Deep dive: equations of motion

For uniform acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at²; v² = u² + 2as. They are derived from the velocity-time graph: the slope gives a and the area under the graph gives s. For a body starting from rest u = 0.
Deep dive: graphs

A distance-time graph with a straight line shows uniform speed, a horizontal line shows rest, and a curve shows changing speed. In a velocity-time graph a horizontal line shows uniform velocity and a sloped line shows uniform acceleration; the area under it is the distance travelled.
Deep dive: circular motion
In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity changes continuously because direction changes, so the motion is accelerated. Speed v = 2πr/T.

Visual lesson

Motion

Motion is the change of position of an object with time

formulas
Q&A

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Describing motion›3Equations of motion›4Graphs›5Circular motion
km/h to m/smultiply by 5/18
🔑

Big idea

  • Motion is the change of position of an object with time
  • Distance is the total path length (scalar)
  • Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance with direction (vector)
  • Speed is distance per unit time
Read the full explanation

Motion is the change of position of an object with time. Distance is the total path length (scalar); displacement is the shortest straight-line distance with direction (vector). Speed is distance per unit time; velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For uniform acceleration the three equations of motion are v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at² and v² = u² + 2as. Motion can be shown on distance-time and velocity-time graphs; the slope of a distance-time graph gives speed, the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration and the area under it gives distance.

🚀

Describing motion

  • Position is described relative to a reference point
  • Distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector
  • A car travelling round a circular track and returning to the start has zero displacement but non-zero distance
  • Speed = distance/time, velocity = displacement/time and acceleration = (v - u)/t
🧮

Equations of motion

  • For uniform acceleration: v = u + at
  • S = ut + (1/2)at²
  • V² = u² + 2as
  • They are derived from the velocity-time graph: the slope gives a and the area under the graph gives s
Read the full explanation

For uniform acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at²; v² = u² + 2as. They are derived from the velocity-time graph: the slope gives a and the area under the graph gives s. For a body starting from rest u = 0.

🌟

Graphs

  • A distance-time graph with a straight line shows uniform speed, a horizontal line shows rest, and a curve shows changing speed
  • In a velocity-time graph a horizontal line shows uniform velocity and a sloped line shows uniform acceleration
  • The area under it is the distance travelled
🚀

Circular motion

  • In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity changes continuously because direction changes, so the motion is accelerated
  • Speed v = 2πr/T
🧮

Formula tiles

Speedv = d/tm/s
Accelerationa = (v - u)/tm/s²
First equationv = u + atvelocity-time
Second equations = ut + 1/2 a t^2position-time
Third equationv^2 = u^2 + 2asposition-velocity
Circular speedv = 2 pi r/Tuniform circular motion

blocks.x: A force changes or tends to change the state of rest or motion of a body. Newton's first law (law of inertia) states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an unbalanced force. The second law states that the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force; F = ma. The third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Momentum p = mv. In an isolated system the total momentum is conserved.
Deep dive: inertia

Galileo observed that a ball rolling on a smooth surface keeps moving. Newton's first law formalised this: a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by an external unbalanced force. Mass measures inertia. Examples: passengers lurch backward when a bus starts and forward when it stops.
Deep dive: second law and momentum

Momentum p = mv. Rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force. F = (mv - mu)/t = ma. One newton gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². Impulse = Ft = change in momentum, so a longer time of contact reduces the force.
Deep dive: third law and conservation

Action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies, so they do not cancel. For an isolated system m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2. A gun recoils with velocity v = -(m_bullet v_bullet)/m_gun.

Visual lesson

Force and Laws of Motion

A force changes or tends to change the state of rest or motion of a body

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Inertia›3Second law and momentum›4Third law and conservation
🔑

Big idea

  • A force changes or tends to change the state of rest or motion of a body
  • Newton's first law (law of inertia) states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an unbalanced force
  • The second law states that the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force
  • The third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
Read the full explanation

A force changes or tends to change the state of rest or motion of a body. Newton's first law (law of inertia) states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an unbalanced force. The second law states that the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force; F = ma. The third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Momentum p = mv. In an isolated system the total momentum is conserved.

📌

Inertia

  • Galileo observed that a ball rolling on a smooth surface keeps moving
  • Newton's first law formalised this: a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by an external unbalanced force
  • Mass measures inertia
  • Examples: passengers lurch backward when a bus starts and forward when it stops
⚖️

Second law and momentum

  • Momentum p = mv
  • Rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force
  • F = (mv - mu)/t = ma
  • One newton gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
Read the full explanation

Momentum p = mv. Rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force. F = (mv - mu)/t = ma. One newton gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². Impulse = Ft = change in momentum, so a longer time of contact reduces the force.

⚖️

Third law and conservation

  • Action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies, so they do not cancel
  • For an isolated system m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2
  • A gun recoils with velocity v = -(m_bullet v_bullet)/m_gun
🧮

lessons.title: Gravitation

blocks.x: Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force called gravitational force. Newton's universal law of gravitation states that this force is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G M m / r². G is the universal gravitational constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². Near the Earth the acceleration due to gravity is g = GM/R² = 9.8 m/s². Weight W = mg. Archimedes' principle gives the buoyant force on a body immersed in a fluid, and explains floatation. Pressure is force per unit area.
Deep dive: universal law

Newton realised that the force that pulls an apple to the ground also holds the Moon in orbit. The force between two masses M and m separated by r is F = GMm/r². The force is attractive, acts along the line joining the masses, and obeys the inverse-square law. Doubling the distance reduces the force to one-fourth.
Deep dive: g and weight

Near Earth, g = GM/R² = 9.8 m/s². g is independent of the falling mass. It varies slightly with latitude and falls with height. Weight W = mg; on the Moon g is about one-sixth, so weight is one-sixth, while mass is the same.
Deep dive: free fall equations
For dropped bodies u = 0, v = gt, s = (1/2)gt² and v² = 2gs. For an upward throw, time to the top is u/g and the maximum height is u²/2g.
Deep dive: pressure and buoyancy

Pressure = thrust/area. Fluids exert buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes). A body floats if its density is less than that of the fluid, sinks if more. Relative density = density of substance/density of water.

Visual lesson

Gravitation

Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force called gravitational force

🔑

Big idea

  • Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force called gravitational force
  • Newton's universal law of gravitation states that this force is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the…
  • G is the universal gravitational constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg²
  • Near the Earth the acceleration due to gravity is g = GM/R² = 9.8 m/s²
Read the full explanation

Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force called gravitational force. Newton's universal law of gravitation states that this force is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G M m / r². G is the universal gravitational constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². Near the Earth the acceleration due to gravity is g = GM/R² = 9.8 m/s². Weight W = mg. Archimedes' principle gives the buoyant force on a body immersed in a fluid, and explains floatation. Pressure is force per unit area.

⚖️

Universal law

  • Newton realised that the force that pulls an apple to the ground also holds the Moon in orbit
  • The force between two masses M and m separated by r is F = GMm/r²
  • The force is attractive, acts along the line joining the masses, and obeys the inverse-square law
  • Doubling the distance reduces the force to one-fourth
🧠

G and weight

  • Near Earth, g = GM/R² = 9.8 m/s²
  • G is independent of the falling mass
  • It varies slightly with latitude and falls with height
  • Weight W = mg
Read the full explanation

Near Earth, g = GM/R² = 9.8 m/s². g is independent of the falling mass. It varies slightly with latitude and falls with height. Weight W = mg; on the Moon g is about one-sixth, so weight is one-sixth, while mass is the same.

🧮

Free fall equations

  • For dropped bodies u = 0, v = gt, s = (1/2)gt² and v² = 2gs
  • For an upward throw, time to the top is u/g and the maximum height is u²/2g
🔬

Pressure and buoyancy

  • Pressure = thrust/area
  • Fluids exert buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes)
  • A body floats if its density is less than that of the fluid, sinks if more
  • Relative density = density of substance/density of water
🧮

lessons.title: Atoms, molecules and the cell (Class 9)

blocks.x: **Law of conservation of mass** and **law of constant proportions** (water is always 1:8 by mass of hydrogen to oxygen). Atom: smallest unit of an element. **Mole** = 6.022 x 10^23 particles. Molecular mass of water = 2 x 1 + 16 = **18 u**. **Atomic structure:** protons (+), neutrons (0) in the nucleus, electrons (-) in shells 2, 8, 8. Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons. Example: sodium (Z = 11) is 2, 8, 1. **Isotopes** have the same Z but different mass numbers (C-12 and C-14). **Cell:** basic unit of life. Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells do not. Tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous.
Deep dive: matter, atoms and molecules

**Laws of chemical combination.** Conservation of mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction. Constant proportions: a compound always has the same elements in the same ratio by mass (water: 1 part hydrogen to 8 parts oxygen). Dalton's atomic theory: matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction. **Symbols and formulae.** Elements have symbols (H, O, Na from natrium, K from kalium, Fe from ferrum). Valency is the combining capacity: Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3, C 4, O 2, Cl 1. Write the symbols, put the valencies crosswise and simplify: Al and O give Al2O3. Atomic mass is in u (1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom). Molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses: H2O = 18 u, CO2 = 44 u, NaCl = 58.5 u, H2SO4 = 98 u. **The mole.** One mole is 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro number). Moles = given mass / molar mass = number of particles / 6.022 x 10^23. 18 g of water is one mole.
Deep dive: structure of the atom

**Subatomic particles.** Electron (-1, negligible mass, J. J. Thomson), proton (+1, mass 1 u, Goldstein), neutron (0, mass 1 u, Chadwick). Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed a small dense positive nucleus with electrons around it; Bohr added fixed orbits (shells) K, L, M, N holding at most 2, 8, 18, 32 electrons (the outermost shell holds at most 8). **Numbers.** Atomic number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A (C-12, C-14; Cl-35, Cl-37); isobars have the same A but different Z (Ar-40, Ca-40). Valence electrons decide valency. Electronic configuration: Na (11) 2, 8, 1; Cl (17) 2, 8, 7; Ar (18) 2, 8, 8.
Deep dive: the cell

**Cell theory.** All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; cells come from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow). Cells were first seen by Robert Hooke in cork. **Parts.** Cell membrane (selective, controls entry and exit). Cell wall (cellulose; plants only). Nucleus (chromosomes, DNA, controls the cell). Cytoplasm (jelly where reactions occur). Mitochondria (powerhouse; respiration, ATP). Endoplasmic reticulum (transport, synthesis; rough has ribosomes). Golgi apparatus (packaging and secretion). Lysosomes (digestion; suicide bags). Ribosomes (protein synthesis). Plastids: chloroplasts (photosynthesis), chromoplasts, leucoplasts. Vacuoles (large in plants, small in animals). **Prokaryotes and eukaryotes.** Bacteria have no true nucleus (a nucleoid) and no membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes do. Osmosis is the movement of water through a semipermeable membrane towards the higher solute concentration; diffusion is movement from high to low concentration. **Tissues.** Plant: meristematic (growth) and permanent (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem, phloem). Animal: epithelial (covering), connective (blood, bone, cartilage, tendons), muscular (striated, smooth, cardiac) and nervous (neurons).

Laws of chemical combination. Conservation of mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction. Constant proportions: a compound always has the same elements in the same ratio by mass (water: 1 part hydrogen to 8 parts oxygen). Dalton's atomic theory: matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction. Symbols and formulae. Elements have symbols (H, O, Na from natrium, K from kalium, Fe from ferrum). Valency is the combining capacity: Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3, C 4, O 2, Cl 1. Write the symbols, put the valencies crosswise and simplify: Al and O give Al2O3. Atomic mass is in u (1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom). Molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses: H2O = 18 u, CO2 = 44 u, NaCl = 58.5 u, H2SO4 = 98 u. The mole. One mole is 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro number). Moles = given mass / molar mass = number of particles / 6.022 x 10^23. 18 g of water is one mole.

Subatomic particles. Electron (-1, negligible mass, J. J. Thomson), proton (+1, mass 1 u, Goldstein), neutron (0, mass 1 u, Chadwick). Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed a small dense positive nucleus with electrons around it; Bohr added fixed orbits (shells) K, L, M, N holding at most 2, 8, 18, 32 electrons (the outermost shell holds at most 8). Numbers. Atomic number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A (C-12, C-14; Cl-35, Cl-37); isobars have the same A but different Z (Ar-40, Ca-40). Valence electrons decide valency. Electronic configuration: Na (11) 2, 8, 1; Cl (17) 2, 8, 7; Ar (18) 2, 8, 8.

The cell

  • The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
  • Cells come from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow)
  • Cells were first seen by Robert Hooke in cork
Read the full explanation

Cell theory. All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; cells come from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow). Cells were first seen by Robert Hooke in cork. Parts. Cell membrane (selective, controls entry and exit). Cell wall (cellulose; plants only). Nucleus (chromosomes, DNA, controls the cell). Cytoplasm (jelly where reactions occur). Mitochondria (powerhouse; respiration, ATP). Endoplasmic reticulum (transport, synthesis; rough has ribosomes). Golgi apparatus (packaging and secretion). Lysosomes (digestion; suicide bags). Ribosomes (protein synthesis). Plastids: chloroplasts (photosynthesis), chromoplasts, leucoplasts. Vacuoles (large in plants, small in animals). Prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Bacteria have no true nucleus (a nucleoid) and no membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes do. Osmosis is the movement of water through a semipermeable membrane towards the higher solute concentration; diffusion is movement from high to low concentration. Tissues. Plant: meristematic (growth) and permanent (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem, phloem). Animal: epithelial (covering), connective (blood, bone, cartilage, tendons), muscular (striated, smooth, cardiac) and nervous (neurons).

yt: class 9 science structure of the atom

blocks.x: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in shells. Atomic number Z = number of protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. Electrons fill shells K, L, M, N with a maximum of 2n^2 (2, 8, 18, 32), with the outermost shell holding at most 8 electrons. Valency is the number of electrons lost, gained or shared to complete the octet. Isotopes have the same Z but different A; isobars the same A but different Z.
Deep dive: models of the atom

Thomson proposed the plum-pudding model: a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it. Rutherford bombarded a thin gold foil with alpha particles: most passed straight through (the atom is mostly empty space), a few were deflected by small angles, and very few (about 1 in 12000) bounced back (a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus). His model has a central nucleus with electrons revolving around it, but could not explain why the atom is stable. Bohr proposed that electrons revolve only in certain special orbits (shells) without radiating energy; each shell has fixed energy and is labelled K, L, M, N or n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932; Goldstein discovered the canal rays (protons) and J. J. Thomson the electron.
Deep dive: subatomic particles and electronic configuration

Electron: charge -1, mass about 1/1837 of a proton, found outside the nucleus. Proton: charge +1, mass 1 u. Neutron: no charge, mass 1 u. Atomic number Z = protons = electrons in a neutral atom; mass number A = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A - Z. The Bohr-Bury scheme: the maximum number of electrons in the nth shell is 2n^2 (K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32); the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons (2 for the first shell); electrons fill a new shell only after the previous inner shell is full. Valency: elements with 1, 2, 3 electrons in the outermost shell have valency 1, 2, 3 (lose electrons); with 5, 6, 7 electrons the valency is 3, 2, 1 (gain electrons); with 4 electrons valency 4 (share); noble gases have valency 0 as their shells are complete.
Deep dive: isotopes, isobars and atomic mass

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (hydrogen: protium 1, deuterium 2, tritium 3; chlorine-35 and chlorine-37; carbon-12 and carbon-14). They have the same chemical properties but different physical properties. Applications: uranium-235 in nuclear reactors, cobalt-60 in cancer treatment, iodine-131 for goitre, carbon-14 dating. Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers (argon-40 and calcium-40). Average atomic mass = sum of (isotope mass x abundance). For chlorine: 35 x 0.75 + 37 x 0.25 = 35.5 u. Isotones have the same number of neutrons.

blocks.x: Matter has mass and occupies space; it exists as solid, liquid and gas, made of tiny particles with spaces between them that attract each other and are always moving. Melting point of ice is 273 K, boiling point of water is 373 K; K = C + 273. Latent heat of fusion and vaporisation hide heat during change of state. Evaporation cools; humidity and wind speed affect its rate.
Deep dive: particle nature of matter

Matter is made of very small particles (the particle size is about 10^-9 m or less); a few crystals of potassium permanganate colour a whole beaker of water, showing how tiny and numerous the particles are. Particles have spaces between them (sugar dissolves in water without the level rising much), are continuously moving (diffusion of ink in water, smell of perfume spreading, faster in hot water) and attract each other (the force of attraction is strong in solids and weak in gases; an iron nail is hard to break while a gas spreads freely). Rate of diffusion is greater in gases than in liquids, and rises with temperature.
Deep dive: states of matter and changes

Solid: definite shape and volume, negligible compressibility, particles tightly packed in fixed positions. Liquid: definite volume but no definite shape, small compressibility, particles slide past each other. Gas: no definite shape or volume, highly compressible (LPG, CNG), particles far apart moving randomly at high speed. Plasma and Bose-Einstein condensate are other states. Melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes to liquid at atmospheric pressure (ice 273.15 K); boiling point is where a liquid changes to gas (water 373 K). Latent heat of fusion is the heat needed to convert 1 kg of solid to liquid at its melting point without raising temperature (ice: 3.34 x 10^5 J/kg); latent heat of vaporisation is for liquid to gas at the boiling point (water: 22.5 x 10^5 J/kg), so steam at 373 K has more energy than water at the same temperature. Sublimation: solid to gas directly (camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride, dry ice).
Deep dive: evaporation and temperature scales

Evaporation is a surface phenomenon: particles near the surface with enough kinetic energy escape. Factors raising its rate: larger surface area, higher temperature, lower humidity and higher wind speed. It causes cooling (sweating cools the body, water in an earthen pot or desert cooler stays cool, cotton clothes in summer absorb sweat). Boiling is a bulk phenomenon at a fixed temperature. Temperature conversion: K = C + 273 and C = K - 273; Fahrenheit F = 9C/5 + 32. Pressure also affects the state: increasing pressure and decreasing temperature can liquefy gases; solid CO2 is called dry ice because it sublimes on reducing pressure to 1 atm.

lessons.title: Is matter around us pure?
yt: class 9 science is matter around us pure

blocks.x: A pure substance has a single kind of particle: elements and compounds. A mixture has two or more substances in any proportion: homogeneous (solution) or heterogeneous (suspension, colloid). Concentration of a solution: mass percent = (mass of solute/mass of solution) x 100; volume percent = (volume of solute/volume of solution) x 100. Separation methods: filtration, evaporation, centrifugation, distillation, fractional distillation, chromatography, sublimation and crystallisation.
Deep dive: pure substances and mixtures

A pure substance has constant composition and properties throughout. Elements (hydrogen, iron, oxygen) cannot be broken down further by chemical means; compounds (water, sodium chloride) are formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio, with properties different from those of the elements. Mixtures are formed by physical mixing in any ratio; components keep their properties and can be separated by physical methods. Homogeneous mixtures (solutions, alloys, air) have uniform composition; heterogeneous mixtures (sand and water, oil and water, chalk powder in water) do not.
Deep dive: solutions, suspensions and colloids

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent: particles are below 1 nm, the path of light is not visible, it is stable and passes through filter paper (sugar in water). A suspension is heterogeneous: particles larger than 100 nm are visible, scatter light, settle on standing and can be filtered (chalk in water). A colloid has particles of size 1 to 100 nm; it appears homogeneous but scatters light (Tyndall effect), is stable, does not settle and cannot be filtered (milk, fog, smoke, ink). Concentration of a solution = amount of solute in a given amount of solution: mass by mass percentage = (mass of solute/mass of solution) x 100; mass by volume percent; volume by volume percent. A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature; solubility generally rises with temperature.
Deep dive: separation techniques and changes

Filtration: insoluble solid from liquid. Evaporation: a soluble solid from its solution (salt from sea water). Centrifugation: cream from milk. Separating funnel: two immiscible liquids (oil and water). Sublimation: ammonium chloride from salt. Chromatography: dyes in ink; Rf = distance by solute/distance by solvent. Distillation: miscible liquids with boiling points differing by more than 25 K (acetone and water); fractional distillation for closer boiling points (petroleum fractions, gases of air). Crystallisation: purifying copper sulphate or alum from impure samples. A physical change affects the form but not the composition (melting, freezing); a chemical change forms new substances (burning, rusting, digestion). Air is a mixture: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide.
Hindi saransh
Mixture = 2+ substances. Solution = homogeneous. Concentration = solute/solution x 100.
Physical change: no new substance. Chemical change: a new substance forms.

qa.q: What is a pure substance?
qa.a: A substance made of only one kind of particle.

qa.q: What is a mixture?
qa.a: A substance made of two or more pure substances mixed in any proportion.

qa.q: What is an element?
qa.a: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances.

qa.q: What is a compound?
qa.a: A pure substance of two or more elements combined chemically in a fixed ratio.

qa.q: What is a solution?
qa.a: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.

qa.q: What is a solute?
qa.a: The component present in the smaller amount in a solution.

qa.q: What is a solvent?
qa.a: The component present in the larger amount in a solution.

qa.q: What is a suspension?
qa.a: A heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles settle on standing.

qa.q: What is a colloid?
qa.a: A heterogeneous-looking mixture with particles of 1 to 100 nm that scatter light.

qa.q: What is the Tyndall effect?
qa.a: The scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles.

qa.q: Give an example of a colloid.
Give an example of a suspension.
qa.a: Chalk powder in water or muddy water.

qa.q: What is an alloy?
qa.a: A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals.

qa.q: What is a saturated solution?
qa.a: A solution that cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature.

qa.q: What is solubility?
qa.a: The amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to give a saturated solution.

qa.q: What is filtration used for?
qa.a: To separate an insoluble solid from a liquid.

qa.q: What is distillation used for?
qa.a: To separate miscible liquids with different boiling points.

qa.q: What is fractional distillation?
qa.a: Distillation used for liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 K.

qa.q: What is chromatography used for?
qa.a: To separate mixtures of dyes or pigments.

qa.q: What is crystallisation?
qa.a: A method of purifying a solid by forming its crystals from solution.

qa.q: What is a physical change?
qa.a: A change in which no new substance is formed.

qa.q: What is a chemical change?
qa.a: A change in which a new substance is formed.

Visual lesson

Is matter around us pure?

A pure substance has a single kind of particle: elements and compounds

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Pure substances and mixtures›3Solutions, suspensions and…›4Separation techniques and…
Solutionparticles < 1 nm
Colloidparticles 1 to 100 nm
Suspensionparticles > 100 nm
🔑

Big idea

  • A pure substance has a single kind of particle: elements and compounds
  • A mixture has two or more substances in any proportion: homogeneous (solution) or heterogeneous (suspension, colloid)
  • Concentration of a solution: mass percent = (mass of solute/mass of solution) x 100
  • Volume percent = (volume of solute/volume of solution) x 100
Read the full explanation

A pure substance has a single kind of particle: elements and compounds. A mixture has two or more substances in any proportion: homogeneous (solution) or heterogeneous (suspension, colloid). Concentration of a solution: mass percent = (mass of solute/mass of solution) x 100; volume percent = (volume of solute/volume of solution) x 100. Separation methods: filtration, evaporation, centrifugation, distillation, fractional distillation, chromatography, sublimation and crystallisation.

🧪

Pure substances and mixtures

  • A pure substance has constant composition and properties throughout
  • Elements (hydrogen, iron, oxygen) cannot be broken down further by chemical means
  • Compounds (water, sodium chloride) are formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio, with properties different from…
  • Mixtures are formed by physical mixing in any ratio
Read the full explanation

A pure substance has constant composition and properties throughout. Elements (hydrogen, iron, oxygen) cannot be broken down further by chemical means; compounds (water, sodium chloride) are formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio, with properties different from those of the elements. Mixtures are formed by physical mixing in any ratio; components keep their properties and can be separated by physical methods. Homogeneous mixtures (solutions, alloys, air) have uniform composition; heterogeneous mixtures (sand and water, oil and water, chalk powder in water) do not.

🧪

Solutions, suspensions and colloids

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent: particles are below 1 nm, the path of light is not visible, it is stable and passes…
  • A suspension is heterogeneous: particles larger than 100 nm are visible, scatter light, settle on standing and can be filtered (chalk in water)
  • A colloid has particles of size 1 to 100 nm
  • It appears homogeneous but scatters light (Tyndall effect), is stable, does not settle and cannot be filtered (milk, fog, smoke, ink)
Read the full explanation

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent: particles are below 1 nm, the path of light is not visible, it is stable and passes through filter paper (sugar in water). A suspension is heterogeneous: particles larger than 100 nm are visible, scatter light, settle on standing and can be filtered (chalk in water). A colloid has particles of size 1 to 100 nm; it appears homogeneous but scatters light (Tyndall effect), is stable, does not settle and cannot be filtered (milk, fog, smoke, ink). Concentration of a solution = amount of solute in a given amount of solution: mass by mass percentage = (mass of solute/mass of solution) x 100; mass by volume percent; volume by volume percent. A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature; solubility generally rises with temperature.

🧪

Separation techniques and changes

  • Filtration: insoluble solid from liquid
  • Evaporation: a soluble solid from its solution (salt from sea water)
  • Centrifugation: cream from milk
  • Separating funnel: two immiscible liquids (oil and water)
Read the full explanation

Filtration: insoluble solid from liquid. Evaporation: a soluble solid from its solution (salt from sea water). Centrifugation: cream from milk. Separating funnel: two immiscible liquids (oil and water). Sublimation: ammonium chloride from salt. Chromatography: dyes in ink; Rf = distance by solute/distance by solvent. Distillation: miscible liquids with boiling points differing by more than 25 K (acetone and water); fractional distillation for closer boiling points (petroleum fractions, gases of air). Crystallisation: purifying copper sulphate or alum from impure samples. A physical change affects the form but not the composition (melting, freezing); a chemical change forms new substances (burning, rusting, digestion). Air is a mixture: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Atoms and Molecules

blocks.x: Matter is made of atoms and molecules. Antoine Lavoisier gave the law of conservation of mass and Joseph Proust gave the law of constant proportions. Dalton's atomic theory explained these laws. Atoms combine in fixed ratios decided by valency to form molecules and compounds. The atomic mass unit u is 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. A mole is 6.022 × 10^23 particles (the Avogadro constant); the mass of one mole of a substance in grams equals its atomic or molecular mass in u. Formulae are written by crossing over valencies.
Deep dive: laws of chemical combination

In a closed system the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products (Lavoisier). A given compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass (Proust): water has H:O = 1:8 and CO2 has C:O = 3:8 by mass.
Deep dive: atoms, molecules and ions

Dalton's theory: matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios. Molecules of elements are O2, N2, O3, P4, S8; molecules of compounds are H2O, CO2. Ions are charged atoms or groups.
Deep dive: writing formulae
Write symbols with valencies, cross them over and reduce to simplest ratio: Mg (2) and Cl (1) give MgCl2; Al (3) and O (2) give Al2O3; Ca (2) and (OH) (1) give Ca(OH)2.
Deep dive: mole concept

Atomic masses: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40. Molecular mass of H2O is 18 u, of CO2 is 44 u. One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles and has mass equal to its molar mass in grams. n = m/M and N = n × NA.

Visual lesson

Atoms and Molecules

Matter is made of atoms and molecules

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Laws of chemical combination›3Atoms, molecules and ions›4Writing formulae›5Mole concept
🔑

Big idea

  • Matter is made of atoms and molecules
  • Antoine Lavoisier gave the law of conservation of mass and Joseph Proust gave the law of constant proportions
  • Dalton's atomic theory explained these laws
  • Atoms combine in fixed ratios decided by valency to form molecules and compounds
Read the full explanation

Matter is made of atoms and molecules. Antoine Lavoisier gave the law of conservation of mass and Joseph Proust gave the law of constant proportions. Dalton's atomic theory explained these laws. Atoms combine in fixed ratios decided by valency to form molecules and compounds. The atomic mass unit u is 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. A mole is 6.022 × 10^23 particles (the Avogadro constant); the mass of one mole of a substance in grams equals its atomic or molecular mass in u. Formulae are written by crossing over valencies.

⚖️

Laws of chemical combination

  • In a closed system the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products (Lavoisier)
  • A given compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass (Proust): water has H:O = 1:8 and CO2 has C:O = 3:8 by mass
⚛️

Atoms, molecules and ions

  • Dalton's theory: matter consists of indivisible atoms
  • Atoms of an element are identical
  • Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios
  • Molecules of elements are O2, N2, O3, P4, S8
Read the full explanation

Dalton's theory: matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios. Molecules of elements are O2, N2, O3, P4, S8; molecules of compounds are H2O, CO2. Ions are charged atoms or groups.

🧮

Writing formulae

  • Write symbols with valencies, cross them over and reduce to simplest ratio: Mg (2) and Cl (1) give MgCl2
  • Al (3) and O (2) give Al2O3
  • Ca (2) and (OH) (1) give Ca(OH)2
📘

Mole concept

  • Atomic masses: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40
  • Molecular mass of H2O is 18 u, of CO2 is 44 u
  • One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles and has mass equal to its molar mass in grams
  • N = m/M and N = n × NA
🧮

Formula tiles

Number of molesn = m / Mm mass, M molar mass
Number of particlesN = n × 6.022 × 10^23Avogadro
Molecular masssum of atomic massesu
WaterH2O = 18 u
Carbon dioxideCO2 = 44 u
🎯 Remember 1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles = molar mass in grams.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

पदार्थ परमाणुओं और अणुओं से बना है। द्रव्यमान संरक्षण का नियम लवोज़ियर ने और स्थिर अनुपात का नियम प्राउस्ट ने दिया। एक मोल में 6.022 × 10^23 कण होते हैं।

lessons.title: Diversity in Living Organisms
yt: class 9 science diversity in living organisms

blocks.x: Living organisms are classified on the basis of cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition and reproduction. R. H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Plants are divided into Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms. Animals are divided into phyla from Porifera to Chordata. Carolus Linnaeus gave the binomial system of naming. The hierarchy is kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus and species.
Deep dive: need for classification

Classification makes the study of the huge diversity of life easier. Organisms are grouped by characteristics: cell type (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular or multicellular), mode of nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic) and reproduction. Characteristics that appeared earlier in evolution are more basic.
Deep dive: five kingdoms

Monera: prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria). Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Euglena). Fungi: heterotrophic, chitin cell wall (yeast, mushroom). Plantae: multicellular autotrophs with cell walls. Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls.
Deep dive: plant kingdom
Thallophyta (algae), Bryophyta (moss), Pteridophyta (ferns), Gymnosperms (pine, Cycas) and Angiosperms (flowering plants, monocots and dicots).
Deep dive: animal kingdom

Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Protochordata and Vertebrata. Vertebrates: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. Nomenclature: Genus species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
Hindi saransh
जीवों को कोशिका संरचना, शारीरिक संगठन, पोषण और प्रजनन के आधार पर वर्गीकृत किया जाता है। व्हिटेकर ने पाँच जगत बताए: मोनेरा, प्रोटिस्टा, कवक, पादप और जन्तु।
Kingdom > Phylum > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species.

  • Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia
  • Plants are divided into Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms
  • Animals are divided into phyla from Porifera to Chordata
Read the full explanation

Living organisms are classified on the basis of cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition and reproduction. R. H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Plants are divided into Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms. Animals are divided into phyla from Porifera to Chordata. Carolus Linnaeus gave the binomial system of naming. The hierarchy is kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus and species.

📌

Need for classification

  • Classification makes the study of the huge diversity of life easier
  • Organisms are grouped by characteristics: cell type (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular or multicellular), mode of nutrition…
  • Characteristics that appeared earlier in evolution are more basic
🧠

Five kingdoms

  • Monera: prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria)
  • Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Euglena)
  • Fungi: heterotrophic, chitin cell wall (yeast, mushroom)
  • Plantae: multicellular autotrophs with cell walls
Read the full explanation

Monera: prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria). Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Euglena). Fungi: heterotrophic, chitin cell wall (yeast, mushroom). Plantae: multicellular autotrophs with cell walls. Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls.

🧬

Plant kingdom

  • Thallophyta (algae), Bryophyta (moss), Pteridophyta (ferns), Gymnosperms (pine, Cycas) and Angiosperms (flowering plants, monocots and dicots)
🧬

Animal kingdom

  • Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Protochordata and Vertebrata
  • Vertebrates: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia
  • Nomenclature: Genus species, e.g. Homo sapiens

yt: class 9 science why do we fall ill

blocks.x: Health is a state of physical, mental and social well-being. Diseases may be acute or chronic and may be infectious (caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa or worms) or non-infectious. Immediate causes are the pathogens, while contributory causes include poor hygiene, poverty and poor nutrition. Infectious diseases spread through air, water, vectors and contact. Treatment kills the cause and relieves symptoms. Prevention is general (clean water, food, vector control) and specific (vaccination). Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine.
Deep dive: health and disease

Health depends on physical, mental and social well-being, which in turn depend on clean surroundings, food, income and social equality. Disease is a disturbance of body functions. Acute diseases (cold, cough) are short-lived; chronic diseases (TB, elephantiasis) are long-lasting and affect general health.
Deep dive: causes and spread

Infectious diseases have immediate causes (pathogens) and contributory causes (poverty, bad hygiene). Pathogens spread through air (cold, TB), water (cholera, typhoid), vectors (mosquitoes for malaria and dengue) and contact (AIDS). Viruses cause cold, dengue, AIDS and polio; bacteria cause typhoid, cholera and TB; fungi cause ringworm; protozoa cause malaria and kala-azar; worms cause elephantiasis.
Deep dive: treatment and prevention

Treatment relieves symptoms and kills the cause. Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses. Prevention includes general measures (clean water and surroundings, nutrition) and specific measures (vaccination). Jenner introduced smallpox vaccination in 1796; vaccines exist for DPT, polio, measles, BCG, hepatitis and others.
Deep dive: public health
Community health is protected by sanitation, safe water, vector control and immunisation programmes. Early diagnosis and good nutrition help the immune system resist infection.

What is health?
qa.a: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being.

qa.q: What is disease?
qa.a: A condition in which normal functioning of the body is disturbed.

qa.q: What are acute diseases?
qa.a: Diseases lasting for a short time, like common cold.

qa.q: What are chronic diseases?
qa.a: Diseases lasting a long time, like tuberculosis and elephantiasis.

qa.q: Why do chronic diseases affect health more?
qa.a: They drain the body over a long period.

qa.q: Name the immediate cause of infectious disease.
qa.a: A pathogen such as virus or bacteria.

qa.q: What are contributory causes?
qa.a: Poverty, poor hygiene, malnutrition and overcrowding that make people susceptible.

qa.q: What are non-infectious diseases?
qa.a: Diseases not spread from person to person, like cancer or hypertension.

qa.q: What are infectious diseases?
qa.a: Diseases caused by organisms that spread from one person to another.

qa.q: Name the pathogens causing infectious diseases.
qa.a: Viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa and worms.

qa.q: Name diseases caused by viruses.
qa.a: Common cold, influenza, dengue, AIDS, polio and hepatitis.

qa.q: Name diseases caused by bacteria.
qa.a: Typhoid, cholera, tuberculosis, anthrax and tetanus.

lessons.title: Natural Resources

blocks.x: Natural resources include air, water and soil. The atmosphere is a blanket of air that regulates temperature and protects life; it contains nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), carbon dioxide (0.03%) and other gases. The greenhouse effect warms the Earth. The ozone layer shields us from UV rays. Water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen move through biogeochemical cycles between living and non-living components. Pollution (acid rain, smog, water and soil pollution) harms these resources. Soil forms by weathering of rocks and is affected by erosion.
Deep dive: air

The atmosphere is mainly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. It regulates temperature, supports respiration and photosynthesis and shields us from UV rays. The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm, but excess CO2 and methane cause global warming. Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs UV; CFCs damage it. Burning fuels releases SO2 and nitrogen oxides, causing acid rain and smog.
Deep dive: water

About 71% of the Earth is covered with water. The water cycle includes evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation. Groundwater, rivers, lakes and glaciers are sources of fresh water. Sewage, industrial waste and chemicals pollute water.
Deep dive: soil
Soil forms by weathering of rocks aided by sun, wind, water and organisms; humus makes it fertile. Soil erosion is checked by trees and terrace farming.
Deep dive: biogeochemical cycles

Nitrogen is fixed by Rhizobium and lightning, converted by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter to nitrate, absorbed by plants, and returned to the air by denitrification (Pseudomonas). Carbon moves by photosynthesis, respiration, combustion and decay. Oxygen moves between photosynthesis and respiration.

Read the full explanation

Natural resources include air, water and soil. The atmosphere is a blanket of air that regulates temperature and protects life; it contains nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), carbon dioxide (0.03%) and other gases. The greenhouse effect warms the Earth. The ozone layer shields us from UV rays. Water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen move through biogeochemical cycles between living and non-living components. Pollution (acid rain, smog, water and soil pollution) harms these resources. Soil forms by weathering of rocks and is affected by erosion.

📌

Air

  • The atmosphere is mainly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour
  • It regulates temperature, supports respiration and photosynthesis and shields us from UV rays
  • The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm, but excess CO2 and methane cause global warming
  • Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs UV
Read the full explanation

The atmosphere is mainly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. It regulates temperature, supports respiration and photosynthesis and shields us from UV rays. The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm, but excess CO2 and methane cause global warming. Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs UV; CFCs damage it. Burning fuels releases SO2 and nitrogen oxides, causing acid rain and smog.

🧠

Water

  • About 71% of the Earth is covered with water
  • The water cycle includes evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation
  • Groundwater, rivers, lakes and glaciers are sources of fresh water
  • Sewage, industrial waste and chemicals pollute water
🗺️

Soil

  • Soil forms by weathering of rocks aided by sun, wind, water and organisms
  • Humus makes it fertile
  • Soil erosion is checked by trees and terrace farming
🔄

Biogeochemical cycles

  • Nitrogen is fixed by Rhizobium and lightning, converted by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter to nitrate, absorbed by plants, and returned to the air by…
  • Carbon moves by photosynthesis, respiration, combustion and decay
  • Oxygen moves between photosynthesis and respiration

lessons.title: The Fundamental Unit of Life (Cell)
yt: class 9 science the fundamental unit of life (cell)

blocks.x: The cell is the structural and functional unit of life. Robert Hooke first saw cells in cork in 1665. Cells may be prokaryotic (no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles) or eukaryotic (true nucleus and organelles). A cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and organelles such as the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, mitochondria, plastids and vacuoles. Plant cells also have a cell wall. The plasma membrane is selectively permeable and controls diffusion and osmosis.
Deep dive: discovery and cell theory

Robert Hooke (1665) examined thin slices of cork under a self-designed microscope and named the box-like compartments cells. Leeuwenhoek (1674) saw free-living cells in pond water. Robert Brown (1831) discovered the nucleus, and Purkinje (1839) named the cell substance protoplasm. Schleiden and Schwann presented the cell theory in 1838-39 and Virchow (1855) added that new cells come from pre-existing cells.
Deep dive: plasma membrane and transport

The plasma membrane, made of lipids and proteins, is selectively permeable. Small molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion. Water moves by osmosis. In a hypotonic medium the cell gains water, in a hypertonic medium it loses water, and in an isotonic medium there is no net movement. Plant cells survive hypotonic media because of the cell wall. Amoeba takes in food by endocytosis.
Deep dive: organelles

The nucleus has a double membrane with pores, chromatin, and a nucleolus. Rough ER carries ribosomes and makes proteins, while smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials. Lysosomes digest waste and are called suicide bags. Mitochondria produce ATP and have their own DNA. Plastids include chloroplasts with chlorophyll, chromoplasts with pigments and leucoplasts for storage. Plant cells have a large central vacuole.
Deep dive: prokaryotes versus eukaryotes

Prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae) have a nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles and small ribosomes. Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

Visual lesson

The Fundamental Unit of Life (Cell)

The cell is the structural and functional unit of life

Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Discovery and cell theory›3Plasma membrane and…›4Organelles›5Prokaryotes versus…
🔑

Big idea

  • The cell is the structural and functional unit of life
  • Robert Hooke first saw cells in cork in 1665
  • Cells may be prokaryotic (no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles) or eukaryotic (true nucleus and organelles)
  • A cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and organelles such as the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, mitochondria, plastids…
Read the full explanation

The cell is the structural and functional unit of life. Robert Hooke first saw cells in cork in 1665. Cells may be prokaryotic (no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles) or eukaryotic (true nucleus and organelles). A cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and organelles such as the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, mitochondria, plastids and vacuoles. Plant cells also have a cell wall. The plasma membrane is selectively permeable and controls diffusion and osmosis.

🧬

Discovery and cell theory

  • Robert Hooke (1665) examined thin slices of cork under a self-designed microscope and named the box-like compartments cells
  • Leeuwenhoek (1674) saw free-living cells in pond water
  • Robert Brown (1831) discovered the nucleus, and Purkinje (1839) named the cell substance protoplasm
  • Schleiden and Schwann presented the cell theory in 1838-39 and Virchow (1855) added that new cells come from pre-existing cells
Read the full explanation

Robert Hooke (1665) examined thin slices of cork under a self-designed microscope and named the box-like compartments cells. Leeuwenhoek (1674) saw free-living cells in pond water. Robert Brown (1831) discovered the nucleus, and Purkinje (1839) named the cell substance protoplasm. Schleiden and Schwann presented the cell theory in 1838-39 and Virchow (1855) added that new cells come from pre-existing cells.

🧠

Plasma membrane and transport

  • The plasma membrane, made of lipids and proteins, is selectively permeable
  • Small molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion
  • Water moves by osmosis
  • In a hypotonic medium the cell gains water, in a hypertonic medium it loses water, and in an isotonic medium there is no net movement
Read the full explanation

The plasma membrane, made of lipids and proteins, is selectively permeable. Small molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion. Water moves by osmosis. In a hypotonic medium the cell gains water, in a hypertonic medium it loses water, and in an isotonic medium there is no net movement. Plant cells survive hypotonic media because of the cell wall. Amoeba takes in food by endocytosis.

🧬

Organelles

  • The nucleus has a double membrane with pores, chromatin, and a nucleolus
  • Rough ER carries ribosomes and makes proteins, while smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies
  • The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials
  • Lysosomes digest waste and are called suicide bags
Read the full explanation

The nucleus has a double membrane with pores, chromatin, and a nucleolus. Rough ER carries ribosomes and makes proteins, while smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials. Lysosomes digest waste and are called suicide bags. Mitochondria produce ATP and have their own DNA. Plastids include chloroplasts with chlorophyll, chromoplasts with pigments and leucoplasts for storage. Plant cells have a large central vacuole.

🔬

Prokaryotes versus eukaryotes

  • Prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae) have a nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles and small ribosomes
  • Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles

lessons.title: Tissues: Plant Tissues

blocks.x: A tissue is a group of cells with similar structure and function. Plant tissues are of two main types. Meristematic tissue (apical, lateral and intercalary) has dividing cells and causes growth. Permanent tissue is formed when cells stop dividing and differentiate; it may be simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, epidermis, cork) or complex (xylem and phloem). Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food.
Deep dive: meristematic tissue

Meristematic cells divide continuously. Apical meristem lengthens roots and shoots, lateral meristem (cambium) thickens the stem and intercalary meristem at the base of leaves and internodes helps regrowth of grasses. Cells are small, thin-walled, with dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei.
Deep dive: simple permanent tissues

Parenchyma stores food, and chlorenchyma and aerenchyma are its special forms. Collenchyma gives flexibility with pectin thickening. Sclerenchyma is dead with lignin and gives hardness, for example the coconut husk. Epidermis protects; stomata with guard cells allow gas exchange; the cuticle reduces water loss. Cork replaces epidermis in older stems.
Deep dive: complex tissues

Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, parenchyma and fibres; it carries water and minerals upward. Phloem consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres and carries food (translocation). Xylem is mainly dead, phloem mainly living.

qa.a: At the base of leaves or internodes, as in grasses.

qa.q: What is differentiation?
qa.a: Taking up of a permanent shape, size and function by cells.

qa.q: What kind of cells do meristematic tissues have?
qa.a: Thin-walled cells with dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei, with little or no vacuole.

qa.q: What are the two types of permanent tissues?
What is parenchyma?
qa.a: Simple tissue of loosely packed, thin-walled living cells.

qa.q: What is the function of parenchyma?
What is chlorenchyma?
qa.a: Parenchyma with chloroplasts that carries out photosynthesis.

qa.q: What is aerenchyma?
qa.a: Parenchyma with large air cavities that helps aquatic plants float.

qa.q: What is collenchyma?
qa.a: Living tissue with cells thickened at the corners with pectin.

qa.q: What is the function of collenchyma?
qa.a: Provides flexibility and mechanical support, as in leaf stalks.

qa.q: What is sclerenchyma?
qa.a: Dead tissue with thick, lignified walls.

qa.q: What is the function of sclerenchyma?
qa.a: Makes plant hard and stiff, as in husk of coconut.

qa.q: What substance makes sclerenchyma walls hard?
What is epidermis?
qa.a: The outermost protective layer of cells in plants.

qa.q: What is the function of stomata?
What are guard cells?
qa.a: Bean-shaped cells that open and close the stomata.

qa.q: What is cuticle?
qa.a: A waxy water-resistant layer on the epidermis.

qa.q: What is cork?
qa.a: Dead protective tissue of the bark with suberin in walls.

qa.q: Why is cork impervious to gases and water?
qa.a: Suberin in the cell walls makes it so.

qa.q: What are complex tissues?
qa.a: Tissues made of more than one type of cells working together.

qa.q: Name the two complex tissues.
What are the components of xylem?
qa.a: Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

qa.q: Which xylem components are dead?
What are the components of phloem?
qa.a: Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.

qa.q: What is the function of companion cells?
qa.a: They help sieve tubes in conduction of food.

qa.q: What is translocation?
qa.a: Transport of food from leaves to other parts through phloem.

qa.q: Which phloem component is dead?
What is the role of root hairs?
qa.a: To absorb water and minerals from the soil.

qa.q: What is the epidermis like in desert plants?
qa.a: It has a thick waxy coating to reduce water loss.

qa.q: Which tissue is responsible for secondary growth?

Visual lesson

Tissues: Plant Tissues

A tissue is a group of cells with similar structure and function

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Meristematic tissue›3Simple permanent tissues›4Complex tissues
🔑

Big idea

  • A tissue is a group of cells with similar structure and function
  • Plant tissues are of two main types
  • Meristematic tissue (apical, lateral and intercalary) has dividing cells and causes growth
  • Permanent tissue is formed when cells stop dividing and differentiate
Read the full explanation

A tissue is a group of cells with similar structure and function. Plant tissues are of two main types. Meristematic tissue (apical, lateral and intercalary) has dividing cells and causes growth. Permanent tissue is formed when cells stop dividing and differentiate; it may be simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, epidermis, cork) or complex (xylem and phloem). Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food.

🧬

Meristematic tissue

  • Meristematic cells divide continuously
  • Apical meristem lengthens roots and shoots, lateral meristem (cambium) thickens the stem and intercalary meristem at the base of leaves and…
  • Cells are small, thin-walled, with dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei
🧬

Simple permanent tissues

  • Parenchyma stores food, and chlorenchyma and aerenchyma are its special forms
  • Collenchyma gives flexibility with pectin thickening
  • Sclerenchyma is dead with lignin and gives hardness, for example the coconut husk
  • Epidermis protects
Read the full explanation

Parenchyma stores food, and chlorenchyma and aerenchyma are its special forms. Collenchyma gives flexibility with pectin thickening. Sclerenchyma is dead with lignin and gives hardness, for example the coconut husk. Epidermis protects; stomata with guard cells allow gas exchange; the cuticle reduces water loss. Cork replaces epidermis in older stems.

🧬

Complex tissues

  • Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, parenchyma and fibres
  • It carries water and minerals upward
  • Phloem consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres and carries food (translocation)
  • Xylem is mainly dead, phloem mainly living
🧮

lessons.title: Tissues: Animal Tissues

blocks.x: Animal tissues are of four types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous. Epithelial tissue covers and lines organs. Connective tissue binds and supports and includes blood, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, areolar and adipose tissue. Muscular tissue (striated, smooth and cardiac) brings about movement. Nervous tissue, made of neurons, receives and transmits impulses.
Deep dive: epithelial tissue

Epithelia protect and separate. Squamous epithelium lines the mouth and oesophagus; stratified squamous forms the skin. Cuboidal epithelium forms kidney tubules and glands; columnar lines the intestine; ciliated columnar lines the trachea and helps move mucus. Glandular epithelium secretes enzymes and hormones.
Deep dive: connective tissue

Blood has plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets. Bone has a hard matrix rich in calcium and phosphorus. Cartilage smooths joints. Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone. Areolar tissue fills spaces, and adipose tissue stores fat and insulates.
Deep dive: muscular and nervous tissue

Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated with multinucleate cells. Smooth muscle is involuntary and spindle-shaped. Cardiac muscle is involuntary, branched and striated. A neuron has a cell body, dendrites and an axon; impulses travel from dendrites to cell body to axon.

How many types of animal tissues are there?
qa.a: Four: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

qa.q: What is epithelial tissue?
qa.a: Tissue that covers or lines the surfaces of organs and body cavities.

qa.q: How are epithelial cells arranged?
qa.a: Tightly packed with very little intercellular space.

qa.q: What is squamous epithelium?
qa.a: Epithelium of flat cells, as in the skin and lining of mouth and oesophagus.

qa.q: Where is stratified squamous epithelium found?
qa.a: In the skin, to prevent wear and tear.

qa.q: What is cuboidal epithelium?
qa.a: Epithelium of cube-shaped cells, as in kidney tubules and salivary gland ducts.

qa.q: What is columnar epithelium?
qa.a: Epithelium of tall pillar-like cells, as in the lining of the intestine.

qa.q: What is ciliated epithelium?
qa.a: Columnar epithelium with cilia, as in the respiratory tract.

qa.q: What is glandular epithelium?
What is connective tissue?
qa.a: Tissue with scattered cells in a matrix that binds and supports organs.

qa.q: Name the connective tissues.
qa.a: Blood, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, areolar tissue and adipose tissue.

qa.q: What is the matrix of blood called?
What are the components of blood?
qa.a: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

qa.q: What does blood transport?
qa.a: Gases, digested food, hormones and wastes.

qa.q: What is the matrix of bone made of?
What is the function of bone?
qa.a: Supports the body, protects organs and anchors muscles.

qa.q: What is cartilage?
qa.a: Connective tissue with widely spaced cells and a solid matrix.

qa.q: Where is cartilage found?
qa.a: In the nose, ear, trachea, larynx and at joints.

qa.q: What is a ligament?
qa.a: Strong flexible tissue connecting bone to bone.

qa.q: What is a tendon?
qa.a: Fibrous tissue connecting muscle to bone.

qa.q: What is areolar tissue?
qa.a: Loose connective tissue that fills spaces, supports organs and helps repair tissues.

qa.q: What is adipose tissue?
qa.a: Fat-storing tissue below the skin and around organs.

qa.q: What are the functions of adipose tissue?
qa.a: Stores fat and acts as an insulator.

qa.q: What is muscular tissue?
qa.a: Tissue made of elongated cells (muscle fibres) that cause movement.

qa.q: What are the three types of muscle?
What is a voluntary muscle?
qa.a: A muscle that moves under our control, such as skeletal muscle.

qa.q: What are involuntary muscles?
qa.a: Muscles that work without our control, such as smooth and cardiac muscles.

qa.q: Describe skeletal muscle cells.
qa.a: Long, cylindrical, unbranched and multinucleate with stripes.

qa.q: Describe smooth muscle cells.
Describe cardiac muscle cells.
qa.a: Cylindrical, branched, uninucleate, striated and involuntary.

qa.q: Where are smooth muscles found?
qa.a: In the iris, urinary bladder, blood vessels, alimentary canal and ureters.

qa.q: What is a neuron?
qa.a: The structural and functional unit of nervous tissue.

qa.q: What are the parts of a neuron?
What does the axon do?
qa.a: Carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body.

qa.q: What do dendrites do?
qa.a: Receive impulses and carry them to the cell body.

qa.q: What is a nerve impulse?
Which is the longest cell in the human body?
What is an organ?
qa.a: A group of tissues working together for a specific function.

qa.q: What is an organ system?
qa.a: A group of organs working together.

Visual lesson

Tissues: Animal Tissues

Animal tissues are of four types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous

minutes
