Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Epithelial tissue›3Connective tissue›4Muscular and nervous tissue
🔑

Big idea

  • Animal tissues are of four types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous
  • Epithelial tissue covers and lines organs
  • Connective tissue binds and supports and includes blood, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, areolar and adipose tissue
  • Muscular tissue (striated, smooth and cardiac) brings about movement
Read the full explanation

Animal tissues are of four types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous. Epithelial tissue covers and lines organs. Connective tissue binds and supports and includes blood, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, areolar and adipose tissue. Muscular tissue (striated, smooth and cardiac) brings about movement. Nervous tissue, made of neurons, receives and transmits impulses.

🧬

Epithelial tissue

  • Epithelia protect and separate
  • Squamous epithelium lines the mouth and oesophagus
  • Stratified squamous forms the skin
  • Cuboidal epithelium forms kidney tubules and glands
Read the full explanation

Epithelia protect and separate. Squamous epithelium lines the mouth and oesophagus; stratified squamous forms the skin. Cuboidal epithelium forms kidney tubules and glands; columnar lines the intestine; ciliated columnar lines the trachea and helps move mucus. Glandular epithelium secretes enzymes and hormones.

🧬

Connective tissue

  • Blood has plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets
  • Bone has a hard matrix rich in calcium and phosphorus
  • Cartilage smooths joints
  • Ligaments join bone to bone
Read the full explanation

Blood has plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets. Bone has a hard matrix rich in calcium and phosphorus. Cartilage smooths joints. Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone. Areolar tissue fills spaces, and adipose tissue stores fat and insulates.

🧬

Muscular and nervous tissue

  • Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated with multinucleate cells
  • Smooth muscle is involuntary and spindle-shaped
  • Cardiac muscle is involuntary, branched and striated
  • A neuron has a cell body, dendrites and an axon
Read the full explanation

Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated with multinucleate cells. Smooth muscle is involuntary and spindle-shaped. Cardiac muscle is involuntary, branched and striated. A neuron has a cell body, dendrites and an axon; impulses travel from dendrites to cell body to axon.

🧮

lessons.title: Improvement in Food Resources: Crop Production
yt: class 9 science improvement in food resources: crop production

blocks.x: Improvement in crop yield involves crop variety improvement, crop production management and crop protection. Crops are grown in kharif (June to October) and rabi (November to April) seasons. Plants need 16 nutrients, of which 13 come from soil. Manure and fertilisers supply nutrients. Irrigation, cropping patterns (mixed cropping, inter-cropping, crop rotation), weed and pest control and safe storage help increase production.
Deep dive: crop variety and nutrients

Variety improvement uses hybridisation (intervarietal, interspecific, intergeneric) and genetic modification to get higher yield, better quality, resistance and adaptability. Plants need 16 nutrients: carbon and oxygen from air, hydrogen from water, and 13 from soil; six are macronutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) and seven are micronutrients (Fe, Mn, B, Zn, Cu, Mo, Cl).
Deep dive: manure and fertilisers

Manure, compost, vermicompost and green manure supply organic matter and nutrients and improve soil structure. Fertilisers give nutrients quickly but harm soil and water if overused. Organic farming reduces chemical use.
Deep dive: cropping systems and irrigation
Mixed cropping lowers risk; inter-cropping reduces pest spread; crop rotation maintains fertility. Irrigation comes from wells, canals, rivers and tanks.
Deep dive: protection and storage

Weeds like Xanthium and Parthenium compete with crops. Pests attack by cutting, sucking and boring. Pesticides and herbicides must be used with care. Grain storage losses come from insects, rodents, fungi, moisture and temperature; cleaning, drying and fumigation protect stored grain.

Why is crop improvement required?
qa.a: To feed a growing population from limited land.

qa.q: What is the Green Revolution?
qa.a: The large increase in food-grain production, especially wheat and rice, through high-yielding varieties and better inputs.

qa.q: What are the main activities in improvement of crop yield?
qa.a: Crop variety improvement, crop production improvement and crop protection management.

qa.q: What are kharif crops?
qa.a: Crops grown in the rainy season from June to October.

qa.q: Name some kharif crops.
qa.a: Paddy, soybean, pigeon pea, maize, cotton, green gram and black gram.

qa.q: What are rabi crops?
qa.a: Crops grown in winter from November to April.

qa.q: Name some rabi crops.
qa.a: Wheat, gram, peas, mustard and linseed.

qa.q: What is hybridisation?
Name three types of hybridisation.
What is a genetically modified crop?
qa.a: A crop in which a gene from another organism has been introduced.

qa.q: What are the desired traits in variety improvement?
qa.a: Higher yield, improved quality, biotic and abiotic resistance, change in maturity duration, wider adaptability and desirable agronomic traits.

qa.q: What is meant by agronomic traits?
qa.a: Traits such as tallness in fodder crops or dwarfness in cereals.

qa.q: How many nutrients do plants need?
From where do plants get carbon and oxygen?
From where do plants get hydrogen?
How many nutrients come from the soil?
What are macronutrients?
qa.a: Nutrients needed in large quantities: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.

qa.q: Name the micronutrients.
qa.a: Iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum and chlorine.

qa.q: What is manure?
qa.a: Organic material from decomposed animal excreta and plant waste that adds nutrients and humus.

qa.q: What is compost?
qa.a: Manure made by decomposing farm waste in pits.

qa.q: What is vermi-compost?
What is green manure?
qa.a: Plants like sunn hemp or guar ploughed back into soil before sowing.

qa.q: What are fertilisers?
Why should fertiliser use be careful?
qa.a: Excess causes soil and water pollution and loss of fertility.

qa.q: What is organic farming?
qa.a: Farming with minimal or no use of chemicals and with organic manure and biological control.

qa.q: What is irrigation?
qa.a: Artificial supply of water to crops.

qa.q: Name some sources of irrigation.
qa.a: Wells, tube wells, canals, rivers and tanks.

qa.q: What is mixed cropping?
qa.a: Growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same land.

qa.q: What is inter-cropping?
qa.a: Growing two or more crops in definite row patterns.

qa.q: What is crop rotation?
qa.a: Growing different crops on the same land in a planned succession.

qa.q: What are weeds?
qa.a: Unwanted plants growing in the crop field.

qa.q: Name some weeds.
qa.a: Xanthium, Parthenium (gajar ghas) and Cyperus rotundus (motha).

qa.q: What are pests?
Name some ways in which pests attack plants.
qa.a: Cutting roots, stems and leaves, sucking cell sap and boring into stems and fruits.

qa.q: Which are biotic factors in grain storage loss?
qa.a: Insects, rodents, fungi, mites and bacteria.

qa.q: Which are abiotic factors in grain storage loss?
How can grains be protected in storage?
qa.a: By cleaning, drying, fumigation and proper treatment with chemicals.

qa.q: What is fumigation?
qa.a: Treatment of grain with gaseous chemicals to kill pests.

qa.q: What is the role of preventive methods?
qa.a: To avoid pest attack through proper seed bed, resistant varieties and crop rotation.

lessons.title: Improvement in Food Resources: Animal Husbandry
yt: class 9 science improvement in food resources: animal husbandry

blocks.x: Animal husbandry is the scientific management of livestock. It includes cattle farming for milk and draught labour, poultry farming for eggs and meat, fish production (marine and inland) and bee-keeping (apiculture) for honey and wax. Improved breeds, proper feed, shelter and disease control increase production. Cross-breeding of Indian and exotic breeds gives high milk yield and disease resistance.
Deep dive: cattle farming

Cattle are of milch and draught types. Milk yield depends on the lactation period. Cross-breeding of Indian cows (Sahiwal, Red Sindhi) with exotic breeds (Jersey, Brown Swiss) gives high yield and disease resistance. Feed consists of roughage and concentrates. Clean shelter and vaccination prevent diseases.
Deep dive: poultry

Layers give eggs and broilers give meat. Exotic Leghorn and Indian Aseel breeds are crossed for better chicks. Broiler feed is rich in protein with vitamins A and K. Cleanliness and vaccination prevent poultry diseases.
Deep dive: fish production

Marine fisheries catch pomfret, mackerel, tuna, sardines and Bombay duck. Mariculture rears mullets, bhetki, prawns, mussels, oysters and seaweed. Inland composite fish culture uses catla, rohu, mrigal, silver carp, grass carp and common carp together. Induced breeding uses hormones.
Deep dive: bee-keeping

Honeybee species used are Apis cerana indica, Apis dorsata, Apis florea and Apis mellifera. Italian bee collects more honey, stings little and stays in the hive longer. Honey quality depends on pasturage.

blocks.x: Communication is the exchange of information between a sender and a receiver through a channel with feedback. Methods are verbal (oral and written), non-verbal (body language) and visual (charts, signs). Effective communication follows the 7 Cs: clear, concise, correct, complete, courteous, concrete and considerate. Barriers such as noise, language, emotion and culture can distort the message. Good writing skills include correct sentences, parts of speech, paragraphs, e-mails and letters. Active listening and feedback complete the cycle.
Deep dive: communication cycle

The sender encodes an idea into a message and sends it through a channel. The receiver decodes it and gives feedback. Noise can disturb any stage. Two-way communication includes feedback; one-way does not.
Deep dive: methods and the 7 Cs
Verbal (oral, written), non-verbal (gesture, posture, eye contact, tone) and visual (charts, symbols). The 7 Cs are clear, concise, correct, complete, courteous, concrete and considerate.
Deep dive: barriers and listening
Physical, language, emotional, cultural and attitudinal barriers reduce effectiveness. Active listening needs attention, eye contact, no interruption, questions and summarising.
Deep dive: writing skills
Use all four sentence types appropriately, choose the correct part of speech, write paragraphs with a topic sentence, and follow formats for e-mails (subject, salutation, body, closing) and letters.

What is communication?
qa.a: The exchange of information, ideas or feelings between two or more persons.

qa.q: Name the elements of the communication cycle.
qa.a: Sender, message, encoding, channel, decoding, receiver and feedback.

qa.q: What is encoding?
qa.a: Converting an idea into words or symbols.

qa.q: What is decoding?
qa.a: Understanding the meaning of the received message.

qa.q: What is feedback?
qa.a: The receiver's response that shows the message was understood.

qa.q: What is a channel?
qa.a: The medium that carries the message.

qa.q: What is noise in communication?
qa.a: Any disturbance that distorts the message.

qa.q: What are the three methods of communication?
What is verbal communication?
qa.a: Communication using words, spoken or written.

qa.q: What is oral communication?
qa.a: Spoken communication such as a phone call or meeting.

qa.q: What is written communication?
qa.a: Communication through letters, e-mails and reports.

qa.q: What is non-verbal communication?
qa.a: Communication through body language, gestures and expressions.

qa.q: What is visual communication?
qa.a: Communication using pictures, charts, maps and signs.

qa.q: What is meant by clarity in a message?
qa.a: Using simple words to convey one main idea.

qa.q: What does concise mean?
What does courteous mean?
What is a concrete message?
qa.a: A message with specific facts and figures.

qa.q: What is a considerate message?
qa.a: A message that keeps the receiver's needs in mind.

qa.q: Name four types of barriers to communication.
qa.a: Physical, language, emotional and cultural barriers.

qa.q: What is a language barrier?
qa.a: Difficulty because of different languages or jargon.

qa.q: What is a physical barrier?
qa.a: Difficulty caused by noise, distance or poor equipment.

qa.q: What is an emotional barrier?
qa.a: Difficulty caused by anger, fear or stress.

qa.q: What is jargon?
qa.a: Special words used by a group that others may not understand.

qa.q: What is active listening?
qa.a: Listening with full attention, without interruption, and giving feedback.

qa.q: How can active listening be shown?
qa.a: By eye contact, nodding, asking questions and summarising.

qa.q: What is body language?
qa.a: Messages sent through posture, gestures and facial expression.

Communication is the exchange of information between a sender and a receiver through a channel with feedback. lessons.title: Self-Management Skills II
yt: class 10 ai and it self-management skills ii

blocks.x: Self-management skills help a person stay in control of emotions, time and goals. They include self-awareness (knowing strengths and weaknesses through SWOT), self-confidence, positive attitude, goal setting using the SMART method, time management, stress management, work ethics, teamwork, resilience and personal grooming. A person with good self-management is punctual, disciplined, motivated and able to work with others.
Deep dive: self-awareness and confidence

A SWOT analysis lists strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Knowing them helps a student choose a career and improve. Confidence grows through preparation, practice and positive self-talk.
Deep dive: goals and time
SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound. Time management uses to-do lists, priorities and schedules and avoids procrastination.
Deep dive: stress and resilience
Stress passes through alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages. Exercise, sleep, hobbies and support from family reduce stress. Resilience helps people recover from setbacks.
Deep dive: workplace behaviour
Work ethics include honesty, punctuality, discipline and accountability. Teamwork needs communication, respect and shared goals. Grooming and hygiene create a good impression.

lessons.title: ICT Skills II
yt: class 10 ai and it ict skills ii

blocks.x: ICT (Information and Communication Technology) covers devices and tools used to create, store and share information: computers, mobiles, the internet, e-mail and cloud services. Important skills are keyboarding and data entry (touch typing on the home row, ergonomics), using word processors and spreadsheets, safe internet use (netiquette, digital footprint, strong passwords), avoiding plagiarism and respecting copyright. Cyber safety protects users from cyberbullying, phishing and malware.
Deep dive: keyboarding and ergonomics
Touch typing uses the home row keys ASDF and JKL; as base positions. Sit upright, keep wrists straight, screen at eye level and take breaks to avoid strain.
Deep dive: productivity tools

Word processors format documents; spreadsheets calculate with formulas; presentation software shows ideas; cloud tools let people share and edit files together. Shortcuts: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+S.
Deep dive: cyber safety

Use strong passwords, two-factor authentication, updated antivirus and a firewall. Do not click unknown links (phishing). Report cyberbullying. Your digital footprint is permanent, so think before posting.

yt: class 10 ai and it entrepreneurial skills ii

blocks.x: An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a business opportunity, takes risks and sets up an enterprise. Qualities include creativity, risk-taking, leadership, decision-making and perseverance. The steps are idea generation, market research, business plan, funding and marketing. Government schemes such as Startup India, Make in India, Digital India and Mudra loans support entrepreneurs. A business plan covers the idea, market, finance, operations and marketing mix (4 Ps: product, price, place, promotion). Ethical practices and customer satisfaction are essential.
Deep dive: entrepreneurial qualities
Successful entrepreneurs are creative, take calculated risks, lead teams, make timely decisions and persevere through failures. They spot needs in the market and offer solutions.
Deep dive: business steps

Generate an idea, research the market, write a business plan, arrange capital (savings, loans, investors, crowdfunding), choose a legal form (sole proprietorship, partnership, company), launch and market. The 4 Ps of marketing are product, price, place and promotion.
Deep dive: finance basics
Profit = revenue - cost. Profit % = (profit/cost price) × 100. Break-even units = fixed cost ÷ (selling price - variable cost per unit).
Deep dive: government support
Startup India, Make in India, Digital India and Mudra loans help new businesses with funding, skills and infrastructure. Ethical practices build trust and long-term success.

उद्यमी अवसर पहचानकर जोखिम उठाते हुए व्यवसाय शुरू करता है। स्टार्टअप इंडिया और मेक इन इंडिया जैसी योजनाएँ उद्यमियों की सहायता करती हैं।
4 Ps: Product, Price, Place, Promotion.

yt: class 10 ai and it green skills ii

blocks.x: Green skills are the knowledge, abilities and attitudes needed to live in and support a sustainable society. Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations. The United Nations set 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030. Key ideas are renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), the 3 Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), water conservation, waste management, e-waste, circular economy, carbon footprint and green jobs. International agreements include the Kyoto Protocol, Montreal Protocol and Paris Agreement.
Deep dive: sustainability and SDGs

Sustainable development balances economic growth, social well-being and environmental protection. The UN's 17 SDGs (2015, to be achieved by 2030) include no poverty, zero hunger, clean water, clean energy, climate action and life on land.
Deep dive: energy and waste

Use renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro) instead of fossil fuels. Follow the 3 Rs, compost biodegradable waste and recycle e-waste through authorised centres. Choose BEE five-star appliances and LED lights.
Deep dive: climate and agreements

Greenhouse gases cause global warming and climate change. The Montreal Protocol (1987) protects the ozone layer, the Kyoto Protocol (1997) cut emissions and the Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to below 2°C.
Deep dive: green careers
Green jobs include solar technician, waste manager, environmental engineer and organic farmer. Green skills involve energy saving, resource efficiency and eco-friendly design.

lessons.title: AI Project Cycle and Ethics
yt: class 10 ai and it ai project cycle and ethics

blocks.x: The AI project cycle has five stages: Problem Scoping, Data Acquisition, Data Exploration, Modelling and Evaluation, followed by Deployment. Problem scoping uses the 4Ws canvas (Who, What, Where, Why) and a problem statement template. Data features, training and testing data, and visualisation guide modelling. AI models are rule-based or learning-based (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement). AI ethics demands fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, safety and the avoidance of bias; AI bias arises from skewed data or design choices. The three domains of AI are Data, Computer Vision and NLP.
Deep dive: problem scoping
Use the 4Ws canvas: Who (stakeholders), What (nature of problem), Where (context), Why (benefit of solving). Summarise it in a problem statement template. Choose problems linked to the SDGs.
Deep dive: data and exploration
Acquire data from surveys, sensors, cameras, web scraping and APIs. Split it into training and testing sets. Visualise with charts to find patterns and relationships among features.
Deep dive: modelling approaches

Rule-based models follow developer-written rules; learning-based models learn from data. Learning types are supervised (labelled), unsupervised (unlabelled) and reinforcement (rewards). Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks.
Deep dive: ethics
Bias in data leads to unfair outcomes. Ethical AI needs fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability and access for all. Developers must test for bias and protect personal data.
Hindi saransh
AI प्रोजेक्ट साइकिल के चरण: समस्या निर्धारण, डेटा अधिग्रहण, डेटा अन्वेषण, मॉडलिंग और मूल्यांकन। नैतिकता में निष्पक्षता, गोपनीयता और जवाबदेही आवश्यक हैं।
Cycle: Problem Scoping → Data Acquisition → Exploration → Modelling → Evaluation.

Visual lesson

AI Project Cycle and Ethics

The AI project cycle has five stages: Problem Scoping, Data Acquisition, Data Exploration, Modelling and Evaluation, followed by Deployment

🔑

Big idea

  • The AI project cycle has five stages: Problem Scoping, Data Acquisition, Data Exploration, Modelling and Evaluation, followed by Deployment
  • Problem scoping uses the 4Ws canvas (Who, What, Where, Why) and a problem statement template

Read the full explanation

The AI project cycle has five stages: Problem Scoping, Data Acquisition, Data Exploration, Modelling and Evaluation, followed by Deployment. Problem scoping uses the 4Ws canvas (Who, What, Where, Why) and a problem statement template. Data features, training and testing data, and visualisation guide modelling. AI models are rule-based or learning-based (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement). AI ethics demands fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, safety and the avoidance of bias; AI bias arises from skewed data or design choices. The three domains of AI are Data, Computer Vision and NLP.

📌

Problem scoping

  • Use the 4Ws canvas: Who (stakeholders), What (nature of problem), Where (context), Why (benefit of solving)
  • Summarise it in a problem statement template
  • Choose problems linked to the SDGs
🧠

Data and exploration

  • Acquire data from surveys, sensors, cameras, web scraping and APIs
  • Split it into training and testing sets
  • Visualise with charts to find patterns and relationships among features
🌟

Modelling approaches

  • Rule-based models follow developer-written rules
  • Learning-based models learn from data
  • Learning types are supervised (labelled), unsupervised (unlabelled) and reinforcement (rewards)
  • Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks
🔬

Ethics

  • Bias in data leads to unfair outcomes
  • Ethical AI needs fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability and access for all
  • Developers must test for bias and protect personal data
🧮

🎯 Remember Cycle: Problem Scoping → Data Acquisition → Exploration → Modelling → Evaluation.

AI प्रोजेक्ट साइकिल के चरण: समस्या निर्धारण, डेटा अधिग्रहण, डेटा अन्वेषण, मॉडलिंग और मूल्यांकन। नैतिकता में निष्पक्षता, गोपनीयता और जवाबदेही आवश्यक हैं।

lessons.title: Data Science
yt: class 10 ai and it data science

blocks.x: Data science extracts insight from data using statistics, programming and domain knowledge. Data may be structured (tables) or unstructured (text, images). Data is gathered, cleaned, analysed and visualised. Basic statistics include mean, median, mode and range; K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) classifies a new point by looking at the nearest labelled points. Data science is applied in finance, healthcare, agriculture, sports and e-commerce. Python libraries NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib support analysis.
Deep dive: types of data
Structured data fit tables; unstructured data (text, images, audio) do not. Big data is described by volume, velocity and variety.
Deep dive: statistics
Mean = sum/n, median = middle of ordered data, mode = most frequent, range = max - min. Outliers can distort the mean more than the median.
Deep dive: KNN
To classify a new point, compute the distance to each labelled point (Euclidean: √((x2-x1)²+(y2-y1)²)), pick the K nearest and choose the majority class. An odd K avoids ties.
Deep dive: tools
NumPy handles arrays, Pandas handles DataFrames, Matplotlib plots graphs. Data science helps healthcare, agriculture, finance, sports and e-commerce.
Hindi saransh
डेटा साइंस में डेटा से जानकारी निकाली जाती है। माध्य, माध्यिका, बहुलक और KNN इसके मुख्य विषय हैं।
Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle value; mode = most frequent.

Data science extracts insight from data using statistics, programming and domain knowledge. Data may be structured (tables) or unstructured (text, images). Data is gathered, cleaned, analysed and visualised. Basic statistics include mean, median, mode and range; K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) classifies a new point by looking at the nearest labelled points. Data science is applied in finance, healthcare, agriculture, sports and e-commerce. Python libraries NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib support analysis.

📌

Types of data

  • Structured data fit tables
  • Unstructured data (text, images, audio) do not
  • Big data is described by volume, velocity and variety
🧠

Statistics

  • Mean = sum/n, median = middle of ordered data, mode = most frequent, range = max - min
  • Outliers can distort the mean more than the median
🌟

KNN

  • To classify a new point, compute the distance to each labelled point (Euclidean: √((x2-x1)²+(y2-y1)²)), pick the K nearest and choose the majority…
  • An odd K avoids ties
🔬

Tools

  • NumPy handles arrays, Pandas handles DataFrames, Matplotlib plots graphs
  • Data science helps healthcare, agriculture, finance, sports and e-commerce

lessons.title: Natural Language Processing
yt: class 10 ai and it natural language processing

blocks.x: Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language. Applications include chatbots, voice assistants, translation, sentiment analysis and spam filters. Text processing steps: text normalisation (sentence segmentation, tokenisation, removing stopwords, converting to lowercase, stemming and lemmatisation). The bag-of-words model counts word occurrences in a corpus; TF-IDF weighs a word by how often it appears in a document and how rare it is across documents. Challenges include ambiguity, sarcasm and context.
Deep dive: applications
NLP powers chatbots (script-bots and smart-bots), translation, voice assistants, sentiment analysis, summarisation and spam filtering.
Deep dive: text normalisation
Steps: segment sentences, tokenise, remove stopwords, lowercase, then stem or lemmatise. Lemmatisation gives real words ("studies" → "study"), stemming may not ("studies" → "studi").
Deep dive: bag of words and TF-IDF

Create a vocabulary from the normalised corpus and count words per document to form vectors. TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency, so common words score low and distinctive words score high.
Deep dive: challenges
Ambiguity, sarcasm, multiple meanings, context and code-mixed text like Hinglish make NLP hard.
Hindi saransh
NLP में कंप्यूटर मानव भाषा को समझता है। टेक्स्ट नॉर्मलाइज़ेशन, बैग ऑफ वर्ड्स और TF-IDF इसके मुख्य चरण हैं।
Normalisation: segmentation → tokenisation → stopwords → lowercase → stemming/lemmatisation.

qa.q: What does a high TF-IDF mean?

qa.q: What happens to the value of stopwords in TF-IDF?
qa.a: It is low, showing little importance.

qa.q: What is the formula for IDF?
qa.a: IDF = total documents ÷ document frequency (often with log).

🔑

Big idea

  • Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language
  • Applications include chatbots, voice assistants, translation, sentiment analysis and spam filters
  • Text processing steps: text normalisation (sentence segmentation, tokenisation, removing stopwords, converting to lowercase, stemming and…
  • The bag-of-words model counts word occurrences in a corpus
Read the full explanation

Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language. Applications include chatbots, voice assistants, translation, sentiment analysis and spam filters. Text processing steps: text normalisation (sentence segmentation, tokenisation, removing stopwords, converting to lowercase, stemming and lemmatisation). The bag-of-words model counts word occurrences in a corpus; TF-IDF weighs a word by how often it appears in a document and how rare it is across documents. Challenges include ambiguity, sarcasm and context.

💡

Applications

  • NLP powers chatbots (script-bots and smart-bots), translation, voice assistants, sentiment analysis, summarisation and spam filtering
🧠

Text normalisation

  • Steps: segment sentences, tokenise, remove stopwords, lowercase, then stem or lemmatise
  • Lemmatisation gives real words ("studies" → "study"), stemming may not ("studies" → "studi")
✍️

Bag of words and TF-IDF

  • Create a vocabulary from the normalised corpus and count words per document to form vectors
  • TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency, so common words score low and distinctive words score high
🔬

Challenges

  • Ambiguity, sarcasm, multiple meanings, context and code-mixed text like Hinglish make NLP hard
🧮

Formula tiles

Normalisationsegment tokenise stopwords lowercase stem
TF-IDFTF × IDFimportant words score high
Chatbotsscript-bot, smart-bot
🎯 Remember Normalisation: segmentation → tokenisation → stopwords → lowercase → stemming/lemmatisation.
🇮🇳

NLP में कंप्यूटर मानव भाषा को समझता है। टेक्स्ट नॉर्मलाइज़ेशन, बैग ऑफ वर्ड्स और TF-IDF इसके मुख्य चरण हैं।

lessons.title: Evaluating Models
yt: class 10 ai and it evaluating models

blocks.x: Evaluation tests a trained model on unseen test data to see how well it predicts. Predictions are compared with reality in a confusion matrix of True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP) and False Negative (FN). Accuracy = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN) × 100; Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN); F1 = 2 × Precision × Recall/(Precision + Recall). Precision matters when false alarms are costly; recall matters when missing a case is costly. Overfitting means the model memorises training data and fails on new data.
Deep dive: confusion matrix
TP and TN are correct predictions; FP (false alarm) and FN (missed case) are errors. Total = TP+TN+FP+FN.
Deep dive: metrics
Accuracy = (TP+TN)/Total. Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Recall = TP/(TP+FN). F1 = 2PR/(P+R), the harmonic mean, which is high only when both are high.
Deep dive: which metric
Use recall where missing a case is dangerous (disease, fire alarm) and precision where false alarms are costly (spam, court). Accuracy fails on imbalanced data.
Deep dive: over and underfitting
Overfitting gives high training but low test performance; underfitting gives low performance on both. Use more data, simpler models or cross-validation.
Hindi saransh
मूल्यांकन में मॉडल को परीक्षण डेटा पर जाँचा जाता है। कन्फ्यूज़न मैट्रिक्स से accuracy, precision, recall और F1 निकाले जाते हैं।
Accuracy=(TP+TN)/Total; Precision=TP/(TP+FP); Recall=TP/(TP+FN).

  • Accuracy = (TP+TN)/Total
  • Precision = TP/(TP+FP)
  • Recall = TP/(TP+FN)
  • F1 = 2PR/(P+R), the harmonic mean, which is high only when both are high
🌟

Which metric

  • Use recall where missing a case is dangerous (disease, fire alarm) and precision where false alarms are costly (spam, court)
  • Accuracy fails on imbalanced data
🔬

Over and underfitting

  • Overfitting gives high training but low test performance
  • Underfitting gives low performance on both
  • Use more data, simpler models or cross-validation
🧮

Formula tiles

Accuracy(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)overall
PrecisionTP/(TP+FP)positive predictions
RecallTP/(TP+FN)actual positives
🎯 Remember Accuracy=(TP+TN)/Total; Precision=TP/(TP+FP); Recall=TP/(TP+FN).
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

मूल्यांकन में मॉडल को परीक्षण डेटा पर जाँचा जाता है। कन्फ्यूज़न मैट्रिक्स से accuracy, precision, recall और F1 निकाले जाते हैं।

lessons.title: Lists, Dictionaries and Functions
yt: class 10 ai and it lists, dictionaries and functions

blocks.x: A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets; methods include append, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse and index. A tuple is immutable. A dictionary stores key:value pairs in braces. Functions are defined with def, take parameters and return values; they promote reuse. Variables can be local or global. Modules are imported with import (math, random). Files can be opened with open() in modes r, w and a and closed with close().
Deep dive: lists
Lists are mutable; index from 0 or from -1 at the end. Methods: append, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse, count, index, extend. Slicing L[a:b] gives items a to b-1.
Deep dive: tuples and dictionaries
Tuples are immutable. Dictionaries map unique keys to values; use keys(), values(), items(), and d[key] to read.
Deep dive: functions
def name(parameters): body; return value. Arguments can be positional, keyword or default. Local variables live inside the function; global variables are visible everywhere.
Deep dive: modules and files
import math, random. open(name, mode) with r, w, a; read(), readline(), write(), close().

Visual lesson

Lists, Dictionaries and Functions

A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Lists›3Tuples and dictionaries›4Functions›5Modules and files
🔑

Big idea

  • A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets
  • Methods include append, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse and index
  • A tuple is immutable
  • A dictionary stores key:value pairs in braces
Read the full explanation

A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets; methods include append, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse and index. A tuple is immutable. A dictionary stores key:value pairs in braces. Functions are defined with def, take parameters and return values; they promote reuse. Variables can be local or global. Modules are imported with import (math, random). Files can be opened with open() in modes r, w and a and closed with close().

📌

Lists

  • Lists are mutable
  • Index from 0 or from -1 at the end
  • Methods: append, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse, count, index, extend
  • Slicing L[a:b] gives items a to b-1
🧠

Tuples and dictionaries

  • Tuples are immutable
  • Dictionaries map unique keys to values
  • Use keys(), values(), items(), and d[key] to read
🌟

Functions

  • Def name(parameters): body
  • Arguments can be positional, keyword or default
  • Local variables live inside the function
  • Global variables are visible everywhere
🔬

Modules and files

  • Import math, random
  • Open(name, mode) with r, w, a
  • Read(), readline(), write(), close()
🧮

blocks.x: NumPy provides fast n-dimensional arrays (ndarray) with operations like sum, mean, reshape and arange. Pandas offers Series (1-D) and DataFrame (2-D table) with functions read_csv, head, describe, loc, iloc and groupby. Matplotlib's pyplot draws line, bar, scatter, histogram and pie charts with labels, titles and legends. Together they form the basic Python data-science toolkit used with AI projects.
Deep dive: NumPy
Arrays hold same-type values and support vectorised maths: a+b adds element-wise. Create with array, arange, zeros, ones; check shape; reshape; use mean, sum, max.
Deep dive: Pandas
A Series is 1-D and a DataFrame is a table. Load with read_csv, inspect with head, info and describe, select with df['col'], loc and iloc, clean with dropna and fillna, summarise with groupby.
Deep dive: Matplotlib
Use plt.plot, bar, scatter, hist, pie. Always add title, xlabel, ylabel and legend, then plt.show().
Deep dive: workflow
Load → clean → explore → visualise → model. These libraries support the AI project cycle.
Hindi saransh

lessons.title: Digital Documentation (Advanced)
yt: class 10 ai and it digital documentation (advanced)

blocks.x: Advanced word processing (Writer/Word) covers styles, headers and footers, page numbers, table of contents, mail merge, track changes, comments, tables, images, hyperlinks, page layout, columns, templates and printing. Styles keep formatting consistent; mail merge combines a main document with a data source to make personalised letters. Cross-references, footnotes and bookmarks help in long documents.
Deep dive: styles and structure
Apply Heading 1, Heading 2 etc. to create a table of contents automatically. Use headers, footers, page numbers and section breaks for professional layout.
Deep dive: mail merge
Prepare a main letter, connect a data source (spreadsheet or database), insert merge fields such as «Name», preview and merge to a new document or print.
Deep dive: collaboration
Track changes records edits; comments carry reviewer notes; accept or reject changes. Protect with a password and share as PDF.
Deep dive: references
Footnotes, endnotes, bookmarks, hyperlinks and cross-references make long documents easier to navigate.

lessons.title: Electronic Spreadsheet (Advanced)
yt: class 10 ai and it electronic spreadsheet (advanced)

blocks.x: An electronic spreadsheet (Excel/Calc) organises data in cells identified by column letter and row number. Formulas begin with =. Common functions are SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, IF, VLOOKUP and ROUND. Cell references are relative (A1), absolute ($A$1) and mixed. Features include sorting, filtering, conditional formatting, charts, pivot tables, data validation and named ranges. Errors like #DIV/0!, #NAME?, #VALUE! and #REF! indicate problems.
Deep dive: formulas and functions
Formulas start with =. Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, IF, ROUND, VLOOKUP. Relative references shift when copied; absolute ($A$1) do not.
Deep dive: data tools
Sort and filter data; apply conditional formatting; validate input; build charts and pivot tables to summarise large data.
Deep dive: errors
#DIV/0! (divide by zero), #NAME? (unknown name), #VALUE! (wrong type), #REF! (invalid reference), ##### (narrow column).
Deep dive: good practice
Use a header row, named ranges, freeze panes and protect formulas. Check results before presenting.

स्प्रेडशीट में सूत्र = से शुरू होते हैं। SUM, AVERAGE, IF, VLOOKUP और पिवट टेबल प्रमुख उपकरण हैं।
Absolute reference uses $ (e.g. $A$1).

An electronic spreadsheet (Excel/Calc) organises data in cells identified by column letter and row number. Formulas begin with =. Common functions are SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, IF, VLOOKUP and ROUND. Cell references are relative (A1), absolute ($A$1) and mixed. Features include sorting, filtering, conditional formatting, charts, pivot tables, data validation and named ranges. Errors like #DIV/0!, #NAME?, #VALUE! and #REF! indicate problems.

🧮

Formulas and functions

  • Formulas start with =
  • Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, IF, ROUND, VLOOKUP
  • Relative references shift when copied
  • Absolute ($A$1) do not
🧠

Data tools

  • Sort and filter data
  • Apply conditional formatting
  • Validate input
  • Build charts and pivot tables to summarise large data
🌟

Errors

  • (divide by zero), #NAME?
  • (unknown name), #VALUE!
  • (wrong type), #REF!
  • (invalid reference), ##### (narrow column)
🔬

Good practice

  • Use a header row, named ranges, freeze panes and protect formulas
  • Check results before presenting

blocks.x: A database is an organised collection of data managed by a Database Management System (DBMS) such as MySQL, Access or Oracle. In the relational model, data is stored in tables (relations) of rows (records/tuples) and columns (fields/attributes). A primary key uniquely identifies each record; a foreign key links tables. SQL commands: CREATE, INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, with WHERE, ORDER BY and aggregate functions COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN. Data types include INT, VARCHAR, DATE.
Deep dive: relational model
Tables (relations) have rows (records/tuples) and columns (fields/attributes). A primary key uniquely identifies rows; a foreign key refers to another table's primary key to link them.
Deep dive: SQL commands
CREATE TABLE, INSERT INTO ... VALUES, SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY, UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE, DELETE FROM ... WHERE. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN with GROUP BY.
Deep dive: example
SELECT Name, Marks FROM Student WHERE Marks > 80 ORDER BY Marks DESC;
Deep dive: advantages
A DBMS reduces redundancy, improves integrity, allows sharing, security and fast searching.
Hindi saransh
डेटाबेस में तालिकाओं के रूप में डेटा रखा जाता है। प्राइमरी की रिकॉर्ड को अद्वितीय बनाती है। SQL में SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE मुख्य कमांड हैं।

lessons.title: Web Applications and Security
yt: class 10 ai and it web applications and security

blocks.x: A web application runs in a browser and communicates with a server over HTTP/HTTPS. The front end uses HTML (structure), CSS (style) and JavaScript (behaviour); the back end handles logic and databases. Web basics include URL, domain name, IP address, DNS, web server and hosting. Security covers HTTPS/SSL, encryption, authentication and authorisation, strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls, antivirus, backups and safe habits against phishing, SQL injection, malware and ransomware. Indian laws include the IT Act 2000.
Deep dive: how the web works
The browser sends an HTTP request using a URL; DNS finds the IP address of the web server; the server returns HTML, CSS and JavaScript which the browser renders.
Deep dive: building blocks
HTML gives structure (h1, p, a, img, table), CSS gives style (colour, font, layout), JavaScript gives behaviour. The back end uses databases and server logic.
Deep dive: security threats
Phishing, malware, ransomware, spyware, SQL injection and weak passwords are common threats. Defences: HTTPS, strong passwords, 2FA, firewalls, antivirus, updates and backups.
Deep dive: law and ethics
The IT Act 2000 penalises hacking, identity theft and cyber fraud. Respect privacy, avoid plagiarism and report cybercrime at cybercrime.gov.in.
Hindi saransh
वेब एप्लिकेशन ब्राउज़र में चलता है। HTML ढाँचा, CSS शैली और JavaScript व्यवहार देता है। HTTPS, एन्क्रिप्शन और मजबूत पासवर्ड सुरक्षा के उपाय हैं।
HTML structure, CSS style, JavaScript behaviour; HTTPS = secure HTTP.

Visual lesson

Web Applications and Security

A web application runs in a browser and communicates with a server over HTTP/HTTPS

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2How the web works›3Building blocks›4Security threats›5Law and ethics
LawIT Act 2000
🔑

Big idea

  • A web application runs in a browser and communicates with a server over HTTP/HTTPS
  • The front end uses HTML (structure), CSS (style) and JavaScript (behaviour)
  • The back end handles logic and databases
  • Web basics include URL, domain name, IP address, DNS, web server and hosting
Read the full explanation

A web application runs in a browser and communicates with a server over HTTP/HTTPS. The front end uses HTML (structure), CSS (style) and JavaScript (behaviour); the back end handles logic and databases. Web basics include URL, domain name, IP address, DNS, web server and hosting. Security covers HTTPS/SSL, encryption, authentication and authorisation, strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls, antivirus, backups and safe habits against phishing, SQL injection, malware and ransomware. Indian laws include the IT Act 2000.

🚀

How the web works

  • The browser sends an HTTP request using a URL
  • DNS finds the IP address of the web server
  • The server returns HTML, CSS and JavaScript which the browser renders
🧠

Building blocks

  • HTML gives structure (h1, p, a, img, table), CSS gives style (colour, font, layout), JavaScript gives behaviour
  • The back end uses databases and server logic
🌟

Security threats

  • Phishing, malware, ransomware, spyware, SQL injection and weak passwords are common threats
  • Defences: HTTPS, strong passwords, 2FA, firewalls, antivirus, updates and backups
⚖️

Law and ethics

  • The IT Act 2000 penalises hacking, identity theft and cyber fraud
  • Respect privacy, avoid plagiarism and report cybercrime at cybercrime.gov.in
🧮

lessons.title: Development

blocks.x: Development means improvement in the quality of life, but different people have different goals. A rich farmer, a landless labourer and a girl in a village may each want different things, and goals can conflict (a dam helps some and displaces others). Income alone is not enough; people also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and respect. Countries are compared by per capita income (national income ÷ population) and by the World Bank classification: high income above $12,696 per annum is rich, low income $1,045 or less is low (2016 figures). Averages hide inequality. Other indicators are literacy, infant mortality rate, life expectancy, net attendance ratio and the Human Development Index (HDI) of the UNDP combining health, education and income. Kerala has better human development than Haryana despite lower per capita income because of public services. Sustainable development avoids using up resources that future generations need.
Deep dive: different goals

A landless labourer wants regular work and higher wages; a rich farmer wants higher support prices and cheap labour; a girl may want equal chances in education. Because goals differ and can conflict, development is judged differently by different people. For a fair view, we look for goals that benefit all.
Deep dive: national income and averages

National income is total goods and services produced in a year. Dividing by population gives per capita income. The World Bank uses it to classify countries. Averages are useful for comparison but hide inequality.
Deep dive: other indicators

Health (life expectancy, infant mortality), education (literacy, attendance) and nutrition (BMI) matter. The UNDP HDI combines these with income. Kerala has high human development due to public services even though per capita income is lower than in Haryana.
Deep dive: sustainability
Groundwater overuse and fossil fuel depletion threaten future generations. Sustainable development uses resources within their renewal limits.
Hindi saransh

विकास का अर्थ जीवन-स्तर में सुधार है, पर अलग-अलग लोगों के लक्ष्य अलग होते हैं। प्रति व्यक्ति आय = राष्ट्रीय आय ÷ जनसंख्या। HDI में स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा और आय शामिल हैं। सतत विकास भविष्य की पीढ़ियों के संसाधन बचाता है।
Per capita income = total income ÷ population. HDI = health + education + income.

Visual lesson

Development

Development means improvement in the quality of life, but different people have different goals

🔑

Big idea

  • Development means improvement in the quality of life, but different people have different goals
  • A rich farmer, a landless labourer and a girl in a village may each want different things, and goals can conflict (a dam helps some and displaces…
  • Income alone is not enough
  • People also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and respect
Read the full explanation

Development means improvement in the quality of life, but different people have different goals. A rich farmer, a landless labourer and a girl in a village may each want different things, and goals can conflict (a dam helps some and displaces others). Income alone is not enough; people also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and respect. Countries are compared by per capita income (national income ÷ population) and by the World Bank classification: high income above $12,696 per annum is rich, low income $1,045 or less is low (2016 figures). Averages hide inequality. Other indicators are literacy, infant mortality rate, life expectancy, net attendance ratio and the Human Development Index (HDI) of the UNDP combining health, education and income. Kerala has better human development than Haryana despite lower per capita income because of public services. Sustainable development avoids using up resources that future generations need.

📌

Different goals

  • A landless labourer wants regular work and higher wages
  • A rich farmer wants higher support prices and cheap labour
  • A girl may want equal chances in education
  • Because goals differ and can conflict, development is judged differently by different people
Read the full explanation

A landless labourer wants regular work and higher wages; a rich farmer wants higher support prices and cheap labour; a girl may want equal chances in education. Because goals differ and can conflict, development is judged differently by different people. For a fair view, we look for goals that benefit all.

🧠

National income and averages

  • National income is total goods and services produced in a year
  • Dividing by population gives per capita income
  • The World Bank uses it to classify countries
  • Averages are useful for comparison but hide inequality
🌟

Other indicators

  • Health (life expectancy, infant mortality), education (literacy, attendance) and nutrition (BMI) matter
  • The UNDP HDI combines these with income
  • Kerala has high human development due to public services even though per capita income is lower than in Haryana
🔬

Sustainability

  • Groundwater overuse and fossil fuel depletion threaten future generations
  • Sustainable development uses resources within their renewal limits
🧮

yt: class 10 economics sectors of economic activity

blocks.x: Economic activities are grouped into three sectors: primary (agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining), secondary (manufacturing from natural products) and tertiary or service sector (transport, trade, banking, IT, education). The tertiary sector supports the other two. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year; only final goods are counted to avoid double counting. In India, production shifted from the primary to the secondary and then the tertiary sector, so by the 2000s the service sector contributed the largest share of GDP, while the majority of workers remained in agriculture. This leads to underemployment (disguised unemployment) in agriculture. Solutions include irrigation, agro-based industries, cold storage, and creating more non-farm jobs.
Deep dive: classification of sectors
Primary uses natural resources (farming, fishing, mining), secondary processes these (sugar, cloth, steel), and tertiary supports both (transport, storage, banking). Sectors are interdependent.
Deep dive: GDP
GDP sums the value of final goods and services produced in a year. Counting only final goods avoids double counting; for example, the value of wheat is included in biscuits, not counted separately.
Deep dive: structural change
Over time the share of the primary sector in GDP fell and the tertiary sector rose to be largest, but employment stayed mostly in agriculture, causing underemployment.
Deep dive: creating jobs
Irrigation, credit, agro-processing, cold storage, tourism, IT and the MGNREGA 2005 job guarantee help create employment.
Hindi saransh

तीन क्षेत्र हैं: प्राथमिक (कृषि), द्वितीयक (विनिर्माण) और तृतीयक (सेवा)। GDP में केवल अंतिम वस्तुओं का मूल्य गिना जाता है। भारत में GDP में सेवा क्षेत्र सबसे बड़ा है, पर अधिकांश लोग कृषि में कार्यरत हैं, इसलिए अल्प-रोजगार है।
GDP counts only final goods and services (avoids double counting).

What are the three sectors of the economy?
What is the primary sector?
qa.a: The sector producing goods by exploiting natural resources, like agriculture.

qa.q: Why is the primary sector also called the agriculture and related sector?
qa.a: Most of its products come from agriculture, dairy, fishing and forestry.

qa.q: What is the secondary sector?
qa.a: The sector converting natural products into other forms by manufacturing.

qa.q: What is another name for the secondary sector?
What is the tertiary sector?
qa.a: The sector providing services that help the other sectors.

qa.q: Give examples of tertiary activities.
qa.a: Transport, banking, trade, communication, teaching and IT.

qa.q: Why are the sectors interdependent?
qa.a: Each depends on goods or services of the others.

qa.q: What is GDP?
qa.a: The value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year.

qa.q: Why are only final goods counted in GDP?
qa.a: To avoid double counting of intermediate goods.

qa.q: What are intermediate goods?
qa.a: Goods used up in producing final goods.

qa.q: What are final goods?
Which organisation measures GDP in India?
qa.a: The Central Government ministry through the NSO.

qa.q: Which sector was the largest in GDP in India in the early 20th century?
Which sector is the largest contributor to India's GDP today?
What is the historical change in sectors?
qa.a: Primary dominated first, then secondary, now tertiary.

qa.q: Which sector employs most people in India?
What is disguised unemployment?
qa.a: More workers are engaged than required, so some add nothing to output.

qa.q: What is another name for disguised unemployment?
Why does agriculture have underemployment?
qa.a: Small land holdings and large families work on the same land.

qa.q: Give a measure to reduce underemployment.
qa.a: Irrigation and cheap credit for farmers.

qa.q: What is the role of agro-based industries?
qa.a: They create non-farm jobs in rural areas.

qa.q: Which service sectors grew rapidly recently?
Why did the tertiary sector grow?
qa.a: Increased demand for services and the rise of IT.

qa.q: Why are the services sector jobs not equally spread?
qa.a: Only a small number of skilled workers get high-paying jobs.

qa.q: What are the other jobs in services?
qa.a: Cobblers, barbers and domestic helpers with low pay.

qa.q: What is the Right to Work scheme?
qa.a: MGNREGA 2005 guaranteeing 100 days of work in rural areas.

qa.q: What does MGNREGA stand for?
qa.a: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act.

qa.q: What are non-economic activities?
qa.a: Activities not done for earning, like household work.

qa.q: What is double counting?
qa.a: Counting the value of the same product more than once.

qa.q: What is the primary sector's main problem?
What are Cold storage and warehouses examples of?
What is value added?
qa.a: Final value minus the value of intermediate goods.

qa.q: What is a measure of economic activity?
What is a service?
qa.a: An activity that helps production but does not produce a tangible good.

qa.q: Why is the tertiary sector important?
qa.a: It supports production and creates jobs and income.

The tertiary sector supports the other two. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year; only final goods are counted to avoid double counting. In India, production shifted from the primary to the secondary and then the tertiary sector, so by the 2000s the service sector contributed the largest share of GDP, while the majority of workers remained in agriculture. This leads to underemployment (disguised unemployment) in agriculture. Solutions include irrigation, agro-based industries, cold storage, and creating more non-farm jobs.

📌

Classification of sectors

  • Primary uses natural resources (farming, fishing, mining), secondary processes these (sugar, cloth, steel), and tertiary supports both (transport…
  • Sectors are interdependent
🧠

GDP

  • GDP sums the value of final goods and services produced in a year
  • Counting only final goods avoids double counting
  • For example, the value of wheat is included in biscuits, not counted separately
🌟

Structural change

  • Over time the share of the primary sector in GDP fell and the tertiary sector rose to be largest, but employment stayed mostly in agriculture…
🔬

Creating jobs

  • Irrigation, credit, agro-processing, cold storage, tourism, IT and the MGNREGA 2005 job guarantee help create employment

blocks.x: In the organised sector, jobs are regular with fixed hours, job security, benefits such as provident fund, pensions, paid leave, and the enterprise is registered and follows rules like the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act. In the unorganised sector, jobs are irregular, wages low, there is no security or benefits, and rules are not followed. About 90 per cent of India's workers are in the unorganised sector; most farmers, casual labourers, and street vendors belong here. Workers need protection in wages, safe work conditions and health care. By ownership, the public sector (government owns assets and provides services: railways, post, BSNL) and private sector (individuals or companies own: Tata Steel, Reliance). The government must provide basic services such as roads, schools, hospitals, electricity and irrigation and support the weak.
Deep dive: organised vs unorganised

The organised sector has regular, registered, rule-governed jobs with benefits like provident fund, gratuity, pension and paid leave. The unorganised sector has irregular jobs, low wages, no benefits and little regulation; about 90% of workers are there.
Deep dive: protecting workers
Governments protect workers through the Minimum Wages Act, safety rules and support for small farmers and traders; unions and cooperatives help workers bargain.
Deep dive: ownership

Public sector enterprises are government-owned and aim at public welfare; private sector firms aim at profit. The government must provide essential services and support farmers with MSP and procurement.

lessons.title: Money

blocks.x: Money is a medium of exchange that removes the problem of the double coincidence of wants in barter. Modern forms of money are currency (paper notes and coins) and demand deposits in banks. Currency is issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI); in India no one can refuse a payment in rupees, which is called legal tender, and the rupee is accepted because the law guarantees it. Coins and notes: the Government of India mints coins, but RBI issues notes. Demand deposits can be withdrawn on demand by cheque, ATM or net banking; cheques are not money but payment orders. Banks hold only a fraction of deposits as cash and lend the rest to earn interest, as they know that depositors will not all withdraw at once. Money should be safe, accepted and hold value over time.
Deep dive: from barter to money
Barter needs a double coincidence of wants. Money as a medium of exchange removes this difficulty, making trade easy and allowing specialisation.
Deep dive: forms of money

Currency (notes issued by the RBI, coins minted by the government) is legal tender. Demand deposits with banks are also accepted as money because payments can be made by cheque, ATM, UPI or net banking.
Deep dive: banks and deposits
Banks accept deposits, pay interest, keep a fraction as cash reserve and lend the rest at higher interest. The difference is their income.
Deep dive: features of money
Good money is widely accepted, durable, divisible and stable in value. Inflation reduces its purchasing power.

Read the full explanation

Money is a medium of exchange that removes the problem of the double coincidence of wants in barter. Modern forms of money are currency (paper notes and coins) and demand deposits in banks. Currency is issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI); in India no one can refuse a payment in rupees, which is called legal tender, and the rupee is accepted because the law guarantees it. Coins and notes: the Government of India mints coins, but RBI issues notes. Demand deposits can be withdrawn on demand by cheque, ATM or net banking; cheques are not money but payment orders. Banks hold only a fraction of deposits as cash and lend the rest to earn interest, as they know that depositors will not all withdraw at once. Money should be safe, accepted and hold value over time.

📌

From barter to money

  • Barter needs a double coincidence of wants
  • Money as a medium of exchange removes this difficulty, making trade easy and allowing specialisation
🧠

Forms of money

  • Currency (notes issued by the RBI, coins minted by the government) is legal tender
  • Demand deposits with banks are also accepted as money because payments can be made by cheque, ATM, UPI or net banking
🌟

Banks and deposits

  • Banks accept deposits, pay interest, keep a fraction as cash reserve and lend the rest at higher interest
  • The difference is their income
🔬

Features of money

  • Good money is widely accepted, durable, divisible and stable in value
  • Inflation reduces its purchasing power
🧮

lessons.title: Credit, Loans and Self-Help Groups
yt: class 10 economics credit, loans and self-help groups

blocks.x: Credit (loan) is an agreement where the lender supplies money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment. Credit helps people earn more when used productively, as with Salim who borrowed to produce shoes, but it can also push borrowers into a debt trap if the crop fails or income falls. Terms of credit include interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment. Collateral is an asset the borrower owns, such as land or a house, pledged as security. Sources are formal (banks and cooperatives, supervised by the RBI, lower interest) and informal (moneylenders, traders, relatives, employers, with higher rates and no records). Poor households depend more on informal credit. Formal credit should expand. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) of 15 to 20 members, usually women, save regularly and give small loans at reasonable interest; after some time they get bank loans. The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh founded by Muhammad Yunus is an example of group lending without collateral.
Deep dive: credit and its terms

Credit lets people spend now and pay later. Terms include interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment. Credit can raise income if used productively (Salim's shoe order) but can create a debt trap when income falls (Swapna the farmer).
Deep dive: sources
Formal credit from banks and cooperatives is supervised by the RBI and cheaper. Informal credit from moneylenders is costly. The poor depend on informal sources; formal credit must expand.
Deep dive: SHGs
Self-Help Groups of 15-20 members, mostly women, save regularly, lend small amounts, keep records and build credit history for bank loans without collateral. Grameen Bank is a famous example.

Terms of credit include interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment. Collateral is an asset the borrower owns, such as land or a house, pledged as security. Sources are formal (banks and cooperatives, supervised by the RBI, lower interest) and informal (moneylenders, traders, relatives, employers, with higher rates and no records). Poor households depend more on informal credit. Formal credit should expand. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) of 15 to 20 members, usually women, save regularly and give small loans at reasonable interest; after some time they get bank loans. The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh founded by Muhammad Yunus is an example of group lending without collateral.

📌

Credit and its terms

  • Credit lets people spend now and pay later
  • Terms include interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment
  • Credit can raise income if used productively (Salim's shoe order) but can create a debt trap when income falls (Swapna the farmer)
🧠

Sources

  • Formal credit from banks and cooperatives is supervised by the RBI and cheaper
  • Informal credit from moneylenders is costly
  • The poor depend on informal sources
  • Formal credit must expand

blocks.x: Globalisation is the rapid integration among countries through foreign trade and foreign investment. Multinational corporations (MNCs) own or control production in more than one country; they set up offices and factories where costs are low. Foreign trade links markets of different countries, giving consumers more choice and prices. Foreign investment is the money spent by MNCs on assets such as land, buildings and machines; investment in a foreign country is Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) when it builds factories. Technology (transport, information and communication technology) and liberalisation (removal of trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas) in 1991 sped it up. The World Trade Organisation (WTO) sets rules for trade. India set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) with world-class facilities to attract investment. The impact has been unequal: producers in a few sectors benefited (cars, IT, services) while small producers suffered competition. Fair globalisation needs fair rules, labour protection and WTO reform.
Deep dive: what globalisation is
Globalisation links countries through trade, investment and movement of ideas. It is driven by MNCs, technology and liberalisation of trade and investment policies.
Deep dive: MNCs and production

MNCs spread production across countries to cut costs: design in one, manufacture in another, call centres elsewhere. They invest in or tie up with local firms through joint ventures and subcontracting.
Deep dive: 1991 liberalisation and the WTO
India removed trade barriers (tariffs and quotas) in 1991. The WTO frames trade rules, but richer nations have greater influence. SEZs attract foreign investment.
Deep dive: impact

Consumers gained choice; some Indian firms became MNCs; but small producers, workers in the unorganised sector and domestic industries faced competition and insecurity. Fair globalisation needs fair rules, worker protection and support to small producers.

lessons.title: Consumer Rights

blocks.x: Consumers need protection because producers and traders can cheat through adulteration, short weights, high prices and hidden risks. The consumer movement in India grew from hoarding, black marketing and adulteration. The Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) 1986, amended in 2019, set up a three-tier redressal system: District Consumer Commission, State Commission and National Commission. Consumer rights include the right to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal and to consumer education. Agencies such as the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) give the ISI mark, Agmark certifies agricultural goods, and Hallmark certifies gold purity. The Right to Information Act 2005 lets citizens seek government information. Consumer International is a global body. Consumers should check labels, MRP, expiry date, ISI or Agmark and always take a cash memo. The consumer movement grows through consumer forums and awareness: 24 December is National Consumer Day.
Deep dive: why protection is needed
Individual consumers are weak against large producers. Adulteration, short weights, hoarding and false advertising exploit them, so laws and consumer organisations are required.
Deep dive: rights
Safety, information, choice, representation, redressal and consumer education. These are protected by COPRA 1986 and its 2019 update, which covers e-commerce.
Deep dive: redressal
District, State and National Commissions hear cases by value. The consumer can seek refund, replacement or compensation. RTI 2005 gives access to government information.
Deep dive: being a smart consumer
Check MRP, expiry date, quantity, ISI, Agmark and Hallmark; keep the bill; compare prices; complain if cheated; and join consumer forums.

Visual lesson

Consumer Rights

Consumers need protection because producers and traders can cheat through adulteration, short weights, high prices and hidden risks

COPRA1986
Consumer Day24 December
🔑

Big idea

  • Consumers need protection because producers and traders can cheat through adulteration, short weights, high prices and hidden risks
  • The consumer movement in India grew from hoarding, black marketing and adulteration
  • The Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) 1986, amended in 2019, set up a three-tier redressal system: District Consumer Commission, State Commission and…
  • Consumer rights include the right to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal and to consumer education
Read the full explanation

Consumers need protection because producers and traders can cheat through adulteration, short weights, high prices and hidden risks. The consumer movement in India grew from hoarding, black marketing and adulteration. The Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) 1986, amended in 2019, set up a three-tier redressal system: District Consumer Commission, State Commission and National Commission. Consumer rights include the right to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal and to consumer education. Agencies such as the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) give the ISI mark, Agmark certifies agricultural goods, and Hallmark certifies gold purity. The Right to Information Act 2005 lets citizens seek government information. Consumer International is a global body. Consumers should check labels, MRP, expiry date, ISI or Agmark and always take a cash memo. The consumer movement grows through consumer forums and awareness: 24 December is National Consumer Day.

📌

Why protection is needed

  • Individual consumers are weak against large producers
  • Adulteration, short weights, hoarding and false advertising exploit them, so laws and consumer organisations are required
🏛️

Rights

  • Safety, information, choice, representation, redressal and consumer education
  • These are protected by COPRA 1986 and its 2019 update, which covers e-commerce
🌟

Redressal

  • District, State and National Commissions hear cases by value
  • The consumer can seek refund, replacement or compensation
  • RTI 2005 gives access to government information
🔬

Being a smart consumer

  • Check MRP, expiry date, quantity, ISI, Agmark and Hallmark
  • Keep the bill
  • Compare prices
  • Complain if cheated
Read the full explanation

Check MRP, expiry date, quantity, ISI, Agmark and Hallmark; keep the bill; compare prices; complain if cheated; and join consumer forums.

🧮

lessons.title: Tenses

blocks.x: A tense shows the time of an action. English has three main times (present, past, future), each with four forms (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Simple present: base verb (s/es with he/she/it); present continuous: is/am/are + ing; present perfect: has/have + past participle; simple past: second form; past continuous: was/were + ing; past perfect: had + past participle; simple future: will/shall + base verb; future continuous: will be + ing. Use simple present for habits and universal truths, present perfect for recent actions with present relevance, past perfect for the earlier of two past actions. In board exams, tenses are tested in gap-filling and error correction.
Deep dive: the twelve tenses

Present: simple (writes), continuous (is writing), perfect (has written), perfect continuous (has been writing). Past: wrote, was writing, had written, had been writing. Future: will write, will be writing, will have written, will have been writing.
Deep dive: usage

Simple present: habits and facts. Present perfect: recent actions or experience. Simple past: finished actions with time words. Past perfect: earlier past action. Use since for points and for for durations.
Deep dive: common errors
Don't use continuous forms with state verbs (know, want, love). Use present perfect, not simple past, with already, yet, just. Use the correct subject-auxiliary agreement.
Hindi saransh
काल क्रिया के समय को दर्शाता है — वर्तमान, भूतकाल और भविष्यत् — प्रत्येक के चार रूप। Simple present आदत के लिए, present perfect हाल की क्रिया के लिए, past perfect पहले हुई क्रिया के लिए।
Present perfect: has/have + V3. Past perfect: had + V3.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Tenses

A tense shows the time of an action

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2The twelve tenses›3Usage›4Common errors
Present perfecthas/have + V3
Past perfecthad + V3
Future simplewill + V1
🔑

Big idea

  • A tense shows the time of an action
  • English has three main times (present, past, future), each with four forms (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous)
  • Simple present: base verb (s/es with he/she/it)
  • Present continuous: is/am/are + ing
Read the full explanation

A tense shows the time of an action. English has three main times (present, past, future), each with four forms (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Simple present: base verb (s/es with he/she/it); present continuous: is/am/are + ing; present perfect: has/have + past participle; simple past: second form; past continuous: was/were + ing; past perfect: had + past participle; simple future: will/shall + base verb; future continuous: will be + ing. Use simple present for habits and universal truths, present perfect for recent actions with present relevance, past perfect for the earlier of two past actions. In board exams, tenses are tested in gap-filling and error correction.

📌

The twelve tenses

  • Present: simple (writes), continuous (is writing), perfect (has written), perfect continuous (has been writing)
  • Past: wrote, was writing, had written, had been writing
  • Future: will write, will be writing, will have written, will have been writing
🧠

Usage

  • Simple present: habits and facts
  • Present perfect: recent actions or experience
  • Simple past: finished actions with time words
  • Past perfect: earlier past action
Read the full explanation

Simple present: habits and facts. Present perfect: recent actions or experience. Simple past: finished actions with time words. Past perfect: earlier past action. Use since for points and for for durations.

🌟

Common errors

  • Don't use continuous forms with state verbs (know, want, love)
  • Use present perfect, not simple past, with already, yet, just
  • Use the correct subject-auxiliary agreement
🧮

Formula tiles

Present perfecthas/have + V3
Past perfecthad + V3
Future simplewill + V1
🎯 Remember Present perfect: has/have + V3. Past perfect: had + V3.
🇮🇳

हिंदी सार

काल क्रिया के समय को दर्शाता है — वर्तमान, भूतकाल और भविष्यत् — प्रत्येक के चार रूप। Simple present आदत के लिए, present perfect हाल की क्रिया के लिए, past perfect पहले हुई क्रिया के लिए।

lessons.title: Modals

blocks.x: Modal auxiliary verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would, ought to, need, dare, used to) express ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, prohibition, request, offer and probability. A modal is followed by the base form of the verb, has no -s in the third person and no infinitive "to" (except ought to), and forms questions and negatives without do. Can/could show ability; may/might permission and possibility; must obligation and strong deduction; should/ought to advice and moral duty; will/would future and politeness; shall for suggestions and offers with I/we; need not for lack of necessity.
Deep dive: forms
Modal + base verb: He can swim. Negative: cannot, must not, need not. Question: Can he swim?
Deep dive: meanings
Ability: can, could. Permission: may, can. Possibility: may, might. Obligation: must, have to. Advice: should, ought to. Request: could, would. Offer: shall, will.
Deep dive: errors
Never write "can sings" or "to" after modals (except ought to). Don't use two modals together.
Hindi saransh
मोडल सहायक क्रियाएँ योग्यता, अनुमति, संभावना, कर्तव्य और सलाह बताती हैं। इनके बाद क्रिया का मूल रूप आता है।
Modal + base verb; no -s, no to (except ought to).

🔑

Big idea

  • Modal auxiliary verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would, ought to, need, dare, used to) express ability, permission…
  • A modal is followed by the base form of the verb, has no -s in the third person and no infinitive "to" (except ought to), and forms questions and…
  • Can/could show ability

Read the full explanation

Modal auxiliary verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would, ought to, need, dare, used to) express ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, prohibition, request, offer and probability. A modal is followed by the base form of the verb, has no -s in the third person and no infinitive "to" (except ought to), and forms questions and negatives without do. Can/could show ability; may/might permission and possibility; must obligation and strong deduction; should/ought to advice and moral duty; will/would future and politeness; shall for suggestions and offers with I/we; need not for lack of necessity.

📌

Forms

  • Modal + base verb: He can swim
  • Negative: cannot, must not, need not
  • Question: Can he swim?
📘

Meanings

  • Ability: can, could
  • Permission: may, can
  • Possibility: may, might
  • Obligation: must, have to
Read the full explanation

Ability: can, could. Permission: may, can. Possibility: may, might. Obligation: must, have to. Advice: should, ought to. Request: could, would. Offer: shall, will.

🌟

Errors

  • Never write "can sings" or "to" after modals (except ought to)
  • Don't use two modals together
🧮

Formula tiles

Rulelearn the pattern and practise
🎯 Remember Modal + base verb; no -s, no to (except ought to).

lessons.title: Determiners

blocks.x: Determiners are words placed before nouns to show which one or how many. Types: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), quantifiers (some, any, much, many, few, a few, little, a little, all, enough), distributives (each, every, either, neither) and numerals (one, two, first, second). A or an is used with singular countable nouns for something mentioned for the first time; the is used for something specific or unique. Some is used in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions. Few and little have a negative sense; a few and a little have a positive sense; many is used with countable and much with uncountable nouns.
Deep dive: articles
A/an: first mention or any one; the: specific or unique. Use "an" before vowel sounds (an hour, an MLA), "a" before consonant sounds (a university, a one-rupee note).
Deep dive: quantifiers
Many/few with countable; much/little with uncountable. A few/a little = some; few/little = hardly any. Some for positives; any for negatives and questions.
Deep dive: distributives
Each, every, either, neither take singular verbs.
Hindi saransh
निर्धारक (determiner) संज्ञा से पहले आकर बताते हैं कि कौन-सा या कितना। a/an, the, some, any, few, little, much, many मुख्य निर्धारक हैं।
A few/a little = some (positive); few/little = hardly any (negative).

📌

Articles

  • A/an: first mention or any one
  • The: specific or unique
  • Use "an" before vowel sounds (an hour, an MLA), "a" before consonant sounds (a university, a one-rupee note)
🧠

Quantifiers

  • Many/few with countable
  • Much/little with uncountable
  • A few/a little = some
  • Few/little = hardly any
Read the full explanation

Many/few with countable; much/little with uncountable. A few/a little = some; few/little = hardly any. Some for positives; any for negatives and questions.

🌟

Distributives

  • Each, every, either, neither take singular verbs
