lessons.title: Reported Speech

blocks.x: Direct speech gives the exact words of a speaker inside quotation marks; indirect (reported) speech reports them without quotes, usually using "that". When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the tense of the reported clause shifts back: present becomes past, present continuous becomes past continuous, present perfect becomes past perfect, simple past becomes past perfect, will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might. Pronouns change according to the reporter, and time and place words shift: today to that day, tomorrow to the next day, yesterday to the previous day, now to then, here to there, this to that. For questions, use "asked" and normal word order with if/whether or the question word; for commands, use "ordered/told/requested" with an infinitive; for exclamations, use "exclaimed with joy/sorrow that".
Deep dive: statements
He said, "I am tired." → He said that he was tired. Pronouns shift by the reporter, tense by backshift, time and place words as per rules.
Deep dive: questions
She asked, "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived. Yes-no questions use if/whether.
Deep dive: commands, requests, exclamations
Commands: ordered/told + to-infinitive. Requests: requested. Exclamations: exclaimed with joy/sorrow that.

Deep dive: commands, requests, exclamations

Big idea

  • Direct speech gives the exact words of a speaker inside quotation marks
  • Indirect (reported) speech reports them without quotes, usually using "that"
  • When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the tense of the reported clause shifts back: present becomes past, present continuous becomes past…
  • Pronouns change according to the reporter, and time and place words shift: today to that day, tomorrow to the next day, yesterday to the previous…
Read the full explanation

Direct speech gives the exact words of a speaker inside quotation marks; indirect (reported) speech reports them without quotes, usually using "that". When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the tense of the reported clause shifts back: present becomes past, present continuous becomes past continuous, present perfect becomes past perfect, simple past becomes past perfect, will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might. Pronouns change according to the reporter, and time and place words shift: today to that day, tomorrow to the next day, yesterday to the previous day, now to then, here to there, this to that. For questions, use "asked" and normal word order with if/whether or the question word; for commands, use "ordered/told/requested" with an infinitive; for exclamations, use "exclaimed with joy/sorrow that".

📌

Statements

  • He said, "I am tired." → He said that he was tired
  • Pronouns shift by the reporter, tense by backshift, time and place words as per rules
🧠

Questions

  • She asked, "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived
  • Yes-no questions use if/whether
🌟

Commands, requests, exclamations

  • Commands: ordered/told + to-infinitive
  • Requests: requested
  • Exclamations: exclaimed with joy/sorrow that

lessons.title: Active and Passive Voice
yt: class 10 english active and passive voice

blocks.x: In the active voice the subject performs the action; in the passive voice the subject receives the action. To change an active sentence into passive: the object of the active becomes the subject; the verb changes to the form of "be" in the same tense plus the past participle; and the active subject becomes the agent introduced by "by" (often omitted when unknown or unimportant). Structures: simple present - is/am/are + V3; simple past - was/were + V3; present perfect - has/have been + V3; future - will be + V3; present continuous - is/am/are being + V3; past continuous - was/were being + V3; modals - modal + be + V3. Only transitive verbs can be made passive. Imperative sentences use "Let ... be + V3" or "You are requested to". Questions begin with the auxiliary or wh-word in the passive.
Deep dive: steps

x: Identify subject, verb, object. 2. Move object to subject position. 3. Use be (same tense) + V3. 4. Add by + former subject (if needed). 5. Adjust pronouns (I→me, he→him).

blocks.x: Deep dive: structures
Present: is/am/are written. Past: was/were written. Perfect: has/have been written. Future: will be written. Continuous: is being written, was being written. Modal: can be written.
Deep dive: questions and commands
Did he write the letter? → Was the letter written by him? Open the door. → Let the door be opened.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Active and Passive Voice

In the active voice the subject performs the action

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Steps›3Structures›4Questions and commands
🔑

Big idea

  • In the active voice the subject performs the action
  • In the passive voice the subject receives the action
  • To change an active sentence into passive: the object of the active becomes the subject
  • The verb changes to the form of "be" in the same tense plus the past participle
Read the full explanation

In the active voice the subject performs the action; in the passive voice the subject receives the action. To change an active sentence into passive: the object of the active becomes the subject; the verb changes to the form of "be" in the same tense plus the past participle; and the active subject becomes the agent introduced by "by" (often omitted when unknown or unimportant). Structures: simple present - is/am/are + V3; simple past - was/were + V3; present perfect - has/have been + V3; future - will be + V3; present continuous - is/am/are being + V3; past continuous - was/were being + V3; modals - modal + be + V3. Only transitive verbs can be made passive. Imperative sentences use "Let ... be + V3" or "You are requested to". Questions begin with the auxiliary or wh-word in the passive.

🔄

Steps

  • Identify subject, verb, object. 2. Move object to subject position. 3. Use be (same tense) + V3. 4. Add by + former subject (if needed). 5. Adjust…
🧠

Structures

  • Present: is/am/are written
  • Past: was/were written
  • Perfect: has/have been written
  • Future: will be written
Read the full explanation

Present: is/am/are written. Past: was/were written. Perfect: has/have been written. Future: will be written. Continuous: is being written, was being written. Modal: can be written.

🌟

Questions and commands

  • Did he write the letter?
  • → Was the letter written by him?
  • Open the door
  • → Let the door be opened
🧮

🎯 Remember Passive = be (same tense) + V3; object becomes subject.

blocks.x: In CBSE Class 10 grammar, three question types test usage: gap filling (choose the right word or form to complete a passage or sentence), editing (find the error in a line and write the correct word, often involving tense, articles, prepositions, agreement, and a word missing), and omission (find the missing word in a line and write it with the word before and after it). Strategies: read the whole passage first; check tense consistency, subject-verb agreement, prepositions, articles, conjunctions and the logical meaning; use the clues given. For sentence reordering, find the opening sentence, link pronouns to nouns, and use connectors.
Deep dive: gap filling
Read the passage for context and choose forms that fit tense, number and meaning.
Deep dive: editing
Typical errors: tense, subject-verb agreement, prepositions, articles, wrong word forms. Correct only the marked word.
Deep dive: omission
A word is missing in each line; write the word before it, the missing word and the word after it.
Deep dive: reordering
Find the opening line, track pronoun references and connectors, and test the logical flow.

lessons.title: Formal Letter Writing

blocks.x: A formal letter is written to an official, an editor, a principal, a company or the public. The CBSE format has: sender's address, date, receiver's designation and address, subject line, salutation (Sir/Madam), body (introduction, details, request), complimentary close (Yours faithfully) and signature with name. Types are letters of inquiry, placing an order, complaint, application for a job or for a school purpose, and letters to the editor. The language must be polite, concise and to the point, in three paragraphs, with a clear subject line and no abbreviations. Include all details such as quantity, price, delivery and date in orders, and facts, effects and remedy in complaints.
Deep dive: format
Sender's address; date; receiver's designation and address; Subject; Sir/Madam; body in 3 paragraphs; Yours faithfully; signature and name.
Deep dive: types

Inquiry: ask for details, rates, delivery. Order: list items, quantity, price, date. Complaint: facts, effects, action. Application: qualifications and availability. Letter to the editor: issue, cause, suggestions.
Deep dive: tips
Be polite and precise; avoid contractions and slang; write within the word limit; proofread.
Hindi saransh
औपचारिक पत्र प्रधानाचार्य, संपादक, कंपनी या अधिकारी को लिखा जाता है। इसमें प्रेषक का पता, तिथि, प्राप्तकर्ता, विषय, अभिवादन, मूल पाठ और समापन होता है। भाषा विनम्र और संक्षिप्त हो।

lessons.title: Analytical Paragraph

blocks.x: An analytical paragraph (about 100 to 120 words) presents a clear, concise analysis of the data shown in a chart, graph, table or map. Steps: read the title and labels, note the highest and lowest values, trends, comparisons and percentages, write a topic sentence, give 3 to 4 key observations with figures, make a comparison or conclusion, and avoid personal opinions. Use present tense for general facts and past tense for past years, and link ideas with connectors such as whereas, while, however, in contrast, overall and therefore. Useful phrases: "increased steadily", "declined sharply", "remained constant", "accounts for", "the majority of", "comparatively".
Deep dive: steps
Read the title; note highest, lowest and trends; compute percentages if needed; write topic sentence; add 3-4 key details with connectors; end with a conclusion.
Deep dive: language
Increase: rose, grew. Decrease: fell, declined. Constant: remained steady. Compare with: whereas, while, in contrast.
Deep dive: caution
Use only given data; avoid personal opinion; keep within 120 words.
Hindi saransh
विश्लेषणात्मक अनुच्छेद चार्ट, ग्राफ या तालिका के आँकड़ों का संक्षिप्त विश्लेषण होता है। उच्चतम-निम्नतम मान, प्रवृत्ति और तुलना लिखें; अपनी राय न लिखें।
Topic sentence + key data + comparison + conclusion; no personal opinion.

🔑

Big idea

  • An analytical paragraph (about 100 to 120 words) presents a clear, concise analysis of the data shown in a chart, graph, table or map
  • Steps: read the title and labels, note the highest and lowest values, trends, comparisons and percentages, write a topic sentence, give 3 to 4 key…

Read the full explanation

An analytical paragraph (about 100 to 120 words) presents a clear, concise analysis of the data shown in a chart, graph, table or map. Steps: read the title and labels, note the highest and lowest values, trends, comparisons and percentages, write a topic sentence, give 3 to 4 key observations with figures, make a comparison or conclusion, and avoid personal opinions. Use present tense for general facts and past tense for past years, and link ideas with connectors such as whereas, while, however, in contrast, overall and therefore. Useful phrases: "increased steadily", "declined sharply", "remained constant", "accounts for", "the majority of", "comparatively".

🔄

Steps

  • Read the title
  • Note highest, lowest and trends
  • Compute percentages if needed
  • Write topic sentence
Read the full explanation

Read the title; note highest, lowest and trends; compute percentages if needed; write topic sentence; add 3-4 key details with connectors; end with a conclusion.

🧠

Language

  • Increase: rose, grew
  • Decrease: fell, declined
  • Constant: remained steady
  • Compare with: whereas, while, in contrast
🌟

Caution

  • Use only given data
  • Avoid personal opinion
  • Keep within 120 words
🧮

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension and Vocabulary
yt: class 10 english reading comprehension and vocabulary

blocks.x: The reading section tests understanding of unseen factual, discursive and literary passages through multiple-choice questions, short answers, vocabulary-in-context, inference and main-idea questions. Skills: skim for the main idea, scan for specific details, read the questions first, locate evidence in the text, and infer meaning from context. Vocabulary includes synonyms, antonyms, prefixes, suffixes, idioms, one-word substitutes and commonly confused words. Answers should be brief and in your own words, based only on the passage, with correct grammar.
Deep dive: strategies
Read questions first, skim for the main idea, scan for evidence, and answer in your own words. For vocabulary-in-context, test each option in the sentence.
Deep dive: question types
MCQs, short answers, inference, vocabulary, true/false, title. Support answers with evidence.
Deep dive: vocabulary
Synonyms, antonyms, prefixes (un-, re-, dis-), suffixes (-ness, -ment), idioms and one-word substitutes broaden word power.

blocks.x: Literary devices are techniques writers use to create effect. Important devices are simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration, onomatopoeia, hyperbole, irony, imagery, symbolism, repetition, oxymoron, transferred epithet and rhyme. lessons.title: A Letter to God
yt: class 10 english a letter to god

blocks.x: "A Letter to God" by Gregorio Lopez y Fuentes is about Lencho, a poor farmer whose ripe fields of corn and beans are destroyed by a hailstorm after he waits eagerly for the rain. With unshaken faith, he writes a letter to God asking for one hundred pesos to sow his field again. The postmaster, moved by the letter, collects money from employees and friends but manages only seventy pesos. Lencho finds only seventy pesos in the envelope, believes God cannot have made a mistake, and writes again demanding the remaining thirty, blaming the post-office employees as thieves. The story shows faith, human kindness and irony.
Deep dive: summary

Lencho, a farmer, longs for rain to ripen his corn. A sudden hailstorm ruins everything. He writes to God for one hundred pesos. The postmaster collects seventy pesos and sends them as God's reply. Lencho suspects the post office of stealing the remaining thirty and writes again.
Deep dive: characters
Lencho is hard-working, simple and has unshakable faith but is also narrow in judgement. The postmaster is kind and imaginative, taking on the role of God to preserve faith.
Deep dive: themes
Faith, kindness, the helplessness of farmers before nature, and irony: Lencho trusts God but not the people through whom God seems to act.
Deep dive: literary devices
Similes (raindrops like new coins, hail like frozen silver), irony, and a simple third-person narrative.
Hindi saransh

लेंचो एक गरीब किसान है जिसकी फसल ओलावृष्टि से नष्ट हो जाती है। वह भगवान को पत्र लिखकर सौ पेसो माँगता है। पोस्टमास्टर सत्तर पेसो भेज देता है। लेंचो अगले पत्र में शेष तीस पेसो माँगता है और डाकघर कर्मचारियों को चोर कहता है।
Theme: faith, human kindness and irony. Lencho trusts God but distrusts people.

Big idea

  • With unshaken faith, he writes a letter to God asking for one hundred pesos to sow his field again

Read the full explanation

"A Letter to God" by Gregorio Lopez y Fuentes is about Lencho, a poor farmer whose ripe fields of corn and beans are destroyed by a hailstorm after he waits eagerly for the rain. With unshaken faith, he writes a letter to God asking for one hundred pesos to sow his field again. The postmaster, moved by the letter, collects money from employees and friends but manages only seventy pesos. Lencho finds only seventy pesos in the envelope, believes God cannot have made a mistake, and writes again demanding the remaining thirty, blaming the post-office employees as thieves. The story shows faith, human kindness and irony.

📌

Summary

  • Lencho, a farmer, longs for rain to ripen his corn
  • A sudden hailstorm ruins everything
  • He writes to God for one hundred pesos
  • The postmaster collects seventy pesos and sends them as God's reply
Read the full explanation

Lencho, a farmer, longs for rain to ripen his corn. A sudden hailstorm ruins everything. He writes to God for one hundred pesos. The postmaster collects seventy pesos and sends them as God's reply. Lencho suspects the post office of stealing the remaining thirty and writes again.

🧠

Characters

  • Lencho is hard-working, simple and has unshakable faith but is also narrow in judgement
  • The postmaster is kind and imaginative, taking on the role of God to preserve faith
🌟

Themes

  • Faith, kindness, the helplessness of farmers before nature, and irony: Lencho trusts God but not the people through whom God seems to act
🔬

Literary devices

  • Similes (raindrops like new coins, hail like frozen silver), irony, and a simple third-person narrative

blocks.x: This extract from Nelson Mandela's autobiography describes his inauguration as the first democratic, non-racial President of South Africa in May 1994, held in the amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria. Thousands of dignitaries from across the world attended. Mandela reflects on the long struggle against apartheid, the unity of the new nation and the gratitude owed to freedom fighters. He says that the sun must never set on so glorious a human achievement. He recalls the loyalty of the former military generals who saluted him, the singing of two anthems and his learning that courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. He ends with the thought that freedom means liberating both the oppressed and the oppressor, and he describes the four ideals of courage, love of freedom, the role of heroes and the cost of apartheid.
Deep dive: the occasion
The inauguration at Pretoria on 10 May 1994 ended centuries of white-minority rule. Over a hundred international leaders attended; the military saluted the new president.
Deep dive: reflections on courage
Mandela says he learned that bravery is not lack of fear. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.
Deep dive: freedom for all
Freedom means breaking the chains of both oppressed and oppressor. Both are robbed of humanity. The new nation must work for the dignity of all.
Deep dive: values
Gratitude to those who sacrificed, unity of the nation, courage in difficulty and responsibility to build a just society.

lessons.title: Two Stories about Flying
yt: class 10 english two stories about flying

blocks.x: This chapter has two parts. In "His First Flight" by Liam O'Flaherty, a young seagull is afraid to fly while his two brothers and sisters have already learned. His parents, brothers and sisters taunt and encourage him. When his mother tempts him with a piece of fish from a distance, he is hungry and finally leaps off the ledge and discovers that he can fly. In "The Black Aeroplane" by Frederick Forsyth, a pilot flying from France to England at night enters a storm. A mysterious black aeroplane appears and guides him; he follows it and lands safely. At the control tower, the lady says no other plane had been in the sky. The pilot realises that his own guidance may have been a mystery.
Deep dive: His First Flight

The young seagull's fear holds him back; his family cannot persuade him. Hunger and his mother's fish finally make him dive off the ledge. He discovers he can fly. The story shows that fear is overcome by action and encouragement.
Deep dive: The Black Aeroplane
The pilot flies through a storm with failing instruments. A black plane leads him to safety. At the airport nobody saw another plane, leaving a mystery.
Deep dive: themes
Overcoming fear, courage under pressure, support from family, and the unexplained.

His First Flight: fear vs hunger. The Black Aeroplane: mystery and courage.

Two Stories about Flying

Big idea

  • This chapter has two parts

  • His parents, brothers and sisters taunt and encourage him
  • When his mother tempts him with a piece of fish from a distance, he is hungry and finally leaps off the ledge and discovers that he can fly
Read the full explanation

This chapter has two parts. In "His First Flight" by Liam O'Flaherty, a young seagull is afraid to fly while his two brothers and sisters have already learned. His parents, brothers and sisters taunt and encourage him. When his mother tempts him with a piece of fish from a distance, he is hungry and finally leaps off the ledge and discovers that he can fly. In "The Black Aeroplane" by Frederick Forsyth, a pilot flying from France to England at night enters a storm. A mysterious black aeroplane appears and guides him; he follows it and lands safely. At the control tower, the lady says no other plane had been in the sky. The pilot realises that his own guidance may have been a mystery.

🔦

His First Flight

  • The young seagull's fear holds him back
  • His family cannot persuade him
  • Hunger and his mother's fish finally make him dive off the ledge
  • He discovers he can fly
Read the full explanation

The young seagull's fear holds him back; his family cannot persuade him. Hunger and his mother's fish finally make him dive off the ledge. He discovers he can fly. The story shows that fear is overcome by action and encouragement.

🧠

The Black Aeroplane

  • The pilot flies through a storm with failing instruments
  • A black plane leads him to safety
  • At the airport nobody saw another plane, leaving a mystery
🌟

Themes

  • Overcoming fear, courage under pressure, support from family, and the unexplained

lessons.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
yt: class 10 english from the diary of anne frank

blocks.x: Anne Frank, a Jewish girl from Germany, went into hiding in Amsterdam during the Second World War. She received a diary on her thirteenth birthday and addressed it as "Kitty". In these extracts she writes that paper has more patience than people and that she wants to share her thoughts with a true friend. She describes her family: her father Otto, mother, sister Margot, and her life at school, her friend Jacqueline (Jopie), her interest in Peter, and the restrictions imposed by the Nazis on Jews. The diary shows her loneliness, wit, maturity and need for understanding.
Deep dive: background
Anne Frank was born in 1929 in Frankfurt and moved to Amsterdam. During Nazi occupation, her family hid from 1942 to 1944. She kept her diary until August 1944.
Deep dive: reason for the diary
Anne had many friends but no real one; so she writes to Kitty, making it a confidant with whom she can be herself.
Deep dive: restrictions
Jews had to wear the yellow star, hand in bicycles, not use trams or cars, shop only 3-5 p.m., and be home by 8 p.m.
Deep dive: character
Anne is lively, witty, observant, and mature beyond her years; her diary becomes a symbol of hope amid persecution.

ऐनी फ्रैंक यहूदी लड़की थी जिसने अपनी डायरी को "किट्टी" नाम दिया। उसे अकेलापन महसूस होता था और वह एक सच्चे मित्र की तरह डायरी से बात करती थी।
Anne's diary is addressed to Kitty, her imaginary friend.

lessons.title: Glimpses of India

blocks.x: This chapter has three parts. "A Baker from Goa" by Lucio Rodrigues describes the Goan baker, or pader, whose bread, bol and other items remain an essential part of Goan life even after the Portuguese left; the baker comes with a bamboo staff to announce his arrival, wears a kabai, and bakes bread in a furnace. "Coorg" describes the beautiful hill district of Karnataka, its coffee plantations, brave Kodava people who are said to be descended from Arabs or Kurds, and the Kaveri river. "Tea from Assam" follows two friends, Rajvir and Pranjol, on a train to Assam; Pranjol's father is a tea planter, and the boys see vast tea gardens and learn the legend that tea was discovered by a Chinese emperor and its Indian origin in Assam.
Deep dive: A Baker from Goa

The pader and his family are a living link to Goa's Portuguese past. Bread is eaten daily and bol is a gift for marriages. The baker visits twice a day, collects payment at month end and is a part of every household.
Deep dive: Coorg
Coorg is a hill district known for its coffee, spices, rivers and the brave Kodavas. It has given India top army officers. Tourists enjoy trekking, rafting and misty hills.
Deep dive: Tea from Assam

Rajvir and Pranjol take a train to Assam. Mr Barua's estate shows large tea gardens; tea is plucked by workers. The legend says tea was discovered when leaves fell into hot water of a Chinese emperor.
Deep dive: unity
All three parts show diversity of India: food, hills and plantations.
Hindi saransh
तीन भाग हैं: गोवा के बेकर (पादर), कुर्ग (कर्नाटक) और असम की चाय। पादर पुर्तगाली प्रभाव वाला पारंपरिक बेकर है जिसकी रोटी आज भी गोवा के जीवन का हिस्सा है।
A Baker from Goa: pader; Coorg: Kodavas and coffee; Tea from Assam: Pranjol and Rajvir.

  • The baker comes with a bamboo staff to announce his arrival, wears a kabai, and bakes bread in a furnace

Read the full explanation

This chapter has three parts. "A Baker from Goa" by Lucio Rodrigues describes the Goan baker, or pader, whose bread, bol and other items remain an essential part of Goan life even after the Portuguese left; the baker comes with a bamboo staff to announce his arrival, wears a kabai, and bakes bread in a furnace. "Coorg" describes the beautiful hill district of Karnataka, its coffee plantations, brave Kodava people who are said to be descended from Arabs or Kurds, and the Kaveri river. "Tea from Assam" follows two friends, Rajvir and Pranjol, on a train to Assam; Pranjol's father is a tea planter, and the boys see vast tea gardens and learn the legend that tea was discovered by a Chinese emperor and its Indian origin in Assam.

📌

A Baker from Goa

  • The pader and his family are a living link to Goa's Portuguese past
  • Bread is eaten daily and bol is a gift for marriages
  • The baker visits twice a day, collects payment at month end and is a part of every household
🧠

Coorg

  • Coorg is a hill district known for its coffee, spices, rivers and the brave Kodavas
  • It has given India top army officers
  • Tourists enjoy trekking, rafting and misty hills
🌟

Tea from Assam

  • Rajvir and Pranjol take a train to Assam
  • Mr Barua's estate shows large tea gardens
  • Tea is plucked by workers
  • The legend says tea was discovered when leaves fell into hot water of a Chinese emperor
🔬

Unity

  • All three parts show diversity of India: food, hills and plantations
🧮

lessons.title: Mijbil the Otter

blocks.x: In this extract from "Ring of Bright Water", Gavin Maxwell tells how he brought a pet otter named Mij from the marshes of Iraq to England. Maxwell had been given the otter by Wilfred Thesiger and brought it in a box to England. During the flight, Mij escaped from the box, caused chaos in the aircraft, and was recaptured. In London, Mij was kept in Maxwell's flat and loved to play with water, a rubber ball and marbles. He was playful, curious, obstinate and affectionate. Maxwell loved him as a pet, and his fascination for water led him to hold the bath tub filled with water.
Deep dive: the rescue
Maxwell was given an otter in Iraq by Thesiger. He named it Mijbil after the marsh village. He took Mij to England in a box.
Deep dive: the flight
During the flight Mij escaped, creating chaos. Maxwell recaptured him, showing patience and love.
Deep dive: life in London
Mij loved water, played with a ball, learnt to respond and enjoyed bathing. His behaviour showed fascination for water.
Deep dive: themes
Love for animals, patience, humour, and curiosity of nature.

yt: class 10 english madam rides the bus

blocks.x: Vallikkannan's story is about Valli, an eight-year-old girl in a South Indian village who is fascinated by the bus that passes through the village. She saves coins and decides to take a ride to the nearby town and back. She boards the bus, enjoys the scenery, notices people and wonders about the world, and behaves like a mature lady to impress the conductor. On the return journey, she sees a dead cow on the road; this shocks her and ends her joy. The story shows childish enthusiasm, the transition to realism, and the contrast between dreams and harsh truth.
Deep dive: plot
Valli saves coins, boards the bus in the morning, enjoys her ride and arrives in town, then returns, but sees a dead cow, which changes her mood.
Deep dive: characters
Valli is curious, bold and sensitive; the conductor treats her kindly; the old woman and passengers reflect different attitudes.
Deep dive: themes
Childhood curiosity, freedom, change from innocence to awareness, and the harshness of reality.
Deep dive: devices
Contrast (joy vs sorrow), imagery of rural India, and symbolism of the dead cow.

lessons.title: The Sermon at Benares
yt: class 10 english the sermon at benares

blocks.x: Gautama Buddha was born as Prince Siddhartha, left his palace, and attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. His first sermon was at Sarnath near Benares (Varanasi). The chapter narrates the story of Kisa Gotami, a young woman whose only son died. Overcome with grief, she carried the body and begged for medicine. The Buddha asked her to bring a handful of mustard seed from a house where no one had died. She went door to door but found no such house. She realised that death comes to all and accepted it, and then became his disciple. The Buddha taught that life is full of suffering, that desire causes suffering, and that peace comes by following the Eightfold Path.
Deep dive: background
The Buddha preached his first sermon near Benares and told the story of Kisa Gotami to show that death is universal. His teachings focus on suffering, its cause, its end and the path.
Deep dive: the story
Kisa Gotami tried to save her dead son. The Buddha asked for mustard seed from a house untouched by death. She discovered that no such home exists and accepted the truth.
Deep dive: teachings
Life brings suffering; desire is its root; liberation is possible through the Eightfold Path.
Deep dive: moral
Understanding grief as shared helps us bear it.
Hindi saransh
बुद्ध ने बनारस के पास सारनाथ में पहला उपदेश दिया। किसा गौतमी का पुत्र मर गया तो बुद्ध ने उससे ऐसे घर से सरसों के दाने लाने को कहा जहाँ किसी की मृत्यु न हुई हो। उसे समझ आया कि मृत्यु सबके लिए है।
Death is universal; one must accept and move on.

Big idea

  • His first sermon was at Sarnath near Benares (Varanasi)
  • The chapter narrates the story of Kisa Gotami, a young woman whose only son died

Read the full explanation

Gautama Buddha was born as Prince Siddhartha, left his palace, and attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. His first sermon was at Sarnath near Benares (Varanasi). The chapter narrates the story of Kisa Gotami, a young woman whose only son died. Overcome with grief, she carried the body and begged for medicine. The Buddha asked her to bring a handful of mustard seed from a house where no one had died. She went door to door but found no such house. She realised that death comes to all and accepted it, and then became his disciple. The Buddha taught that life is full of suffering, that desire causes suffering, and that peace comes by following the Eightfold Path.

📌

Background

  • The Buddha preached his first sermon near Benares and told the story of Kisa Gotami to show that death is universal
  • His teachings focus on suffering, its cause, its end and the path
✍️

The story

  • Kisa Gotami tried to save her dead son
  • The Buddha asked for mustard seed from a house untouched by death
  • She discovered that no such home exists and accepted the truth
🌟

Teachings

  • Life brings suffering
  • Desire is its root
  • Liberation is possible through the Eightfold Path
🔬

Moral

  • Understanding grief as shared helps us bear it

lessons.title: The Proposal

blocks.x: "The Proposal" is a one-act farce by Anton Chekhov. Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov, a nervous and hypochondriac landowner, visits his neighbour Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov to propose to his daughter Natalya Stepanovna. Before he can finish, he starts quarrelling with Natalya over who owns the Oxen Meadows. Chubukov joins in, and Lomov leaves angrily with palpitations. When they hear that he came to propose, Natalya wants him called back. The quarrel resumes over whose dog, Guess or Squeezer, is better. Finally, Chubukov joins their hands and they agree to marry while still arguing. The play satirises marriage for property.
Deep dive: plot
Lomov comes to propose to Natalya but they quarrel about Oxen Meadows; he faints; after waking he is called back; they quarrel again about dogs; Chubukov joins them and orders champagne.
Deep dive: characters
Lomov is nervous and sensitive; Natalya is proud and quick-tempered; Chubukov is loud and interfering.
Deep dive: themes
The play satirises property-driven marriage, pride, and trivial disputes.
Deep dive: devices
Farce, irony, humour, fast-moving dialogue and comic repetition.

lessons.title: Dust of Snow

blocks.x: "Dust of Snow" by Robert Frost is a short eight-line poem in two stanzas. The speaker is in a bad mood when a crow shakes some snow from a hemlock tree onto him. This small natural event changes his mood and saves part of a day he had regretted. The poem shows that nature has the power to heal sadness through simple things. The crow and hemlock, usually symbols of sorrow and poison, bring joy and hope instead.
Deep dive: summary
A crow sitting on a hemlock tree shakes snow onto the speaker. The simple event cheers him and rescues part of a day he had felt was wasted.
Deep dive: symbols
Crow and hemlock normally suggest gloom, yet they change the speaker's mood.
Deep dive: theme
Nature has the power to heal and renew.
Deep dive: devices
Imagery, symbolism, contrast, and simple rhyme.

फ्रॉस्ट की कविता में कौआ हेमलॉक पेड़ से बर्फ़ गिराता है जिससे कवि का उदास मन प्रसन्न हो जाता है।
A small event in nature changes the mood and saves the day.

Big idea

  • "Dust of Snow" by Robert Frost is a short eight-line poem in two stanzas

  • This small natural event changes his mood and saves part of a day he had regretted

Read the full explanation

"Dust of Snow" by Robert Frost is a short eight-line poem in two stanzas. The speaker is in a bad mood when a crow shakes some snow from a hemlock tree onto him. This small natural event changes his mood and saves part of a day he had regretted. The poem shows that nature has the power to heal sadness through simple things. The crow and hemlock, usually symbols of sorrow and poison, bring joy and hope instead.

📌

Summary

  • A crow sitting on a hemlock tree shakes snow onto the speaker
  • The simple event cheers him and rescues part of a day he had felt was wasted
🧠

Symbols

  • Crow and hemlock normally suggest gloom, yet they change the speaker's mood
🌟

Theme

  • Nature has the power to heal and renew
🔬

Devices

  • Imagery, symbolism, contrast, and simple rhyme

lessons.title: Fire and Ice

blocks.x: In "Fire and Ice", Robert Frost says some people believe the world will end in fire while others say ice. Based on his experience of desire, he favours fire; but if the world had to perish twice, he knows enough of hate to say that ice is also great and would suffice. Fire stands for desire and passion while ice stands for hatred and indifference. Both can destroy humanity. The poem is a warning against uncontrolled desire and hatred.
Deep dive: summary
Frost compares two possible ends of the world. Fire stands for desire; ice for hatred. He favours fire from experience but says ice is equally destructive.
Deep dive: symbols
Fire: greed, lust, anger. Ice: cold hatred, indifference. Both lead to destruction.
Deep dive: message
Human emotions have the power to destroy; we must control them.
Deep dive: devices
Symbolism, understatement, brevity and rhyme.

lessons.title: A Tiger in the Zoo
yt: class 10 english a tiger in the zoo

blocks.x: Leslie Norris's poem contrasts a tiger in a zoo cage with one in the wild. In the cage, the tiger moves with soft strides, stares into the dark and stalks around the bars, full of anger and a thirst for freedom. In his imagination, he stalks the jungle where he would hunt near the village at night; but now he is confined, ignoring the sights of visitors and the sounds of cars on the zoo's outside road. The poem draws sympathy for captive animals and criticises caging wild creatures.
Deep dive: summary
A tiger pacing in a zoo cage is full of rage and longing. In imagination he roams the forest.
Deep dive: contrast
Captive: soft footsteps, silent fury. Wild: power, hunting near villages and moving freely.
Deep dive: message
Keeping wild animals in cages is cruel; they belong in their habitats.
Deep dive: devices
Contrast, imagery, symbolism and personification.
Hindi saransh
चिड़ियाघर के पिंजरे में बाघ आज़ादी के लिए तड़पता है। कवि पिंजरे में कैद और जंगल के बाघ की तुलना करता है।
Captivity vs freedom of wild animals.

Leslie Norris's poem contrasts a tiger in a zoo cage with one in the wild. In the cage, the tiger moves with soft strides, stares into the dark and stalks around the bars, full of anger and a thirst for freedom. In his imagination, he stalks the jungle where he would hunt near the village at night; but now he is confined, ignoring the sights of visitors and the sounds of cars on the zoo's outside road. The poem draws sympathy for captive animals and criticises caging wild creatures.

  • In imagination he roams the forest
🧠

Contrast

  • Wild: power, hunting near villages and moving freely
🌟

Message

  • Keeping wild animals in cages is cruel
  • They belong in their habitats

lessons.title: The Ball Poem

blocks.x: In "The Ball Poem" by John Berryman, the poet watches a little boy whose ball has bounced away and rolled into the water. The boy is deeply upset. The poet thinks of how the boy will learn through loss. He says that money cannot replace the ball because such loss is personal, and that the boy must learn to cope with loss and take responsibility. Standing there, the boy understands that things get lost and growing up involves handling grief. The poem teaches the first lesson in life: how to stand up after loss.
Deep dive: summary
A boy loses his ball in the water. The poet reflects that the boy must learn to bear loss; money cannot replace lost things.
Deep dive: symbolism
Ball: childhood and innocence. Harbour: the larger world of experiences.
Deep dive: message
Growing up means learning to face loss with courage and responsibility.
Deep dive: form
A reflective free-verse poem with a sympathetic tone.
Hindi saransh
एक बच्चे की गेंद पानी में चली जाती है। कवि बताता है कि वह नुकसान सहना और जिम्मेदारी सीख रहा है। पैसे से उसकी गेंद की जगह नहीं भरी जा सकती।
The boy learns about loss and responsibility; money cannot replace feelings.

Read the full explanation

In "The Ball Poem" by John Berryman, the poet watches a little boy whose ball has bounced away and rolled into the water. The boy is deeply upset. The poet thinks of how the boy will learn through loss. He says that money cannot replace the ball because such loss is personal, and that the boy must learn to cope with loss and take responsibility. Standing there, the boy understands that things get lost and growing up involves handling grief. The poem teaches the first lesson in life: how to stand up after loss.

📌

Summary

  • A boy loses his ball in the water
  • The poet reflects that the boy must learn to bear loss
  • Money cannot replace lost things
🧠

Symbolism

  • Ball: childhood and innocence
  • Harbour: the larger world of experiences
🌟

Message

  • Growing up means learning to face loss with courage and responsibility
🔬

Form

The poem is a gentle comment on how adults and children see the world and how constant nagging makes a child long for freedom.

Amanda is told what to do all day. She imagines herself as a mermaid and as an orphan like Rapunzel to escape.

Deep dive: theme
Children need freedom and imagination; constant correction hurts.

Contrast, humour, repetition, imagery and rhyme.

lessons.title: The Trees

blocks.x: In "The Trees", Adrienne Rich describes trees in the forest moving towards the house. Through the night, the trees stir; they are no longer silent, and they push to go outside. Their roots are tangled and the leaves seek their own space. The poet is in the house, and the trees, like women in confined spaces, struggle for freedom. At the end the moon is up and the trees seem to be going out into the forest again. The poem symbolises the desire of women, or any living creature, to escape confinement and be free.
Deep dive: summary
At night the trees inside the house struggle to go back to the forest. Their leaves and roots strain outward. The moon watches their escape.
Deep dive: symbolism
Trees stand for living beings, especially women, who long for freedom from confinement.
Deep dive: theme
Nature's desire for freedom and the need for liberty for all.
Deep dive: devices
Personification, imagery, symbolism and free verse.
Hindi saransh
कविता में पेड़ घर की ओर बढ़ते हैं और बाहर निकलने के लिए संघर्ष करते हैं। यह स्वतंत्रता की चाह का प्रतीक है।
Trees = nature (and women) seeking freedom from confinement.

The Trees

In "The Trees", Adrienne Rich describes trees in the forest moving towards the house

🔑

Big idea

  • In "The Trees", Adrienne Rich describes trees in the forest moving towards the house
  • Through the night, the trees stir
  • They are no longer silent, and they push to go outside
  • Their roots are tangled and the leaves seek their own space
Read the full explanation

In "The Trees", Adrienne Rich describes trees in the forest moving towards the house. Through the night, the trees stir; they are no longer silent, and they push to go outside. Their roots are tangled and the leaves seek their own space. The poet is in the house, and the trees, like women in confined spaces, struggle for freedom. At the end the moon is up and the trees seem to be going out into the forest again. The poem symbolises the desire of women, or any living creature, to escape confinement and be free.

📌

Summary

  • At night the trees inside the house struggle to go back to the forest
  • Their leaves and roots strain outward
  • The moon watches their escape
🧠

Symbolism

  • Trees stand for living beings, especially women, who long for freedom from confinement
🌟

Theme

  • Nature's desire for freedom and the need for liberty for all
🔬

Devices

  • Personification, imagery, symbolism and free verse

blocks.x: Carl Sandburg's very short poem "Fog" compares fog to a cat. The fog comes silently on little cat feet, sits looking over the harbour and city on silent haunches, and then moves on. The metaphor of a cat captures the stillness and sudden disappearance of fog. The poem is an example of imagist poetry with few words and a strong image.

Fog arrives quietly like a cat, rests over the harbour and city, then moves on.

lessons.title: The Tale of Custard the Dragon
yt: class 10 english the tale of custard the dragon

blocks.x: Ogden Nash's ballad tells of Belinda, who lived in a little white house with a black kitten called Ink, a grey mouse called Blink, a yellow dog called Mustard and a dragon called Custard. Belinda was brave as a barrelful of bears and so were Ink, Blink and Mustard, who were all bold, but Custard the dragon cried for a safe cage and was a coward. One day a pirate came; everyone ran away except Custard, who fought and gobbled up the pirate. Everybody praised him but he said he was still a coward and wished for a safe cage.
Deep dive: the characters
Belinda, Ink, Blink and Mustard boast about bravery. Custard, the dragon, admits he wants a cage.
Deep dive: the pirate
When a pirate arrives, everyone runs except Custard, who destroys him.
Deep dive: irony and moral
The one called coward saves everyone. He continues to call himself a coward, so the poem mocks both bravado and labels.
Deep dive: devices
Simile, alliteration, rhyme, humour, ballad form.
Hindi saransh
बेलिंडा के घर में एक कायर ड्रैगन कस्टर्ड था। जब समुद्री डाकू आया तो सब भाग गए पर कस्टर्ड ने उसे खा लिया। फिर भी वह खुद को डरपोक मानता रहा।
Humorous ballad: the supposed coward is the real hero.

Read the full explanation

Ogden Nash's ballad tells of Belinda, who lived in a little white house with a black kitten called Ink, a grey mouse called Blink, a yellow dog called Mustard and a dragon called Custard. Belinda was brave as a barrelful of bears and so were Ink, Blink and Mustard, who were all bold, but Custard the dragon cried for a safe cage and was a coward. One day a pirate came; everyone ran away except Custard, who fought and gobbled up the pirate. Everybody praised him but he said he was still a coward and wished for a safe cage.

📌

The characters

  • Belinda, Ink, Blink and Mustard boast about bravery
  • Custard, the dragon, admits he wants a cage
🧠

The pirate

  • When a pirate arrives, everyone runs except Custard, who destroys him
🌟

Irony and moral

  • The one called coward saves everyone
  • He continues to call himself a coward, so the poem mocks both bravado and labels
🔬

Devices

  • Simile, alliteration, rhyme, humour, ballad form

lessons.title: For Anne Gregory

blocks.x: W. B. Yeats's poem is a conversation between a young man and a girl, Anne Gregory. The young man says that young men would not love her for herself because of her beautiful yellow hair, as hair hides what she really is. Anne says she can dye her hair brown, black or carrot and then they will love her for herself alone. The speaker replies that he has found a text saying only God, and not a young man, can love you for yourself alone and not for your yellow hair. The poem shows the difference between true love and love for outward beauty.
Deep dive: summary
A young Anne Gregory is told that men love her only for her yellow hair. She says she will dye it. The speaker says only God can love one for oneself.
Deep dive: theme
Love should be based on character; outer beauty is superficial.

Dialogue, irony, symbolism of hair, and simple rhymes.

lessons.title: A Triumph of Surgery
yt: class 10 english a triumph of surgery

blocks.x: James Herriot, a veterinary surgeon, tells about Tricki, a small Pekingese dog belonging to rich Mrs Pumphrey. She overfeeds and pampers him with cream cakes, chocolates and biscuits, and he becomes very fat and lazy. Herriot is called when the dog loses appetite and is breathless. He advises exercise and puts Tricki in the hospital with other dogs, and prescribes a strict diet. After three weeks, Tricki becomes healthy and playful. Mrs Pumphrey, who believed that Herriot had performed an operation, praised him as a great surgeon. The story is humorous and shows the harmful effects of over-pampering.
Deep dive: summary
Mrs Pumphrey's overfeeding made her dog Tricki ill. Herriot kept him on a diet and in the company of other dogs, and after three weeks Tricki recovered.
Deep dive: irony
Mrs Pumphrey believes a surgical miracle has occurred, though no surgery was done.
Deep dive: message
Over-pampering harms pets; proper diet and exercise heal.
Deep dive: summary

Overfeeding harms; discipline restores health.

Big idea

  • She overfeeds and pampers him with cream cakes, chocolates and biscuits, and he becomes very fat and lazy

Read the full explanation

James Herriot, a veterinary surgeon, tells about Tricki, a small Pekingese dog belonging to rich Mrs Pumphrey. She overfeeds and pampers him with cream cakes, chocolates and biscuits, and he becomes very fat and lazy. Herriot is called when the dog loses appetite and is breathless. He advises exercise and puts Tricki in the hospital with other dogs, and prescribes a strict diet. After three weeks, Tricki becomes healthy and playful. Mrs Pumphrey, who believed that Herriot had performed an operation, praised him as a great surgeon. The story is humorous and shows the harmful effects of over-pampering.

📌

Summary

  • Mrs Pumphrey's overfeeding made her dog Tricki ill
  • Herriot kept him on a diet and in the company of other dogs, and after three weeks Tricki recovered
🧠

Irony

  • Mrs Pumphrey believes a surgical miracle has occurred, though no surgery was done
🌟

Message

  • Over-pampering harms pets
  • Proper diet and exercise heal

lessons.title: The Midnight Visitor

blocks.x: Robert Arthur's story is a detective tale about Ausable, a clever secret agent, and Max, a rival agent. Fowler, a young writer, thinks Ausable is a boring man. Ausable meets Fowler in a hotel room, expecting a visit from the rival agent Max, who wants a secret paper. When Max arrives at midnight with a gun, Ausable cleverly outwits him with a bold trick and keeps the secret paper safe, showing great presence of mind. The story shows presence of mind.
Deep dive: summary
Ausable, a cool-headed agent, outwits Max, who comes at midnight to steal a paper. Ausable bluffs, and then retrieves his safe paper.
Deep dive: characters
Ausable: clever, calm. Max: greedy and rash. Fowler: naive observer.
Deep dive: theme
Presence of mind and intelligence defeat violence.
Hindi saransh
ऑसेबल एक चतुर गुप्तचर है। मैक्स बंदूक के साथ आता है पर ऑसेबल चालाकी से उसे चकमा देता है। कहानी में सूझबूझ का महत्व दिखाया है।
Presence of mind and cleverness defeat force.

Robert Arthur's story is a detective tale about Ausable, a clever secret agent, and Max, a rival agent. Fowler, a young writer, thinks Ausable is a boring man. Ausable meets Fowler in a hotel room, expecting a visit from the rival agent Max, who wants a secret paper. When Max arrives at midnight with a gun, Ausable cleverly outwits him with a bold trick and keeps the secret paper safe, showing great presence of mind. The story shows presence of mind.

📌

Summary

  • Ausable, a cool-headed agent, outwits Max, who comes at midnight to steal a paper
  • Ausable bluffs, and then retrieves his safe paper
🧠

Characters

  • Ausable: clever, calm
  • Max: greedy and rash
  • Fowler: naive observer
🌟

Theme

  • Presence of mind and intelligence defeat violence

Deep dive: theme
Question of trust and the dangers of blind faith.

lessons.title: Footprints Without Feet

blocks.x: H. G. Wells's story is about Griffin, a scientist who discovers how to make himself invisible but cannot reverse the process. Griffin is the main character in "Footprints without Feet". In the story, Griffin steals clothes, causes chaos in the village, steals money and tries to recover his belongings. He is invisible but his footprints are visible in mud and snow. He also needs to find ways to eat and keep warm. In the end the story shows the loneliness, selfishness and moral problems of invisibility.
Deep dive: summary
Griffin, made invisible by experiment, causes chaos but cannot hide his footprints and faces cold and hunger.
Deep dive: theme
Misuse of science and the loneliness of power.
Deep dive: devices
Science fiction, humour, irony and suspense.
Hindi saransh
ग्रिफिन अदृश्य हो जाता है पर उसके पदचिह्न दिखाई देते हैं। कहानी अदृश्यता के लाभ और खतरे दिखाती है।
Invisibility brings power but also loneliness and trouble.

Read the full explanation

H. G. Wells's story is about Griffin, a scientist who discovers how to make himself invisible but cannot reverse the process. Griffin is the main character in "Footprints without Feet". In the story, Griffin steals clothes, causes chaos in the village, steals money and tries to recover his belongings. He is invisible but his footprints are visible in mud and snow. He also needs to find ways to eat and keep warm. In the end the story shows the loneliness, selfishness and moral problems of invisibility.

📌

Summary

  • Griffin, made invisible by experiment, causes chaos but cannot hide his footprints and faces cold and hunger
🧠

Theme

  • Misuse of science and the loneliness of power
🌟

Devices

  • Science fiction, humour, irony and suspense

yt: class 10 english the making of a scientist

blocks.x: Robert W. Peterson's biography-style essay tells of Richard Ebright, who from childhood was curious, a collector of butterflies, a reader, and an experimenter. His mother encouraged him and he read books, joined the Adult Butterfly Collectors; in school he studied monarch butterflies and won a prize. He studied the cause of the golden spots on the pupa in an experiment, and with the help of Dr Lincoln Brower, he published the result. He later studied at Harvard. The text shows how curiosity, hard work, patience and encouragement make a scientist.
Deep dive: childhood
Richard was curious, collected butterflies and read widely, encouraged by his mother who gave him tools.
Deep dive: the project
He studied monarch butterflies and found why spots appeared, with help from Dr Brower.
Deep dive: qualities
Curiosity, patience, hard work, and support make a scientist.

lessons.title: The Necklace

blocks.x: Guy de Maupassant's story is about Matilda Loisel, a pretty woman who is unhappy with her middle-class life. Her husband gets an invitation to a ball; she borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend Madame Forestier. At the ball she is the centre of attraction but loses the necklace on the way home. They buy a replacement for 36,000 francs by borrowing money and spend ten years in hardship to repay. When Matilda meets Madame Forestier she learns that the original necklace was only paste worth 500 francs. The story shows vanity, pride, and irony.
Deep dive: summary
Matilda borrows a necklace, loses it, and replaces it at the cost of years of hardship. She learns that the original was paste.
Deep dive: irony
Her desire for show leads to ruin, and the original necklace was nearly worthless.
Deep dive: themes
Vanity, honesty, discontent and consequences of appearances.

Guy de Maupassant's story is about Matilda Loisel, a pretty woman who is unhappy with her middle-class life. Her husband gets an invitation to a ball; she borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend Madame Forestier. At the ball she is the centre of attraction but loses the necklace on the way home. They buy a replacement for 36,000 francs by borrowing money and spend ten years in hardship to repay. When Matilda meets Madame Forestier she learns that the original necklace was only paste worth 500 francs. The story shows vanity, pride, and irony.

📌

Summary

  • Matilda borrows a necklace, loses it, and replaces it at the cost of years of hardship
  • She learns that the original was paste
🧠

Irony

  • Her desire for show leads to ruin, and the original necklace was nearly worthless
🌟

Themes

  • Vanity, honesty, discontent and consequences of appearances

lessons.title: The Book That Saved the Earth
yt: class 10 english the book that saved the earth

blocks.x: Claire Boiko's one-act play is set in the year 2200 and is a humorous science-fiction story told from the point of view of Martians. The Martian Captain, Noodle, and the Think-Tank (a talking computer) are sent to invade Earth. A Martian invader who found a book (Mother Goose rhymes) in a library misunderstood it as a violent book. The Think-Tank interprets the nursery rhymes, such as "Hey Diddle Diddle" and "Humpty Dumpty", as threats. The Martians fear Earth's power and retreat. The play satirises how misinterpretation causes fear and war.
Deep dive: summary
In 2200, Martians prepare to invade Earth. They find a nursery-rhyme book and think it is Earth's war manual. Fearing Earth's power, they retreat.
Deep dive: satire
The play mocks misreading, overconfidence and war.
Deep dive: message
Books and knowledge protect civilisation; ignorance causes needless conflict.

Claire Boiko's one-act play is set in the year 2200 and is a humorous science-fiction story told from the point of view of Martians. The Martian Captain, Noodle, and the Think-Tank (a talking computer) are sent to invade Earth. A Martian invader who found a book (Mother Goose rhymes) in a library misunderstood it as a violent book. The Think-Tank interprets the nursery rhymes, such as "Hey Diddle Diddle" and "Humpty Dumpty", as threats. The Martians fear Earth's power and retreat. The play satirises how misinterpretation causes fear and war.

  • Fearing Earth's power, they retreat

Satire

🌟

Message

  • Books and knowledge protect civilisation
  • Ignorance causes needless conflict

Resources are classified by origin (biotic and abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable and non-renewable), ownership (individual, community, national, international) and status of development (potential, developed, stock, reserves). India has varied soils: alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid and forest soils. Soil erosion is checked by contour ploughing, terrace farming, strip cropping and shelter belts.
Deep dive: classification of resources

By origin: biotic and abiotic. By exhaustibility: renewable (continuous or flow) and non-renewable (recyclable like metals, non-recyclable like fossil fuels). By ownership: individual, community, national, international. By development: potential, developed, stock and reserves.
Deep dive: planning and sustainability

Resource planning identifies, surveys and evaluates resources, matches them to technology and development plans. Sustainable development requires equity and care for the environment (Agenda 21, Rio 1992).
Deep dive: land

Land use: forests, land not available for cultivation (barren, non-agricultural use), other uncultivated land (pastures, groves, culturable waste), fallow lands and net sown area. Degradation arises from deforestation, mining, overgrazing, over-irrigation and industrial effluents.

Contour ploughing, terrace farming, strip cropping, shelter belts and afforestation prevent erosion.

qa.q: How are resources classified by origin?
Give examples of biotic resources.
qa.a: Human beings, forests, animals and fisheries.

qa.q: Give examples of abiotic resources.
How are resources classified by exhaustibility?
Give examples of renewable resources.
qa.a: Solar energy, wind, water and forests.

qa.q: Give examples of non-renewable resources.
How are resources classified by ownership?
Give an example of an individual resource.
qa.a: A house, plot or well owned by a person.

qa.q: Give an example of a community resource.
qa.a: Village ponds, public parks and burial grounds.

qa.q: Give an example of a national resource.
qa.a: Minerals, water, forests and land within a country's borders.

qa.q: Up to what distance from the coast is the Exclusive Economic Zone?
What are potential resources?
qa.a: Resources found in a region but not yet used.

qa.q: What are developed resources?
What are stock resources?
qa.a: Materials that can satisfy needs but lack the technology to use them.

qa.q: What are reserves?
qa.a: Part of the stock that can be used with existing technology but is kept for the future.

qa.q: Why is resource planning necessary?
qa.a: Resources are limited and unevenly distributed.

qa.q: What is sustainable development?
qa.a: Development without damaging the environment and meeting needs without compromising future generations.

qa.q: What was the Rio Earth Summit?
qa.a: A 1992 UN conference on environment and development in Rio de Janeiro.

qa.q: What is Agenda 21?
qa.a: A declaration to combat environmental damage and poverty through global cooperation.

qa.q: Who wrote "Small is Beautiful"?
Which book is by the Club of Rome?
What are the land use categories?
qa.a: Forests, land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area.

qa.q: What is net sown area?
qa.a: The area sown with crops, counted once.

qa.q: What is gross cropped area?
qa.a: Net sown area plus area sown more than once.

qa.q: What is current fallow?
qa.a: Land left uncultivated for one or less than one agricultural year.

qa.q: What is the target forest area in the National Forest Policy 1952?
qa.a: 33 per cent of the geographical area.

qa.q: What is a barren and waste land?
qa.a: Rocky, arid and desert land not suitable for cultivation.

qa.q: What is a land degradation?
qa.a: Reduction in the quality of land by human activities.

qa.q: Name the causes of land degradation.
qa.a: Deforestation, overgrazing, mining, over-irrigation and industrial effluents.

qa.q: What is soil?
qa.a: The most important renewable resource that supports plant growth.

qa.q: Which factors form soil?
qa.a: Relief, parent rock, climate, vegetation, time and other life forms.

qa.q: Which soil is most widespread in India?
Where is alluvial soil found?
qa.a: The northern plains and some coastal and delta regions.

qa.q: Which rivers deposited alluvial soil?
What are bangar and khadar?
qa.a: Older alluvium and newer alluvium respectively.

qa.q: Which crops grow in alluvial soil?
Which soil is called regur?
Which crop is best suited to black soil?
What is the black soil made of?
qa.a: Volcanic rock (basalt); it is clayey and retains moisture.

qa.q: Which soil is formed by intense leaching?
Which crops grow in laterite soil?
Where is red soil found?
qa.a: Parts of the Deccan plateau, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.

qa.q: Why is red soil red?
qa.a: Because of diffusion of iron in crystalline and metamorphic rocks.

qa.q: Which soil has kankar layers?
Where are forest soils found?
What is soil erosion?
qa.a: Removal of soil cover by wind or water faster than it forms.

qa.q: What is gully erosion?
qa.a: Running water cutting deep channels called gullies.

qa.q: What is sheet erosion?
qa.a: Water flowing as a sheet removing top soil.

qa.q: What is contour ploughing?
qa.a: Ploughing along contour lines to slow water.

qa.q: What is terrace farming?
qa.a: Cutting steps on steep slopes to cultivate.

qa.q: What is strip cropping?
qa.a: Planting crops in strips with grass bands between.

qa.q: What are shelter belts?
qa.a: Rows of trees planted to check wind speed.

lessons.title: Forest and Wildlife Resources
yt: class 10 geography forest and wildlife resources

blocks.x: India is rich in biodiversity, but forests and wildlife are under threat. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classes species as normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic and extinct. Causes of depletion include colonial exploitation, agricultural expansion, large development projects, mining, grazing and fuelwood collection, environmental destruction and unequal access to resources. Conservation measures include the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, Project Tiger (1973) and community efforts such as Chipko, Beej Bachao Andolan and Joint Forest Management. Forests are legally classified as reserved, protected and unclassed. Sacred groves also protect biodiversity.
Deep dive: biodiversity and depletion

India has about 8 per cent of the world's species. Causes of depletion: colonial railways, shipbuilding and agriculture expansion; post-independence development projects, mining, grazing, fuelwood and large dams; poverty and unequal use of resources.
Deep dive: classification of species
Normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic and extinct (IUCN Red List categories).
Deep dive: conservation
Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Project Tiger 1973, national parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves. Community movements: Chipko, Beej Bachao Andolan and JFM (Odisha 1988); sacred groves.

Visual lesson

Forest and Wildlife Resources

India is rich in biodiversity, but forests and wildlife are under threat

Big idea

Read the full explanation

India is rich in biodiversity, but forests and wildlife are under threat. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classes species as normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic and extinct. Causes of depletion include colonial exploitation, agricultural expansion, large development projects, mining, grazing and fuelwood collection, environmental destruction and unequal access to resources. Conservation measures include the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, Project Tiger (1973) and community efforts such as Chipko, Beej Bachao Andolan and Joint Forest Management. Forests are legally classified as reserved, protected and unclassed. Sacred groves also protect biodiversity.

📌

Biodiversity and depletion

  • India has about 8 per cent of the world's species
  • Causes of depletion: colonial railways, shipbuilding and agriculture expansion
  • Post-independence development projects, mining, grazing, fuelwood and large dams
  • Poverty and unequal use of resources
🧠

Classification of species

  • Normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic and extinct (IUCN Red List categories)
🌟

Conservation

  • Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Project Tiger 1973, national parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves
  • Community movements: Chipko, Beej Bachao Andolan and JFM (Odisha 1988)
  • Sacred groves
🔬

Forests in India

  • Reserved (over half), protected (about one third), unclassed (remainder)
  • Madhya Pradesh has the largest area of permanent forests
🧮

lessons.title: Water Resources

blocks.x: About 96.5 per cent of the Earth's water is in oceans and only about 2.5 per cent is freshwater, of which most is locked as ice. India receives 4 per cent of the world's freshwater and has a high demand because of population and irrigation. Water scarcity arises from over-exploitation, unequal access, pollution and growing demand for irrigation and industry. Multipurpose river projects (Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud, Sardar Sarovar, Tehri) provide irrigation, power, flood control and fisheries but face criticism on displacement, sedimentation and flooding; the Narmada Bachao Andolan protests against them. Rainwater harvesting has traditional forms: guls and kuls in the Western Himalayas, rooftop harvesting in Rajasthan, inundation channels in Bengal, khadins and johads in Rajasthan, bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya and tankas in Rajasthan. Tamil Nadu made rooftop harvesting mandatory.
Deep dive: water scarcity
Water is a renewable resource but demand outpaces supply because of population, irrigation, industry, pollution and unequal access. India's per capita availability is falling.
Deep dive: multipurpose projects

Dams on rivers like the Sutlej (Bhakra-Nangal), Mahanadi (Hirakud), Narmada (Sardar Sarovar) and Bhagirathi (Tehri) bring irrigation and power, but cause displacement, sedimentation, flood risks and conflicts. The Narmada Bachao Andolan opposes displacement.
Deep dive: rainwater harvesting
Traditional systems: guls/kuls, rooftop tanks (tankas), khadins and johads, bamboo drip irrigation. Rooftop harvesting is compulsory in Tamil Nadu; Gendathur is a model.
Hindi saransh
पृथ्वी का लगभग 96.5% जल सागरों में है। भारत में विश्व का 4% मीठा जल है। बहुउद्देशीय परियोजनाएँ सिंचाई, बिजली और बाढ़ नियंत्रण देती हैं। वर्षा जल संग्रहण से जल संकट कम होता है।
Hirakud on Mahanadi; Bhakra Nangal on Sutlej; Sardar Sarovar on Narmada.

Big idea

  • About 96.5 per cent of the Earth's water is in oceans and only about 2.5 per cent is freshwater, of which most is locked as ice
  • India receives 4 per cent of the world's freshwater and has a high demand because of population and irrigation
  • Water scarcity arises from over-exploitation, unequal access, pollution and growing demand for irrigation and industry

Read the full explanation

About 96.5 per cent of the Earth's water is in oceans and only about 2.5 per cent is freshwater, of which most is locked as ice. India receives 4 per cent of the world's freshwater and has a high demand because of population and irrigation. Water scarcity arises from over-exploitation, unequal access, pollution and growing demand for irrigation and industry. Multipurpose river projects (Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud, Sardar Sarovar, Tehri) provide irrigation, power, flood control and fisheries but face criticism on displacement, sedimentation and flooding; the Narmada Bachao Andolan protests against them. Rainwater harvesting has traditional forms: guls and kuls in the Western Himalayas, rooftop harvesting in Rajasthan, inundation channels in Bengal, khadins and johads in Rajasthan, bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya and tankas in Rajasthan. Tamil Nadu made rooftop harvesting mandatory.

📌

Water scarcity

  • Water is a renewable resource but demand outpaces supply because of population, irrigation, industry, pollution and unequal access
  • India's per capita availability is falling
🎯

Multipurpose projects

  • Dams on rivers like the Sutlej (Bhakra-Nangal), Mahanadi (Hirakud), Narmada (Sardar Sarovar) and Bhagirathi (Tehri) bring irrigation and power, but…
  • The Narmada Bachao Andolan opposes displacement
🌟

Rainwater harvesting

  • Traditional systems: guls/kuls, rooftop tanks (tankas), khadins and johads, bamboo drip irrigation
  • Rooftop harvesting is compulsory in Tamil Nadu
  • Gendathur is a model

blocks.x: Agriculture is the primary activity employing about half of India's workforce. Farming types include primitive subsistence (slash and burn, called jhumming in the North-East), intensive subsistence, commercial farming (Punjab, Haryana) and plantation farming (tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane, banana). India has three cropping seasons: Rabi (sown October to December, harvested April to June: wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard), Kharif (sown with monsoon onset, harvested September-October: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soybean) and Zaid (summer: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder). Major crops are rice, wheat, millets, maize, pulses, sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, rubber, cotton, jute and horticulture crops.
Deep dive: farming types

Primitive subsistence (slash and burn), intensive subsistence (high labour inputs in densely populated areas), commercial (modern inputs, high yield per hectare) and plantation (single cash crop, large estates, migrant labour, capital).
Deep dive: cropping seasons
Rabi: sown winter, harvested summer. Kharif: sown with monsoon, harvested autumn. Zaid: between the two, short summer season.
Deep dive: major crops

Rice: hot, humid, 100+ cm rain; alluvial plains. Wheat: cool, 50-75 cm; Ganga-Satluj plains. Millets: poor soils; Maize: food and fodder. Pulses: legumes restore nitrogen. Sugarcane: tropical and subtropical, second in the world. Oilseeds: groundnut leads. Tea, coffee, rubber, cotton, jute: cash and fibre crops.
Deep dive: horticulture
India is among the top producers of fruits and vegetables: mangoes, bananas, oranges, grapes, peas, tomatoes, onions.

lessons.title: Agriculture: Reforms, Technology and Contribution
yt: class 10 geography agriculture: reforms, technology and contribution

blocks.x: Agriculture contributes to national income and employment but faces problems of small holdings, dependence on rain and low investment. Technological and institutional reforms include land reforms (consolidation of holdings, abolition of zamindari, Bhoodan-Gramdan of Vinoba Bhave), the Green Revolution (HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation in the 1960s), White Revolution (Operation Flood), crop insurance, Kisan Credit Card, minimum support price, Grameen banks, and Kisan call centres. Challenges: fragmented holdings, over-use of fertilisers, shrinking land, WTO competition and fluctuations in prices. Globalisation exposes farmers to competition; organic farming and diversification are encouraged. Food security is essential, and the government supports it through procurement and public distribution.
Deep dive: institutional reforms

Land reforms: abolition of zamindari, land ceilings, consolidation, Bhoodan-Gramdan. Credit: Grameen banks, Kisan Credit Card. Insurance: PMFBY. Price support: MSP and procurement. Information: Kisan call centres.
Deep dive: technological reforms
Green Revolution (1960s): HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation, pesticides; raised wheat and rice output in Punjab, Haryana. White Revolution (Operation Flood): increased milk production.
Deep dive: challenges
Fragmentation, rain dependence, soil damage, price instability, competition from imports. Remedies: organic farming, diversification, cooperative farming, irrigation and market support.
Hindi saransh
कृषि सुधारों में भूमि सुधार, हरित क्रांति, श्वेत क्रांति, फसल बीमा, किसान क्रेडिट कार्ड और न्यूनतम समर्थन मूल्य शामिल हैं। भूदान-ग्रामदान आंदोलन विनोबा भावे ने चलाया।
Green Revolution: HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation. Operation Flood: milk.

Big idea

  • Agriculture contributes to national income and employment but faces problems of small holdings, dependence on rain and low investment
  • Technological and institutional reforms include land reforms (consolidation of holdings, abolition of zamindari, Bhoodan-Gramdan of Vinoba Bhave)…

Read the full explanation

Agriculture contributes to national income and employment but faces problems of small holdings, dependence on rain and low investment. Technological and institutional reforms include land reforms (consolidation of holdings, abolition of zamindari, Bhoodan-Gramdan of Vinoba Bhave), the Green Revolution (HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation in the 1960s), White Revolution (Operation Flood), crop insurance, Kisan Credit Card, minimum support price, Grameen banks, and Kisan call centres. Challenges: fragmented holdings, over-use of fertilisers, shrinking land, WTO competition and fluctuations in prices. Globalisation exposes farmers to competition; organic farming and diversification are encouraged. Food security is essential, and the government supports it through procurement and public distribution.

📌

Institutional reforms

  • Land reforms: abolition of zamindari, land ceilings, consolidation, Bhoodan-Gramdan
  • Credit: Grameen banks, Kisan Credit Card
  • Insurance: PMFBY
  • Price support: MSP and procurement
Read the full explanation

Land reforms: abolition of zamindari, land ceilings, consolidation, Bhoodan-Gramdan. Credit: Grameen banks, Kisan Credit Card. Insurance: PMFBY. Price support: MSP and procurement. Information: Kisan call centres.

  • Green Revolution (1960s): HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation, pesticides
  • Raised wheat and rice output in Punjab, Haryana
  • White Revolution (Operation Flood): increased milk production

Challenges

  • Fragmentation, rain dependence, soil damage, price instability, competition from imports
  • Remedies: organic farming, diversification, cooperative farming, irrigation and market support

lessons.title: Minerals and Energy Resources
yt: class 10 geography minerals and energy resources

blocks.x: A mineral is a homogeneous naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure. Minerals are classified as metallic (ferrous: iron ore, manganese, nickel, cobalt; non-ferrous: copper, lead, zinc, bauxite), non-metallic (mica, salt, limestone) and energy minerals (coal, petroleum, natural gas). Iron ore (magnetite is the best) is mainly found in Odisha-Jharkhand, Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur, Bellary-Chitradurga-Chikmagaluru-Tumakuru, and Maharashtra-Goa belts. Conventional energy: coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity (thermal, hydro, nuclear). Non-conventional: solar, wind, biogas, tidal, geothermal and biomass. India's Gondwana coal fields are in Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro), Mahanadi, Godavari and Son valleys; lignite at Neyveli. Petroleum comes from Mumbai High, Gujarat and Assam (Digboi). Conservation of minerals and energy is vital.
Deep dive: minerals

Metallic ferrous: iron ore, manganese. Non-ferrous: copper, bauxite. Non-metallic: mica, limestone. Minerals occur in igneous and metamorphic rocks (veins), sedimentary rocks (layers), alluvial deposits and ocean waters.
Deep dive: iron ore and other minerals

Magnetite (70% iron) is best; hematite is most important. Belts: Odisha-Jharkhand, Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur, Bellary-Chitradurga-Tumakuru, Maharashtra-Goa. Manganese: Odisha. Copper: Balaghat, Khetri. Bauxite: Koraput, Amarkantak. Mica: Koderma.
Deep dive: conventional energy

Coal: peat, lignite, bituminous, anthracite; Gondwana coal in Damodar valley; Neyveli lignite. Petroleum: Mumbai High, Gujarat, Assam. Gas: Krishna-Godavari, HVJ pipeline. Thermal, hydro and nuclear electricity.
Deep dive: non-conventional energy
Solar (Bhuj), wind (Nagercoil, Jaisalmer), biogas, tidal, geothermal (Manikaran, Puga), biomass.
Deep dive: conservation
Use minerals judiciously, recycle metals, use substitutes and efficient technology; save energy.
Hindi saransh
खनिज धात्विक, अधात्विक और ऊर्जा खनिज होते हैं। लौह अयस्क ओडिशा-झारखंड में मिलता है। ऊर्जा के पारंपरिक स्रोत कोयला, पेट्रोलियम, गैस और विद्युत हैं; गैर-पारंपरिक स्रोत सौर, पवन, बायोगैस आदि हैं।

lessons.title: Lifelines of National Economy
yt: class 10 geography lifelines of national economy

blocks.x: Transport, communication and trade are the lifelines of the economy. India has one of the largest road networks in the world; roads are classified as Golden Quadrilateral, National Highways, State Highways, District roads and Border roads (BRO). Railways are the principal mode of transport; the first train ran in 1853 between Mumbai and Thane. Pipelines carry crude oil and gas; waterways include National Waterway 1 (Prayagraj-Haldia), 2 (Sadiya-Dhubri) and 3 (West Coast Canal). Major ports are Kandla, Mumbai, JNPT, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Chennai, Tuticorin, Visakhapatnam, Paradwip, Kolkata and Haldia. Airways are the fastest mode. Communication includes post, telecom and mass media. International trade is the exchange of goods between countries; tourism is a major trade; the government promotes it as an industry.
Deep dive: roadways
Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi-Kolkata-Chennai-Mumbai), NS-EW corridors, national and state highways, district roads and BRO roads. Roads are cheaper for short distances and give door-to-door service.
Deep dive: railways, pipelines, waterways

Railways: 17 zones; first train 1853. Pipelines carry oil and gas. Waterways: NW1, NW2, NW3. Ports: Kandla, Mumbai, JNPT, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Chennai, Tuticorin, Visakhapatnam, Paradwip, Kolkata-Haldia.
Deep dive: airways and communication
Air transport is fastest; Pawan Hans serves remote areas. India Post has the world's largest network; telecom, radio, TV and the internet link the country.
Deep dive: trade and tourism
International trade: exports, imports and balance of trade. Tourism creates jobs, foreign exchange and national integration; types: cultural, medical, eco, adventure.
Hindi saransh
परिवहन, संचार और व्यापार अर्थव्यवस्था की जीवन रेखाएँ हैं। स्वर्णिम चतुर्भुज सड़कें, पहली रेलगाड़ी 1853 में मुंबई-ठाणे के बीच, राष्ट्रीय जलमार्ग 1, 2 और 3 तथा प्रमुख बंदरगाह इसके भाग हैं।

Visual lesson

Lifelines of National Economy

Transport, communication and trade are the lifelines of the economy

minutes

Q&A
