cosec A1 / sin A
sec A1 / cos A
🔑

Big idea

  • In a right triangle: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent
  • Standard values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = 1/sqrt 2, sin 60 = sqrt 3/2
  • Tan 30 = 1/sqrt 3
  • Identity sin2 + cos2 = 1
Read the full explanation

In a right triangle: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. Standard values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = 1/sqrt 2, sin 60 = sqrt 3/2; cos 60 = 1/2; tan 45 = 1; tan 30 = 1/sqrt 3. Identity sin^2 + cos^2 = 1. Heights and distances: angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal. Example: standing 20 m from a tower with an angle of elevation 30 degrees: height = 20 tan 30 = 20/sqrt 3 = 11.55 m. Probability: P(E) = favourable / total. A card from 52: P(heart) = 13/52 = 1/4.

📌

Trigonometric ratios

  • In a right triangle, for an acute angle A: sin A = opposite / hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent / hypotenuse, tan A = opposite / adjacent
  • Reciprocals: cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A
  • Also tan A = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A
  • Standard angles
Read the full explanation

Definitions. In a right triangle, for an acute angle A: sin A = opposite / hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent / hypotenuse, tan A = opposite / adjacent. Reciprocals: cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A. Also tan A = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A. Standard angles. sin: 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt 2, sqrt 3/2, 1 for 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees. cos is the same list reversed. tan: 0, 1/sqrt 3, 1, sqrt 3, not defined. A memory trick: sin = sqrt(0/4), sqrt(1/4), sqrt(2/4), sqrt(3/4), sqrt(4/4). Complementary angles. sin (90 - A) = cos A; cos (90 - A) = sin A; tan (90 - A) = cot A; cot (90 - A) = tan A; sec (90 - A) = cosec A; cosec (90 - A) = sec A. So sin 35 = cos 55 and tan 20 x tan 70 = 1. Identities. sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1; 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A; 1 + cot^2 A = cosec^2 A. To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side, write everything in sin and cos, and simplify. Behaviour. As A rises from 0 to 90 degrees sin A rises from 0 to 1, cos A falls from 1 to 0, tan A rises from 0 without limit. The value of sin A and cos A never exceeds 1; sec A and cosec A are never below 1.

🧠

Heights and distances

  • The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight upward to an object
  • The angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal to an object below
  • The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (alternate angles)
  • Draw a clear figure
Read the full explanation

Angles. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight upward to an object. The angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal to an object below. The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (alternate angles). Method. Draw a clear figure; mark the right angle, the known side and the angle; choose the ratio that links the known and unknown sides: height and distance use tan, height and line of sight use sin, distance and line of sight use cos. Typical forms: height = distance x tan (angle); two observation points give two equations that share the height. Common values. At 45 degrees height equals distance. At 30 degrees height = distance / sqrt 3. At 60 degrees height = distance x sqrt 3. Take sqrt 3 = 1.732 and sqrt 2 = 1.414 for numerical answers.

🌟

Probability

  • P(E) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of equally likely outcomes
  • 0 <= P(E) <= 1
  • P(sure event) = 1
  • P(impossible event) = 0
Read the full explanation

Definition. P(E) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of equally likely outcomes. 0 <= P(E) <= 1; P(sure event) = 1; P(impossible event) = 0; P(E) + P(not E) = 1. Standard sample spaces. A coin: 2 outcomes. A die: 6. Two coins: 4. Two dice: 36. A pack of cards: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 12 face cards, 26 red, 26 black, 4 aces, 4 kings.

lessons.title: Coordinate geometry, circles and similar triangles

blocks.x: **Distance formula:** d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2); e.g. (0, 0) to (3, 4) is **5**. **Section formula:** point dividing (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in ratio m:n = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); midpoint is the case m = n. Area of triangle = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **Similar triangles:** corresponding sides in the same ratio; areas in the ratio of the squares of sides. **Circle:** tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; tangents from an external point are equal. If tangent length is 12 and radius 5, the distance from the centre is sqrt(144 + 25) = **13**.
Deep dive: coordinate geometry

**Cartesian plane.** Two perpendicular axes meet at the origin O (0, 0). A point is (x, y): x is the abscissa and y the ordinate. The quadrants are I (+,+), II (-,+), III (-,-), IV (+,-). Points on the x-axis have y = 0; points on the y-axis have x = 0. **Distance formula.** PQ = sqrt ((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2). Distance from the origin to (x, y) is sqrt (x^2 + y^2). Use it to test shapes: an isosceles triangle has two equal sides; a right triangle satisfies Pythagoras; a parallelogram has equal opposite sides and bisecting diagonals; a rhombus has four equal sides; a rectangle has equal diagonals; three points are collinear when the sum of two distances equals the third. **Section formula.** The point dividing A (x1, y1) and B (x2, y2) internally in the ratio m : n is ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)). The midpoint is ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). The centroid of a triangle is ((x1 + x2 + x3)/3, (y1 + y2 + y3)/3). To find the ratio in which a line divides a segment, let the ratio be k : 1 and solve. **Area of a triangle.** Area = (1/2) |x1 (y2 - y3) + x2 (y3 - y1) + x3 (y1 - y2)|. Three points are collinear when this area is 0. The area of a quadrilateral is found by splitting it into two triangles.
Deep dive: similar triangles and circles

**Similar triangles.** Two triangles are similar if their angles are equal; then corresponding sides are proportional. Criteria: AAA (or AA), SSS (sides in the same ratio) and SAS (two sides in the same ratio and the included angle equal). The ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of corresponding sides. The basic proportionality (Thales) theorem: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. **Tangents.** A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point, the point of contact. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. From an external point exactly two tangents can be drawn and they are equal in length. If the distance from the centre to the external point is d and the radius r then the tangent length is sqrt (d^2 - r^2). A circle has infinitely many tangents; from a point inside it none.

Visual lesson

Coordinate geometry, circles and similar triangles

Distance formula: d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)

🔑

Big idea

  • Distance formula: d = sqrt((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2)
  • E.g. (0, 0) to (3, 4) is 5
  • Section formula: point dividing (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in ratio m:n = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n))
  • Midpoint is the case m = n
Read the full explanation

Distance formula: d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2); e.g. (0, 0) to (3, 4) is 5. Section formula: point dividing (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in ratio m:n = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); midpoint is the case m = n. Area of triangle = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. Similar triangles: corresponding sides in the same ratio; areas in the ratio of the squares of sides. Circle: tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; tangents from an external point are equal. If tangent length is 12 and radius 5, the distance from the centre is sqrt(144 + 25) = 13.

📐

Coordinate geometry

  • Cartesian plane
  • Two perpendicular axes meet at the origin O (0, 0)
  • A point is (x, y): x is the abscissa and y the ordinate
  • The quadrants are I (+,+), II (-,+), III (-,-), IV (+,-)
Read the full explanation

Cartesian plane. Two perpendicular axes meet at the origin O (0, 0). A point is (x, y): x is the abscissa and y the ordinate. The quadrants are I (+,+), II (-,+), III (-,-), IV (+,-). Points on the x-axis have y = 0; points on the y-axis have x = 0. Distance formula. PQ = sqrt ((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2). Distance from the origin to (x, y) is sqrt (x^2 + y^2). Use it to test shapes: an isosceles triangle has two equal sides; a right triangle satisfies Pythagoras; a parallelogram has equal opposite sides and bisecting diagonals; a rhombus has four equal sides; a rectangle has equal diagonals; three points are collinear when the sum of two distances equals the third. Section formula. The point dividing A (x1, y1) and B (x2, y2) internally in the ratio m : n is ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)). The midpoint is ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). The centroid of a triangle is ((x1 + x2 + x3)/3, (y1 + y2 + y3)/3). To find the ratio in which a line divides a segment, let the ratio be k : 1 and solve. Area of a triangle. Area = (1/2) |x1 (y2 - y3) + x2 (y3 - y1) + x3 (y1 - y2)|. Three points are collinear when this area is 0. The area of a quadrilateral is found by splitting it into two triangles.

📐

Similar triangles and circles

  • Similar triangles
  • Two triangles are similar if their angles are equal
  • Then corresponding sides are proportional
  • Criteria: AAA (or AA), SSS (sides in the same ratio) and SAS (two sides in the same ratio and the included angle equal)
Read the full explanation

Similar triangles. Two triangles are similar if their angles are equal; then corresponding sides are proportional. Criteria: AAA (or AA), SSS (sides in the same ratio) and SAS (two sides in the same ratio and the included angle equal). The ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of corresponding sides. The basic proportionality (Thales) theorem: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. Tangents. A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point, the point of contact. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. From an external point exactly two tangents can be drawn and they are equal in length. If the distance from the centre to the external point is d and the radius r then the tangent length is sqrt (d^2 - r^2). A circle has infinitely many tangents; from a point inside it none.

(0, 0) થી (3, 4) સુધીનું અંતર **5**. **વિભાજન સૂત્ર:** (x1, y1) અને (x2, y2) ને m:n ગુણોત્તરમાં વહેંચતો બિંદુ = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); m = n હોય ત્યારે તે મધ્યબિંદુ. ત્રિકોણનું ક્ષેત્રફળ = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **સમરૂપ ત્રિકોણ:** અનુરૂપ બાજુઓ સમાન ગુણોત્તરમાં; ક્ષેત્રફળનો ગુણોત્તર બાજુઓના વર્ગના ગુણોત્તર જેટલો. **વર્તુળ:** સ્પર્શક સ્પર્શબિંદુએ ત્રિજ્યાને લંબ હોય છે; બહારના બિંદુથી દોરેલા સ્પર્શકો સમાન હોય છે. સ્પર્શકની લંબાઈ 12 અને ત્રિજ્યા 5 હોય તો કેન્દ્રથી અંતર √(144 + 25) = **13**.
બહારના બિંદુથી દોરેલા સ્પર્શકોની લંબાઈ સમાન હોય છે.

quiz.q: સ્પર્શકની લંબાઈ 12 અને ત્રિજ્યા 5 હોય તો બાહ્ય બિંદુનું અંતર

hi.title: निर्देशांक ज्यामिति, वृत्त और समरूप त्रिभुज

blocks.x: **दूरी सूत्र:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); जैसे (0, 0) से (3, 4) की दूरी **5**। **विभाजन सूत्र:** बिंदुओं (x1, y1), (x2, y2) को m:n अनुपात में बाँटने वाला बिंदु = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); मध्य बिंदु m = n की स्थिति है। त्रिभुज का क्षेत्रफल = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|। **समरूप त्रिभुज:** संगत भुजाएँ समान अनुपात में; क्षेत्रफल भुजाओं के वर्गों के अनुपात में। **वृत्त:** स्पर्श रेखा स्पर्श बिंदु पर त्रिज्या पर लंब होती है; बाह्य बिंदु से खींची गई स्पर्श रेखाएँ बराबर होती हैं। यदि स्पर्श रेखा की लंबाई 12 और त्रिज्या 5 हो तो केंद्र से दूरी √(144 + 25) = **13**।
बाह्य बिंदु से खींची स्पर्श रेखाओं की लंबाई समान होती है।

qa.a: स्पर्श बिंदु पर वे परस्पर लंब होती हैं।

kn.title: ನಿರ್ದೇಶಾಂಕ ರೇಖಾಗಣಿತ, ವೃತ್ತ ಮತ್ತು ಸಮರೂಪ ತ್ರಿಭುಜಗಳು

blocks.x: **ದೂರ ಸೂತ್ರ:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); ಉದಾ. (0, 0) ರಿಂದ (3, 4) ವರೆಗಿನ ದೂರ **5**. **ವಿಭಜನಾ ಸೂತ್ರ:** (x1, y1) ಮತ್ತು (x2, y2) ಬಿಂದುಗಳನ್ನು m:n ಅನುಪಾತದಲ್ಲಿ ವಿಭಾಗಿಸುವ ಬಿಂದು = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); m = n ಆದರೆ ಅದು ಮಧ್ಯಬಿಂದು. ತ್ರಿಭುಜದ ವಿಸ್ತೀರ್ಣ = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **ಸಮರೂಪ ತ್ರಿಭುಜಗಳು:** ಅನುರೂಪ ಭುಜಗಳು ಒಂದೇ ಅನುಪಾತದಲ್ಲಿರುತ್ತವೆ; ವಿಸ್ತೀರ್ಣಗಳ ಅನುಪಾತ ಭುಜಗಳ ವರ್ಗಗಳ ಅನುಪಾತಕ್ಕೆ ಸಮ. **ವೃತ್ತ:** ಸ್ಪರ್ಶಕವು ಸ್ಪರ್ಶ ಬಿಂದುವಿನಲ್ಲಿ ತ್ರಿಜ್ಯಕ್ಕೆ ಲಂಬವಾಗಿರುತ್ತದೆ; ಹೊರಗಿನ ಬಿಂದುವಿನಿಂದ ಎಳೆದ ಸ್ಪರ್ಶಕಗಳು ಸಮ. ಸ್ಪರ್ಶಕದ ಉದ್ದ 12 ಮತ್ತು ತ್ರಿಜ್ಯ 5 ಆದರೆ ಕೇಂದ್ರದಿಂದ ದೂರ √(144 + 25) = **13**.
ಹೊರಗಿನ ಬಿಂದುವಿನಿಂದ ಎಳೆದ ಸ್ಪರ್ಶಕಗಳ ಉದ್ದ ಸಮ.

qa.q: (0, 0) ಮತ್ತು (3, 4) ನಡುವಿನ ದೂರ ಎಷ್ಟು?
ಸ್ಪರ್ಶಕ ಮತ್ತು ತ್ರಿಜ್ಯದ ನಡುವಿನ ಸಂಬಂಧ ಏನು?

quiz.q: ಸ್ಪರ್ಶಕದ ಉದ್ದ 12, ತ್ರಿಜ್ಯ 5 ಆದರೆ ಹೊರಗಿನ ಬಿಂದುವಿನ ದೂರ
ಭುಜಗಳ ಅನುಪಾತ 1:2 ಇರುವ ಸಮರೂಪ ತ್ರಿಭುಜಗಳ ವಿಸ್ತೀರ್ಣದ ಅನುಪಾತ

blocks.x: **ദൂര സൂത്രവാക്യം:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); ഉദാ. (0, 0) മുതൽ (3, 4) വരെയുള്ള ദൂരം **5**. **വിഭജന സൂത്രവാക്യം:** (x1, y1), (x2, y2) ബിന്ദുക്കളെ m:n അനുപാതത്തിൽ വിഭജിക്കുന്ന ബിന്ദു = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); m = n ആയാൽ അത് മധ്യബിന്ദു. ത്രികോണത്തിന്റെ വിസ്തീർണ്ണം = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **സദൃശ ത്രികോണങ്ങൾ:** അനുബന്ധ വശങ്ങൾ ഒരേ അനുപാതത്തിലായിരിക്കും; വിസ്തീർണ്ണങ്ങളുടെ അനുപാതം വശങ്ങളുടെ വർഗ്ഗങ്ങളുടെ അനുപാതത്തിന് തുല്യം. **വൃത്തം:** സ്പർശരേഖ സ്പർശബിന്ദുവിൽ ആരത്തിന് ലംബമാണ്; പുറത്തെ ബിന്ദുവിൽ നിന്നുള്ള സ്പർശരേഖകൾ തുല്യമാണ്. സ്പർശരേഖയുടെ നീളം 12, ആരം 5 ആയാൽ കേന്ദ്രത്തിൽ നിന്നുള്ള ദൂരം √(144 + 25) = **13**.
പുറത്തെ ബിന്ദുവിൽ നിന്നുള്ള സ്പർശരേഖകളുടെ നീളം തുല്യമാണ്.

qa.q: (0, 0), (3, 4) എന്നിവയ്ക്കിടയിലെ ദൂരം എത്ര?
(2, 4), (6, 8) എന്നിവയുടെ മധ്യബിന്ദു ഏത്?
സ്പർശരേഖയും ആരവും തമ്മിലുള്ള ബന്ധം എന്ത്?
സദൃശ ത്രികോണങ്ങളുടെ വിസ്തീർണ്ണങ്ങളുടെ അനുപാതം എത്ര?

quiz.q: സ്പർശരേഖയുടെ നീളം 12, ആരം 5 ആയാൽ പുറത്തെ ബിന്ദുവിന്റെ ദൂരം
വശങ്ങളുടെ അനുപാതം 1:2 ആയ സദൃശ ത്രികോണങ്ങളുടെ വിസ്തീർണ്ണ അനുപാതം

mr.title: निर्देशक भूमिती, वर्तुळ आणि समरूप त्रिकोण

blocks.x: **अंतर सूत्र:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); उदा. (0, 0) ते (3, 4) अंतर **5**. **विभाजन सूत्र:** (x1, y1) आणि (x2, y2) यांना m:n गुणोत्तरात विभागणारा बिंदू = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); मध्यबिंदू म्हणजे m = n ही स्थिती. त्रिकोणाचे क्षेत्रफळ = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **समरूप त्रिकोण:** संगत बाजू समान गुणोत्तरात; क्षेत्रफळांचे गुणोत्तर बाजूंच्या वर्गांच्या गुणोत्तराइतके. **वर्तुळ:** स्पर्शिका स्पर्शबिंदूत त्रिज्येला लंब असते; बाह्य बिंदूपासून काढलेल्या स्पर्शिका समान असतात. स्पर्शिकेची लांबी 12 आणि त्रिज्या 5 असल्यास केंद्रापासून अंतर √(144 + 25) = **13**.

pa.title: ਧੁਰਾ ਜਿਓਮੈਟਰੀ, ਚੱਕਰ ਅਤੇ ਸਮਰੂਪ ਤਿਕੋਣ

blocks.x: **ਦੂਰੀ ਸੂਤਰ:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); ਜਿਵੇਂ (0, 0) ਤੋਂ (3, 4) ਤੱਕ ਦੂਰੀ **5**। **ਵੰਡ ਸੂਤਰ:** (x1, y1) ਅਤੇ (x2, y2) ਨੂੰ m:n ਅਨੁਪਾਤ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੰਡਣ ਵਾਲਾ ਬਿੰਦੂ = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); m = n ਹੋਵੇ ਤਾਂ ਇਹ ਮੱਧ ਬਿੰਦੂ ਹੈ। ਤਿਕੋਣ ਦਾ ਖੇਤਰਫਲ = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|। **ਸਮਰੂਪ ਤਿਕੋਣ:** ਸੰਗਤ ਭੁਜਾਵਾਂ ਇੱਕੋ ਅਨੁਪਾਤ ਵਿੱਚ; ਖੇਤਰਫਲਾਂ ਦਾ ਅਨੁਪਾਤ ਭੁਜਾਵਾਂ ਦੇ ਵਰਗਾਂ ਦੇ ਅਨੁਪਾਤ ਜਿੰਨਾ। **ਚੱਕਰ:** ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਰੇਖਾ ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਬਿੰਦੂ ਉੱਤੇ ਅਰਧ ਵਿਆਸ ਉੱਤੇ ਲੰਬ ਹੁੰਦੀ ਹੈ; ਬਾਹਰੀ ਬਿੰਦੂ ਤੋਂ ਖਿੱਚੀਆਂ ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਰੇਖਾਵਾਂ ਬਰਾਬਰ ਹੁੰਦੀਆਂ ਹਨ। ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਰੇਖਾ ਦੀ ਲੰਬਾਈ 12 ਅਤੇ ਅਰਧ ਵਿਆਸ 5 ਹੋਵੇ ਤਾਂ ਕੇਂਦਰ ਤੋਂ ਦੂਰੀ √(144 + 25) = **13**।
ਬਾਹਰੀ ਬਿੰਦੂ ਤੋਂ ਖਿੱਚੀਆਂ ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਰੇਖਾਵਾਂ ਦੀ ਲੰਬਾਈ ਬਰਾਬਰ ਹੁੰਦੀ ਹੈ।

qa.q: ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਰੇਖਾ ਅਤੇ ਅਰਧ ਵਿਆਸ ਦਾ ਸੰਬੰਧ ਕੀ ਹੈ?
qa.a: ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਬਿੰਦੂ ਉੱਤੇ ਉਹ ਇੱਕ ਦੂਜੇ ਉੱਤੇ ਲੰਬ ਹੁੰਦੇ ਹਨ।

qa.q: ਸਮਰੂਪ ਤਿਕੋਣਾਂ ਦੇ ਖੇਤਰਫਲਾਂ ਦਾ ਅਨੁਪਾਤ ਕੀ ਹੈ?

quiz.q: ਸਪਰਸ਼ ਰੇਖਾ ਦੀ ਲੰਬਾਈ 12 ਅਤੇ ਅਰਧ ਵਿਆਸ 5 ਹੋਵੇ ਤਾਂ ਬਾਹਰੀ ਬਿੰਦੂ ਦੀ ਦੂਰੀ

ta.title: ஆயத்தொலை வடிவியல், வட்டம் மற்றும் வடிவொத்த முக்கோணங்கள்

blocks.x: **தூர சூத்திரம்:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); எ.கா. (0, 0) முதல் (3, 4) வரை தூரம் **5**. **பிரிவு சூத்திரம்:** (x1, y1), (x2, y2) புள்ளிகளை m:n விகிதத்தில் பிரிக்கும் புள்ளி = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); m = n ஆனால் அது நடுப்புள்ளி. முக்கோணத்தின் பரப்பு = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **வடிவொத்த முக்கோணங்கள்:** ஒத்த பக்கங்கள் ஒரே விகிதத்தில்; பரப்புகளின் விகிதம் பக்கங்களின் வர்க்க விகிதம். **வட்டம்:** தொடுகோடு தொடுபுள்ளியில் ஆரத்துக்குச் செங்குத்து; வெளிப்புள்ளியிலிருந்து வரையும் தொடுகோடுகள் சமம். தொடுகோட்டின் நீளம் 12, ஆரம் 5 எனில் மையத்திலிருந்து தூரம் √(144 + 25) = **13**.
வெளிப்புள்ளியிலிருந்து வரையும் தொடுகோடுகளின் நீளம் சமம்.

blocks.x: **దూర సూత్రం:** d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²); ఉదా. (0, 0) నుండి (3, 4) వరకు దూరం **5**. **విభజన సూత్రం:** (x1, y1), (x2, y2) బిందువులను m:n నిష్పత్తిలో విభజించే బిందువు = ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)); m = n అయితే అది మధ్య బిందువు. త్రిభుజ వైశాల్యం = (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. **సరూప త్రిభుజాలు:** సంబంధిత భుజాలు ఒకే నిష్పత్తిలో ఉంటాయి; వైశాల్యాల నిష్పత్తి భుజాల వర్గాల నిష్పత్తికి సమానం. **వృత్తం:** స్పర్శరేఖ స్పర్శ బిందువు వద్ద వ్యాసార్ధానికి లంబంగా ఉంటుంది; బాహ్య బిందువు నుండి గీసిన స్పర్శరేఖలు సమానం. స్పర్శరేఖ పొడవు 12, వ్యాసార్ధం 5 అయితే కేంద్రం నుండి దూరం √(144 + 25) = **13**.
బాహ్య బిందువు నుండి గీసిన స్పర్శరేఖల పొడవులు సమానం.

lessons.title: Real numbers

blocks.x: **Euclid division lemma:** for positive integers a and b there are unique q and r with a = b q + r, 0 <= r < b. Euclid algorithm finds HCF by repeating this. **Fundamental theorem of arithmetic:** every composite number is a product of primes in a unique way (apart from order). Example: 140 = 2^2 x 5 x 7.
Deep dive: Euclid division lemma and algorithm

**Lemma.** For any positive integers a (dividend) and b (divisor) there exist unique whole numbers q and r with a = b q + r and 0 <= r < b. When r = 0, b divides a. **Algorithm for HCF.** To find HCF (c, d) with c > d: divide c by d to get remainder r; if r = 0 the HCF is d; otherwise replace (c, d) by (d, r) and repeat. Example: HCF (455, 42): 455 = 42 x 10 + 35; 42 = 35 x 1 + 7; 35 = 7 x 5 + 0, so HCF = 7. Uses: show that every positive odd integer is 2q + 1 and every even integer 2q; any positive integer is of the form 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2; the square of any positive integer is of the form 3m or 3m + 1; the cube is of the form 9m, 9m + 1 or 9m + 8.
Deep dive: fundamental theorem of arithmetic

**Statement.** Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique except for the order of the primes. Example: 32760 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5 x 7 x 13. **HCF and LCM by prime factorisation.** HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime that appears. For two numbers: HCF x LCM = product of the numbers (this does not hold for three numbers). Numbers of the form 4^n can never end in 0 because 4^n = 2^(2n) has no factor 5. **Irrational numbers.** If a prime p divides a^2 then p divides a. Using this, sqrt 2, sqrt 3, sqrt 5 and every sqrt p (p prime) are irrational (proof by contradiction). The sum or difference of a rational and an irrational is irrational; so are the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and an irrational. Example: 3 + 2 sqrt 5 is irrational. The sum of two irrationals can be rational: (2 + sqrt 3) + (2 - sqrt 3) = 4. **Decimal expansions.** A rational number p/q (in lowest terms) has a terminating decimal if and only if q = 2^m x 5^n; otherwise the decimal is non-terminating and repeating. An irrational number has a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal. The number of decimal places in the terminating expansion is the larger of m and n. **Common mistakes.** Forgetting that the factorisation must be into primes (1 is not prime); taking the larger power of each prime for the HCF (that is for LCM); applying HCF x LCM = product to three numbers.

qa.q: State Euclid's division lemma.
qa.a: For positive integers a and b there are unique q and r with a = bq + r, 0 <= r < b.

qa.q: What is Euclid's division algorithm used for?
qa.a: To find the HCF of two positive integers.

qa.q: What is a composite number?
qa.a: A number with more than two factors.

qa.q: Is 1 prime?
qa.a: No. 1 is neither prime nor composite.

qa.q: State the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
qa.a: Every composite number is a product of primes, uniquely apart from the order.

qa.q: How do you find the HCF by prime factorisation?
qa.a: Multiply the smallest power of each common prime.

qa.q: How do you find the LCM by prime factorisation?
qa.a: Multiply the greatest power of every prime that appears.

qa.q: State the product rule for HCF and LCM.
qa.a: HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers.

qa.q: Does HCF x LCM = product hold for three numbers?
What is an irrational number?
qa.a: A number that cannot be written as p/q; its decimal never ends or repeats.

qa.q: Prove that sqrt 3 is irrational.
qa.a: Assume sqrt 3 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 3b^2 = a^2, so 3 divides a, a = 3c, giving b^2 = 3c^2, so 3 divides b. This contradicts lowest terms.

qa.q: Show that 5 - sqrt 3 is irrational.
qa.a: If it were rational r then sqrt 3 = 5 - r would be rational, which is false.

qa.q: Show that 3 + 2 sqrt 5 is irrational.
qa.a: If it were rational r then sqrt 5 = (r - 3)/2 would be rational, which is false.

qa.q: Show that 1/sqrt 2 is irrational.
qa.a: It equals sqrt 2 / 2; if rational then sqrt 2 would be rational, which is false.

qa.q: Show that any positive odd integer is of the form 4q + 1 or 4q + 3.
qa.a: Dividing by 4 gives remainders 0, 1, 2, 3; remainders 0 and 2 give even numbers.

🔑

Big idea

  • Euclid division lemma: for positive integers a and b there are unique q and r with a = b q + r, 0 <= r < b
  • Euclid algorithm finds HCF by repeating this
  • Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every composite number is a product of primes in a unique way (apart from order)
  • Example: 140 = 22 x 5 x 7
📌

Euclid division lemma and algorithm

  • For any positive integers a (dividend) and b (divisor) there exist unique whole numbers q and r with a = b q + r and 0 <= r < b
  • When r = 0, b divides a
  • Algorithm for HCF
  • To find HCF (c, d) with c > d: divide c by d to get remainder r
Read the full explanation

Lemma. For any positive integers a (dividend) and b (divisor) there exist unique whole numbers q and r with a = b q + r and 0 <= r < b. When r = 0, b divides a. Algorithm for HCF. To find HCF (c, d) with c > d: divide c by d to get remainder r; if r = 0 the HCF is d; otherwise replace (c, d) by (d, r) and repeat. Example: HCF (455, 42): 455 = 42 x 10 + 35; 42 = 35 x 1 + 7; 35 = 7 x 5 + 0, so HCF = 7. Uses: show that every positive odd integer is 2q + 1 and every even integer 2q; any positive integer is of the form 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2; the square of any positive integer is of the form 3m or 3m + 1; the cube is of the form 9m, 9m + 1 or 9m + 8.

⚖️

Fundamental theorem of arithmetic

  • Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique except for the order of the primes
  • Example: 32760 = 23 x 32 x 5 x 7 x 13
  • HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
  • HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime
Read the full explanation

Statement. Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique except for the order of the primes. Example: 32760 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5 x 7 x 13. HCF and LCM by prime factorisation. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime that appears. For two numbers: HCF x LCM = product of the numbers (this does not hold for three numbers). Numbers of the form 4^n can never end in 0 because 4^n = 2^(2n) has no factor 5. Irrational numbers. If a prime p divides a^2 then p divides a. Using this, sqrt 2, sqrt 3, sqrt 5 and every sqrt p (p prime) are irrational (proof by contradiction). The sum or difference of a rational and an irrational is irrational; so are the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and an irrational. Example: 3 + 2 sqrt 5 is irrational. The sum of two irrationals can be rational: (2 + sqrt 3) + (2 - sqrt 3) = 4. Decimal expansions. A rational number p/q (in lowest terms) has a terminating decimal if and only if q = 2^m x 5^n; otherwise the decimal is non-terminating and repeating. An irrational number has a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal. The number of decimal places in the terminating expansion is the larger of m and n. Common mistakes. Forgetting that the factorisation must be into primes (1 is not prime); taking the larger power of each prime for the HCF (that is for LCM); applying HCF x LCM = product to three numbers.

lessons.title: Areas related to circles

blocks.x: Circumference of a circle is 2 pi r and area is pi r^2. A sector with angle theta has arc length (theta/360) x 2 pi r and area (theta/360) x pi r^2. Area of segment = area of sector - area of triangle. Use pi = 22/7 unless told otherwise.
Deep dive: circle, sector, segment

Circumference C = 2 pi r = pi d. Area A = pi r^2. For a sector of angle theta at the centre: arc length l = (theta/360) x 2 pi r and area = (theta/360) x pi r^2 = (1/2) l r. A minor segment is the region between a chord and its arc: area = area of sector - area of triangle formed by the radii and the chord = (theta/360) pi r^2 - (1/2) r^2 sin theta. The major segment area = pi r^2 - minor segment area.
Deep dive: special figures

Ring (annulus) between radii R and r: area = pi (R^2 - r^2). Distance moved by a wheel in one rotation = circumference; in n rotations = n x 2 pi r. A minute hand of length l sweeps an angle of 6 degrees per minute, so in t minutes it sweeps area (6t/360) pi l^2. An equilateral triangle of side a has area (sqrt 3 / 4) a^2; a square of side a inscribed in a circle has diagonal a sqrt 2 = 2r. Combined figures: find each area separately, then add or subtract. **Common mistakes:** using diameter instead of radius, forgetting to subtract the triangle for a segment, mixing units (cm and m).

Parridhi 2 pi r, kshetrafal pi r^2. Sector = (theta/360) x circle.
Segment = sector - triangle.

Big idea

  • Circumference of a circle is 2 pi r and area is pi r2
  • A sector with angle theta has arc length (theta/360) x 2 pi r and area (theta/360) x pi r2
  • Area of segment = area of sector - area of triangle
  • Use pi = 22/7 unless told otherwise
📐

Circle, sector, segment

  • Circumference C = 2 pi r = pi d
  • Area A = pi r2
  • For a sector of angle theta at the centre: arc length l = (theta/360) x 2 pi r and area = (theta/360) x pi r2 = (1/2) l r
  • A minor segment is the region between a chord and its arc: area = area of sector - area of triangle formed by the radii and the chord = (theta/360)…
Read the full explanation

Circumference C = 2 pi r = pi d. Area A = pi r^2. For a sector of angle theta at the centre: arc length l = (theta/360) x 2 pi r and area = (theta/360) x pi r^2 = (1/2) l r. A minor segment is the region between a chord and its arc: area = area of sector - area of triangle formed by the radii and the chord = (theta/360) pi r^2 - (1/2) r^2 sin theta. The major segment area = pi r^2 - minor segment area.

🧠

Special figures

  • Ring (annulus) between radii R and r: area = pi (R2 - r2)
  • Distance moved by a wheel in one rotation = circumference
  • In n rotations = n x 2 pi r
  • A minute hand of length l sweeps an angle of 6 degrees per minute, so in t minutes it sweeps area (6t/360) pi l2
Read the full explanation

Ring (annulus) between radii R and r: area = pi (R^2 - r^2). Distance moved by a wheel in one rotation = circumference; in n rotations = n x 2 pi r. A minute hand of length l sweeps an angle of 6 degrees per minute, so in t minutes it sweeps area (6t/360) pi l^2. An equilateral triangle of side a has area (sqrt 3 / 4) a^2; a square of side a inscribed in a circle has diagonal a sqrt 2 = 2r. Combined figures: find each area separately, then add or subtract. Common mistakes: using diameter instead of radius, forgetting to subtract the triangle for a segment, mixing units (cm and m).

lessons.title: Surface areas and volumes

blocks.x: Combine solids such as cone on cylinder, hemisphere on cylinder, and find the frustum of a cone. Curved surface area of cylinder 2 pi r h, cone pi r l, sphere 4 pi r^2, hemisphere 2 pi r^2. Volumes: cylinder pi r^2 h, cone one-third pi r^2 h, sphere (4/3) pi r^3, hemisphere (2/3) pi r^3.
Deep dive: standard solids

Cylinder (radius r, height h): CSA 2 pi r h, TSA 2 pi r (r + h), volume pi r^2 h. Cone: slant height l = sqrt (r^2 + h^2), CSA pi r l, TSA pi r (l + r), volume (1/3) pi r^2 h. Sphere: surface 4 pi r^2, volume (4/3) pi r^3. Hemisphere: CSA 2 pi r^2, TSA 3 pi r^2, volume (2/3) pi r^3.
Deep dive: combination of solids

For a toy made of a cone on a hemisphere, or a tent made of a cylinder and a cone, find the total surface area by adding the curved surfaces only for the joined parts (the circular faces that are joined are hidden). Total volume is the sum of volumes. For a capsule (cylinder with two hemispheres): TSA = 2 pi r h + 4 pi r^2 and volume = pi r^2 h + (4/3) pi r^3.
Deep dive: conversion of solids and frustum

When a solid is melted and recast into another, the volume stays the same: a sphere of radius R recast into n small spheres of radius r gives n = R^3/r^3. For a frustum of a cone with radii r1 > r2 and height h: slant height l = sqrt (h^2 + (r1 - r2)^2); volume (1/3) pi h (r1^2 + r2^2 + r1 r2); CSA pi (r1 + r2) l; TSA = CSA + pi r1^2 + pi r2^2. **Common mistakes:** using height instead of slant height in CSA of a cone, forgetting the joined faces are not exposed, and mixing units (cm to m means cubic factors).

blocks.x: For grouped data, mean = sum(f x) / sum f using class marks x. Median = l + ((n/2 - cf)/f) x h. Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2 f1 - f0 - f2)) x h. Empirical relation: 3 median = mode + 2 mean. Cumulative frequency curves (ogives) give the median graphically.
Deep dive: mean of grouped data

Direct method: x = class mark, mean = sum (f x)/sum f. Assumed mean method: d = x - a, mean = a + sum (f d)/sum f. Step-deviation: u = (x - a)/h, mean = a + h x sum (f u)/sum f. All three give the same answer.
Deep dive: mode and median

Modal class is the class with the highest frequency. Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2 f1 - f0 - f2)) x h, where l is the lower limit of the modal class, f1 its frequency, f0 and f2 the frequencies of the classes before and after, and h the class size. Median class is the class whose cumulative frequency first exceeds n/2. Median = l + ((n/2 - cf)/f) x h where cf is the cumulative frequency of the class before it. Relationship: Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean.
Deep dive: ogives

A less-than ogive plots upper class limits against cumulative frequency (less than type); a more-than ogive plots lower limits against cumulative frequency (more than type). The x-coordinate of the intersection of the two ogives is the median; so is the x-value for n/2 on either curve. **Common mistakes:** using class limits instead of class marks, forgetting to make classes continuous, and taking cf of the median class rather than the class before it.
Hindi saransh

lessons.title: Electricity and light (Class 10)

blocks.x: **Ohm's law** V = IR; power P = VI = I^2 R. For V = 5 V and R = 10 ohm: I = **0.5 A**, P = **2.5 W**. Resistors in series add; in parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2: 2 ohm and 3 ohm give **1.2 ohm**. Heating effect H = I^2 R t. **Light:** mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = -v/u. Concave mirror f = -15 cm, object at u = -30 cm: v = **-30 cm**, m = **-1** (real, inverted, same size). **Refraction:** Snell's law; refractive index n = c / v: if light travels at 2 x 10^8 m/s in glass, n = **1.5**. Lens power P = 1/f (metres), in dioptres. **Magnetic effects:** field around a current carrying wire; motor, generator, electromagnetic induction.
Deep dive: electricity

**Charge and current.** Current I is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q / t. One ampere is one coulomb per second. The charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C, so 1 C is about 6.25 x 10^18 electrons. Conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to the electron flow. **Potential difference.** V = W / Q: the work done to move one coulomb between two points. Unit: volt (1 V = 1 J/C). A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component; an ammeter is connected in series. **Ohm's law.** At constant temperature V is proportional to I, so V = I R. The graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. Resistance depends on length, area and material: R = rho L / A. Doubling the length doubles R; doubling the area halves R. Resistivity rho depends only on the material and temperature (metals: low, alloys: higher, insulators: very high). **Series and parallel.** Series: the same current passes through every resistor, R = R1 + R2 + ... and the voltages add. Parallel: every resistor has the same voltage, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... and the currents add; the combined resistance is smaller than the smallest. Household appliances are in parallel so each gets 220 V and works independently. **Heating effect.** H = I^2 R t = V I t = V^2 t / R (Joule's law). Used in heaters, geysers, irons and fuses. A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point in series with the appliance that melts when the current is too high. **Electric power and energy.** P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R, in watts. Energy E = P t. The commercial unit is the kilowatt hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J = 1 unit of electricity.
Deep dive: light

**Reflection.** The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. **Spherical mirrors.** Focal length f = R / 2. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from the pole; in the direction of the incident light is positive, against it is negative. For a concave mirror f is negative; for a convex mirror f is positive. Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. A concave mirror gives a real inverted image when the object is beyond f; with the object between pole and f it gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image (shaving mirror, dentist's mirror). A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image (rear-view mirrors). **Refraction.** Light bends when it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes. Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n21 = constant. Absolute refractive index n = c / v with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Going into a denser medium the ray bends towards the normal. Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. **Lenses.** Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = v/u. Power P = 1/f with f in metres; the unit is the dioptre. Convex lens: f positive, converging, P positive. Concave lens: f negative, diverging, P negative. Lenses placed in contact add their powers: P = P1 + P2. **Human eye.** Myopia (short sight) is corrected by a concave lens; hypermetropia (long sight) by a convex lens. Presbyopia comes with age and needs bifocal lenses. Dispersion by a prism splits white light into VIBGYOR; a rainbow is dispersion plus internal reflection in raindrops; the sky is blue because shorter wavelengths scatter most.

qa.q: What does the slope of a V-I graph show?
qa.a: The resistance R of the conductor.

qa.q: On what factors does the resistance of a wire depend?
qa.a: Its length, area of cross-section, the material, and the temperature.

qa.q: What is resistivity?
qa.a: The resistance of a wire of unit length and unit area of cross-section; it depends only on the material and temperature.

qa.q: Why are alloys used in heating elements?

qa.q: Why is tungsten used for bulb filaments?

qa.q: How should an ammeter be connected?

qa.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?

qa.q: What is the use of a fuse?

qa.q: State Joule's law of heating.

Why does the filament of a bulb glow but the connecting wires do not?

qa.q: Why do parallel resistors have a smaller combined resistance?
qa.a: More paths are available for the current, so the total opposition falls below the smallest single resistance.

qa.q: What is a short circuit?
qa.a: A path of almost zero resistance across the supply, causing a very large current and overheating.

qa.q: Why is the earth wire used?

qa.q: What is the direction of conventional current?
qa.a: From the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the cell.

qa.q: What are the properties of an image in a plane mirror?

qa.q: Which mirror is used by dentists and in shaving?
qa.a: A concave mirror: with the object within the focal length it gives an erect, enlarged, virtual image.

qa.q: What is refraction?
qa.a: The bending of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another because its speed changes.

qa.q: State Snell's law.
qa.a: The ratio sin i / sin r is a constant for a given pair of media and light colour.

qa.q: Define absolute refractive index.
qa.a: n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in the medium = c / v.

What causes the blue colour of the sky?
qa.a: Scattering of light: the shorter blue wavelengths scatter most by air molecules.

qa.q: Why does the Sun appear red at sunrise and sunset?
qa.a: Light travels through more atmosphere, so blue is scattered away and red reaches the eye.

qa.q: How does a rainbow form?
qa.a: By dispersion, refraction and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets.

qa.q: What is dispersion?
qa.a: The splitting of white light into its seven colours when passing through a prism.

Visual lesson

Electricity and light (Class 10)

Ohm's law V = IR

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Electricity›3Light
🔑

Big idea

  • Ohm's law V = IR
  • Power P = VI = I2 R
  • For V = 5 V and R = 10 ohm: I = 0.5 A, P = 2.5 W
  • Resistors in series add
Read the full explanation

Ohm's law V = IR; power P = VI = I^2 R. For V = 5 V and R = 10 ohm: I = 0.5 A, P = 2.5 W. Resistors in series add; in parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2: 2 ohm and 3 ohm give 1.2 ohm. Heating effect H = I^2 R t. Light: mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = -v/u. Concave mirror f = -15 cm, object at u = -30 cm: v = -30 cm, m = -1 (real, inverted, same size). Refraction: Snell's law; refractive index n = c / v: if light travels at 2 x 10^8 m/s in glass, n = 1.5. Lens power P = 1/f (metres), in dioptres. Magnetic effects: field around a current carrying wire; motor, generator, electromagnetic induction.

⚡

Electricity

  • Charge and current
  • Current I is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q / t
  • One ampere is one coulomb per second
  • The charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10-19 C, so 1 C is about 6.25 x 1018 electrons
Read the full explanation

Charge and current. Current I is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q / t. One ampere is one coulomb per second. The charge of one electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C, so 1 C is about 6.25 x 10^18 electrons. Conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to the electron flow. Potential difference. V = W / Q: the work done to move one coulomb between two points. Unit: volt (1 V = 1 J/C). A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component; an ammeter is connected in series. Ohm's law. At constant temperature V is proportional to I, so V = I R. The graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. Resistance depends on length, area and material: R = rho L / A. Doubling the length doubles R; doubling the area halves R. Resistivity rho depends only on the material and temperature (metals: low, alloys: higher, insulators: very high). Series and parallel. Series: the same current passes through every resistor, R = R1 + R2 + ... and the voltages add. Parallel: every resistor has the same voltage, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... and the currents add; the combined resistance is smaller than the smallest. Household appliances are in parallel so each gets 220 V and works independently. Heating effect. H = I^2 R t = V I t = V^2 t / R (Joule's law). Used in heaters, geysers, irons and fuses. A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point in series with the appliance that melts when the current is too high. Electric power and energy. P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R, in watts. Energy E = P t. The commercial unit is the kilowatt hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J = 1 unit of electricity.

🔦

Light

  • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
  • The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane
  • A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
  • Spherical mirrors
Read the full explanation

Reflection. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Spherical mirrors. Focal length f = R / 2. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from the pole; in the direction of the incident light is positive, against it is negative. For a concave mirror f is negative; for a convex mirror f is positive. Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. A concave mirror gives a real inverted image when the object is beyond f; with the object between pole and f it gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image (shaving mirror, dentist's mirror). A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image (rear-view mirrors). Refraction. Light bends when it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes. Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n21 = constant. Absolute refractive index n = c / v with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Going into a denser medium the ray bends towards the normal. Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. Lenses. Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = v/u. Power P = 1/f with f in metres; the unit is the dioptre. Convex lens: f positive, converging, P positive. Concave lens: f negative, diverging, P negative. Lenses placed in contact add their powers: P = P1 + P2. Human eye. Myopia (short sight) is corrected by a concave lens; hypermetropia (long sight) by a convex lens. Presbyopia comes with age and needs bifocal lenses. Dispersion by a prism splits white light into VIBGYOR; a rainbow is dispersion plus internal reflection in raindrops; the sky is blue because shorter wavelengths scatter most.

lessons.title: Chemical reactions, acids and bases, and heredity

blocks.x: **Balanced equation:** atoms of each element equal on both sides. Example: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (displacement). Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox. **Acids and bases:** acids turn blue litmus red; pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Neutralisation: acid + base -> salt + water; e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Common salt, baking soda (NaHCO3) and washing soda (Na2CO3.10H2O). **Heredity:** Mendel's monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation; human sex is determined by XY (male) and XX (female); the sex of the child depends on the father's chromosome.
Deep dive: chemical reactions and equations

**Equations.** A chemical equation uses formulae for reactants and products. It must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides (law of conservation of mass). Balance by trial: balance elements that appear once first, hydrogen and oxygen last. State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conditions such as heat or catalyst are written over the arrow. Example: 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. **Types.** Combination: A + B -> AB (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, exothermic). Decomposition: AB -> A + B, by heat (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), light (2 AgCl -> 2 Ag + Cl2) or electricity (electrolysis of water). Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one (Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu). Double displacement: ions exchange and often a precipitate forms (Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2 NaCl). Redox: oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they occur together (CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O). **Everyday changes.** Corrosion is slow oxidation of metals (rusting of iron needs air and water; prevent by painting, galvanising). Rancidity is oxidation of fats and oils; prevent with antioxidants, airtight containers, nitrogen flushing. Exothermic reactions release heat (burning, respiration); endothermic reactions absorb heat (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition).
Deep dive: acids, bases and salts

**Acids** taste sour, turn blue litmus red, give H+ ions in water (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH). **Bases** are bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue and give OH- in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2); a water-soluble base is an alkali. Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein (pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base), turmeric (red in base). **Reactions.** Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the gas burns with a pop). Acid + metal carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide (which turns lime water milky). Acid + base -> salt + water (neutralisation). Acid + metal oxide -> salt + water. Non-metal oxides are acidic; metal oxides are basic. **pH scale.** pH = -log [H+]. 0 to 7 acidic, 7 neutral, 7 to 14 basic. Each unit is a tenfold change. Gastric juice about 1.5-3, lemon juice 2.2, milk 6.5, pure water 7, blood 7.4, baking soda solution 8.3, milk of magnesia 10, NaOH 14. Uses: antacids for acidity, tooth enamel decays below pH 5.5, soil pH, acid rain below 5.6. **Salts.** Common salt NaCl (from brine; chlor-alkali process gives NaOH, Cl2 and H2). Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Cl2 + Ca(OH)2). Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl); on heating gives Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; used in antacids and baking powder. Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O. Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2 H2O (gypsum heated at 373 K) sets as CaSO4.2H2O. Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt (CuSO4.5H2O is blue and turns white when heated).
Deep dive: heredity

**Basics.** Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring; variation is the difference between individuals. Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction and are the raw material of evolution. Genes on chromosomes are the units of heredity. A gene has alleles (dominant and recessive). **Mendel.** Worked on garden pea (Pisum sativum) with seven contrasting pairs of traits. Monohybrid cross: tall (TT) x dwarf (tt) gives all tall Tt in F1; selfing F1 gives F2 with phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf and genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Dihybrid cross (round yellow RRYY x wrinkled green rryy): F2 phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 shows independent assortment. Laws: dominance, segregation of alleles, independent assortment. **Sex determination.** Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). The mother always gives X; the father gives X or Y, so the sex of the child depends on the father. The chance of a boy or a girl is 50% each. **Evolution points.** Acquired traits are not inherited. Speciation arises from variation, natural selection and isolation. Homologous organs (forelimb of man, bat, whale) show common ancestry; analogous organs (wing of bird and insect) have the same function with different origin. Fossils and carbon dating give evidence of evolution.

Visual lesson

Chemical reactions, acids and bases, and heredity

Balanced equation: atoms of each element equal on both sides

🔑

Big idea

  • Balanced equation: atoms of each element equal on both sides
  • Example: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO
  • Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (displacement)
  • Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox
Read the full explanation

Balanced equation: atoms of each element equal on both sides. Example: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (displacement). Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox. Acids and bases: acids turn blue litmus red; pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Neutralisation: acid + base -> salt + water; e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Common salt, baking soda (NaHCO3) and washing soda (Na2CO3.10H2O). Heredity: Mendel's monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation; human sex is determined by XY (male) and XX (female); the sex of the child depends on the father's chromosome.

🧮

Chemical reactions and equations

  • A chemical equation uses formulae for reactants and products
  • It must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides (law of conservation of mass)
  • Balance by trial: balance elements that appear once first, hydrogen and oxygen last
  • State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq)
Read the full explanation

Equations. A chemical equation uses formulae for reactants and products. It must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides (law of conservation of mass). Balance by trial: balance elements that appear once first, hydrogen and oxygen last. State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conditions such as heat or catalyst are written over the arrow. Example: 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O; Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. Types. Combination: A + B -> AB (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, exothermic). Decomposition: AB -> A + B, by heat (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), light (2 AgCl -> 2 Ag + Cl2) or electricity (electrolysis of water). Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one (Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu). Double displacement: ions exchange and often a precipitate forms (Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2 NaCl). Redox: oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they occur together (CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O). Everyday changes. Corrosion is slow oxidation of metals (rusting of iron needs air and water; prevent by painting, galvanising). Rancidity is oxidation of fats and oils; prevent with antioxidants, airtight containers, nitrogen flushing. Exothermic reactions release heat (burning, respiration); endothermic reactions absorb heat (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition).

⚗️

Acids, bases and salts

  • Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, give H+ ions in water (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH)
  • Bases are bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue and give OH- in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2)
  • A water-soluble base is an alkali
  • Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein (pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base), turmeric (red in base)
Read the full explanation

Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, give H+ ions in water (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH). Bases are bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue and give OH- in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2); a water-soluble base is an alkali. Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein (pink in base), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base), turmeric (red in base). Reactions. Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the gas burns with a pop). Acid + metal carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide (which turns lime water milky). Acid + base -> salt + water (neutralisation). Acid + metal oxide -> salt + water. Non-metal oxides are acidic; metal oxides are basic. pH scale. pH = -log [H+]. 0 to 7 acidic, 7 neutral, 7 to 14 basic. Each unit is a tenfold change. Gastric juice about 1.5-3, lemon juice 2.2, milk 6.5, pure water 7, blood 7.4, baking soda solution 8.3, milk of magnesia 10, NaOH 14. Uses: antacids for acidity, tooth enamel decays below pH 5.5, soil pH, acid rain below 5.6. Salts. Common salt NaCl (from brine; chlor-alkali process gives NaOH, Cl2 and H2). Bleaching powder CaOCl2 (Cl2 + Ca(OH)2). Baking soda NaHCO3 (NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl); on heating gives Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; used in antacids and baking powder. Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O. Plaster of Paris CaSO4.1/2 H2O (gypsum heated at 373 K) sets as CaSO4.2H2O. Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt (CuSO4.5H2O is blue and turns white when heated).

🌟

Heredity

  • Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring
  • Variation is the difference between individuals
  • Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction and are the raw material of evolution
  • Genes on chromosomes are the units of heredity
Read the full explanation

Basics. Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring; variation is the difference between individuals. Variations arise from DNA copying errors and sexual reproduction and are the raw material of evolution. Genes on chromosomes are the units of heredity. A gene has alleles (dominant and recessive). Mendel. Worked on garden pea (Pisum sativum) with seven contrasting pairs of traits. Monohybrid cross: tall (TT) x dwarf (tt) gives all tall Tt in F1; selfing F1 gives F2 with phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf and genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Dihybrid cross (round yellow RRYY x wrinkled green rryy): F2 phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 shows independent assortment. Laws: dominance, segregation of alleles, independent assortment. Sex determination. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). The mother always gives X; the father gives X or Y, so the sex of the child depends on the father. The chance of a boy or a girl is 50% each. Evolution points. Acquired traits are not inherited. Speciation arises from variation, natural selection and isolation. Homologous organs (forelimb of man, bat, whale) show common ancestry; analogous organs (wing of bird and insect) have the same function with different origin. Fossils and carbon dating give evidence of evolution.

blocks.x: **Photosynthesis:** 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2. Light reaction (thylakoid membranes): water splits, O2 released, ATP and NADPH made. Calvin cycle (stroma): CO2 fixed by RuBisCO into 3-PGA and then sugars. C4 plants (maize, sugarcane) use PEP carboxylase and show Kranz anatomy. **Respiration:** C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. Glycolysis (cytoplasm) gives 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate; Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix); electron transport chain (inner membrane) makes most ATP. Net about **30-32 ATP** per glucose in eukaryotes (older textbooks say 36-38).

lessons.title: Some basic concepts: mole and stoichiometry

blocks.x: **Mole:** the amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro number N_A). Molar mass in g/mol equals the relative atomic/molecular mass: water (18 g/mol), 18 g = 1 mol.
Concentration terms

x: **Molarity** (M) = moles of solute / litres of solution. 5.85 g NaCl (58.5 g/mol) in 500 mL: moles = 0.1; M = 0.1 / 0.5 = **0.2 M**.
Molality = moles / kg of solvent; mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B); mass percent.

blocks.x: Percentage composition and empirical formula

H2SO4: M = 98.08 g/mol; H 2.06%, S 32.69%, O 65.26%. Empirical formula example: C 40%, H 6.7%, O 53.3%. Moles: C 40/12 = 3.33, H 6.7/1 = 6.7, O 53.3/16 = 3.33. Ratio 1 : 2 : 1, so empirical formula **CH2O**.
Limiting reagent
In 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O, with 4 g H2 (2 mol) and 16 g O2 (0.5 mol), O2 needs 1 mol H2 so O2 is limiting; it forms 1 mol (18 g) of water.
Gas laws
At STP (0 C, 1 atm) 1 mol of ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L. PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K): 2 mol at 300 K and 1 atm occupies 49.3 L.
Hindi saransh
1 mol = 6.022 x 10^23 kan. Molarity = mol / L. Empirical formula mole ratio se. Limiting reagent product decide karta hai.
Always convert to moles first.

lessons.title: Structure of the atom and the Bohr model

blocks.x: **Subatomic particles:** electron (-1), proton (+1), neutron (0). **Atomic number Z** = protons; **mass number A** = protons + neutrons.
Bohr model (hydrogen-like)

Electrons move in fixed orbits; energy E_n = -13.6 Z^2 / n^2 eV. Radius r_n = 0.529 n^2 / Z angstrom. Transition energy dE = 13.6 Z^2 (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) eV. Wavelength lambda (nm) = 1240 / dE (eV). Example: n = 3 to n = 2 in hydrogen: dE = 13.6 (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.889 eV, lambda = **656 nm** (red H-alpha line of the Balmer series).
Quantum numbers
n (shell), l (subshell: 0 s, 1 p, 2 d, 3 f), m_l (-l to +l), m_s (+/- 1/2). Each shell holds 2n^2 electrons.
Electron configuration rules

**Aufbau** (fill lowest energy first), **Pauli exclusion** (no two electrons share all four quantum numbers), **Hund's rule** (fill degenerate orbitals singly first). Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1, Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1.
de Broglie and uncertainty
lambda = h / (m v). Heisenberg: dx x dp >= h / 4 pi.
Hindi saransh
E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. Quantum numbers n, l, m, s. Aufbau, Pauli, Hund ke niyam.
Cr and Cu are the common exceptions.

lessons.title: Chemical equilibrium, acids and bases, pH

blocks.x: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations stay constant. For a A + b B <=> c C + d D, **K_c = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b)**. K depends only on temperature. **Le Chatelier's principle:** a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change in concentration, pressure or temperature. A catalyst does not shift equilibrium; it only speeds approach.
Example
pH

pH = -log [H+]; pH + pOH = 14 at 25 C. 0.01 M HCl has pH **2**. For a weak acid, [H+] = sqrt(K_a C): 0.1 M acetic acid (K_a = 1.8 x 10^-5): [H+] = 1.34 x 10^-3, pH = **2.87**. **Buffer** (Henderson-Hasselbalch): pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).
Hindi saransh
K_c = products / reactants. Le Chatelier: system badlav ka virodh karta hai. pH = -log[H+]. Weak acid mein [H+] = sqrt(Ka C).
A catalyst changes speed, not the position of equilibrium.

lessons.title: Thermodynamics and enthalpy

blocks.x: **First law:** dU = q + w (internal energy). **Enthalpy** H = U + PV; at constant pressure q_p = dH. Exothermic: dH < 0. **Hess's law:** total enthalpy change is independent of the path. **Standard enthalpy of reaction** = sum of formation enthalpies of products minus reactants. Example (methane combustion): CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O(l). dH = (-393.5) + 2 (-285.8) - (-74.8) = **-890.3 kJ/mol**. **Entropy** S measures disorder. **Gibbs free energy** dG = dH - T dS; reaction is spontaneous if dG < 0. At equilibrium dG = 0.

dU = q + w. Hess ka niyam: path se koi fark nahi. dG = dH - T dS < 0 to spontaneous.
Spontaneous means dG is negative, not that the reaction is fast.

lessons.title: States of matter: gases and liquids

blocks.x: Boyle: P V = constant (T, n fixed); Charles: V/T = constant; Gay-Lussac: P/T = constant; Avogadro: V proportional to n. Combined: PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K) = 8.314 J/(mol K). Dalton: P_total = sum of partial pressures; Graham: r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1). Real gases follow (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT.
Deep dive: gas laws

Boyle law: at constant temperature P1 V1 = P2 V2. Charles law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2 (T in kelvin). Gay-Lussac law: at constant volume P1/T1 = P2/T2. Avogadro law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules; molar volume at STP (0 C, 1 atm) is 22.4 L and at 1 bar 22.7 L. Combined gas law P1 V1/T1 = P2 V2/T2 and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT = (m/M) RT, giving density d = PM/(RT). R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1 = 8.314 J K^-1 mol^-1 = 0.0831 L bar K^-1 mol^-1.
Deep dive: mixtures, diffusion and kinetic energy

Dalton law of partial pressures: P_total = P1 + P2 + ...; the partial pressure P_i = x_i P_total where x_i is the mole fraction. Graham law of diffusion: r1/r2 = sqrt (M2/M1) = sqrt (d2/d1) (at equal pressure). Kinetic molecular theory: pressure arises from molecular collisions; average kinetic energy is (3/2) k T, so it depends only on temperature. Speeds: u_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), u_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), u_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with u_mp < u_avg < u_rms.
Deep dive: real gases and liquids

Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature. The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 where attractions dominate and above 1 where repulsion dominates. van der Waals equation (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT, where a measures attraction and b is the excluded volume. Boyle temperature T_B = a/(R b). Critical constants: T_c = 8a/(27 R b), P_c = a/(27 b^2), V_c = 3 b. Liquids: vapour pressure rises with temperature (boiling when it equals external pressure); surface tension and viscosity decrease with temperature; intermolecular forces include London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding.

PV = nRT. Dalton: P = P1 + P2 + ... Graham: rate proportional to 1/sqrt(M).
At STP (273 K, 1 atm) one mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L.

Big idea

  • Boyle: P V = constant (T, n fixed)
  • Charles: V/T = constant

Read the full explanation

Boyle: P V = constant (T, n fixed); Charles: V/T = constant; Gay-Lussac: P/T = constant; Avogadro: V proportional to n. Combined: PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K) = 8.314 J/(mol K). Dalton: P_total = sum of partial pressures; Graham: r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1). Real gases follow (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT.

⚖️

Gas laws

  • Boyle law: at constant temperature P1 V1 = P2 V2
  • Charles law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2 (T in kelvin)
  • Gay-Lussac law: at constant volume P1/T1 = P2/T2
  • Avogadro law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules
Read the full explanation

Boyle law: at constant temperature P1 V1 = P2 V2. Charles law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2 (T in kelvin). Gay-Lussac law: at constant volume P1/T1 = P2/T2. Avogadro law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules; molar volume at STP (0 C, 1 atm) is 22.4 L and at 1 bar 22.7 L. Combined gas law P1 V1/T1 = P2 V2/T2 and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT = (m/M) RT, giving density d = PM/(RT). R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1 = 8.314 J K^-1 mol^-1 = 0.0831 L bar K^-1 mol^-1.

🚀

Mixtures, diffusion and kinetic energy

  • Dalton law of partial pressures: P_total = P1 + P2 +
  • The partial pressure P_i = x_i P_total where x_i is the mole fraction
  • Graham law of diffusion: r1/r2 = sqrt (M2/M1) = sqrt (d2/d1) (at equal pressure)
  • Kinetic molecular theory: pressure arises from molecular collisions
Read the full explanation

Dalton law of partial pressures: P_total = P1 + P2 + ...; the partial pressure P_i = x_i P_total where x_i is the mole fraction. Graham law of diffusion: r1/r2 = sqrt (M2/M1) = sqrt (d2/d1) (at equal pressure). Kinetic molecular theory: pressure arises from molecular collisions; average kinetic energy is (3/2) k T, so it depends only on temperature. Speeds: u_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), u_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), u_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with u_mp < u_avg < u_rms.

🌟

Real gases and liquids

  • Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature
  • The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 where attractions dominate and above 1 where repulsion dominates
  • Van der Waals equation (P + a n2/V2)(V - n b) = nRT, where a measures attraction and b is the excluded volume
  • Boyle temperature T_B = a/(R b)
Read the full explanation

Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature. The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 where attractions dominate and above 1 where repulsion dominates. van der Waals equation (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - n b) = nRT, where a measures attraction and b is the excluded volume. Boyle temperature T_B = a/(R b). Critical constants: T_c = 8a/(27 R b), P_c = a/(27 b^2), V_c = 3 b. Liquids: vapour pressure rises with temperature (boiling when it equals external pressure); surface tension and viscosity decrease with temperature; intermolecular forces include London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding.

lessons.title: Sets, relations and functions

blocks.x: Sets

A **set** is a well-defined collection. Operations: union, intersection, difference, complement. Laws: commutative, associative, distributive, **De Morgan: (A U B)' = A' n B'** and (A n B)' = A' U B'. **Inclusion-exclusion:** n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B). Example: n(A) = 30, n(B) = 25, n(A n B) = 10 gives n(A U B) = **45**. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets.
Relations

A relation from A to B is a subset of A x B. If |A| = m and |B| = n there are 2^(mn) relations. A relation on a set is **reflexive**, **symmetric**, **transitive**; if all three, it is an **equivalence relation**.
Functions

A function assigns each element of the domain exactly one element of the codomain. **One-one** (injective), **onto** (surjective), **bijective** (both). The number of functions from a set of m elements to one of n elements is n^m; the number of one-one functions is nPm.

Prove or disprove that the relation R = {(a, b): a - b is divisible by 3} on the integers is an equivalence relation.

lessons.title: Complex numbers and quadratic equations

blocks.x: A complex number is z = a + ib with i^2 = -1. Its modulus is |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), its conjugate is a - ib, and its argument is the angle theta with tan theta = b/a (in the correct quadrant). The quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = 0 has roots (-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/2a, which are complex when the discriminant is negative.
Deep dive: algebra of complex numbers

A complex number z = a + ib has real part a and imaginary part b. Two complex numbers are equal when their real and imaginary parts are equal. Addition and subtraction are done part by part; multiplication uses (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc). The powers of i repeat with period 4: i^1 = i, i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1, so i^n depends on n mod 4. The conjugate of z is z-bar = a - ib, and z x z-bar = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2, which is how division is done: (a + ib)/(c + id) = (a + ib)(c - id)/(c^2 + d^2).
Deep dive: modulus, argument and the Argand plane

Each complex number is a point (a, b) on the Argand plane. The modulus |z| = sqrt (a^2 + b^2) is the distance from the origin; the argument is the angle the line from the origin makes with the positive real axis; the principal argument lies in (-pi, pi]. Polar form: z = r (cos theta + i sin theta). Properties: |z1 z2| = |z1||z2|, |z1/z2| = |z1|/|z2|, |z-bar| = |z|, z + z-bar = 2 Re(z), z - z-bar = 2i Im(z), |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2| (triangle inequality). The square root of a complex number a + ib is found by assuming x + iy and equating squares.
Deep dive: quadratic equations with complex roots

For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with real a, b, c the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac decides the roots: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal real roots, D < 0 two complex conjugate roots (-b +- i sqrt(-D))/2a. Sum of roots = -b/a and product = c/a hold for complex roots too. A quadratic with given roots p and q is x^2 - (p + q)x + pq = 0. The cube roots of unity are 1, w and w^2 where w = (-1 + i sqrt 3)/2, with 1 + w + w^2 = 0 and w^3 = 1. **Common mistakes:** taking i^2 as 1, forgetting to change the sign of the imaginary part for the conjugate, and reading the argument from the wrong quadrant.

lessons.title: Linear inequalities

blocks.x: An inequality compares two expressions with <, >, <= or >=. Adding or subtracting the same number keeps the sign; multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it. Solutions are written as intervals; two-variable inequalities represent half-planes bounded by a line.
Deep dive: rules and intervals

Rules: (i) equal numbers can be added to or subtracted from both sides; (ii) both sides can be multiplied or divided by a positive number; (iii) multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Solution sets are intervals: (a, b) open, [a, b] closed, [a, b) half-open; infinity is never included. For example x >= 2 is [2, infinity) and x < 5 is (-infinity, 5). Integer solutions: list the integers inside the interval. Natural number solutions begin at 1.
Deep dive: compound and modulus inequalities

A compound inequality a < x < b means x > a and x < b together (intersection). For |x| < a (a > 0): -a < x < a. For |x| > a: x < -a or x > a. For |x - c| <= d: c - d <= x <= c + d. Always check the endpoints against the original strict or non-strict sign.
Deep dive: graphical solution of two-variable inequalities

To graph ax + by <= c, draw the line ax + by = c (dashed for strict, solid for non-strict), test the origin (0, 0) and shade the side that satisfies the inequality; if the line passes through the origin test another point. The solution of a system is the common shaded region, which can be bounded or unbounded.

blocks.x: **Fundamental principle:** if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, together they can be done in m x n ways (multiplication) or m + n ways (either one, addition).
**Permutations (order matters):** nPr = n! / (n - r)!. **Combinations (order does not matter):** nCr = n! / (r! (n - r)!). nCr = nC(n-r).
Examples

Choose 3 from 10: 10C3 = **120**.
Choose 2 men from 8 and 3 women from 6: 8C2 x 6C3 = 28 x 20 = **560**.
Arrangements of the letters of MISSISSIPPI: 11! / (4! 4! 2!) = 34650.
Circular arrangements of n objects: (n - 1)!.

lessons.title: Straight lines, limits and derivatives

blocks.x: Straight lines

Slope m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1) = tan t. Forms: slope-intercept y = m x + c; point-slope y - y1 = m (x - x1); intercept x/a + y/b = 1. Distance from point (x1, y1) to line A x + B y + C = 0: |A x1 + B y1 + C| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2). Example: distance of (1, 2) from 3x + 4y - 5 = 0 is |3 + 8 - 5| / 5 = **1.2**. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m1 m2 = -1.
Limits
lim x->0 sin x / x = 1; lim x->0 (1 + x)^(1/x) = e; lim x->a (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n-1).
Derivatives

d/dx of x^n = n x^(n-1); sin x -> cos x; cos x -> -sin x; product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv'; quotient rule (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2. Example: derivative of x^2 at x = 1 from the definition: lim h->0 ((1 + h)^2 - 1)/h = lim (2 + h) = **2**.

lessons.title: Conic sections

blocks.x: A conic is the section of a double cone by a plane: a circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. Standard forms: circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2; parabola y^2 = 4ax; ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 with b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2); hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 with b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1).
Deep dive: how conics arise

Cutting a double-napped cone by a plane gives: a circle (plane perpendicular to the axis), an ellipse (tilted plane cutting one nappe), a parabola (plane parallel to a generator) and a hyperbola (plane cutting both nappes). Every conic is the locus of a point whose distance from a fixed point (the focus) is e times its distance from a fixed line (the directrix): e = 0 circle, e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola.
Deep dive: circle and parabola

Circle with centre (h, k) and radius r: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2; the general form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt (g^2 + f^2 - c). Parabola y^2 = 4ax: vertex (0, 0), focus (a, 0), directrix x = -a, axis the x-axis, length of latus rectum 4a. Other forms: y^2 = -4ax (opens left), x^2 = 4ay (opens up), x^2 = -4ay (opens down).
Deep dive: ellipse and hyperbola

Ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (a > b): centre origin, vertices (+-a, 0), foci (+-ae, 0), major axis length 2a, minor axis 2b, eccentricity e = sqrt (1 - b^2/a^2), latus rectum 2b^2/a, directrices x = +-a/e. Hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1: vertices (+-a, 0), foci (+-ae, 0), transverse axis 2a, conjugate axis 2b, e = sqrt (1 + b^2/a^2), latus rectum 2b^2/a, asymptotes y = +- (b/a) x. For the ellipse the sum of focal distances is 2a; for the hyperbola their difference is 2a.
Hindi saransh
Parabola y^2 = 4ax, ellipse e < 1, hyperbola e > 1.
Eccentricity: circle 0, ellipse < 1, parabola 1, hyperbola > 1.

Visual lesson

Conic sections

A conic is the section of a double cone by a plane: a circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola

🔑

Big idea

  • A conic is the section of a double cone by a plane: a circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola
  • Standard forms: circle x2 + y2 = r2
  • Parabola y2 = 4ax
  • Ellipse x2/a2 + y2/b2 = 1 with b2 = a2(1 - e2)
Read the full explanation

A conic is the section of a double cone by a plane: a circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. Standard forms: circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2; parabola y^2 = 4ax; ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 with b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2); hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 with b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1).

📌

How conics arise

  • Cutting a double-napped cone by a plane gives: a circle (plane perpendicular to the axis), an ellipse (tilted plane cutting one nappe), a parabola…
  • Every conic is the locus of a point whose distance from a fixed point (the focus) is e times its distance from a fixed line (the directrix): e = 0…
Read the full explanation

Cutting a double-napped cone by a plane gives: a circle (plane perpendicular to the axis), an ellipse (tilted plane cutting one nappe), a parabola (plane parallel to a generator) and a hyperbola (plane cutting both nappes). Every conic is the locus of a point whose distance from a fixed point (the focus) is e times its distance from a fixed line (the directrix): e = 0 circle, e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola.

📐

Circle and parabola

  • Circle with centre (h, k) and radius r: (x - h)2 + (y - k)2 = r2
  • The general form x2 + y2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt (g2 + f2 - c)
  • Parabola y2 = 4ax: vertex (0, 0), focus (a, 0), directrix x = -a, axis the x-axis, length of latus rectum 4a
  • Other forms: y2 = -4ax (opens left), x2 = 4ay (opens up), x2 = -4ay (opens down)
Read the full explanation

Circle with centre (h, k) and radius r: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2; the general form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt (g^2 + f^2 - c). Parabola y^2 = 4ax: vertex (0, 0), focus (a, 0), directrix x = -a, axis the x-axis, length of latus rectum 4a. Other forms: y^2 = -4ax (opens left), x^2 = 4ay (opens up), x^2 = -4ay (opens down).

🌟

Ellipse and hyperbola

  • Ellipse x2/a2 + y2/b2 = 1 (a > b): centre origin, vertices (+-a, 0), foci (+-ae, 0), major axis length 2a, minor axis 2b, eccentricity e = sqrt…
  • Hyperbola x2/a2 - y2/b2 = 1: vertices (+-a, 0), foci (+-ae, 0), transverse axis 2a, conjugate axis 2b, e = sqrt (1 + b2/a2), latus rectum…
  • For the ellipse the sum of focal distances is 2a
  • For the hyperbola their difference is 2a
Read the full explanation

Ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (a > b): centre origin, vertices (+-a, 0), foci (+-ae, 0), major axis length 2a, minor axis 2b, eccentricity e = sqrt (1 - b^2/a^2), latus rectum 2b^2/a, directrices x = +-a/e. Hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1: vertices (+-a, 0), foci (+-ae, 0), transverse axis 2a, conjugate axis 2b, e = sqrt (1 + b^2/a^2), latus rectum 2b^2/a, asymptotes y = +- (b/a) x. For the ellipse the sum of focal distances is 2a; for the hyperbola their difference is 2a.

lessons.title: Probability

blocks.x: Probability of an event E is P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally likely outcomes. 0 <= P(E) <= 1, P(not E) = 1 - P(E), P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; exhaustive events cover the whole sample space.
Deep dive: sample space and events

An experiment has outcomes forming the sample space S. An event is a subset of S. A simple event has one outcome; a compound event has more. The complement of E is E-bar (not E); A or B is the union, A and B is the intersection. Events A and B are mutually exclusive if A and B cannot both happen (A intersect B is empty), and exhaustive if their union is S. Typical sample spaces: a coin (2 outcomes), a die (6), two coins (4), two dice (36), three coins (8), a pack of 52 cards (4 suits x 13 ranks).
Deep dive: rules of probability

For equally likely outcomes P(E) = n(E)/n(S). Axioms: P(E) >= 0, P(S) = 1, and for mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Addition law: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Complement: P(A-bar) = 1 - P(A). P(A but not B) = P(A) - P(A and B). P(neither A nor B) = 1 - P(A or B). Odds in favour of E = P(E) : P(E-bar).
Deep dive: counting methods in probability

Use the multiplication principle and combinations: choosing r objects from n gives C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n - r)!). Drawing 2 cards from 52: total C(52, 2) = 1326. Two dice: the sum 7 occurs in 6 of 36 ways. P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). Dice sums: 2 and 12 occur once each; 7 occurs 6 times, the most likely sum. **Common mistakes:** treating outcomes as equally likely when they are not (the sum of two dice), double-counting overlap in P(A or B), and forgetting to use combinations for selections.

Visual lesson

Probability

Probability of an event E is P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally likely outcomes

🔑

Big idea

  • Probability of an event E is P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally likely outcomes
  • 0 <= P(E) <= 1, P(not E) = 1 - P(E), P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
  • Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together
  • Exhaustive events cover the whole sample space
📌

Sample space and events

  • An experiment has outcomes forming the sample space S
  • An event is a subset of S
  • A simple event has one outcome
  • A compound event has more
Read the full explanation

An experiment has outcomes forming the sample space S. An event is a subset of S. A simple event has one outcome; a compound event has more. The complement of E is E-bar (not E); A or B is the union, A and B is the intersection. Events A and B are mutually exclusive if A and B cannot both happen (A intersect B is empty), and exhaustive if their union is S. Typical sample spaces: a coin (2 outcomes), a die (6), two coins (4), two dice (36), three coins (8), a pack of 52 cards (4 suits x 13 ranks).

⚖️

Rules of probability

  • For equally likely outcomes P(E) = n(E)/n(S)
  • Axioms: P(E) >= 0, P(S) = 1, and for mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
  • Addition law: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
  • Complement: P(A-bar) = 1 - P(A)
Read the full explanation

For equally likely outcomes P(E) = n(E)/n(S). Axioms: P(E) >= 0, P(S) = 1, and for mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Addition law: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Complement: P(A-bar) = 1 - P(A). P(A but not B) = P(A) - P(A and B). P(neither A nor B) = 1 - P(A or B). Odds in favour of E = P(E) : P(E-bar).

🔄

Counting methods in probability

  • Use the multiplication principle and combinations: choosing r objects from n gives C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n - r)!)
  • Drawing 2 cards from 52: total C(52, 2) = 1326
  • Two dice: the sum 7 occurs in 6 of 36 ways
  • P(at least one) = 1 - P(none)
