lessons.title: Introduction to three dimensional geometry

blocks.x: A point in space is (x, y, z) in three mutually perpendicular axes forming eight octants. The distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2). The section formula divides a segment in the ratio m:n.
Deep dive: coordinate system in space

Three mutually perpendicular axes X, Y, Z meet at the origin O. The coordinate planes XY, YZ, ZX divide space into eight octants. A point P (x, y, z) has distances |x|, |y|, |z| from the YZ, ZX and XY planes. Points on the x-axis are (x, 0, 0), on the y-axis (0, y, 0), on the z-axis (0, 0, z). Points in the XY plane have z = 0, in YZ plane x = 0, in ZX plane y = 0. The octant of a point is decided by the signs of x, y, z.
Deep dive: distance and section formulae

Distance between P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) is PQ = sqrt ((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2). The distance of P from the origin is sqrt (x^2 + y^2 + z^2). The point dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n is ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n), (m z2 + n z1)/(m + n)); the mid-point is the average of the coordinates, and for external division change n to -n. The centroid of a triangle is the mean of the three vertices.
Deep dive: applications

Three points are collinear if the sum of two of the distances equals the third. Triangle shape: if all three sides are equal it is equilateral; two equal, isosceles; a^2 + b^2 = c^2, right-angled. The locus of points at a fixed distance r from a given point is a sphere.
Hindi saransh
Distance: sqrt of sum of three squares. Section formula: (m x2 + n x1)/(m + n).
Mid-point = average of coordinates.

lessons.html:
Visual lesson

Introduction to three dimensional geometry

A point in space is (x, y, z) in three mutually perpendicular axes forming eight octants

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Coordinate system in space›3Distance and section…›4Applications
Distance from originsqrt (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)
Centroid((x1 + x2 + x3)/3, ...)
Number of octants8
🔑

Big idea

  • A point in space is (x, y, z) in three mutually perpendicular axes forming eight octants
  • The distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is sqrt((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2 + (z2 - z1)2)
  • The section formula divides a segment in the ratio m:n
📐

Coordinate system in space

  • Three mutually perpendicular axes X, Y, Z meet at the origin O
  • The coordinate planes XY, YZ, ZX divide space into eight octants
  • A point P (x, y, z) has distances |x|, |y|, |z| from the YZ, ZX and XY planes
  • Points on the x-axis are (x, 0, 0), on the y-axis (0, y, 0), on the z-axis (0, 0, z)
Read the full explanation

Three mutually perpendicular axes X, Y, Z meet at the origin O. The coordinate planes XY, YZ, ZX divide space into eight octants. A point P (x, y, z) has distances |x|, |y|, |z| from the YZ, ZX and XY planes. Points on the x-axis are (x, 0, 0), on the y-axis (0, y, 0), on the z-axis (0, 0, z). Points in the XY plane have z = 0, in YZ plane x = 0, in ZX plane y = 0. The octant of a point is decided by the signs of x, y, z.

🧮

Distance and section formulae

  • Distance between P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) is PQ = sqrt ((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2 + (z2 - z1)2)
  • The distance of P from the origin is sqrt (x2 + y2 + z2)
  • The point dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n is ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n), (m z2 + n z1)/(m + n))
  • The mid-point is the average of the coordinates, and for external division change n to -n
Read the full explanation

Distance between P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) is PQ = sqrt ((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2). The distance of P from the origin is sqrt (x^2 + y^2 + z^2). The point dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n is ((m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n), (m z2 + n z1)/(m + n)); the mid-point is the average of the coordinates, and for external division change n to -n. The centroid of a triangle is the mean of the three vertices.

💡

Applications

  • Three points are collinear if the sum of two of the distances equals the third
  • Triangle shape: if all three sides are equal it is equilateral
  • Two equal, isosceles
  • A2 + b2 = c2, right-angled
Read the full explanation

Three points are collinear if the sum of two of the distances equals the third. Triangle shape: if all three sides are equal it is equilateral; two equal, isosceles; a^2 + b^2 = c^2, right-angled. The locus of points at a fixed distance r from a given point is a sphere.

🧮

lessons.title: Statistics: measures of dispersion

blocks.x: Range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation measure how spread out data are. Variance = (1/n) sum (x - mean)^2, standard deviation is its square root, and coefficient of variation = (s / mean) x 100.
Deep dive: measures of dispersion

Range = largest - smallest. Mean deviation about the mean = sum |x - mean| / n; about the median = sum |x - M| / n. Variance sigma^2 = sum (x - mean)^2 / n = (sum x^2)/n - mean^2. Standard deviation sigma = sqrt (variance). For a frequency table: sigma^2 = sum f (x - mean)^2 / N, N = sum f. For continuous data use class marks as x. Coefficient of variation CV = (sigma / mean) x 100 compares the variability of two series: the series with smaller CV is more consistent.
Deep dive: effect of change of origin and scale

If every value is increased by a constant, the mean increases by it but the variance and SD stay the same. If every value is multiplied by k, the mean and SD are multiplied by |k| and the variance by k^2. For a combined group of n1 and n2 items with means m1, m2, the combined mean is (n1 m1 + n2 m2)/(n1 + n2). The shortcut method: with a assumed mean, sigma^2 = (sum f d^2)/N - (sum f d / N)^2 where d = x - a. **Common mistakes:** dividing by n - 1 (not used in this syllabus), forgetting the square root, and comparing variability using SD instead of CV when the means differ.

Statistics: measures of dispersion

Range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation measure how spread out data are

Coefficient of variation(sigma / mean) x 100
Combined mean(n1 m1 + n2 m2)/(n1 + n2)
🔑

Big idea

  • Range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation measure how spread out data are
  • Variance = (1/n) sum (x - mean)2, standard deviation is its square root, and coefficient of variation = (s / mean) x 100
📌

Measures of dispersion

  • Range = largest - smallest
  • Mean deviation about the mean = sum |x - mean| / n
  • About the median = sum |x - M| / n
  • Variance sigma2 = sum (x - mean)2 / n = (sum x2)/n - mean2
Read the full explanation

Range = largest - smallest. Mean deviation about the mean = sum |x - mean| / n; about the median = sum |x - M| / n. Variance sigma^2 = sum (x - mean)^2 / n = (sum x^2)/n - mean^2. Standard deviation sigma = sqrt (variance). For a frequency table: sigma^2 = sum f (x - mean)^2 / N, N = sum f. For continuous data use class marks as x. Coefficient of variation CV = (sigma / mean) x 100 compares the variability of two series: the series with smaller CV is more consistent.

🧠

Effect of change of origin and scale

  • If every value is increased by a constant, the mean increases by it but the variance and SD stay the same
  • If every value is multiplied by k, the mean and SD are multiplied by |k| and the variance by k2
  • For a combined group of n1 and n2 items with means m1, m2, the combined mean is (n1 m1 + n2 m2)/(n1 + n2)
  • The shortcut method: with a assumed mean, sigma2 = (sum f d2)/N - (sum f d / N)2 where d = x - a
Read the full explanation

If every value is increased by a constant, the mean increases by it but the variance and SD stay the same. If every value is multiplied by k, the mean and SD are multiplied by |k| and the variance by k^2. For a combined group of n1 and n2 items with means m1, m2, the combined mean is (n1 m1 + n2 m2)/(n1 + n2). The shortcut method: with a assumed mean, sigma^2 = (sum f d^2)/N - (sum f d / N)^2 where d = x - a. Common mistakes: dividing by n - 1 (not used in this syllabus), forgetting the square root, and comparing variability using SD instead of CV when the means differ.

lessons.title: Motion in a plane: vectors and projectile motion

blocks.x: Vectors

A vector has magnitude and direction. Add by the **triangle/parallelogram law**; resolve into components A_x = A cos t, A_y = A sin t. Resultant of two vectors with angle t: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos t). Dot product A.B = AB cos t (scalar); cross product has magnitude AB sin t (vector).
Projectile motion
A body thrown with speed u at angle t above the horizontal moves under gravity only. Horizontal velocity is constant; vertical motion has acceleration -g.

x: Time of flight T = 2 u sin t / g
Maximum height H = u^2 sin^2 t / (2 g)
Range R = u^2 sin 2t / g (maximum at 45 degrees, equal for t and 90 - t)
Path is a parabola.

blocks.x: Worked example (u = 20 m/s, t = 30 degrees, g = 10)
Circular motion
Uniform circular motion: speed constant, direction changes. Centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / r = w^2 r directed to the centre.

Projectile mein horizontal velocity constant, vertical mein g ka acceleration. T = 2u sin t / g, H = u^2 sin^2 t / 2g, R = u^2 sin 2t / g.

lessons.title: Laws of motion and friction
yt: newton laws of motion atwood machine

blocks.x: Newton's laws

x: **First law (inertia):** a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a net external force acts.
**Second law:** F = m a (net force equals rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt).
**Third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction (acting on different bodies).

blocks.x: Free-body diagrams
Draw only forces on one body: weight mg, normal N, tension T, friction f, applied force. Resolve along and perpendicular to motion, then apply F = ma.
Friction
Static friction f_s <= mu_s N (self-adjusting); kinetic friction f_k = mu_k N. On a rough incline of angle t: a = g (sin t - mu cos t); a block just starts to slide when tan t = mu_s.
Atwood machine
Masses m1 < m2 over a light pulley: a = (m2 - m1) g / (m1 + m2), T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2). For 3 kg and 5 kg (g = 10): a = 2 x 10 / 8 = **2.5 m/s^2**, T = 2 x 15 x 10 / 8 = **37.5 N**.
Incline example
Block on a 30 degree incline with mu = 0.2: a = 10 (0.5 - 0.2 x 0.866) = **3.27 m/s^2** down the slope.
Circular motion and banking
Needed centripetal force F = m v^2 / r. On a level road, friction supplies it: v_max = sqrt(mu g r).
Hindi saransh
F = ma. Friction f = mu N. Atwood machine mein a = (m2 - m1)g/(m1 + m2). Incline par a = g(sin t - mu cos t).
Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other.

qa.a: The net force on a body equals its mass times acceleration, F = ma, or the rate of change of momentum.

qa.a: They act on two different bodies.

lessons.title: Work, energy and power

blocks.x: **Work** W = F d cos t (scalar). Positive if force has a component along the displacement. **Kinetic energy** K = (1/2) m v^2. **Work-energy theorem:** net work = change in kinetic energy. **Potential energy:** gravitational U = m g h; spring U = (1/2) k x^2. Conservative forces conserve mechanical energy K + U. **Power** P = W / t = F v. 1 horsepower is about 746 W.
Examples

x: A 2 kg body at rest pushed by 10 N over 5 m (no friction): W = **50 J**, so v = sqrt(2 x 50 / 2) = **7.07 m/s**.
Spring k = 200 N/m compressed 0.1 m stores (1/2)(200)(0.01) = **1 J**.
Free fall from 80 m (g = 10): speed at the ground from energy: v = sqrt(2 g h) = 40 m/s.

blocks.x: Collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision. **Elastic:** kinetic energy also conserved. **Perfectly inelastic:** bodies stick together; maximum KE loss. Coefficient of restitution e = (speed of separation) / (speed of approach).
Hindi saransh
Work = F d cos t. Work-energy theorem: net work = change in KE. Spring energy = kx^2/2. Collision mein momentum hamesha conserve hota hai.
Energy is scalar; momentum is a vector.

🔑

Big idea

  • Work W = F d cos t (scalar)
  • Positive if force has a component along the displacement
  • Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v2
  • Work-energy theorem: net work = change in kinetic energy
Read the full explanation

Work W = F d cos t (scalar). Positive if force has a component along the displacement. Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2. Work-energy theorem: net work = change in kinetic energy. Potential energy: gravitational U = m g h; spring U = (1/2) k x^2. Conservative forces conserve mechanical energy K + U. Power P = W / t = F v. 1 horsepower is about 746 W.

💡

Examples

  • A 2 kg body at rest pushed by 10 N over 5 m (no friction): W = 50 J, so v = sqrt(2 x 50 / 2) = 7.07 m/s.
  • Spring k = 200 N/m compressed 0.1 m stores (1/2)(200)(0.01) = 1 J.
  • Free fall from 80 m (g = 10): speed at the ground from energy: v = sqrt(2 g h) = 40 m/s.
🧠

Collisions

  • Momentum is conserved in every collision
  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick together
  • Maximum KE loss
Read the full explanation

Momentum is conserved in every collision. Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved. Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick together; maximum KE loss. Coefficient of restitution e = (speed of separation) / (speed of approach).

🎯 Remember Energy is scalar; momentum is a vector.
🇮🇳

Work = F d cos t. Work-energy theorem: net work = change in KE. Spring energy = kx^2/2. Collision mein momentum hamesha conserve hota hai.

lessons.title: Gravitation and satellites

blocks.x: **Newton's law of gravitation:** F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. **Acceleration due to gravity:** g = G M / R^2 (about 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth). Variation: g decreases with height (g' = g (R/(R+h))^2), decreases with depth (g' = g (1 - d/R)), and varies with latitude. **Gravitational potential energy** of two masses U = - G M m / r.
Escape and orbital velocity

x: Orbital velocity near the surface v_o = sqrt(g R) = sqrt(G M / R) = about **7.9 km/s**.
Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2 g R) = sqrt(2) v_o = about **11.2 km/s**.

blocks.x: Computed with G = 6.67e-11, M = 5.97e24 kg, R = 6.371e6 m: v_e = 11.18 km/s and v_o = 7.91 km/s.
Kepler's laws

x: Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times (angular momentum conserved).
T^2 is proportional to a^3.

blocks.x: Satellites
Time period T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / G M). A **geostationary** satellite has period 24 h, orbits in the equatorial plane at about 36,000 km above the surface.

lessons.title: Mechanical properties of solids and fluids
yt: class 11 physics mechanical properties of fluids

blocks.x: Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain. Fluid pressure P = P0 + rho g h; Pascal law transmits pressure equally; Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced. Continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2; Bernoulli P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. Surface tension S = F/l, capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g r), terminal velocity v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).
Deep dive: elasticity

When a deforming force acts on a body, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area (N/m^2 = Pa). Strain = fractional change: longitudinal (change in length/length), volumetric (change in volume/volume) or shear (angle of shear). Hooke law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain. Young modulus Y = (F/A)/(DL/L), bulk modulus B = -P/(DV/V) with compressibility 1/B, shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain. Poisson ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, with a value between -1 and 0.5. Elastic energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain. Work done in stretching a wire = (1/2) F x DL = (1/2) Y A DL^2/L. Steel is more elastic than rubber because it has a higher modulus.
Deep dive: fluid statics and dynamics

Pressure P = F/A; in a fluid at rest P = P0 + rho g h and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Pascal law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished (hydraulic lift F2/F1 = A2/A1). Archimedes principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced; a body floats when its density is less than the fluid (fraction submerged = rho_body/rho_fluid). Steady (streamline) flow of an incompressible fluid satisfies the equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2. Bernoulli theorem: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline; speed of efflux from a hole at depth h is v = sqrt (2 g h) (Torricelli). Applications: venturimeter, aerofoil lift, atomiser, Magnus effect.
Deep dive: viscosity and surface tension

Viscous force F = eta A (dv/dx); the SI unit of viscosity eta is Pa s (poise in CGS: 1 Pa s = 10 poise). Stokes law: F = 6 pi eta r v. Terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a fluid v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta). Reynolds number Re = rho v d/eta decides laminar (< 1000) or turbulent (> 2000) flow. Surface tension S = F/l = energy per unit area; excess pressure inside a drop is 2S/R, inside a soap bubble 4S/R. Capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(r rho g). Angle of contact is acute for liquids that wet glass (water), obtuse for non-wetting liquids (mercury). Surface energy of a drop = S x area; work to form a bubble of radius R is 8 pi R^2 S.
Hindi saransh
Stress/strain = modulus. P = rho g h. Bernoulli: P + 1/2 rho v^2 + rho g h = constant.
Pressure at depth h: P = P0 + rho g h.

qa.q: What is stress?
qa.a: The restoring force per unit area.

qa.q: What is strain?
qa.a: The fractional change in the dimension of the body.

qa.q: State Hooke's law.
qa.a: Within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain.

qa.q: What is Young's modulus?
qa.a: The ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain.

qa.q: What is the bulk modulus?
qa.a: The ratio of volume stress (pressure) to volume strain.

qa.q: What is the shear modulus?
qa.a: The ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

qa.q: What is Poisson's ratio?
qa.a: The ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
State Pascal's law.
qa.a: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished in every direction.

qa.q: State Archimedes' principle.
qa.a: A body in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid it displaces.

qa.q: What is the equation of continuity?
State Bernoulli's theorem.
qa.a: For streamline flow of an ideal fluid, P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h is constant.

qa.q: What is viscosity?
qa.a: The internal friction of a fluid that opposes relative motion of its layers.

qa.q: What is Stokes' law?
qa.a: The viscous drag on a sphere is 6 pi eta r v.

qa.q: What is terminal velocity?
qa.a: The constant velocity reached when drag and buoyancy balance weight.

qa.q: What is surface tension?
qa.a: The force per unit length acting along the surface of a liquid.

qa.q: Why do liquid drops become spherical?
qa.a: Surface tension minimises the surface area.

qa.q: What is the angle of contact?
qa.a: The angle between the liquid surface and the solid surface at the point of contact.

qa.q: Why is steel more elastic than rubber?
qa.a: Steel has a larger Young's modulus.

qa.q: What is capillarity?
qa.a: The rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube.

qa.q: What is the unit of viscosity?
What is the Reynolds number?
qa.a: rho v d / eta, which decides if the flow is laminar or turbulent.

qa.q: Why does an aerofoil get lift?
qa.a: Faster air above lowers the pressure there (Bernoulli).

Mechanical properties of solids and fluids

🔑

Big idea

  • Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain
  • Fluid pressure P = P0 + rho g h
  • Pascal law transmits pressure equally
  • Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced
Read the full explanation

Stress = force/area, strain = change/original, Young modulus Y = stress/strain. Fluid pressure P = P0 + rho g h; Pascal law transmits pressure equally; Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced. Continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2; Bernoulli P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. Surface tension S = F/l, capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g r), terminal velocity v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).

📌

Elasticity

  • When a deforming force acts on a body, internal restoring forces appear
  • Stress = restoring force per unit area (N/m2 = Pa)
  • Strain = fractional change: longitudinal (change in length/length), volumetric (change in volume/volume) or shear (angle of shear)
  • Hooke law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain
Read the full explanation

When a deforming force acts on a body, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area (N/m^2 = Pa). Strain = fractional change: longitudinal (change in length/length), volumetric (change in volume/volume) or shear (angle of shear). Hooke law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain. Young modulus Y = (F/A)/(DL/L), bulk modulus B = -P/(DV/V) with compressibility 1/B, shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain. Poisson ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, with a value between -1 and 0.5. Elastic energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain. Work done in stretching a wire = (1/2) F x DL = (1/2) Y A DL^2/L. Steel is more elastic than rubber because it has a higher modulus.

🧠

Fluid statics and dynamics

  • Pressure P = F/A
  • In a fluid at rest P = P0 + rho g h and acts equally in all directions at a given depth
  • Pascal law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished (hydraulic lift F2/F1 = A2/A1)
  • Archimedes principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced
Read the full explanation

Pressure P = F/A; in a fluid at rest P = P0 + rho g h and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Pascal law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished (hydraulic lift F2/F1 = A2/A1). Archimedes principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced; a body floats when its density is less than the fluid (fraction submerged = rho_body/rho_fluid). Steady (streamline) flow of an incompressible fluid satisfies the equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2. Bernoulli theorem: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline; speed of efflux from a hole at depth h is v = sqrt (2 g h) (Torricelli). Applications: venturimeter, aerofoil lift, atomiser, Magnus effect.

🌟

Viscosity and surface tension

  • Viscous force F = eta A (dv/dx)
  • The SI unit of viscosity eta is Pa s (poise in CGS: 1 Pa s = 10 poise)
  • Stokes law: F = 6 pi eta r v
  • Terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a fluid v_t = 2 r2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta)
Read the full explanation

Viscous force F = eta A (dv/dx); the SI unit of viscosity eta is Pa s (poise in CGS: 1 Pa s = 10 poise). Stokes law: F = 6 pi eta r v. Terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a fluid v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta). Reynolds number Re = rho v d/eta decides laminar (< 1000) or turbulent (> 2000) flow. Surface tension S = F/l = energy per unit area; excess pressure inside a drop is 2S/R, inside a soap bubble 4S/R. Capillary rise h = 2 S cos theta/(r rho g). Angle of contact is acute for liquids that wet glass (water), obtuse for non-wetting liquids (mercury). Surface energy of a drop = S x area; work to form a bubble of radius R is 8 pi R^2 S.

lessons.title: Oscillations and waves

blocks.x: Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega^2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2). For a spring T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); for a simple pendulum T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). A wave has speed v = f lambda; on a string v = sqrt(T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt(gamma P/rho); stationary waves, beats and the Doppler effect follow.
Deep dive: simple harmonic motion

In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, so a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = k/m. Displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi); velocity v = A omega cos (omega t + phi) = omega sqrt (A^2 - x^2), maximum A omega at the mean position; maximum acceleration A omega^2 at the extremes. Time period T = 2 pi/omega, frequency f = 1/T, and omega = 2 pi f. Energy: kinetic (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), potential (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, total (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = (1/2) k A^2, constant. Kinetic and potential energies each oscillate at twice the frequency of the motion; their time-average is half the total.
Deep dive: spring, pendulum and combinations

A mass m on a spring: T = 2 pi sqrt (m/k). Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2; in parallel: k = k1 + k2. Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small angles); the seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) has length about 1 m. In an accelerating lift g becomes g +- a; on the Moon g is one-sixth so T is larger by sqrt 6. Physical pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (I/(m g d)). Damped oscillations lose amplitude exponentially; forced oscillations show resonance when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.
Deep dive: wave motion

A progressive wave y = A sin (k x - omega t) has wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, speed v = omega/k = f lambda. Transverse waves (particles move perpendicular to propagation) travel in solids on strings; longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) such as sound need a medium. Speed on a stretched string v = sqrt (T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt (gamma P/rho) = sqrt (gamma R T/M), increasing about 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius near 20 C. Stationary waves arise from superposition of two opposite waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum), adjacent nodes lambda/2 apart. A string fixed at both ends: f_n = n v/(2L); an open pipe: f_n = n v/(2L); a closed pipe: f_n = (2n - 1) v/(4L) (odd harmonics only). Beats: two close frequencies f1 and f2 give beat frequency |f1 - f2|. Doppler effect: f' = f (v +- v_o)/(v -+ v_s).

Visual lesson

Oscillations and waves

Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega^2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)

🔑

Big idea

  • Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A2 - x2)
  • For a spring T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)

Read the full explanation

Simple harmonic motion has acceleration a = -omega^2 x, period T = 2 pi/omega, displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi), speed v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2). For a spring T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); for a simple pendulum T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). A wave has speed v = f lambda; on a string v = sqrt(T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt(gamma P/rho); stationary waves, beats and the Doppler effect follow.

🚀

Simple harmonic motion

  • In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, so a = -omega2 x with omega2 = k/m
  • Displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi)
  • Velocity v = A omega cos (omega t + phi) = omega sqrt (A2 - x2), maximum A omega at the mean position
  • Maximum acceleration A omega2 at the extremes
Read the full explanation

In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, so a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = k/m. Displacement x = A sin (omega t + phi); velocity v = A omega cos (omega t + phi) = omega sqrt (A^2 - x^2), maximum A omega at the mean position; maximum acceleration A omega^2 at the extremes. Time period T = 2 pi/omega, frequency f = 1/T, and omega = 2 pi f. Energy: kinetic (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), potential (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, total (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = (1/2) k A^2, constant. Kinetic and potential energies each oscillate at twice the frequency of the motion; their time-average is half the total.

🧠

Spring, pendulum and combinations

  • A mass m on a spring: T = 2 pi sqrt (m/k)
  • Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2
  • In parallel: k = k1 + k2
  • Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small angles)
Read the full explanation

A mass m on a spring: T = 2 pi sqrt (m/k). Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2; in parallel: k = k1 + k2. Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small angles); the seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) has length about 1 m. In an accelerating lift g becomes g +- a; on the Moon g is one-sixth so T is larger by sqrt 6. Physical pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt (I/(m g d)). Damped oscillations lose amplitude exponentially; forced oscillations show resonance when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.

🌊

Wave motion

  • A progressive wave y = A sin (k x - omega t) has wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, speed v = omega/k = f lambda
  • Transverse waves (particles move perpendicular to propagation) travel in solids on strings
  • Longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) such as sound need a medium
  • Speed on a stretched string v = sqrt (T/mu)
Read the full explanation

A progressive wave y = A sin (k x - omega t) has wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, speed v = omega/k = f lambda. Transverse waves (particles move perpendicular to propagation) travel in solids on strings; longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) such as sound need a medium. Speed on a stretched string v = sqrt (T/mu); in a gas v = sqrt (gamma P/rho) = sqrt (gamma R T/M), increasing about 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius near 20 C. Stationary waves arise from superposition of two opposite waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum), adjacent nodes lambda/2 apart. A string fixed at both ends: f_n = n v/(2L); an open pipe: f_n = n v/(2L); a closed pipe: f_n = (2n - 1) v/(4L) (odd harmonics only). Beats: two close frequencies f1 and f2 give beat frequency |f1 - f2|. Doppler effect: f' = f (v +- v_o)/(v -+ v_s).

lessons.title: Heat, kinetic theory and thermodynamics

blocks.x: Heat Q = m c DT; PV = nRT; the kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2) k T and v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M). First law: Q = DU + W. Efficiency of a Carnot engine = 1 - T2/T1. Heat flow by conduction H = k A DT/L; Stefan law E = sigma T^4; Wien law lambda_m T = b.
Deep dive: temperature, heat and calorimetry

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. Scales: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 = (K - 273)/5. Heat required Q = m c DT; for a phase change Q = m L (latent heat of fusion for ice 336 kJ/kg, of vaporisation of water 2260 kJ/kg). Principle of calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained. Specific heat of water is 4200 J/(kg K). Thermal expansion: DL = alpha L DT, DA = 2 alpha A DT, DV = 3 alpha V DT. Water shows anomalous expansion between 0 and 4 C, with maximum density at 4 C.
Deep dive: kinetic theory of gases

Ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k T with R = 8.31 J/(mol K) and k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Pressure P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2. Average kinetic energy per molecule (3/2) k T; v_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), v_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), v_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt 3 : sqrt (8/pi) : sqrt 2. Degrees of freedom f: energy per mole (f/2) R T; monatomic f = 3, diatomic f = 5 at room temperature. C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = C_v + R (Mayer), gamma = C_p/C_v = 1 + 2/f: 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic. Mean free path lambda = 1/(sqrt 2 pi d^2 n).
Deep dive: thermodynamics and transfer

First law: Q = DU + W where W = integral P dV. Isothermal: DU = 0, W = nRT ln (V2/V1), PV = constant. Adiabatic: Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant, W = (P1 V1 - P2 V2)/(gamma - 1). Isobaric: W = P DV. Isochoric: W = 0. Heat engine efficiency = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1; a Carnot engine between T1 and T2 has efficiency 1 - T2/T1 (maximum). Refrigerator coefficient of performance = T2/(T1 - T2). Second law: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot (Clausius); no engine converts all heat to work (Kelvin-Planck). Conduction H = k A (T1 - T2)/L; convection; radiation: a black body emits E = sigma T^4 per unit area (Stefan), with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/(m^2 K^4); Wien displacement lambda_m T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K; Newton law of cooling: rate of cooling proportional to temperature difference.

Big idea

  • Heat Q = m c DT

Heat Q = m c DT; PV = nRT; the kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2) k T and v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M). First law: Q = DU + W. Efficiency of a Carnot engine = 1 - T2/T1. Heat flow by conduction H = k A DT/L; Stefan law E = sigma T^4; Wien law lambda_m T = b.

🌡️

Temperature, heat and calorimetry

  • Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules
  • Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference
  • Scales: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 = (K - 273)/5
  • Heat required Q = m c DT
Read the full explanation

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. Scales: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 = (K - 273)/5. Heat required Q = m c DT; for a phase change Q = m L (latent heat of fusion for ice 336 kJ/kg, of vaporisation of water 2260 kJ/kg). Principle of calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained. Specific heat of water is 4200 J/(kg K). Thermal expansion: DL = alpha L DT, DA = 2 alpha A DT, DV = 3 alpha V DT. Water shows anomalous expansion between 0 and 4 C, with maximum density at 4 C.

🧠

Kinetic theory of gases

  • Ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k T with R = 8.31 J/(mol K) and k = 1.38 x 10-23 J/K
  • Pressure P = (1/3) rho v_rms2
  • Average kinetic energy per molecule (3/2) k T
  • V_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), v_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), v_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt 3 : sqrt (8/pi) : sqrt 2
Read the full explanation

Ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k T with R = 8.31 J/(mol K) and k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Pressure P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2. Average kinetic energy per molecule (3/2) k T; v_rms = sqrt (3RT/M), v_avg = sqrt (8RT/(pi M)), v_mp = sqrt (2RT/M), with v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt 3 : sqrt (8/pi) : sqrt 2. Degrees of freedom f: energy per mole (f/2) R T; monatomic f = 3, diatomic f = 5 at room temperature. C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = C_v + R (Mayer), gamma = C_p/C_v = 1 + 2/f: 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic. Mean free path lambda = 1/(sqrt 2 pi d^2 n).

🌡️

Thermodynamics and transfer

  • First law: Q = DU + W where W = integral P dV
  • Isothermal: DU = 0, W = nRT ln (V2/V1), PV = constant
  • Adiabatic: Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant, W = (P1 V1 - P2 V2)/(gamma - 1)
  • Isobaric: W = P DV
Read the full explanation

First law: Q = DU + W where W = integral P dV. Isothermal: DU = 0, W = nRT ln (V2/V1), PV = constant. Adiabatic: Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant, W = (P1 V1 - P2 V2)/(gamma - 1). Isobaric: W = P DV. Isochoric: W = 0. Heat engine efficiency = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1; a Carnot engine between T1 and T2 has efficiency 1 - T2/T1 (maximum). Refrigerator coefficient of performance = T2/(T1 - T2). Second law: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot (Clausius); no engine converts all heat to work (Kelvin-Planck). Conduction H = k A (T1 - T2)/L; convection; radiation: a black body emits E = sigma T^4 per unit area (Stefan), with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/(m^2 K^4); Wien displacement lambda_m T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K; Newton law of cooling: rate of cooling proportional to temperature difference.

lessons.title: Mendelian genetics and Hardy-Weinberg

blocks.x: **Law of segregation:** alleles separate during gamete formation. **Law of independent assortment:** genes on different chromosomes assort independently. Monohybrid cross Aa x Aa gives 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic ratio. Dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb gives **9:3:3:1**. Test cross identifies an unknown genotype using a homozygous recessive. **Beyond Mendel:** incomplete dominance (1:2:1), codominance (ABO blood groups: I^A and I^B codominant), polygenic traits. **Sex linkage:** colour blindness and haemophilia are X-linked recessive. **Hardy-Weinberg:** p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1. If q^2 = 0.04 then q = 0.2, p = 0.8 and carriers 2pq = **0.32**.

lessons.title: DNA replication, transcription and translation

blocks.x: **DNA structure:** double helix of two antiparallel strands joined by hydrogen bonds: A pairs with T (2 bonds), G with C (3 bonds). **Replication** is semi-conservative (Meselson and Stahl): helicase unwinds, primase makes RNA primer, DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides 5' to 3'; leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase. **Central dogma:** DNA -> RNA -> protein. **Transcription:** RNA polymerase makes mRNA from the template strand. **Genetic code:** triplet codons, 64 codons, start AUG (methionine), stop UAA, UAG, UGA; code is degenerate and universal. **Translation:** ribosome reads mRNA, tRNA brings amino acids. **Lac operon** shows gene regulation in bacteria: lactose acts as inducer, binding the repressor.

lessons.title: Haloalkanes, alcohols and key organic reactions

blocks.x: **SN2:** one step, backside attack, inversion of configuration, rate = k[RX][Nu], favoured by primary halides and strong nucleophiles. **SN1:** two steps via a carbocation, racemisation, rate = k[RX], favoured by tertiary halides and polar protic solvents. Order of SN1 reactivity: tertiary > secondary > primary. **Alcohols:** oxidation of a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde then a carboxylic acid; a secondary alcohol gives a ketone; a tertiary alcohol resists oxidation. **Lucas test** (ZnCl2/HCl): tertiary reacts immediately, secondary in about 5 min, primary does not react at room temperature. Dehydration with conc. H2SO4 at 443 K gives an alkene (Saytzeff rule: more substituted alkene).

lessons.title: Matrices and determinants

blocks.x: A matrix is a rectangular array. Product AB is defined when columns of A equal rows of B; in general AB is not equal to BA. **Determinant** of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad - bc. The **inverse** exists only if det is non-zero: A^-1 = adj(A)/det(A). Properties: det(AB) = det A det B; det(kA) = k^n det A for n x n.

lessons.title: Determinants and inverse of a matrix

blocks.x: The determinant of a square matrix is a single number: for [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc. A matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero, and then A^-1 = adj(A)/|A|. Cramer-style solutions use A^-1 B for the system AX = B. The area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) is half the absolute value of a determinant.
Deep dive: determinants and their properties

For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc; for a 3 x 3 matrix expand along any row or column using minors and cofactors with the sign pattern (+ - +, - + -, + - +). Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; a row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0; multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k; adding a multiple of a row to another does not change the value; |A^T| = |A|; |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = k^n |A| for an n x n matrix; the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of the diagonal entries.
Deep dive: adjoint and inverse

The minor M_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i + j) M_ij. The adjoint adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Then A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I, so A^-1 = adj A / |A| exists only if A is non-singular (|A| != 0). Properties: (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, (A^-1)^-1 = A, |adj A| = |A|^(n - 1), |A^-1| = 1/|A|.
Deep dive: solving equations and areas

For AX = B with |A| != 0 the unique solution is X = A^-1 B. If |A| = 0 and (adj A) B is non-zero the system is inconsistent; if (adj A) B = 0 it has infinitely many solutions (or none, check). Area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2) |det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|; three points are collinear when this determinant is 0.

|AB| = |A||B| and |kA| = k^n |A| for an n x n matrix.

Visual lesson

Determinants and inverse of a matrix

The determinant of a square matrix is a single number: for [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Determinants and their…›3Adjoint and inverse›4Solving equations and areas
Triangle area(1/2)
🔑

Big idea

  • The determinant of a square matrix is a single number: for [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc
  • A matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero, and then A-1 = adj(A)/|A|
  • Cramer-style solutions use A-1 B for the system AX = B
  • The area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) is half the absolute value of a determinant
📌

Determinants and their properties

  • For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc
  • For a 3 x 3 matrix expand along any row or column using minors and cofactors with the sign pattern (+ - +, - + -, + - +)
  • Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign
  • A row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0
Read the full explanation

For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc; for a 3 x 3 matrix expand along any row or column using minors and cofactors with the sign pattern (+ - +, - + -, + - +). Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; a row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0; multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k; adding a multiple of a row to another does not change the value; |A^T| = |A|; |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = k^n |A| for an n x n matrix; the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of the diagonal entries.

🧠

Adjoint and inverse

  • The minor M_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j
  • The cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i + j) M_ij
  • The adjoint adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix
  • Then A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I, so A-1 = adj A / |A| exists only if A is non-singular (|A| != 0)
Read the full explanation

The minor M_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i + j) M_ij. The adjoint adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Then A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I, so A^-1 = adj A / |A| exists only if A is non-singular (|A| != 0). Properties: (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, (A^-1)^-1 = A, |adj A| = |A|^(n - 1), |A^-1| = 1/|A|.

🧮

Solving equations and areas

  • For AX = B with |A| != 0 the unique solution is X = A-1 B
  • If |A| = 0 and (adj A) B is non-zero the system is inconsistent
  • If (adj A) B = 0 it has infinitely many solutions (or none, check)
  • Area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2) |det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|
Read the full explanation

For AX = B with |A| != 0 the unique solution is X = A^-1 B. If |A| = 0 and (adj A) B is non-zero the system is inconsistent; if (adj A) B = 0 it has infinitely many solutions (or none, check). Area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2) |det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|; three points are collinear when this determinant is 0.

lessons.title: Continuity and differentiability

blocks.x: A function f is continuous at x = a if the limit as x tends to a equals f(a). It is differentiable at a if the derivative exists there; differentiable implies continuous but not conversely. Standard derivatives: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1), sin x -> cos x, cos x -> -sin x, e^x -> e^x, log x -> 1/x. Rules: sum, product, quotient and chain rules.
Deep dive: continuity

f is continuous at x = a if lim (x -> a-) f(x) = lim (x -> a+) f(x) = f(a). A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it. Polynomials, sin x, cos x and e^x are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous except where the denominator is zero; |x| is continuous everywhere. Sums, differences, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and so are quotients where the denominator is non-zero. To make a piecewise function continuous, equate the left and right limits at the join and solve for the unknown constant.
Deep dive: differentiability and rules

f is differentiable at a if the left and right derivatives exist and are equal. Differentiability implies continuity, but |x| is continuous and not differentiable at 0. Rules: (u + v)' = u' + v'; (uv)' = u'v + uv'; (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2; chain rule (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) g'(x). Standard results: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1), (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = -sin x, (tan x)' = sec^2 x, (e^x)' = e^x, (a^x)' = a^x log a, (log x)' = 1/x, (sin^-1 x)' = 1/sqrt (1 - x^2), (tan^-1 x)' = 1/(1 + x^2).
Deep dive: special techniques

Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x and treat y as a function of x (use dy/dx). Logarithmic differentiation is used for y = f(x)^g(x) and long products: take log first. Parametric form: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Second derivative d^2y/dx^2 is the derivative of dy/dx. Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b) then some c satisfies f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a).
Hindi saransh
Continuous: LHL = RHL = f(a). Differentiable => continuous.
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) g'(x).

Visual lesson

Continuity and differentiability

A function f is continuous at x = a if the limit as x tends to a equals f(a)

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Continuity›3Differentiability and rules›4Special techniques
Inverse sine1/sqrt (1 - x^2)
Inverse tangent1/(1 + x^2)
🔑

Big idea

  • A function f is continuous at x = a if the limit as x tends to a equals f(a)
  • It is differentiable at a if the derivative exists there
  • Differentiable implies continuous but not conversely
  • Standard derivatives: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1), sin x -> cos x, cos x -> -sin x, e^x -> e^x, log x -> 1/x
Read the full explanation

A function f is continuous at x = a if the limit as x tends to a equals f(a). It is differentiable at a if the derivative exists there; differentiable implies continuous but not conversely. Standard derivatives: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1), sin x -> cos x, cos x -> -sin x, e^x -> e^x, log x -> 1/x. Rules: sum, product, quotient and chain rules.

📌

Continuity

  • F is continuous at x = a if lim (x -> a-) f(x) = lim (x -> a+) f(x) = f(a)
  • A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it
  • Polynomials, sin x, cos x and e^x are continuous everywhere
  • Rational functions are continuous except where the denominator is zero
Read the full explanation

f is continuous at x = a if lim (x -> a-) f(x) = lim (x -> a+) f(x) = f(a). A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it. Polynomials, sin x, cos x and e^x are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous except where the denominator is zero; |x| is continuous everywhere. Sums, differences, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and so are quotients where the denominator is non-zero. To make a piecewise function continuous, equate the left and right limits at the join and solve for the unknown constant.

⚖️

Differentiability and rules

  • F is differentiable at a if the left and right derivatives exist and are equal
  • Differentiability implies continuity, but |x| is continuous and not differentiable at 0
  • Rules: (u + v)' = u' + v'
  • (uv)' = u'v + uv'
Read the full explanation

f is differentiable at a if the left and right derivatives exist and are equal. Differentiability implies continuity, but |x| is continuous and not differentiable at 0. Rules: (u + v)' = u' + v'; (uv)' = u'v + uv'; (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2; chain rule (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) g'(x). Standard results: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1), (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = -sin x, (tan x)' = sec^2 x, (e^x)' = e^x, (a^x)' = a^x log a, (log x)' = 1/x, (sin^-1 x)' = 1/sqrt (1 - x^2), (tan^-1 x)' = 1/(1 + x^2).

🌟

Special techniques

  • Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x and treat y as a function of x (use dy/dx)
  • Logarithmic differentiation is used for y = f(x)^g(x) and long products: take log first
  • Parametric form: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
  • Second derivative d2y/dx2 is the derivative of dy/dx
Read the full explanation

Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x and treat y as a function of x (use dy/dx). Logarithmic differentiation is used for y = f(x)^g(x) and long products: take log first. Parametric form: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Second derivative d^2y/dx^2 is the derivative of dy/dx. Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b) then some c satisfies f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a).

blocks.x: Vectors

Dot product a.b = |a||b| cos t (scalar); cross product a x b has magnitude |a||b| sin t, perpendicular to both. For a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (2, -1, 1): a.b = 2 - 2 + 3 = **3**; a x b = (2x1 - 3x(-1), 3x2 - 1x1, 1x(-1) - 2x2) = **(5, 5, -5)**. Two vectors are perpendicular if a.b = 0.
Probability

P(A) = favourable / total. Conditional P(A|B) = P(A n B)/P(B). **Bayes' theorem:** P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B). Example: machine A makes 60% of items with 2% defects, machine B makes 40% with 5% defects. P(defect) = 0.6 x 0.02 + 0.4 x 0.05 = **0.032**. Given a defective item, P(it came from A) = 0.012 / 0.032 = **0.375**. **Binomial distribution:** P(X = r) = nCr p^r q^(n-r); mean np, variance npq.
Hindi saransh
Dot product scalar, cross product vector. Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
Independent events: P(A n B) = P(A) P(B).

lessons.title: Three dimensional geometry

blocks.x: Direction ratios (a, b, c) of a line are any numbers proportional to its direction cosines l, m, n, where l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. The line through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c) is (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. The plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 has normal (a, b, c); the distance of (x1, y1, z1) from it is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
Deep dive: direction cosines and direction ratios

If a line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the axes, then l = cos alpha, m = cos beta, n = cos gamma are its direction cosines, with l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Direction ratios a, b, c are proportional to l, m, n, so l = a/sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) and so on. For the points P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) the direction ratios of PQ are (x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1). The angle theta between two lines with direction ratios (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c2) satisfies cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (sqrt (a1^2 + b1^2 + c1^2) sqrt (a2^2 + b2^2 + c2^2)). Lines are perpendicular if a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0 and parallel if a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.
Deep dive: equations of a line in space

Cartesian form through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c): (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. Vector form r = a + t b. Through two points the direction ratios are the differences of coordinates. The shortest distance between skew lines r = a1 + t b1 and r = a2 + s b2 is |(a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2)| / |b1 x b2|; for parallel lines it is |(a2 - a1) x b| / |b|. Skew lines are non-parallel, non-intersecting lines.
Deep dive: planes

The plane with unit normal n at distance d from the origin: r . n = d; Cartesian form lx + my + nz = d. General form ax + by + cz + d = 0 with normal (a, b, c). Plane through (x1, y1, z1) with normal (a, b, c): a (x - x1) + b (y - y1) + c (z - z1) = 0. Plane through three points: use the determinant of coordinates. The distance from (x1, y1, z1) to the plane is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d| / sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2). The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals. Angle between a line and a plane: sin theta = |a l + b m + c n| / (|normal| |direction|).
Hindi saransh
Direction cosines: l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Plane: ax + by + cz + d = 0.
Angle between two lines uses cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (|v1||v2|).

Visual lesson

Three dimensional geometry

Direction ratios (a, b, c) of a line are any numbers proportional to its direction cosines l, m, n, where l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1

minutes
formulas
Q&A
quiz
Flat concept map (2D)
1Big idea›2Direction cosines and…›3Equations of a line in space›4Planes
Direction ratios of PQ(x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1)
🔑

Big idea

  • Direction ratios (a, b, c) of a line are any numbers proportional to its direction cosines l, m, n, where l2 + m2 + n2 = 1
  • The line through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c) is (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c
  • The plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 has normal (a, b, c)
  • The distance of (x1, y1, z1) from it is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d|/sqrt(a2 + b2 + c2)
Read the full explanation

Direction ratios (a, b, c) of a line are any numbers proportional to its direction cosines l, m, n, where l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. The line through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c) is (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. The plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 has normal (a, b, c); the distance of (x1, y1, z1) from it is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).

📌

Direction cosines and direction ratios

  • If a line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the axes, then l = cos alpha, m = cos beta, n = cos gamma are its direction cosines, with l2 + m2 +…
  • Direction ratios a, b, c are proportional to l, m, n, so l = a/sqrt (a2 + b2 + c2) and so on
  • For the points P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) the direction ratios of PQ are (x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1)
  • The angle theta between two lines with direction ratios (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c2) satisfies cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (sqrt (a12 +…
Read the full explanation

If a line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the axes, then l = cos alpha, m = cos beta, n = cos gamma are its direction cosines, with l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Direction ratios a, b, c are proportional to l, m, n, so l = a/sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) and so on. For the points P (x1, y1, z1) and Q (x2, y2, z2) the direction ratios of PQ are (x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1). The angle theta between two lines with direction ratios (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c2) satisfies cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (sqrt (a1^2 + b1^2 + c1^2) sqrt (a2^2 + b2^2 + c2^2)). Lines are perpendicular if a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0 and parallel if a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.

🧮

Equations of a line in space

  • Cartesian form through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c): (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c
  • Vector form r = a + t b
  • Through two points the direction ratios are the differences of coordinates
  • The shortest distance between skew lines r = a1 + t b1 and r = a2 + s b2 is |(a2 - a1)
Read the full explanation

Cartesian form through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios (a, b, c): (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. Vector form r = a + t b. Through two points the direction ratios are the differences of coordinates. The shortest distance between skew lines r = a1 + t b1 and r = a2 + s b2 is |(a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2)| / |b1 x b2|; for parallel lines it is |(a2 - a1) x b| / |b|. Skew lines are non-parallel, non-intersecting lines.

🌟

Planes

  • The plane with unit normal n at distance d from the origin: r
  • Cartesian form lx + my + nz = d
  • General form ax + by + cz + d = 0 with normal (a, b, c)
  • Plane through (x1, y1, z1) with normal (a, b, c): a (x - x1) + b (y - y1) + c (z - z1) = 0
Read the full explanation

The plane with unit normal n at distance d from the origin: r . n = d; Cartesian form lx + my + nz = d. General form ax + by + cz + d = 0 with normal (a, b, c). Plane through (x1, y1, z1) with normal (a, b, c): a (x - x1) + b (y - y1) + c (z - z1) = 0. Plane through three points: use the determinant of coordinates. The distance from (x1, y1, z1) to the plane is |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d| / sqrt (a^2 + b^2 + c^2). The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals. Angle between a line and a plane: sin theta = |a l + b m + c n| / (|normal| |direction|).

lessons.title: Current electricity and circuits

blocks.x: **Current** I = Q/t. **Ohm's law** V = I R. Resistivity: R = rho L / A. Series: R = R1 + R2; parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Example: 4 ohm and 6 ohm in parallel = 24/10 = **2.4 ohm**. **Cell:** terminal voltage V = E - I r. For E = 12 V, r = 1 ohm, R = 5 ohm: I = 12/6 = **2 A**, V = 12 - 2 = **10 V**. **Kirchhoff's laws:** junction rule (sum of currents at a node is zero) and loop rule (sum of potential drops around a loop is zero). **Power** P = V I = I^2 R. **Wheatstone bridge** is balanced when P/Q = R/S. **Potentiometer** compares EMFs accurately because it draws no current at balance.

lessons.title: Photoelectric effect and nuclei

blocks.x: **Photoelectric effect:** light of frequency above the **threshold frequency** ejects electrons instantly. Einstein: h f = phi + K_max. Photon energy E (eV) = 1240 / lambda (nm). Example: lambda = 400 nm, work function 2.0 eV: E = 3.1 eV, K_max = **1.1 eV**. Stopping potential V_0 = K_max / e = 1.1 V. Intensity changes the number of electrons, not their maximum energy. **de Broglie:** lambda = h / p. **Nuclei:** mass defect gives binding energy E = (dm) c^2 (1 u = 931.5 MeV). **Radioactive decay:** N = N0 e^(-lambda t); half-life T = 0.693 / lambda. After 3 half-lives, 64 g becomes **8 g**. Alpha decay: Z falls by 2 and A by 4; beta decay: Z rises by 1. **Semiconductor:** doping gives n-type (donor) and p-type (acceptor); a p-n junction conducts in forward bias only.

Biot-Savart gives B = (mu0/4 pi) I dl x r / r^3; a long straight wire gives B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), a circular loop centre B = mu0 I/(2R), a solenoid B = mu0 n I. A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = B I L sin theta; a loop has torque tau = N I A B sin theta.
Deep dive: force on charges and currents

The magnetic force on a charge is F = q (v x B), magnitude q v B sin theta, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work. In a uniform field a charge moves in a circle when v is perpendicular to B: radius r = m v/(q B), period T = 2 pi m/(q B) (independent of speed), frequency f = qB/(2 pi m) (cyclotron frequency). If v has a component along B the path is a helix with pitch p = v cos theta T. With both E and B (velocity selector) the charge moves straight when q E = q v B, i.e. v = E/B. A straight wire of length L carrying current I in field B feels F = B I L sin theta; two parallel wires carrying currents I1 and I2 at distance d attract (same direction) or repel with force per unit length mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d), which defines the ampere.
Deep dive: field due to currents

Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta / r^2. Long straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r). Centre of a circular loop of radius R: B = mu0 I/(2R); N turns: mu0 N I/(2R). On the axis of a loop: B = mu0 I R^2/(2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)). Ampere circuital law: closed integral of B . dl = mu0 I_enclosed. Solenoid: B = mu0 n I inside (n turns per metre), almost zero outside; toroid: B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r). Semicircular arc of radius R at its centre: B = mu0 I/(4R).
Deep dive: torque, galvanometer and magnetic materials

A rectangular loop of N turns, area A, current I in field B has torque tau = N I A B sin theta = m x B where m = N I A is the magnetic dipole moment; potential energy U = -m . B. The moving-coil galvanometer has deflection proportional to current: N I A B = k phi, so current sensitivity phi/I = N A B/k. A galvanometer converts to an ammeter with a small shunt S = G Ig/(I - Ig) in parallel, and to a voltmeter by a large series resistance R = V/Ig - G. Materials: diamagnetic (weakly repelled, chi negative), paramagnetic (weakly attracted, chi small positive, Curie law chi proportional to 1/T), ferromagnetic (strongly attracted, hysteresis, Curie temperature). Bar magnet: B on the axis = (mu0/4 pi) 2m/r^3 and on the equator (mu0/4 pi) m/r^3 for r >> length. Earth field: horizontal component BH = B cos delta, vertical component B sin delta.
Hindi saransh
F = q v B sin theta. B = mu0 I/(2 pi r). Solenoid B = mu0 n I.
mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A.

Read the full explanation

The magnetic force on a charge is F = q (v x B), magnitude q v B sin theta, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work. In a uniform field a charge moves in a circle when v is perpendicular to B: radius r = m v/(q B), period T = 2 pi m/(q B) (independent of speed), frequency f = qB/(2 pi m) (cyclotron frequency). If v has a component along B the path is a helix with pitch p = v cos theta T. With both E and B (velocity selector) the charge moves straight when q E = q v B, i.e. v = E/B. A straight wire of length L carrying current I in field B feels F = B I L sin theta; two parallel wires carrying currents I1 and I2 at distance d attract (same direction) or repel with force per unit length mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d), which defines the ampere.

⚡

Field due to currents

  • Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta / r2
  • Long straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r)
  • Centre of a circular loop of radius R: B = mu0 I/(2R)
  • N turns: mu0 N I/(2R)
Read the full explanation

Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta / r^2. Long straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r). Centre of a circular loop of radius R: B = mu0 I/(2R); N turns: mu0 N I/(2R). On the axis of a loop: B = mu0 I R^2/(2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)). Ampere circuital law: closed integral of B . dl = mu0 I_enclosed. Solenoid: B = mu0 n I inside (n turns per metre), almost zero outside; toroid: B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r). Semicircular arc of radius R at its centre: B = mu0 I/(4R).

⚡

Torque, galvanometer and magnetic materials

  • A rectangular loop of N turns, area A, current I in field B has torque tau = N I A B sin theta = m x B where m = N I A is the magnetic dipole moment
  • Potential energy U = -m
  • The moving-coil galvanometer has deflection proportional to current: N I A B = k phi, so current sensitivity phi/I = N A B/k
  • A galvanometer converts to an ammeter with a small shunt S = G Ig/(I - Ig) in parallel, and to a voltmeter by a large series resistance R = V/Ig - G
Read the full explanation

A rectangular loop of N turns, area A, current I in field B has torque tau = N I A B sin theta = m x B where m = N I A is the magnetic dipole moment; potential energy U = -m . B. The moving-coil galvanometer has deflection proportional to current: N I A B = k phi, so current sensitivity phi/I = N A B/k. yt: class 12 physics electromagnetic induction and ac

blocks.x: Faraday law: induced emf = -N d(phi)/dt; motional emf = B l v; self-inductance L gives emf = -L dI/dt and energy (1/2) L I^2. In an AC circuit with series L, C and R the impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/(omega C); resonance at omega = 1/sqrt(LC); average power P = V_rms I_rms cos phi; transformer Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
Deep dive: induction laws

Magnetic flux phi = B A cos theta (unit weber). Faraday laws: an emf is induced whenever the flux through a circuit changes; its magnitude is e = -N d(phi)/dt. Lenz law gives the minus sign: the induced current opposes the change in flux (conservation of energy). Motional emf in a rod of length l moving with speed v perpendicular to B is e = B l v; a rod rotating about one end with angular speed omega gives e = (1/2) B omega l^2. Eddy currents are induced in bulk conductors and cause heating (used in induction furnaces and electromagnetic braking, reduced by laminating cores). Charge flowing in a coil q = N Dphi/R, independent of time.
Deep dive: inductance

Self-inductance L is defined by phi = L I; induced emf = -L dI/dt; energy stored U = (1/2) L I^2; for a long solenoid L = mu0 n^2 A l. Mutual inductance M gives emf in coil 2 = -M dI1/dt, with M = mu0 N1 N2 A/l for two coaxial solenoids. Time constant of an LR circuit is L/R; the current grows as I = I0 (1 - e^(-t R/L)). Inductors in series add; in parallel combine like resistors if there is no mutual coupling.
Deep dive: alternating current

An AC source V = V0 sin omega t has rms values V_rms = V0/sqrt 2 = 0.707 V0 and average value over a half cycle 0.637 V0. Reactances: X_L = omega L (current lags voltage by 90 degrees), X_C = 1/(omega C) (current leads by 90 degrees). Series LCR: Z = sqrt (R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), tan phi = (X_L - X_C)/R, I_rms = V_rms/Z. Resonance at omega_0 = 1/sqrt (LC) where Z = R is minimum and current maximum; quality factor Q = omega_0 L/R = (1/R) sqrt (L/C). Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos phi, where cos phi = R/Z is the power factor (zero for a pure L or C: wattless current). A transformer works by mutual induction: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is for an ideal one; step-up if Ns > Np. Losses: copper, iron (eddy and hysteresis), flux leakage, humming.

qa.q: State Faraday's law of induction.
qa.a: The induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit.

qa.q: State Lenz's law.
qa.a: The induced current flows so as to oppose the change in flux that produces it.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?
What is motional emf?
qa.a: The emf induced in a conductor moving across a magnetic field, e = B l v.

qa.q: What are eddy currents?
qa.a: Circulating currents induced in a bulk conductor by changing flux.

qa.q: How are eddy currents reduced?
What is self-inductance?
qa.a: The property of a coil by which it opposes a change in its own current.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of inductance?
What is the energy stored in an inductor?
What is mutual inductance?
qa.a: The emf induced in one coil due to a changing current in a neighbouring coil.

qa.q: What is the rms value of an alternating current?
Does a pure inductor consume power?
qa.a: No, the average power is zero.

qa.q: What is the phase difference between voltage and current in a pure inductor?
What is the phase difference in a pure capacitor?
What is resonance in an LCR circuit?
qa.a: The condition X_L = X_C at which the impedance is minimum and the current is maximum.

qa.q: What is the resonant frequency?
What is the power factor?
What is wattless current?
qa.a: Current in a circuit with zero power factor, so no average power is consumed.

qa.q: What is a transformer?
qa.a: A device that changes AC voltage using mutual induction.

qa.q: What is a step-up transformer?
qa.a: A transformer with more secondary turns than primary turns.

qa.q: What are the losses in a transformer?
qa.a: Copper loss, iron loss, flux leakage and humming.

qa.q: What is the quality factor?
qa.a: A measure of the sharpness of resonance, omega_0 L/R.

qa.q: What is an AC generator?
qa.a: A device that converts mechanical energy into alternating current using induction.

qa.q: Why is AC preferred for power transmission?
qa.a: Its voltage can be changed easily by transformers, reducing losses.
